items.title: Roy Lichtenstein’s Witty Critiques of Masculinity
items.description: “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New” (at the Whitney through May 10th) is a masterpiece of curation and design, an exhibition that positions Lichtenstein as the last happy white man in American art. Organized with esprit and imagination by the artist Alex Da Corte and
items.author: Hilton Als
paragraphs: “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New” (at the Whitney through May 10th) is a masterpiece of curation and design, an exhibition that positions Lichtenstein as the last happy white man in American art. Organized with esprit and imagination by the artist Alex Da Corte and the curator Meg Onli, it’s the first retrospective of Lichtenstein’s work in New York since his splash at the Guggenheim in 1993. The show takes up the museum’s entire fifth floor and ends as it begins: with the artist’s signature brightly colored brushstrokes, lines, and Benday dots causing pleasurable kinetic movements in the mind. Lichtenstein’s dynamic style is ubiquitous by now—as are his professional sheen and finish—but that doesn’t cancel out his winning charm, which, like most charm, can warm you up or wear you out. At “Like New,” you may experience both feelings. It’s a show that aims to keep the real world, our gothic political climate included, at bay, while also distracting us from what one might call the grief porn of contemporary art and its constant reminders of our failures as humans.

For years now, the Whitney has foregrounded race- and gender-based political art, and it’s a little trippy to walk around this show’s pearl-gray-painted rooms, looking at Lichtenstein’s Fantastik-clean white world of orderly studios, shiny blondes, and square-jawed men, in a place where white male power has been repeatedly denounced and the sins of past neglect redressed. No one can make up for the past—certainly not by demanding that it be corrected in the present—and it was perhaps inevitable that the Whitney would have to turn, or return, to white men with name recognition to get people back into its galleries post-COVID. Exhibitions devoted to Jasper Johns and Andy Warhol helped, and still fit the Whitney framework: both artists were queer. And although Lichtenstein wasn’t gay, there’s enough irony about gender in his early work to qualify him as being interestingly gay-adjacent.

Still, it’s difficult to entirely undo the way we’ve been viewing art for a while now, and, after having a great time at “Like New,” you may find yourself feeling slightly guilty about it. But one of the more poignant subtexts of the show is that it’s a reminder of the New York avant-garde in the sixties, and of what a beautiful, forceful energy there was to its various voices, with Lichtenstein the least dirty and anarchic of them all. There’s a sweetness in that, and a sadness, too.

I first spent time with Lichtenstein’s work in the early eighties, when I took a class at Columbia on the art of the nineteen-sixties. The professor led us from the glory days of Abstract Expressionism in the fifties, through the emergence of Robert Rauschenberg and Johns by the end of that decade, to this new era in American art. Inspired by Marcel Duchamp and his poetry of the everyday, Rauschenberg and Johns used commonplace objects—a flashlight, a bedspread—in their creations. But artists working under the Pop-art banner in the sixties, including Lichtenstein, Claes Oldenburg, James Rosenquist, Tom Wesselmann, Marisol, and Warhol, picked at the surface of the world that had made them, in order to show us how much it could reveal about what lay beneath it. You can still feel, in the memorable work produced during that period, the critical embrace of all those dance-lesson diagrams, Campbell’s soup cans, ice-cream cones, and Coca-Cola bottles, alongside images of electric chairs, car crashes, and atomic-bomb detonations.

In the Cold War universe, where everyone was isolated and class was defined by the power to acquire (and to oppress), Pop artists painted or sculpted what they saw and heard. The artist’s “aura” had no place in those works; instead, Pop art was a kind of supersonic whistle heralding the disasters to come, that had already come. But unlike, for instance, Rosenquist, in such charged political pieces as “F-111” (1964-65), which juxtaposes consumer objects with missiles, Lichtenstein made work that was less about conscience than about control, and the eradication of mess, of feeling.

Lichtenstein became Lichtenstein in 1961, when he made “Look Mickey.” He had flirted with cartoon characters before then, but “Look Mickey” took things further. Four feet by nearly six, the painting features the brightest of reds, blues, and yellows. In it, Mickey Mouse and the bombastic Donald Duck are standing on a dock, fishing. Mickey covers his laughing mouth because Donald thinks he’s hooked a fish, but the hook is caught on his own coat. The delight of the painting is the pleasure that Lichtenstein took in the joke—and in this new way of making work that was both free and not free of the artist’s hand. (In the age of Pop, achieving an automated look was part of the process.)

Decades before Richard Prince made his fantastic and forlorn cartoon paintings, Lichtenstein was already exploring the idea of entertainment and raising questions: If cartoons were a form of entertainment, was painting a cartoon a form of entertainment, too? Was modern art a put-on? Or something that could be put on? One question that the Whitney show didn’t answer for me was how Lichtenstein got to cartoons, and then to his comic-strip paintings, with their speech balloons, women in distress, and silent men—whose reserve makes us wonder if their creator was a silent man, too.

Born in 1923, into an upper-middle-class German Jewish family in New York, Lichtenstein grew up on the Upper West Side, with easy access to museums and other cultural institutions. He loved music and art, and in 1940 he enrolled at Ohio State University, where he studied life drawing, painting, and the work of the masters, including Picasso. If he insisted on pursuing art, his parents felt, it would be good for him to get a degree, in case he had to teach to get by.

The Whitney retrospective includes “Drawing by Seeing,” a short film about Lichtenstein’s artistic education, made by Da Corte, whose own work includes video, performance, and installations, driven by the kind of avant-gardism that Lichtenstein espoused for a time. The film is shot in color, but with the performers and their costumes colored a “Twilight Zone” gray. It features a voice-over drawn from a text by Hoyt L. Sherman, Lichtenstein’s teacher and mentor at Ohio State. Sherman’s work centered on perception; he’d flash an image on a screen and then have his students draw what they had seen. Or hadn’t. Da Corte’s film also animates some of Lichtenstein’s early works, including “Step-on Can with Leg” (1961), a two-panel painting that shows a woman’s high-heeled foot stepping on the pedal of a closed garbage can, and then the same image with the lid open. Like Warhol, in “Before and After,” a study of a nose job, also from 1961, Lichtenstein was interested in how time can be represented in a static medium, thus changing how we see a thing, or making us realize that we weren’t really looking.

Lichtenstein’s studies were interrupted when he was drafted, in 1943, but he returned in 1946 to finish his degree on the G.I. Bill. By 1949, he was married to the artist Isabel Wilson Sarisky, with whom he had two sons. (Divorced in 1965, he married Dorothy Herzka, a philanthropist, in 1968.) Lichtenstein, shy and reclusive, was a responsible fellow; he supported his family by teaching, while making art that was at first representational, then a little abstract, not terribly distinguished. The breakthrough came in 1960, when he was teaching at Douglass College (which later became part of Rutgers), where he met the performance artist Allan Kaprow, who introduced him to Claes Oldenburg and George Segal, artists who were as taken with the look and signs of masculinity as Lichtenstein was. (Oldenburg’s 1959 work “ ‘Empire’ (‘Papa’) Ray Gun,” for instance, plays on the phallic shape of a firearm.) Surely the freedom that Lichtenstein saw in those sculptors’ work and at Kaprow’s “happenings” helped to release him and open him up to his strongest qualities as an artist: his interest in gender and his amused wit.

Lichtenstein’s wonderful early work “Masterpiece” (1962) still makes me laugh. In it, a couple are looking at a canvas. The woman, a blonde, has a speech balloon issuing from her red lips: “Why, Brad darling, this painting is a masterpiece! My, soon you’ll have all of New York clamoring for your work!” The man is silent, only partially visible, in profile; the woman is our focus. She may be the kind of woman who needs her man to be a success, in order to validate her power as a woman, one who, unlike Donald Duck, has caught a big one. It’s a joke on the bright and shiny, profit-driven art world, where nothing resonates like success. Among other great early works, there’s the funny, ’tude-filled “Ohhh . . . Alright . . .” (1964)—a closeup of a red-haired woman on the phone, looking slightly annoyed as she speaks the title—and “Drowning Girl” (1963), in which a blue-haired woman with tears falling from her closed eyes drowns as much in misbegotten love as in a swirl of black-and-white waves. A thought bubble reads, “I don’t care! I’d rather sink—than call Brad for help!”

These are not really paintings about distress or isolation. They’re about fake feelings in a manufactured world. What was real in Pop? What wasn’t? I liked these works so much when I was younger, and still do, because, for me, Lichtenstein was at his strongest when he wasn’t just a straight man but, rather, a Warhol-adjacent straight man who could critique both masculinity and the self-consciously feminine. The truth is that when Lichtenstein stopped painting “gay,” I stopped looking. From the seventies on, in work that seemed influenced by Léger, Matisse, Picasso, and others, he appeared to be more at play with the straight boys than questioning their performative creativity. (The Whitney curators have put some of the gay back into his work by treating it as a kind of exquisite California-modern decoration; all that’s missing are gray throw pillows.) Still, at the end of the show, I stood by Da Corte’s replica of Lichtenstein’s enormous 1967 work “Super Sunset Billboard,” which shows a horizon and, above it, white streams of light shooting up and out, like klieg lights announcing a show. The painting is the show. Da Corte and Onli have placed the piece in front of a wall of windows overlooking the Hudson; it’s a calming, lovely thing to see a “real” sky echoing Lichtenstein’s. It’s also a thrilling and moving coda to his work—so much so that I got goosebumps. It was the first time I’d ever thought of goosebumps as Benday dots. ♦

items.title: A Song of Grief and Union in “Lincoln in the Bardo”
items.description: A measure of vitality in opera—or any creative form—is the number of interesting artists it carries into the open space of mid-career. The innovations of early work are frequently flukes. The middle years bring longer strides and deepening ambitions. The sixth
items.author: Nathan Heller
paragraphs: A measure of vitality in opera—or any creative form—is the number of interesting artists it carries into the open space of mid-career. The innovations of early work are frequently flukes. The middle years bring longer strides and deepening ambitions. The sixth opera by the forty-six-year-old American composer Missy Mazzoli premièred, last month, at the Metropolitan Opera, with an air of arrival that seemed leavened by relief. Mazzoli, once best known for her indie-electro band, Victoire, has emerged as one of our leading dramatic composers, and the opera, “Lincoln in the Bardo,” written with her longtime librettist, Royce Vavrek, is both her first Met commission and the company’s first première by a woman. An occasion like that deserves a charismatic, openhearted work, and Mazzoli and Vavrek deliver one in the form of a comedy with a melancholy guise. Based on the novel by George Saunders and set a year into the Civil War, the opera follows Abraham Lincoln as he visits his deceased eleven-year-old, Willie, in the cemetery where the boy lies amid restless ghosts. The President has not resigned himself to the death, and neither has his son.

“Bardo” is a Tibetan term, referring to an intermediate state following death, but its assonance with the English “bard”—one who recites, or sings, tales of lives and deeds—can’t have been lost on Saunders. The residents of the graveyard rehash their pasts obsessively, ritualistically, and all the time. In a basic sense, they can’t let go; they linger, fretting about experiences never tasted, errors left unremedied, vindications not received. Their self-absorption is so great that they do not realize they are dead. (They think they’re convalescing.) They refer to their coffins as “sick-boxes” and complain, like captious hostel guests, about the lack of blankets.

Opera is a hybrid form, allowing for storytelling approaches not available to the novel. In the early scenes, Mazzoli and Vavrek weave two supporting characters, Vollman and Bevins, into a single aria of aggrievement. Vollman, a homely middle-aged printer (sung by the baritone Ryan McKinny), was on the verge of consummating his marriage when a falling beam killed him. Now he rests in a purgatorial state of sexual excitement, fitted onstage with a buffa penis that disturbingly resembles a piñata. (The appendage, lofted by a valiant puppeteer, is briefly played for laughs and never seen again.) Bevins, sung by the tenor Jonah Hoskins, is a young gay man who slit his wrists after being jilted by a lover. His song is an overwrought lament of curlicues and tortured intervals dancing around Vollman’s squarer line, for an effect both dreamlike and uncanny. Their two complaints—love without sex and sex without love—mark a barycenter of human loss, the stuff of operatic duets.

Elsewhere in the Bardo we find three Black people who had lived through slavery and were buried in coffinless graves, and a ghoulish pair of boozy sadists, Mr. and Mrs. Baron, imagined somewhere between the Dickensian and the Dahlian as they teeter in a sick, odd-meter duet. But the heart of this production is the dramatic soprano Christine Goerke, who plays a deceased clergyman known as the Reverend. Goerke is a wonderful actress, funny and free, who can project irony while projecting her voice. The bravura aria that Mazzoli gives her at the start of the second act—soaring and droll, and slowly intensifying—is a musical delight. In another gender-swapped role, the celebrated countertenor Anthony Roth Costanzo plays Miss Elise Traynor, a fourteen-year-old trapped in the Bardo. Her lilting, clucking vocal line may not contribute much to Costanzo’s musical reputation, but the part adds mightily to his repertoire of outré costuming, which includes singing Philip Glass’s “Akhnaten” nude. Miss Traynor—a kind of nightmare version of the Queen of the Night—appears swathed in an enormous, mildewing white dress, its hems nibbled by rubber pig heads. She’s a cautionary tale of what awaits children who “tarry” in this world of irresolution, and the dramatic arc of the opera follows Bevins, Vollman, and the Reverend’s scheme to compel the President and his son to move on.

To Lincoln, Willie’s death is weighted with the Civil War. “I have exported this grief / three thousand times,” he laments. When he enters the crypt and embraces his son’s corpse, his shirtfront glows and throbs like a linked Bluetooth device—the way the production, directed with a marvellous contemporary edge by Lileana Blain-Cruz, signals Saunders’s concept of “occupation,” in which ghosts enter living people and their thoughts. The Swedish baritone Peter Mattei, who sings Lincoln, is tall and rightly renowned for his rich, unmuddy voice, here channelled into plausible Midwestern vowels. Yet his aspect onstage, vexed and exercised and diligently in tempo, is nearer in spirit to the Wagnerian mountaintops than to the lonely terrors of a plainsman, and the dazzling performance he delivers ends up seeming less specific than so singular an opera might call for.

Mazzoli, who has trained as a death doula, is known for burrowing deep into specific worlds. (For the reputation-making “Breaking the Waves,” based on the Lars von Trier movie, she and Vavrek studied the language and the music of the Scottish Highlands.) In “Lincoln in the Bardo,” she has produced a rich twenty-first-century score with musical shadows of both the Civil War era and the Halloween graveyard, opening with a spooky stacked minor tone cluster (made spookier by knitting needles rattling the percussion) and extending to gorgeous snatches of chocolatey writing in the low brass, befitting a bereaved President. The orchestra, under the direction of Yannick Nézet-Séguin, comes at this music with terrific confidence, delivering the sort of fully conceived performance that rarely awaits brand-new work (and only occasionally overpowering the singers). Mazzoli’s setting of text can be a mixed bag; her melodies now and then seem to take a purgatorial path themselves, patiently cycling among set intervals when the ear, and the libretto, might wish them to move. But the intelligence of her dramatic writing haunts the score. She makes much of big glissandos, in which the men and women of the chorus slide together through a scale, like a winding siren. Heading upward, these slides impart moments of ecstatic, unworldly levitation. Sent downward, they plummet us into the earth.

Saunders’s novel mixes his characters’ epitaph-like accounts of their lives and other dialogue with real text from the historical record, blurring the boundary between speech, which rises in living time, and writing, which exists outside it. The page, we are meant to see, is an inherently ghostly place, at once a paltry shadow of the world it describes and a realm of empathetic reach. The written word, like the Bardo, carries both life, in all its specificity and imperfection, and abstractions of the sort that might define a nation, affording people trapped within themselves a chance to step into other points of view. In a climactic effort to enjoin Willie and the President to go on without each other, the spirits—not least Thomas Havens, a Black freedman, movingly sung by the young tenor Joshua Blue—gather in an effort to occupy Lincoln together. Union is the governing metaphor, and, in the book, it’s a union carried by the intermingling of voice and text, of varied experience and inky phrase. “Lincoln in the Bardo,” published in the first weeks of the first Trump Administration, today reads distinctly as a novel of the Obama years.

Despite an occasional groan of narrative machinery, Vavrek ably repaces Saunders’s story line and carries its texty voices into song. Gnarled, consonant-laden phrases such as “conjoined, mass-minded, positive intention” and “two passing temporarinesses” are hard to say, let alone sing. They are retained here as if to underscore the messy peculiarity of the world left behind. The language of the afterlife, by contrast, seems flat and stutteringly insistent: “Lingering lingering lingering,” the dead intone. “Worthy worthy worthy.” In one of the opera’s lovelier ensemble arias, the ghosts praise “the things of the world,” enumerating the small, sticky details that they miss from human existence: “beerfroth,” “toweling off one’s clinging shirt post June rain.” Language, like irresolution, is a thing that belongs to the living world. ♦

items.title: Dustin Hoffman on Surviving “The Graduate”
items.description: When I went down to the pool at the Chateau Marmont, it seemed like everyone knew each other and was having fun in the sun.
items.author: Dustin Hoffman
paragraphs: When I went down to the pool at the Chateau Marmont, it seemed like everyone knew each other and was having fun in the sun.

I had been staying with my parents in L.A., shooting “The Graduate,” but my father was driving me crazy. Every day, I’d get home from the set, and he’d grill me, wanting to know every detail of what happened. And he’d be very critical: Why did you do that? That’s not the way to do it. I lasted maybe five days, and then I couldn’t take it anymore. I was trapped in the house where I’d grown up, totally alienated by the previous generation, just like my character. So I’d moved to the hotel where the cast and crew were staying.

Out by the pool, it was like a cabana party on Mount Olympus: the people looked like golden gods among the palm trees. I felt immediately uncomfortable, unworthy. Here I was, playing a starring role in a movie by Mike Nichols, who was the director of the moment, but I felt like I had no right to be there.
The shoot went on for months. Mike was in no rush; he had all the time and money he wanted. But I never went down to the pool again.

“The Graduate” exacerbated all my insecurities from the start. When my agent said that Mike was interested in me, I didn’t even want to try out for the part. I had read the Charles Webb novel that Mike was adapting, and it was obvious that I was all wrong for Benjamin. A track star and straight-A student, the head of the debate team—this was an affluent, all-American kid, whose surname was “Braddock.” Why would you cast a person who looks as ethnic as I do to play the ultimate Wasp? It made absolutely no sense.

It was impossible to be unimpressed by Mike, though. His first film, “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?,” had just been nominated for thirteen Academy Awards, including Best Directing and Best Picture. I’d enjoyed his version of “Barefoot in the Park” on Broadway, and I loved the comedy routines he’d done with Elaine May. Still—me, playing a six-foot gentile? I had to draw the line somewhere.
“I hear you don’t think you’re right for the part,” Mike said on the phone. “So who is right for it?”

There happened to be a copy of Time on the coffee table in front of me; on the cover was a sketch of a handsome, blond, athletic fellow meant to represent Americans “Twenty-five and Under.” “The guy on the cover of Time,” I said.
“You’re saying you’re not right for it because you’re Jewish,” Mike said.
“Well, because Benjamin’s so not Jewish.”
There was a pause. Then Mike said, “Maybe he’s Jewish inside.”

By that time, they’d been trying to cast the part for almost two years. “Robert Redford and Candice Bergen, the ideal couple—that’s what we were thinking,” Buck Henry, the film’s co-screenwriter, said about casting Benjamin and his love interest, Elaine. But they’d already seen Redford—and pretty much everyone else—by the time they got around to me and Katharine Ross. Nothing had clicked. I still maintain that if I’d read for them at the beginning of their search, instead of at the bitter end, I never would have got the part.

The irony is that I was just starting to become successful in theatre, the world I’d inhabited for almost a decade. I was in “Eh?” Off Broadway, and I was having a great experience: lots of laughs, standing ovations almost nightly, my face on the cover of the Arts section of the Times. I was finally making a living doing what I loved. It was as if I’d been hiking up a mountain and, just when I could finally see the summit, here comes Mike in a helicopter, offering me a ride to a different peak.

Hollywood had never been my endgame. As far as I was concerned, the studios kept beautiful people imprisoned in seven-year contracts. I wasn’t beautiful, and I didn’t want to be trapped. To be honest, I looked down on American movies, compared with theatre. When it came to breakthrough cinema, the kind made in Europe by greats like Truffaut, Buñuel, Antonioni, and Godard, Hollywood had yet to see the light.

My agent convinced me that I should screen-test for Mike, despite my reservations. I told my castmates in “Eh?” not to worry; I was sure they wouldn’t need to replace me. Then I walked to my neighbor on Eleventh Street, Mel Brooks, who’d suggested that I play a small part in “The Producers.” I called up to his window: “They’re flying me out to audition for a Mike Nichols movie.”
“Good luck!” he said, suppressing a laugh. “Keep me posted!”

I had to learn ten pages in less than forty-eight hours. I stayed up the entire night running lines; by the time I landed in Los Angeles, I hadn’t slept in two days. Mike’s office was a series of palatial rooms with high ceilings, and in my memory it included a bar, which is where I first saw him. “Oh, hi, would you like a drink?” he said. He was always so casual, almost seductive. Then they brought in Katharine Ross, who was outrageously beautiful. I felt foolish, like I had to apologize to her for looking like I did.

They took us to get our makeup done in a long room with rows of upholstered chairs. Today, you get made up in a trailer, without a trace of glamour, but this room was a remnant of Old Hollywood. It seemed likely that Betty Grable’s ass had been on the chair before mine.

They had these famous makeup artists, the Westmores—six brothers who’d learned their trade from their father. I can’t remember how many of them were there that day, but they were at it for hours. And it’s not like I was getting prosthetics or a toupee. It took them that long just to do something with what little I offered.

Mike came in, watched them for a while, and looked at my face in the mirror. Quietly, in his singsong voice, he said, “Can’t you do something with his eyebrows?” Bobby Duvall always said that I had only one. They started plucking me to make two.

Then Mike said that my neck looked too thick, so they put me in a turtleneck. But he was still unhappy with what he was seeing. (I, too, was increasingly unhappy.) Mike sounded almost innocent when he asked the Westmores, “Now, what are we going to do about the nose?”

I remember thinking, They’re trying to take the Jew off my face, and it ain’t going to happen. All I wanted to do was go home, to ethnic New York, where I belonged. I knew I was no leading man. I knew my place.

The scene I did with Katharine was endless. Both of us kept screwing up because—for God knows what reason—Mike wanted to shoot a ten-minute scene in one take. At one point, he took me aside and said, “Why are you nervous? This isn’t a play; the curtain’s not opening. It’s not a movie. It won’t go any farther than this room. So just relax!” I felt that he understood completely, and I thanked him and shook his hand. It was so slippery with sweat that it literally slid out of mine. That’s when I realized that he was more anxious than I was, and this did not put me at ease.

It wasn’t just paranoia: everyone thought I was wrong for the part. “I looked at it, and it was just this ugly boy playing the part, and I thought, Ugh,” the film’s editor, Sam O’Steen, later said of my screen test. People imagined the Braddocks as prototypical California gentiles. “All blonde, all healthy,” Buck Henry said. “A family of surfboards is what we called them. And here comes Dustin: clearly not a surfboard.” To save the film, they hoped Benjamin’s parents might be played by Ronald Reagan and Doris Day. “We immediately rationalized it: he’s a genetic throwback,” Buck continued. “Doris Day and Ronald Reagan have had this mutt.”

I was so relieved when we finished the screen test. I couldn’t wait to get out of there. As I was thanking the propman, a few subway tokens dropped out of my pocket. He very nicely picked them up, then said, “Here, kid, you’re gonna need these.”

Soon after I got home to New York, my agent told me to call Mike at nine o’clock on Sunday morning. It was snowing out, and I was going uptown to my girlfriend’s apartment for breakfast. Obviously, the agent meant Pacific time, but I was such an anxious wreck that I didn’t think it through. When I got to my girlfriend’s place, I called Mike at precisely 9 A.M. New York time and woke him up.
I mumbled an apology. There was a long silence. “Well,” Mike said, “you got it.”

Stunned is too weak a word. Mike had apparently seen something in the footage. “He had this thing I’d only seen in Elizabeth Taylor, and that I’d certainly not seen in any of the other tests,” he later told his biographer, Mark Harris. “That secret. That deal with Technicolor where you do nothing and it turns out you were doing everything. He was compelling and hilarious and impassive. It was startling. That’s what a great movie actor does. They don’t know how they do it, and I don’t know how they do it, but the difference is shocking.”
I hung up the phone feeling like I’d been hit in the head. I looked at my girlfriend, who was holding a spatula, making our breakfast. “I got it,” I told her.
“I knew you would,” she said.
We had three weeks of rehearsal, which was unheard of for a film—a testament to just how revered Mike was, how much leverage he had in the industry.

“Don’t try to do a character, don’t try to be funny,” he told us. “Start from zero.” Mike took me back to my adolescence—my acne, my barely suppressed horniness. He asked me if I thought Benjamin Braddock was a virgin. I said no, but that I didn’t think he’d ever screwed his mother’s friend before, either. (He liked that response.)

Mike was completely open and unusually perceptive. I struggled, for instance, with the scene in the hotel lobby when Benjamin is registering for the room where he will have his first illicit encounter with Mrs. Robinson, the seductive, alienated housewife played by Anne Bancroft. Mike asked me all kinds of questions: What was it like when I lost my virginity? When had I experienced sexual shame? I told him that I could never bring myself to buy rubbers from a female pharmacist—if I was at the register and a woman appeared behind the counter, I had to make a break for it. Mike told me to think of the hotel clerk (played, to hilarious effect, by Buck Henry) as a woman pharmacist. It was such a useful piece of direction, such a helpful way of working.

Mike also asked me if I had a role model as a kid. I told him it was my brother Ronny. He had me try a scene as Ronny, who I could imitate perfectly; I used to pretend I was him when girls called him, hoping to see how long I could keep them on the phone. Then Mike asked me if Ronny ever got uptight, and he absolutely did. “Try it again, as your brother, uptight,” Mike said. So I did what Ronny did whenever he was nervous: I held my breath. Finally, Mike said, “Now forget all that and just do the scene.”

This time, I still held my breath a lot, but I also let out a little squeak periodically. Mike liked it so much he put in a few extra squeaks in the final edit. You can hear them throughout “The Graduate,” like gas escaping from Benjamin Braddock, who is a balloon of tension.

Mike was so wonderful during rehearsal that it was shocking, destabilizing, when we started shooting the film and he was an entirely different person. We weren’t allowed to see any dailies—I later found out it was because Mike didn’t want Anne Bancroft to see the way they were lighting her. (She was only thirty-five, and I was about to turn thirty; Mike had to make that five-year age gap look more like fifteen.) So we had nothing to go on but Mike’s mood, which was frequently sour.

I often felt that I was about to be fired. When we were shooting some of the film’s most famous sequences, I remember thinking, I have no fucking idea what I’m doing. The first scene that we shot featured Benjamin in front of a fish tank in his room, where he’s escaped from a party his parents have thrown to celebrate his college graduation. I just sat there on the bed while Mike told me, “O.K., look at the fish. Now look down. Move toward the fish.” We probably spent a whole day on it, and not for one second did I have a handle on what I was meant to be conveying or how to go about it.

I did make Mike laugh sometimes, and those were moments of great relief for me. When we started working on Benjamin and Mrs. Robinson’s first scene in the hotel room, I did what I’d done when I had my “first feel” as a teen-ager: I awkwardly and abruptly put my hand on Anne’s bra-covered breast, with absolutely no finesse or passion, without even making eye contact with her. Anne’s response was incredible: without missing a beat, she looked down at the sweater in her hands, noticed a stain, and paid it all of her attention, rubbing the fabric together and fussing with it, while I continued to hold her breast in my paw like a paralyzed animal.

It was so funny that I had to walk away, trying to avoid bursting into laughter. That was the worst thing you could do: break character. I started knocking my head against the wall in an attempt to collect myself. Don’t break! Don’t break! Mike interpreted it as an artistic choice, and it cracked him up. When Mike was laughing, I felt he loved the character I was trying to create. It was the only time I knew I was doing something he was happy with.
But his mood would shift dramatically. I don’t remember the scene, but I will never forget Mike’s acid voice saying to me, after one take: “What were you doing?”
I tried to defend myself: I’d been taught that to give your character depth, you don’t play the text—you play the subtext, which can sometimes be the opposite of the text.
“Well, do me a favor,” Mike said. “The next time you get a thought, do the opposite of that.”

This is the kind of comment that kept me in a state of constant anxiety. And it wasn’t just my own experience. When we shot a scene in which Benjamin drags Elaine, Mrs. Robinson’s daughter, to a strip club for their first date, Mike overheard Robert Surtees, the cinematographer, say something to the crew. Surtees was a mentor to Mike, the man who taught him all about the possibilities of light and filmmaking. “I said something snotty, as I often did, to the crew,” Mike recalled later. “And Surtees—I heard him say to them, but it wasn’t for me—he said, ‘It’s O.K. It’s not much longer.’ I thought, Oh man. How could I have been such a shit that this man that I revere feels that way about me? But I was.”

Mike was irritable with everyone, but with me a certain sadism seemed to creep in. There was a scene in which Katharine Ross had to slap me, and he made us do twenty-seven takes. The scene has Benjamin run into Elaine’s room, soaking wet from the rain, to tell her that he’s had an affair with an older woman; within seconds, Elaine realizes the woman is her mother. Mike just kept telling Katharine to hit me, to hit me harder. Katharine worried she would hurt me, and I told her, “I’m O.K. Just don’t hit my ear.” Unfortunately, she missed a few times. I was dizzy by the end of that day, and Mike didn’t even use the slap in the film.

The next day, we shot an underwater scene in the pool: Benjamin is being forced to try the scuba suit his father has bought for him. The scene was meant to symbolize the way that Benjamin’s parents gave their children material things instead of love. Mike didn’t want me to keep popping up out of the water, so I had to hold myself down: if you watch the movie, you can see that one hand is behind me the whole time I’m underwater, because I’m holding on to the ladder behind me. When I came up for air after a few takes, there was blood trickling out of my ear. Between all the slapping during the previous day and all the water pressure at the bottom of the pool, I’d punctured an eardrum. (They sent me to the best ear doctor in Beverly Hills, and I remember him telling me, “The eardrum is like a pie: you have a slice of pie missing.”)

By summer, we were shooting in La Verne, California. We got there the week of the Six-Day War—we all thought the world was going to end. The sound guy, Jack Solomon, heard about it on the radio, on the way to the set, and was so upset that he had to pull over to throw up. It was scorching hot. Anne Bancroft actually fainted when we were shooting a scene. She had to be resuscitated with oxygen, and we stopped shooting for a few days while she recovered.

I nearly passed out myself doing the scene where Benjamin, on his way to stop Elaine’s wedding, runs out of gas, has to ditch his Alfa Romeo, and sprints as fast as he can from the highway to the church. Mike could not be satisfied. I remember Sam O’Steen saying to him, “I don’t think Dusty can keep running in this heat.” But we did it over and over and over again, until I was absolutely trashed from exhaustion and dehydration. I remember lying down in the grass in front of the church because I thought I was going to lose consciousness.

It was a terrible experience making the movie that changed my life. The whole time, I felt Mike was angry at me, either because I was doing something wrong or because he had realized what everybody else already knew, that he had miscast the lead in his film. My friend Ulu Grosbard, a distinguished theatre director, came and visited toward the end of the shoot, and I told him, “If this is what it’s like doing a movie, I will never make another movie again for the rest of my life.” Ulu was taking Mike out to lunch, and I begged him to do some reporting: Was Mike regretting that he’d hired me? Ulu told me later that Mike had said, Yes, very much.
But apparently, after a few decades and some therapy, Mike arrived at a different explanation:

Mike lived in the Waspiest part of Connecticut. He collected antiques and cars and Arabian horses—the ultimate gentile status symbols. But he was very much a Jew, who’d fled Germany in 1939 and arrived in the United States, speaking not a word of English, at the age of seven. Born Mikhail Igor Peschkowsky, Mike always felt ugly. He had alopecia, and he was extremely self-conscious about his hairlessness. (He had a collection of incredible wigs that started with what his fantasy hair would look like freshly cut; on each successive day, the wig would be a little longer, until it was time for a “haircut.” Then he’d start the wig cycle again from the beginning.)

Eventually, he realized that he had made a self-portrait out of “The Graduate.” “My unconscious was making that movie,” he said once. He didn’t notice for years that, not long after his professional breakup with Elaine May—his partner in crime, his artistic collaborator since college—he made a movie in which the hero bangs against the glass wall of a church screaming, in anguish, “Elaine! Elaine! Elaine!” He was looking for an alter ego—that’s why Benjamin had taken years to cast, and maybe that’s why he was so hard on me. I was a stand-in, there to absorb Mike’s own self-loathing.

The first time that I saw “The Graduate” in a theatre was at a sneak preview on Eighty-sixth Street in Manhattan. My girlfriend and I sat in the back of the balcony, because I was very self-conscious and tense. My teeth were literally chattering when I saw the first shot, a closeup of my face.

At first, there was a weak reception. None of the humor seemed to be landing. I heard a spattering of laughter. Then more people joined in. About twenty minutes into the picture, the laughs started building. It was as though, little by little, the audience was figuring out where we were coming from. . . . There was a little more laughter, and then quite a lot more, and by the time Benjamin was screaming, “Elaine! Elaine! Elaine!” and she screams, “Ben!” and runs to him, the audience was standing up and screaming, too. It was like they had come to see a fight and had been waiting the whole time on the edge of their seats for this: the knockout.
I’ve been doing this for sixty years now. I don’t think I’ve ever seen anything like that since. I sat there, buried in my chair, and then I walked out with my girlfriend into the snow. ♦
This is drawn from “Look at Me.”

items.title: Nothing Is Stopping the Flood of A.I. Political Ads
items.description: In August, the reëlection campaign of the North Carolina state senator Michael Lee, a Republican, released an ad attacking his Democratic opponent, a yoga-studio owner named Jessica Bichler. The ad, titled “Bonkers Bichler,” seems to show Bichler, a middle-age
items.author: Kyle Chayka
paragraphs: In August, the reëlection campaign of the North Carolina state senator Michael Lee, a Republican, released an ad attacking his Democratic opponent, a yoga-studio owner named Jessica Bichler. The ad, titled “Bonkers Bichler,” seems to show Bichler, a middle-aged woman with graying straight hair, doing yoga in a well-equipped, gently lit studio. The figure onscreen is not Bichler, though; it’s a hyperrealistic, animated A.I. rendering of her. The next frame shows her body twisting into an impossible knot, even as she maintains a vacant-eyed grin. Bichler told me recently that, when she first encountered the ad imagery, “I was thinking, who was even advising on this? Because it was really bizarre.” Five seconds into the ad there is a written disclaimer noting that A.I. was used to make “these silly video clips,” but the footage still deceived some local voters, who asked Bichler why she had let Lee into her yoga studio. With A.I., “people can make any image of you doing anything that they want you to be doing, and put that out in the public sphere,” Bichler said. “There is just a huge vulnerability.” (There was a whiff of hypocrisy about the ad, too: Lee and his wife have been known to frequent yoga studios themselves.)

Bichler has noticed apparently A.I.-generated imagery in other North Carolina election ads, including ones targeting the state Senate candidates April Cook and James Gailliard. Even Lee himself has been a target of a kind of impersonation; according to Bichler, a group not connected with her campaign has put up cardboard cutouts of the senator gripping handfuls of money and wearing a shirt that says “I <3 special interest.” (He also appears to have peed his pants.) Whatever the outcome of the races on Tuesday, this year’s midterms season marks a tipping point for A.I. in campaigning. AdImpact, an organization that tracks political advertising, has identified fifty-eight unique ads across the country that deployed A.I.; more than ten million dollars has been spent to air them. (Lee’s campaign spent a total of more than a hundred thousand dollars on “Bonkers Bichler” and two follow-up ads.)

This is not the first election cycle to be touched by misleading A.I. content. In January, 2024, thousands of New Hampshire voters received a recorded message from a voice that sounded just like then President Joe Biden, discouraging listeners from voting in the local primary election. In reality, it was a deepfake created by Paul Carpenter, a magician from New Orleans, using the audio-generating A.I. tool ElevenLabs, on behalf of a consultant associated with Dean Phillips’s long-shot Presidential campaign. But, as A.I. models have grown more powerful, more accessible, and more affordable, releasing fake messages from one’s opponents has become something of a default political strategy. In October, 2025, Andrew Cuomo’s mayoral campaign posted a series of A.I. spots targeting Zohran Mamdani: one depicted him as an “Austin Powers” Mini-Me to Bill de Blasio; another showed a silent Mamdani running through the streets of Manhattan with a giant set of keys and messily eating rice with his hands. Like the infamous “Trump Gaza” slopaganda video that the President shared earlier last year, these were blatant and shoddy A.I. creations, with blurry, color-saturated backgrounds and overly smooth faces. The Cuomo videos were criticized as racist and quickly taken down, but they proliferated online regardless, playing a role similar to that of extreme political cartoons: exaggerated and offensive provocations that could be played off as jokes.

Today’s A.I. ads are more easily mistaken as real. Compare the Mamdani content to a recent attack ad against the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro, by his opponent Stacy Garrity’s campaign. An A.I.-generated Shapiro, outfitted in a blue suit and casually tieless white shirt, with realistically coiffed hair and facial wrinkles, seems to testify to “deleting incriminating e-mails” and supporting “boys in girls sports.” There are no six-fingered hands here as a tell (though the imperfect voice replication might be a hint.) Lambasting an opponent’s record in office is the bread and butter of political attack ads, but candidates used to have to put their criticisms into the mouths of actors playing salt-of-the-earth voters—a plumber, say, or a factory worker. Now they can deposit any unflattering idea into the A.I.-generated mouth of the opponents themselves. Manuel Bonder, a spokesperson for Shapiro for Pennsylvania, described the ad to me as “cheap, dishonest AI bullshit” and pointed out Garrity’s support for “aggressive data center deregulation.”

Two-thirds of the A.I. ads identified by AdImpact are from Republicans, which might explain why they often fixate on aspects of personal identity, enlisting an opponent’s likeness to help depict him as a reductive trope. One such attack ad shows the Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed playing a Risk-type board game with his sister and the left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, flashing cards saying “DEATH TO AMERICA.” “The destruction of Israel and the West isn’t just a game for them, it’s a mission,” a voice-over narrates. Another depicts James Talarico, a Democrat running for U.S. Senate in Texas, wearing a T-shirt supporting trans people and eating tofu cubes at a football game, presumably to mock his masculinity and build on false rumors that he is a vegan. (The Talarico campaign said in a statement that his opponents are “slandering him with AI deepfakes, foreign bots, and conspiracy theories.”) Yet another video depicts Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia in a salon, getting his hair done and his nails filed, as a fictional illustration of the “makeup services” that Ossoff has reportedly paid for while in office—a sign, the ad alleges, that “he’s hiding something else.” In the ad, Ossoff appears perfectly real, as if he’d signed up for a walk-on role in his opponent’s campaign. Only a careful viewer would notice that the technicians seem to be filing his hands, not his nails.

As with the A.I. agents spreading across the internet or the A.I. software assisting in warfare, A.I. imagery in politics has gone largely unregulated. The 2025 Take It Down Act requires online platforms to remove sexually explicit deepfake content, but machine-generated political ads are treated as examples of free speech, granted the same protections as political cartoons. There have been some efforts toward halting the flood; after the 2024 fake-Biden robocall, Steve Kramer, the consultant who commissioned the ad, was ejected from the campaign and faced criminal charges of voter suppression and impersonation of a candidate, as well as millions of dollars in fines from the Federal Communications Commission. (He was later acquitted.) Not long after the fake-Biden phone message, the F.C.C. banned A.I.-generated voices in robocalls. Jessica Bichler’s campaign sent a cease-and-desist letter to Michael Lee’s campaign on the ground that the A.I. ad misrepresented her affiliation with a nonprofit. In regard to the actual A.I. impersonation, “there are no laws on the books to say he can’t do that,” Bichler said, noting that Lee voted to table an amendment to a state bill which would have required disclosure for generative-A.I. use in media. Bichler worries that even voters who know that such ads are unreal will be subtly influenced by their imagery. On the algorithmic internet, voters already live within their own bubbles and struggle to find common ground. A.I. attack ads provide further fuel for that fragmentation, Bichler said: “We’re talking across each other, but oftentimes we’re talking with such conviction. We feel like, ‘I’ve seen this with my own eyes.’ ” ♦

items.title: “Chronovisor” Captures the Terror of Thinking
items.description: In my former life as a Ph.D. candidate in philosophy, I spent a lot of time doing what looked like a lot of nothing. I read; I ruminated; I sat in apparent idleness, unknotting skeins of arguments in my head. At my most gregarious, I talked with other graduate
items.author: Becca Rothfeld
paragraphs: In my former life as a Ph.D. candidate in philosophy, I spent a lot of time doing what looked like a lot of nothing. I read; I ruminated; I sat in apparent idleness, unknotting skeins of arguments in my head. At my most gregarious, I talked with other graduate students; we had a habit of contorting our fingers into what those in the business call “philosophy hands,” which at least looked like something, if not exactly like most people’s idea of a meaningful contribution to society. Physicists and chemists could produce pictures of themselves manifestly Doing Science, wearing white coats and wielding pipettes. What did we have to show for ourselves? What did thinking look like, which is another way of wondering, What is thinking, anyway? Is it a substance? A spirit? A shiver?

Whatever it is, it is maddeningly spectral, which is why it was so hard for me to convince anyone (not least my parents and the administrators of my erstwhile university, who refused to provide dental insurance for graduate students until we went on strike) that what I was doing when I was sitting in silence was work, labor in want of compensation or at least dental insurance, alchemy that had the potential to alter the world, however impalpably. The philosopher and critic Elaine Scarry once wrote that “to have great pain is to have certainty; to hear that another person has pain is to have doubt.” We could say almost the same of thinking: from the inside, there is nothing more undeniable (though the thinker may come to doubt her conviction in the face of so much skepticism); from the outside, it is wispier than vapor.

But the difficulty of visualizing thinking hasn’t dissuaded filmmakers from attempting to stage thought’s convolutions onscreen. Cue montages of cryptographers staring at strings of numbers that light up suggestively (the film “A Beautiful Mind”), detectives taking stock of the corpses of murder victims as the camera zooms into the details that strike them as salient (the series “Sherlock”), chess prodigies hallucinating games on the ceiling (the series “The Queen’s Gambit”), and policemen affixing bits of yarn to bulletin boards with thumbtacks (innumerable crime procedurals). In movies and television shows, tortured geniuses think for brief, febrile stretches; then their paroxysms end, and the product of their toil (a cracked code, a jailed murderer, an especially clever checkmate) sets a more readily legible plot into motion. Thought is invariably the handmaiden of action, and the experimental contrivances that dramatize mental exertion—the closeups, the animations, the glowing numbers—are impatiently retired in favor of more standard fare.

“Chronovisor” is one of the few movies about thinking to deviate from this formula. In Jack Auen and Kevin Walker’s mesmerizing directorial début, mental foment is not a prelude to car chases or crime-fighting but an event in its own right. The film has just one character: Béatrice Courte (played by the real-life academic Anne-Laure Sellier), a philosophy professor at Columbia who is hard at work on a monograph about memory. In the opening scene, she describes her project to her peers over drinks in a dark, loud restaurant. She tells them that she is interested in ancient theories of the mind, which hold that different regions of the brain give rise to distinct mental functions—but above all, she continues, she is fascinated by memory palaces. According to the Roman rhetorician Quintilian, Béatrice explains, “an orator wishing to fixate an oration in memory should plan an itinerary through a large imaginary building, all of whose rooms and galleries, courtyards and corridors, statuary and adornments, are as clearly lined out as possible.” Thus a speaker’s roving thoughts are fixed, outfitted with an architecture. But Béatrice’s peers are not interested in memory palaces, and they are not impressed by her fervent monologue: they make their excuses and beg off, leaving her to return home to her desk.

Soon, however, she happens upon an even more ambitious effort to instantiate the insubstantial, to endow memory with form: the chronovisor, a real device that the Benedictine monk Pellegrino Ernetti claimed, in 1972, to have invented. Ernetti hypothesized that events emit electromagnetic waves that linger in the ether, and the chronovisor is intended to record these traces and reconstruct them, creating audiovisual documentation of history, much like a camera shooting a film. “Each one of us gradually leaves behind what happens in a span of seconds, hours, days, months and years, as a visual-acoustic double track,” Ernetti is quoted as saying in one of the sources that Béatrice consults in the course of her manic research. Exploiting this “visual-acoustic double track,” both the real and the filmic Ernetti took what he insisted was a kind of “photograph” of Jesus.

In reality, Ernetti was outed as a fake—the image was revealed to be a doctored reproduction of a sculpture by the Spanish artist Lorenzo Coullaut Valera—but in “Chronovisor” this verdict comes to seem wavering and indeterminate, at least as elusive as the residue of history that he purported to synthesize into images. As Béatrice combs through the archives, always alone, always in the dead of night, always in libraries dense with darkness, she becomes skeptical of the many attempts to discredit the monk and his discovery. “Chronovisor” accelerates and syncopates as she reads on and on—at an ever faster and more scrabbling clip, in increasing desperation—about the Vatican’s determination to silence him and suppress his findings, about threats and subterfuges, about the makings of a great conspiracy. The chronovisor, Ernetti and his supporters claim, was capable of recording not just history but also memories and fantasies, affording whoever controlled it the ultimate means of surveillance. “If I could reach into my heart, take hold of my thoughts, and with my bare hands lay them without further embellishment in your own, then, I confess, the innermost desire of my soul would be fulfilled,” the German Romantic novelist and playwright Heinrich von Kleist wrote, in 1811. Ernetti’s device intrigues and appalls us because it seems to be a means of both satisfying this desire and realizing the fears that it raises: the machine promises, horribly and redemptively, to transmute our inner intangibilities into something that others might see and touch.

Perhaps “Chronovisor” is one of its emanations. The film has the soft, blurred texture of a dream, and it teems not with things themselves but with their echoes. Shadows flit over a curtain in Béatrice’s apartment, and beams cast by a pair of headlights extend into the offing of a road while the car from which they emanate remains out of sight. In place of people’s bodies or faces, we see photographs from the archive and hear voices issuing from offscreen. When Béatrice meets her colleagues at the restaurant, they are positioned behind the camera; in another scene, she delivers a lecture, but the shot conceals her audience, which declines to ask her any questions during the period designated for Q. & A.

What “Chronovisor” captures is not quite the past so much as an oneiric alternative to the present—a place where time detaches from linearity and twines into unrecognizable loops, doubling back on itself. Béatrice is curiously out of synch with the world around her. Night after night, she sits and works. Her life consists of compulsive repetition, of what might even be regarded as a single event: she reads and reads. Her frenzied reading is set outside of time, in an epoch eerily adjacent to our own. Instead of a laptop, she takes notes with a typewriter; instead of searching for references in a digital database, she consults a librarian. All of her sources—books, photographs, magazine articles—are physical, many of them faded with evident age. She uses an iPhone, but only to make calls, never to send texts or summon Ubers or look up directions. She is as much at odds with the norms of her era as she is with the daily rhythms of the city. “Chronovisor” is set almost exclusively at night, when Béatrice sits in gloomy libraries that are otherwise empty, or works in the smudged chiaroscuro solitude of her apartment.

There are many reasons that this ruminative film surpasses previous efforts to portray the vellications of thinking. For one thing, contemplation—not the sheer fact of it but its content—drives the plot. “Chronovisor” makes no capitulations to conventional action; the only drama is the drama of research. (“We view the act of research and scholarship itself as high adventure in its own right,” Auen told an interviewer.) As Béatrice reads, racing toward discovery, we are obliged to read along with her. Passages are limned in white as her gaze passes over them. Sometimes the surrounding text fades away as she homes in on a sentence or phrase. She reads in French, German, and Italian, and the film translates for us in real time, overlaying the words with their English renderings until the pages on the screen become palimpsests. Our eyes move as Béatrice’s do: as she grows hysterical, an enigmatic snippet that she encountered in a book apparently unrelated to Ernetti at the beginning of the film fragments into its rudiments. At first, she reads,

Later, each word is isolated in its own shot: “I,” “carefully,” “collected,” “information,” and so on and on. The words flash onto the screen slowly, then accelerate frenetically. “I lay down quietly on my bed and died,” “I lay down quietly on my bed and died,” repeats faster and faster. As Béatrice sits at her desk, phantasmagoric music—selections from Gustav Holst’s orchestral suite “The Planets” and the Gregorian chants that Ernetti studied when he was not too busy inventing occult machines to devote himself to his other interest, musicology—swells and surges. “Chronovisor” is both a patient movie—a steady accretion of atmosphere—and a feverish one. It has the cadence of a burgeoning obsession.

But, above all, it succeeds because Auen and Walker have finally hit on the ideal genre in which to depict the pangs of thinking: horror. At one point, Béatrice listens intently to a 1977 interview with the philosopher Willard Van Orman Quine. The interviewer asks the eminence what he thinks of dualism—the view, hegemonic for much of the history of Western thought, that “there were bodies and there were minds, and that these were two fundamentally different kinds of thing.” Quine rejects dualism on the ground that it cannot explain the mind’s influence on the body, and opts instead for a thoroughgoing physicalism. But Béatrice takes the opposite tack: for her, thought and memory wreak havoc on dualism’s neat dichotomies—and thereby suggest that there is some interstitial entity quivering at the junction of the corporeal and the incorporeal. What is so chilling about this entity is that it always tempts us to suspect that it may not actually exist.

“Chronovisor” is, after all, a chronicle of bruising failures of acknowledgment. Béatrice gives a lecture, and no one asks her any questions; she explains her research to her colleagues, and they leave the restaurant as fast as possible. The academic speaks—and is so resoundingly ignored that she is justified in wondering if she has only imagined it. Most of what happens in “Chronovisor,” like most of what happens when Béatrice is entombed in the library, may or may not have really happened at all, which is another way of saying that “Chronovisor” is a ghost movie, which is another way of saying that it is a film about scholarship. Horror is the ideal genre in which to represent thinking because the true terror of the life of the mind, like the true terror of a haunting, is the sneaking suspicion that nothing is there, that all the agonies of rumination are mere phantoms. Contra Descartes’s famous dictum, to think is to inherit a sliver of the anti-intellectual’s uncertainty—to wonder helplessly if one has in fact accomplished anything at all. I think, therefore I worry that thinking is illusory.

In “Chronovisor,” we eventually come to see some of the images that the device has supposedly recorded—and then we wonder if we are watching a reel of Béatrice’s hallucinations, and then we wonder if the existence of a reel of Béatrice’s hallucinations proves that the chronovisor is real enough to have recorded them. The film is ingeniously ambiguous between these possibilities. But, whether Ernetti’s opus is a momentous innovation or a cheap hoax, whether Béatrice devolves into delusion or comes to see the truth, “Chronovisor” provides what the machine promises, what would be in equal measure harrowing and consoling, what will in any case remain elusive once we leave the cinema and return to the library: proof, for once, that the ghosts are real. ♦

items.title: Guess Who’s Coming to Washington
items.description: When Claire Valdez recently made her way to Washington, D.C., to prepare for her new life in Congress, she quickly got a taste of how unwelcome she was — at least among many of her future colleagues. That day, a majority of the House, including nearly every Re
items.author: Nia Prater
paragraphs: When Claire Valdez recently made her way to Washington, D.C., to prepare for her new life in Congress, she quickly got a taste of how unwelcome she was — at least among many of her future colleagues. That day, a majority of the House, including nearly every Republican and eight Democrats, voted in favor of a GOP-led “condemnation and denouncement of socialism in all its forms,” including the Democratic Socialists of America.

“When I joined DSA in 2019, I thought I was basically joining a reading group, and now we’re being condemned on the floor of Congress,” Valdez tells me with a hint of amusement. The soon-to-be congresswoman-elect mocked the symbolic vote by posting a photo of herself grinning and flashing a peace sign in front of the Capitol. “It was surreal, mostly because I think people are really scared of us,” she says, then adds, “I think some of them should be.”

We’re sitting in Peg’s Cavalier, a small bar in Ridgewood, one of several Queens and Brooklyn neighborhoods the 37-year-old will soon represent in D.C. The area has been playfully nicknamed New York City’s “Commie Corridor,” but Valdez points out that the people in her district aren’t the only ones demanding dramatic change. She says the members of Congress attacking her and DSA are “so out of touch with what’s happening in the United States right now,” not just because polls show Americans with a more favorable impression of socialism, but because of how angry people are.

“People are pissed that they’re not getting paid more money, that more and more of their lives are being dedicated to working shitty jobs,” she says. “They’re pissed that rent is going up, that they can’t afford retirement, they can’t afford their health care, and we have this unimaginable income inequality.”

Valdez is one of several democratic socialists set to be sworn into Congress in January, part of a growing bloc that, depending on how many seats Democrats win in the midterms, could soon wield significant leverage over their more moderate colleagues. She’s already been having conversations with other incoming DSA House members, including fellow New Yorker Darializa Avila Chevalier, who ousted Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair Adriano Espaillat this summer; Chris Rabb from Philadelphia; and Melat Kiros, who primaried and defeated a 15-term Democratic incumbent in Denver. “We’re building this new vision of what politics can and should be: one that’s about solidarity and cooperation and working together and not about ego and the kind of careerism that I think motivates a lot of politicians,” she said.

It obviously won’t be the first time idealistic outsiders have arrived in Washington intent on transforming its politics, nor would it be the first time if the swamp ends up swallowing them whole. But Valdez insists she and her DSA peers are ready for what they’re getting themselves into. “D.C. is really designed to literally pull you out of your district, literally pull you out of your community, away from your home, to isolate you in various ways, to intimidate you in various ways,” she says. “Staying together, it makes you more powerful,” she continues. “It protects you from backlash. It allows you to take bigger swings. You can take bigger risks together. I hope we can do the same thing in Congress.”

When we talk, Valdez reveals little about whether or not she intends to support House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’s bid to become Speaker, assuming Democrats do indeed flip the House, but she’s clear about what she wants, pointing back to her primary victory in her neighboring district. “We won by a 20-point margin,” she says. “This is a real mandate. This district, we want ICE abolished. We want Medicare for All. We want permanent, affordable social housing. These are things I’m going to keep fighting for, and I would like leadership that reflects those priorities as well.”
Valdez does confirm she’s spoken with Jeffries, and that they met for coffee over the summer. “I’m not going to negotiate in public,” she says, “but we’ll see how the midterms shake out.”

Valdez’s road to politics began with an ordinary union meeting. She was almost 30. After growing up in a liberal Mexican American family in conservative Lubbock, Texas, a winding path of art school in Chicago, jobs at Taco Bell and Trader Joe’s, and a yearslong stint at a Long Island City museum led her to Columbia University, where she took on an administrative-assistant role that provided the opportunity to join a local chapter of the United Auto Workers. Her first meeting in an auditorium with hundreds of new faces, she recalls, beaming, “was just the most democratic thing that I’d ever seen in my life.” Workers posed questions about a new contract and what was left on the bargaining table, standard talk for any unit gathering. But to Valdez, it was revelatory. It was the first time, she says, that she felt like she had some input over her future.

It was 2018, the same year the DSA upended the city’s politics when two first-time candidates, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Julia Salazar, ousted a pair of long-entrenched Establishment Democrats.“These punks built a campaign and learned how to use the tools that you use to run campaigns, and they won,” Valdez recalls. “It was a huge shot across the bow.” She joined DSA the following year, canvassing for local candidates in Brooklyn and for Bernie Sanders in New Hampshire. She describes DSA meetings as “a lot of nerds from all over the city who really want health care for everyone” and are “sick of people telling us that we don’t have the right degree or the right credentials, or the right experience to be fighting for it.”

While Valdez’s political organizing led her to becoming more deeply involved in her union, she initially didn’t envision herself as the one on the ballot. When she was approached in 2021 about running for the State Assembly, she rejected the overture as she planned to go to grad school for labor studies and continue her work with UAW. But a DSA friend at the time challenged her, pointing out that there were plenty of people in their movement going to grad school, but they also needed people willing to aim higher. When Valdez was approached again in 2023, she was ready, defeating a Democratic incumbent and another competitor in the 37th Assembly district primary by double digits.

She even found herself, in October 2024, as the lone elected official at the small, undercovered launch of a long-shot mayoral campaign by her Assembly colleague Zohran Mamdani. He then went from pulling just one percent in the polls to winning City Hall with a campaign built on their shared DSA principles, and this year he vigorously backed Valdez’s congressional campaign.

We’re actually sitting in the same bar where Mamdani joined Valdez to watch game four of the Knicks’ NBA Finals run this past spring. She occasionally offers small waves to other patrons but otherwise still seems to be enjoying — for now — the relative anonymity of being a state legislator.

“It was really instructive,” Valdez says of Mamdani’s success. “I think it showed we shouldn’t be afraid of taking big swings. We shouldn’t be stupid, but we should be ambitious. We should organize and govern with real moral clarity around issues, and we shouldn’t run away from our politics.”
“New York City elected a democratic socialist,” she adds. “That’s profound.”

When Nydia Velázquez first announced her intention to retire as U.S. representative for New York’s Seventh Congressional District, running for her seat was far from the first thing on Valdez’s mind. “Damn, those are big shoes to fill. Good luck to whoever is going to do that,” she recalls thinking, with a laugh. She says she ultimately decided to enter the race because she thought she could be a force for unions in Congress. “There was kind of a project there. How do we build union density in the United States? How do we protect our neighbors? Why do we need an organizer in Congress? That was my motivation,” she says.

When she gets to the House, Valdez said she intends to push for passage of the Protecting the Right to Organize Act and hopes to join the House Education and Workforce Committee if possible. She also hopes her congressional office will unionize like her campaign staff did. “I don’t love being a boss,” she admits. “What I tell all of my staff all the time is you will never be more powerful than when you are not on the clock, and you should take your time off and organize against me.”

There are more mundane concerns, too, as she plots out life in the capital, where members often live together to save money. “I have been fighting my whole life to be able to live alone in my apartment, and now I’m gonna have roommates,” she says.
“Today, I was making coffee and I was like, Wait, I need another coffee maker. Like, I need two coffee makers,” she adds, with a laugh.

She will also have to contend with future colleagues, who, like current Speaker Mike Johnson, have been warning about the dangers of socialists riding the blue wave to the U.S. Capitol. “I hoped and prayed it would never come to this, but here we are,” Johnson said over the summer. “The barbarians are in the gate.”

Valdez believes a lot of that fearmongering only works from afar. “I think most people, they meet us and they’re very disarmed,” she says. “I think that they realize that we’re real people who, honestly, truly want to get things done.”

But she also has a warning for any Democrats in Congress who are wary of the kind of economic populist agenda she and her DSA colleagues aim to pursue. “I think it’s not inconceivable that, in the next couple of years, we could have a Democratic president,” she says, taking a moment to knock on the wood bar table. “If we have a trifecta and we don’t use it for something, it’s game over. The working class is never going to come back,” she says.

“Trump will be gone in a couple of years, but the circumstances that brought him to power won’t,” she worries. “So, I think if we fail to address those root causes, we’re going to end up in the same position, and we’re running out of time.”

items.title: The House, Senate, and Texas All Turn Blue: Live Updates
items.description: It’s a historic night in America, with a massive blue wave propelling Democrats in unlikely places and serving as a repudiation of Donald Trump’s agenda. There has been one stunner after another, from South Carolina to Kansas. And history made in Texas and Geo
items.author: Intelligencer Staff
paragraphs: It’s a historic night in America, with a massive blue wave propelling Democrats in unlikely places and serving as a repudiation of Donald Trump’s agenda. There has been one stunner after another, from South Carolina to Kansas. And history made in Texas and Georgia. Democrats have already taken the House and Senate, but there are still major races to call. So follow along below for the latest results, reporting, and insights as power shifts in Washington.
Max Miller is going away, too

Neither a Trump endorsement or a family fortune could save the Ohio congressman from a blue wave and the consequences of his own actions. Domestic violence allegations haunted Miller for months, and on Tuesday night, he lost his seat in the U.S. House of Representatives to union ironworker Brian Poindexter. It’s a final humiliation for Miller, who rose to prominence as Trump’s “Music Man” and married Emily Moreno, daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno, in 2022. Moreno later accused him of throwing boiling water on her and holding a gun to her head; the two have since divorced. Miller denies the allegations, but Moreno is not the first woman to accuse him of violent behavior. Stephanie Grisham, a former Trump White House press secretary, said he pushed her against a wall and slapped her face during their romantic relationship. (Miller says she’s lying, too.) Voters gave him a pass at the time, but he couldn’t survive Moreno’s story – or his close ties to the unpopular Trump. Shame is not dead after all.
Cold comfort for Maine Republicans: LePage is back

In the shadow of Susan Collins’s titanic fall from power, another Maine GOP legend of some ill-repute, former two-term governor Paul LePage, looks like he’s probably taking his cantankerous and reactionary act to Washington. He’s pulling off what may be the only Republican flip of a un-gerrymandered Democratic House seat. It’s Maine’s rural/small town 2nd congressional district, a Republican-leaning seat occupied by conservative Democrat Jared Golden, who retired.
Jon Husted’s fine ass was no defense against Sherrod Brown

The blue onslaught was so intense for a moment there that we almost forgot to specifically mark the other big blue victory in Ohio tonight. Brown lost his Senate seat two years ago, but now he’s going to take Husted’s. This was despite — or perhaps partly because of — President Trump’s repeated praise for Husted’s posterior in the final weeks before the midterms. With 90 percent of results in, Brown currently has a 2.5 percentage point lead.
Democrats will have a Fetterman-proof Senate majority
“Always bet on the underdog”

In his victory speech, Senator-elect James Talarico reflected on his campaign and invoked the Biblical story of David and Goliath, positioning his longshot bid as one locked in a fight against the many political forces that emerged in the cycle’s most expensive and most high-profile races.

“In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths: the richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world, and the entire Washington D.C. establishment. David wasn’t as big or as strong as Goliath. He didn’t have as many weapons, but he had hope. He had faith, and he had a slingshot,” the former seminarian told the crowd. “You were my slingshot. The people of Texas were my slingshot. And tonight, we defeated Goliath.”

The senator-elect also emphasized the hurdles that his campaign faced beyond the money, getting people to believe that a Democratic win in Texas was actually possible. “We went up against nearly 40 years of doubt and disillusionment. We went up against more than $300 million, more than any Senate campaign in American history, we went up against all the negative ads, smear campaigns, foreign bots, and AI deepfakes that money can buy,” he said.

Talarico continued, “Those attacks were the final howls of a dying establishment, the death rattle of a status quo that knows its days are numbered. They played dirty because they were desperate, but we never lost hope. We never lost faith, and against big money and long odds, we took our power back.”
The billionaire tax is crashing and burning in California

It’s not a big surprise, since the ballot initiative has been losing altitude steadily after extensive and expensive strafing from some of its wealthy targets, but Prop 40, California’s “billionaire tax,” a one-time 5 percent levy on the wealth of the state’s wealthiest residents, appears to be going down to defeat. With about half the vote in, “No” is leading “Yes” by a 13 percent margin. It’s barely ahead in very liberal San Francisco, is narrowly losing in Los Angeles. Prominent backers Bernie Sanders, Ro Khanna, and the state’s biggest health care union are taking a big hit.
Susan Collins is done, too

For 30 years, Senator Collins has cultivated a reputation as a senator willing to buck her party. She has steered vast amounts of federal money to Maine, and repeatedly outperformed polls that showed her losing in past elections. But her cooperation with Trump on key issues proved too much of a millstone this time around. Democrat Troy Jackson, who replaced the scandal-ridden Graham Platner, will be going to Washington.
Democrats win a trifecta in Pennsylvania, as well

Governor Josh Shapiro, who won reelection earlier Tuesday night, confirmed that the Democratic Party flipped the state Senate, handing the party a trifecta in state government for the first time in more than thirty years. “TRIFECTA DELIVERED,” he wrote on social media.
Trump is going through it on Fox News
He’s a little bit surprised:
He took a shot at a host, on air:
And Fox News had to fact check him:
DeSantis rubbing Trump’s nose in his losses, again
Guess who’s going to some trouble to underline the disaster that has struck the GOP Senate? Meatball Ron:

If this feels familiar, recall that in 2022 DeSantis and his supporters were quick to contrast RDS’s boffo reelection win with the Senate losses attributed to Donald Trump’s poor choice of candidates. Then he ran for president against Trump. Could he be thinking about running the same play, again?
New Yorkers have taken over America
Flanagan holds Tina Smith’s Senate seat in Minnesota

NBC News is projecting Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan will become Minnesota’s next senator, defeating former sports broadcaster and Republican nominee Michele Tafoya. Flanagan will succeed the retiring incumbent Tina Smith and ensure the seat stays in Democratic Party hands, further strengthening its margin in the Senate.
RIP to Bipartisan Trump, 11:05 p.m. – 11:35 p.m.

Moments after telling Politico he’s eager to work with Democrats and doesn’t want to blame anyone in his party for their historic losses, Trump took to Truth Social to taunt Democrats and lash out at specific GOP losers.
He posted a photo of a “VETO”-fied MAGA hat:
He called Texas Governor Greg Abbott a RINO:
And promised to unload on other Republicans:
Now four for four in Pennsylvania

While the AP has yet to officially call the race, Bucks County commissioner Bob Harvie is claiming victory in PA’s First District, marking a stunning end to Republican incumbent Brian Fitzpatrick’s tenure in the House. Fitzpatrick, a moderate known for his independent streak, has long avoided the fallout of Pennsylvania’s constantly shifting political landscape. While anti-Trump sentiment loomed large in tonight’s contests, Fitzpatrick likely fell victim to the electorate’s strong anti-incumbent push that was also a persistent trend this cycle. If confirmed, this marks a clean sweep of four swing House districts for Democrats.
