There’s no doubt now: the 120th Congress will be run by Democrats.

CNN has officially called it for Democratic control of the U.S. Senate. Even with races in Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, and Alaska uncalled, Democrats have flipped six GOP-held Senate seats (in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas) to secure at least 51 seats. Combined with their conquest of the House, Democrats have now taken away the congressional underpinnings of Donald Trump’s second term, and will be able to deny his executive-branch and judicial appointments unless he chooses to work with them. In this reduced position, Trump will resemble George W. Bush in his sad last two years as president after the Democratic landslide of 2006. And Democrats should be in an excellent position to hang onto Congress in 2028 and seek a trifecta with a presidential win.
Trump tired, shockingly conciliatory in call with Politico
In a very surprising turn of events, Trump sounded more defeated than “defiant” in a phone interview with Dasha Burns during Politico’s live election night broadcast.

Trump began by reiterating that the GOP’s massive losses aren’t really his fault. “I wasn’t on the ballot,” he said. “And we didn’t get the people out. But I wasn’t on the ballot. If I was on the ballot we would have won. We would have won it all very easily.”
The Burns pointed out the obvious counterpoint, saying, “You told voters that you were on the ballot, to go vote as if you were on the ballot.”
Trump conceded, “Yeah, I said, ‘say you’re on the ballot, think about me being on the ballot.’” But they didn’t agree and they didn’t like the candidates in most cases. So, just one of those things.”
When asked if he thinks certain candidates didn’t do enough, Trump — stunningly — opted not to scapegoat others.
“Nah, I don’t want to blame anybody,” he said.”I just want to say, it was a very interesting period of time. I watched with great interest, learned from it, but I wasn’t on the ballot.”
So what exactly did he learn? That he wants to play nice with Democrats, who are suddenly his “friends” not “Dumocrats.”

“Well, we’re going to work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for our country,” Trump said. “Very important. They’ve already called and they want to work with me. I have a right to veto everything. But I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything. They want to see things happen too. So I’ve already spoken to certain leaders of the Democrat Party … and you know, I have a lot of friends in the Democrats. It’s an interesting phenomenon.
We’ll work with the Democrats and we’ll make things work out well for the country.
Spoken like a man who really, really doesn’t want to get impeached again.
And here was the crowd’s reaction at Talarico’s Election Night event:

In a result (much like Annie Andrews’ win in South Carolina) that could have barely been imagined at the beginning of the midterm cycle, Methodist megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton defeated incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall in deep-red Kansas, becoming the first Democrat to represent the Sunflower State in the Senate since 1932. Hamilton deployed his outstanding communications skills, projected bipartisan bonafides, and benefited from the flaws of his opponent, an OB/GYN who during the campaign was revealed as having sued many patients for non-payment of medical bills. Hamilton will join Raphael Warnock of Georgia as an ordained minister in the Senate, and he’ll also have a lot in common with seminarian James Talarico. Together the three will battle the stereotype that organized Christianity is the Republican Party at prayer.
Jeffries heralds ‘great American comeback’
On the eve of the Democratic Party’s seismic flip of the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries—who is poised to make history as the chamber’s first Black speaker, relished in the cycle’s results.
“Today begins the great American comeback,” he said to applause.

He continued, “The American people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption. They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January.”
He did not bring his baseball bat.
Polls close on the Left Coast

Polls have now closed in California, Oregon and Washington. The only competitive statewide race in the bunch is in Oregon, where Democratic Governor Tina Kotek has been in a close race, but surely can hope the national Democratic wave can save her. There are competitive House races in the Republican-held seats of CA-22 and CA-48, and Democratic-held WA-03. And many eyes will be on California’s Prop 40, a first-of-its-kind billionaire tax that has struggled against lavishly funded opposition.
Bluenami? The Midterm Massacre? Trump’s Folly-Flood?
The Flipocalypse? A Blue-Out?
The race is on to come up with the best way to describe tonight’s events. “Blue wave” just doesn’t seem to cut it anymore.
Gina Hinojosa has ousted Abbott in Texas
Incumbent Republican governor Greg Abbott has lost his bid for a fourth term.

Hinojosa will be the first Latina governor to lead Texas, and the first Democrat to hold that office in over three decades, according to Houston Public Media. Her victory marks a stunning night for Texas Democrats, as James Talarico looks set to win his Senate race against Ken Paxton, whose wife, Angela, recently filed for divorce on “Biblical grounds.” (He cheated. He’s also pretty corrupt.)

Hinojosa ran a savvy campaign focused less on the historic nature of her candidacy and more on a version of economic populism. As she said at a rally, “Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people? Or is this a billionaire’s world and we just live here? That is the one fight. It is the one fight of this election. It is the fight in America. And it is the fight for Texas.”
Elon Musk probably didn’t like that. Oh well!
Trump says he’s “absolutely willing to accept” election results
The president was considerably less “defiant” in an interview with the Times:

“I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” he said in an interview with The New York Times. He added: “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.”
Trump spoke to the outlet around 10:30 p.m., right before Texas was called for Talarico. He seemed stunned by Darline Graham’s loss in South Carolina:
“I’m just looking at these results as I’m talking,” he said. “I see that Darline lost. Wow, that’s amazing. How do you think Lindsey would have done if he ran?”
Mr. Trump said he thought Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July, most likely would have prevailed in his race.
Insane that “President of United States accepts election results” is news that requires a push alert, but here we are.

It’s now official, and Texas Democrats can stop fearing they can never have good things. The massively outspent and endlessly demonized Texas seminarian James Talarico has defeated Texas Attorney General and Trump favorite Ken Paxton to win the first Democratic Senate victory in the Lone Star State since Lloyd Bentsen retired.

It was a long road for the Austin state legislator who caught the imagination of Democrats everywhere with his resistance to Republican gerrymandering in 2025, and then won a tough primary against Jasmine Crockett, showing exceptional message discipline and an outstanding temperament. It’s impossible at this point to count the number of smears and insults Talarico had to deal with during this long campaign, targeted as he was by Donald Trump and Elon Musk, who believed the only way to save Paxton was to turn the Democrat into a cartoon villain. But it didn’t work, and where Beto O’Rourke and Colin Allred fell short, Talarico went the extra mile, and now heads to Washington already a celebrity.
Lawler concedes in New York’s lone toss-up race

Mike Lawler, the Republican incumbent representing New York’s 17th congressional district, has conceded the race to his Democratic challenger Cait Conley. Lawler first took office in 2022, defeating then-DCCC chairman Sean Patrick Maloney in a stunning victory that helped flip control of the House to Republicans.

The once highly-competitive and even Democratic-leaning state of Iowa (it was carried by Michael Dukakis in 1988!) has been exhibit A of white working-class and farm areas going hard right in the Trump era. It started in the 2014 midterms with a Republican sweep of statewide races, and just kept getting worse, with Trump carrying Iowa three times by big margins (13 percent in 2024, when Republicans won every House race).

Thanks to a lot of things that affected living costs in this part of the country, and some high-quality candidates, the worm turned today. Democrats seem sure to flip the Senate seat once held by Tom Harkin; the governorship (for the first time since 2006) and likely three of the state’s four House seats. Along with the even more startling Democratic gains in nearby Kansas, the results showed once again that you should never take the farm belt for granted, as Trump surely did.
Amy Acton defeats Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio

The Associated Press just called Ohio’s gubernatorial race for Democrat Amy Acton, a physician and public health official who helped the state’s response to COVID. Her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, set his campaign on fire late last month after releasing an ad with Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur. Why are they estranged? Well, Arthur’s husband raped Acton when she was 12 years old, then fled the state to escape justice. Arthur lost custody of Acton and her brother, and remained married to their stepfather until his death – facts that did not make it into the Ramaswamy ad. Although Trump and Vice President JD Vance defended the move, it backfired spectacularly, and likely clinched Ramaswamy’s loss to Acton. MAGA bet big on venom this cycle, but Acton’s victory may be an early sign that the cruel kids’ table doesn’t look that attractive right now.
A vaguepost from Texas’ outgoing senator
As James Talarico is expected to flip Texas’s open Senate race, John Cornyn — who made his disappointment in Republican nominee Ken Paxton known — shares a photo of the Texas Capitol building.
And officially disavows any responsibility for tonight’s GOP disaster. After three hours of silence on Truth Social, he posted:
Do you remember a certain commander-in-chief repeatedly saying voters should pretend Trump’s on the ballot in this election? Trump sure doesn’t!
Three out of four in Pennsylvania

Former news anchor Janelle Stelton is projected to defeat Republican Congressman Scott Perry in Pennsylvania’s 10th congressional district, further expanding the Democratic Party’s gains in the House. Perry, the one-time chair of the House Freedom Caucus, narrowly defeated Stelton in the swing district in 2024. Perry gained notoriety in 2020 as one of the leading members supporting President Trump’s push to overturn the presidential election results.
Democrats are winning in some very unexpected places

When there’s an electoral tsunami like the one happening now, incumbents who thought they were safe suddenly find themselves in great danger. A few illustrative examples so far tonight — though there are many more.
Fox News pundits acknowledge Trump’s war in Iran is to blame

Sean Hannity was quick to add that he believes, “the president will be proven correct” someday, “just like Reagan was.” But it’s notable that Fox isn’t rolling with the White House’s delusional claim that Trump deserves no blame for this GOP bloodbath.
The GOP officially needs an ark
Robert Garcia, the ranking member on House Oversight Committee, appeared to give a preview of the panel’s likely focus under a Democratic-controlled House:
Don’t think Trump is going to declare victory tonight

One of the most important by-products of the size and speed of the Democratic wave tonight is that Donald Trump was robbed of any opportunity to claim an election victory that he might subsequently use to argue that Democrats stole the results with late-counted results, especially mail ballots. He made that argument famously in 2020, but also in 2018, when he attributed a next-day surge in Democratic votes in close House races to ballot-box stuffing, especially in California.

This time around, the overall results are clear long before a single vote was counted in California. And even Donald Trump would be hard-pressed to claim that non-citizen voting was a big factor in red-state losses in places like South Carolina, Kansas and Texas. There may be some Trump administration post-election chicanery and denial still ahead of us, but nobody’s going to believe Trump and his party actually won.
Bob Brooks wins PA-7 back for Democrats, too

NBC News is projecting that Democratic nominee Bob Brooks has won Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, flipping back a seat that the party lost in 2024. Brooks, a moderate former firefighter who emphasized his working class roots, defeated Republican incumbent Ryan Mackenzie in the district that spans the Lehigh Valley.
Trump has gone silent on social media

It turns out predictions that he’d been Truthing through it were premature. He dropped a few criticisms of Fox News early in the night, but now his Truth Social feed is unusually inactive. He hasn’t posted anything in three hours.
When the Needle goes far left
Democrats do indeed conquer the House

CNN was the first major media outlet to officially project that Democrats will indeed flip control of the House. The Senate is more likely than not to follow. How big could that House majority be? It could be significantly bigger than much of anyone predicted. At present, the New York Times “needle” projects 251 House Democrats winning the midterms. That’s a net gain of 36 seats, and a 33-seat majority. Silver Bulletin, an outfit considered bullish on Democratic odds, had predicted ten fewer Democratic wins. If it turns out that way, this will be the largest Democratic House majority since the 111th Congress, which enacted Obamacare before Republicans “shellacked” them in 2010.
Annie Andrews flips Lindsey Graham’s seat

Darline Graham, the sister of the late Lindsay Graham, lost her bid for her brother’s South Carolina seat to pediatrician Annie Andrews, handing Democrats a crucial and stunning win in the party’s pursuit of Senate control. Graham, a political novice, won the Republican nomination over Congressman Ralph Norman with the crucial backing of President Trump. The last Democrat to represent the state in the Senate was Fritz Hollings who was first elected in 1966 and retired in 2005.
Mood in White House is “defiant,” delusional
A White House official released this statement to multiple networks:

Basically, the White House is saying Trump deserves none of the blame, though he promoted terrible candidates in key races, insisted voters’ affordability concerns were a “hoax,” and repeatedly instructed voters to pretend that he is on the ballot, to name just a few of his missteps in this election cycle.
How will Republicans react to Trump making their nightmare a reality then insisting he’s totally innocent? Buckle up!
Elon’s ROI on Texas Republicans was zilch

There are a lot of uncalled races still yet, but at present Democrats could well be on the brink of a truly astounding victory in Texas. This very red state, which has tantalized and frustrated Democrats for years, even as its Republican politicians became more outlandishly extremist every year, could flip blue in every statewide race, including the potential defeat of three-term Governor Greg Abbott, thought to be invincible. But on top of every other advantage the GOP had and squandered, this is where Elon Musk spent an estimated $224 million of his own money to make absolutely sure what happened couldn’t happen. The business chops that made him the world’s richest person certainly eluded him, and he might want to pull up roots and get out of this money-sink of a state as quickly as possible.
Now closing: Montana and Nevada
Just three states close polls at 10:00 p.m. ET. And just two of them — Montana and Nevada — have competitive congressional or gubernatorial races.
• In Montana, MT-01 is an open Republican-controlled seat in a toss-up election, as rated by Cook.

• In Nevada, the governorship is a toss-up race between Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo and Democrat Aaron Ford. And NV-02 is a GOP-controlled House seat in a competitive race that leans Republican. Like Virginia, Nevada also has an abortion rights constitutional amendment on the ballot that is expected to pass.
What if Angie Nixon hadn’t been written off?

Nixon has lost her bid for U.S. Senate in Florida, but her surprisingly narrow margin of defeat — less than three points, according to most projections — is already raising questions about what could have been. A major theme in the home stretch of this race was how hesitant the national Democratic Party and its top donors were to invest in the former Jacksonville state representative. Now, there is reason to believe they were too gun shy.

Many progressive pundits certainly think so. “Imagine if anyone in Democratic leadership had lifted a finger to help Angie Nixon in Florida,” tweeted Lydia Polgreen. “The minute that Angie Nixon won the primary, they cast her aside and said she wasn’t electable,” said reporter Ari Berman on Democracy Now! “I think a lot of Democrats are going to feel like they should have invested more.”

It’s impossible to say with confidence how much better Nixon would have performed with the same resources as, say, Jon Ossoff in Georgia, whose campaign had nearly $120 million more than hers. But this is clearly not the same Florida we’re used to seeing. Earlier this year, Republicans in the state legislature gerrymandered four congressional districts to make them easy GOP pickups. They now appear to have lost all four of them.

In what is shaping up to be an incredibly favorable electoral environment for Democrats, the decision to play “wait-and-see” with Nixon’s race — as Chuck Schumer did after her upset win in the Democratic primary — could haunt the party. Many Democrats had written Florida off as either too red or too expensive to claw back, and Nixon’s campaign looked forbiddingly polarizing — she joined the DSA this summer and supports the kind of big government agenda long associated with Bernie Sanders.

Yet she appears to be running about even with David Jolly, the former Republican who was the Democratic nominee for governor, and came remarkably close to winning for a candidate who basically had to build her entire campaign infrastructure from scratch. One thing feels certain: The bad feelings generated by this race towards party leadership aren’t going away any time soon.
Paige Cognetti wins PA-8 in crucial Dem flip

NBC News projects that Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti has defeated Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan, flipping Pennsylvania’s 8th district which spans the state’s Luzerne, Wayne and Lackawanna Counties. Bresnahan, a freshman member, was hit heavily for his controversial stock trading despite his campaign promise to ban stock trading in Congress.
Part of Ossoff’s victory speech tonight:
The missing congressman will soon no longer be a congressman

Democratic nominee Rebecca Bennett soundly defeated Republican Congressman Tom Kean, Jr. to win New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District seat, per projections from NBC News. Kean’s campaign was engulfed by one of the election cycle’s strangest controversies as the incumbent congressman missed numerous votes amid a four-month absence from Congress. Kean would later reveal that he was seeking treatment for depression.
“It’s very hard to read, I think, into these midterms, a lot about the economy.”
I don’t know, seems like voters aren’t loving it?
An important subplot of tonight’s results
Prediction markets are very sure about a lot of big races that haven’t been officially called

The “official” callers of winners and losers, the AP and the major media networks, are often cautious about announcing winners on election night. Not so the prediction markets, where data combine with vibe and social media talk to produce more certainty, and earlier.

• There hasn’t been an official call in either of the big statewide races in Texas. Kalshi has James Talarico as a 98.5 percent likely winner over Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa as a 93.2 percent likely winner over Greg Abbott.
• The South Carolina Senate race is still uncalled too. Not at Kalshi, where Annie Andrews is at 98.3 percent.
• How about Kansas, where Adam Hamilton has an early but tentative lead over Roger Marshall? Kalsh has Hamilton at 96.3 percent.
• Michigan? It’s uncalled, but Kalshi has Abdul El-Sayed at 93.8 percent.
Now if any of these early predictions crashes, maybe future betters will be more careful. But for right now, prediction markets have a pretty good record of just being rapidly ahead of the curve.

items.title: Trump Ponders Pardoning Elon Musk and Many, Many Others
items.description: Facing the prospect of a massive Republican defeat in Congress — and a likely blizzard of investigations and subpoenas by Democrats — Donald Trump declared this week that he will not hesitate to pardon anyone who’s ever worked for him. And yes, he includes the
items.author: Bess Levin
paragraphs: Facing the prospect of a massive Republican defeat in Congress — and a likely blizzard of investigations and subpoenas by Democrats — Donald Trump declared this week that he will not hesitate to pardon anyone who’s ever worked for him. And yes, he includes the 20-year-old known as “Big Balls” on that list.

In an interview with the New York Post released the day before the midterm elections, Trump said that should Democrats go after Elon Musk, former DOGE employee Eddie Coristine (a.k.a. Mr. Balls), or any member of his administration, he would “protect those people” with preemptive pardons. “That’s what Biden did — he gave everyone a pardon,” Trump told Post columnist Miranda Devine, who suggested Democrats “want to arrest Elon Musk … seize his factories, nationalize SpaceX,” as well as arrest “Big Balls” and “anyone around you who enabled you.”

Referring to his blanket pardon of the nearly 1,600 individuals convicted (or awaiting trial or sentencing) for crimes connected to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, Trump told Devine, “I wouldn’t even think about it. I did it for J6.”

Naturally, Trump did not mention his previous claim that he had “terminated” the preemptive pardons Joe Biden issued for the members of the House committee tasked with investigating the Capitol attack, claiming any orders signed using an autopen were not legal. (Legal experts said at the time that there was zero basis for him to do so.)

In October, Senator Alex Padilla called for an investigation into Musk following reports that SpaceX had restricted Ukraine’s ability to operate military drones. (Musk later said Ukraine had violated the company’s terms of service.) According to the Washington Post, Democrats are “preparing sweeping investigations of Trump’s growing wealth in office, his remaking of the federal government and his pursuit of his political enemies.”

Last week, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee indicated they plan to go after the president for his ties to Jeffrey Epstein, accusing him of committing crimes “alongside, and in coordination with, the most infamous sex trafficker in history.” (A spokesperson for the White House told MS NOW that “none” of the allegations are true.)

items.title: Trump Says We’re ‘Not Fighting a War’ As He Bombs Iran Again
items.description: If you ask Donald Trump, his war with Iran has been over, or just about over, almost since the very start. Just ten days after the first missile strike in February, the president announced, “The war is very complete — pretty much.” He’s been offering kaleidosc
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: If you ask Donald Trump, his war with Iran has been over, or just about over, almost since the very start. Just ten days after the first missile strike in February, the president announced, “The war is very complete — pretty much.” He’s been offering kaleidoscopic assessments ever since; the war may be long over or on the verge of wrapping up, depending on the day and who’s asking.

So it’s fitting that on the eve of a midterms election that may be heavily influenced by voters’ distaste for the Iran war — or at least its economic impact — Trump delivered a condensed version of his “all of the above” answer on the state of the conflict.

On Monday night, Trump called into Fox News for an interview with Sean Hannity. After displaying a list of Trump’s purported second-term accomplishments, the host set the president up to argue that the Iran war doesn’t actually violate his “no forever wars” campaign pledge.

Hannity noted, at the six-minute mark in the video below, that many administration officials have argued they simply “had no choice” on launching a war with Iran. “Both Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury were to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon … [the conflict] will come to an end. How can you assure the American people on that point tonight?”

Trump gave it a shot, but his point on Iran was lost in some hard-to-follow weaving on the stock market, Greenland, and Venezuela. He concluded by hinting that the war actually isn’t coming to an end, as the U.S. might soon strike Pickaxe Mountain, the site of an underground facility linked to Tehran’s nuclear program.
“Now, we might have to go after Pickaxe, but that’s not a big deal,” Trump said. “We can do it in literally — we can do that in one hour, okay, as soon as we want, at any time we want.”
So aside from this potential nuclear-weapon-related bombing, the war is over? Well, according to Trump, that’s really a semantic question.

“I mean, what’s a war?” Trump said. “A war is — a war is fighting. Take a look at World War I, World War II, these were — when was the last time you saw us fighting with them? … We’re not fighting a war. Everyone says ‘You’re at war.’ Well, when was the last time we fired anything?”
Inconveniently for Trump, the last time the U.S. fired something at Iran was actually Monday. Shortly after the Hannity interview aired, The Wall Street Journal reported:

The U.S. attacked Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials said, in the latest of a series of limited strikes Washington has secretly carried out against the country in recent weeks as President Trump touted the possibility of a diplomatic deal.
But it seems air strikes on Qeshm Island don’t meet Trump’s new definition of military engagement. Trump also told Hannity the situation with Iran is merely a “soft war”:

This isn’t a war, this is a very soft war. We did have a big hit on them, and we hit them very hard and that took out their navy. 159 ships are gone, but this isn’t like a war that’s going on. There’s no war raging.

Could happen if they don’t make a deal, but they want to make a deal very badly and there’s a very good chance we make a deal. But they want to — but here’s the thing, we’re dealing from total strength. We can end it at any time. If I can make a deal, I’d rather do it, save a lot of lives, but we can — but think about a war, this isn’t war. … So this is not much of a war, Sean, because there hasn’t been shooting for months.

This is what Trump has been saying all along. There hasn’t been any Saving Private Ryan–style fighting, so the Iran War is “very complete — pretty much.” (Except for yesterday’s strikes on Qeshm Island, the potential bombing of Pickaxe Mountain, and the fact that gas prices are at a new high for an Election Day — which are all no big deal!) Why are voters having such a hard time grasping this?

items.title: The Big Strong Man Who Likes Big Strong Men
items.description: In 2016, Donald Trump, in an effort to illustrate the loyalty of his base, remarked, “I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I still wouldn’t lose any voters.” What else, in 2026, does he think could do in the streets of Manhattan?
items.author: Paul McAdory
paragraphs: In 2016, Donald Trump, in an effort to illustrate the loyalty of his base, remarked, “I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I still wouldn’t lose any voters.” What else, in 2026, does he think could do in the streets of Manhattan? Could he walk to Hell’s Kitchen and gush over the burly queens flitting between bars? Could he cruise the Ramble in Central Park?

I ask because the president recently has moved on from the bog-standard compliments (“handsome,” “good-looking”) he’s laden on supporters and military personnel in public appearances for years. Now, Trump is likening the ass of former footballer Jon Husted, the GOP’s candidate for Senate in Ohio, to “a pile of muscle,” exclaiming that his feet are so big, that his fingers resemble sausages. On the campaign trail, he has called Georgia’s Rick Jackson a “beautiful-looking guy,” praised Mike Collins’s “big strong build,” and deemed Kentucky’s Ed Gallrein “a perfect man.” He even brought back his bit from 2024 about golfer Arnold Palmer’s fleshy long iron: “When he took showers with the other pros, they came out of there and said, ‘Oh my God. That’s unbelievable.’” What is the meaning of his tumescing man-love, and how deep does it penetrate?

I do not mean to imply that Trump is gay. He is a camp icon and camera chaser, a diva who lives for the musical Cats, for “Y.M.C.A.,” for the applause and for the lines that garner it. He has cavorted with players for the other team: His mentor, Roy Cohn, set the bar for odious gay guys everywhere, and Jimmy Lasalvia and Christopher Barron, founders of the now-defunct gay Republican organization GOProud, invited Trump to speak at his first Conservative Political Action Conference in 2011. But he has not regressed in his dotage to a state of infantile bisexuality; he does not have “gay dementia,” as some have half-joked; he is straight.

Rather, I’d like to posit that his vocal appreciation for toned male bodies and square jaws fulfills two purposes, consciously pursued or not. One is to display his continued freedom from conventions and from the consequences that, once upon a time, were supposed to obtain when politicians breached those conventions. The other is to remind receptive audiences that their only hope in a scary world rests in the arms of big strong white men with granitic asses.

“You watch him calculating, yet not seeming to care about the consequences of what he says, and you listen to his supporters enjoying the feel of his freedom,” the late cultural theorist Lauren Berlant wrote of then-candidate Trump more than a decade ago in a piece for The New Inquiry. Trump had already called Mexican immigrants “rapists,” drug mules, and criminals; he had mocked a disabled Times reporter; he had called for “the total and complete shutdown of Muslims coming into the U.S.” Cataloguing his statements since seems at once banal and absurd, like listing out a city’s weather conditions for every day of the past ten years. He has been every temperature, blown in all possible directions, rained and shined.

But if his open racism appealed to certain voters precisely for its openness, for the sense of emotional possibility it unleashed in them, and if his reign has since helped uncloseted racists attain power and influence, then his latter-day man ogling has a “then as farce” tenor to it. I can play at being fruity because I’m me, the most potent specimen, and anyway you — my fans, liberal vermin, the Fake News Media — you like it, you laugh at it, you cover it breathlessly and post jokes about it, you want me to carry on. You conservative straight men out there, despite your groomer fearmongering, you too notice and at moments savor the looks of other men because you have eyes, because you are human, and now perhaps you too may do so more openly — or just cynically and servilely, as Senate Majority Leader John Thune did last week when he referred to a colleague as “eye candy.” Conservatives are free to get a little gay with it, no “no homo” required, even if, lacking Trump’s chutzpah and platform, they will never be as fierce or mother as him.

Indeed, one of the minor consolatory pleasures of Trump 2.0 involves watching his subordinates prove their dearth of charisma as they slavishly riff on his absurd talking points — a pleasure marred somewhat by the sense that Trump likewise enjoys watching his right-wing drag daughters perform their listless variations on his assophilia. They can’t hack it like he can, but they must try all the same. Chief among the chronically un-fierce anti-comediennes is JD Vance, who has lately told a rally crowd that Representative Ryan Zinke complimented his “beautiful blue eyes earlier today” and, in a town hall, joked that he is “jealous” of the attention his boss has lavished on Husted’s wild rump. This misshapen shadow of the Great Leader lacks the self-confidence required to engage in both jockish, ostensibly jocular ball-grabbing and high-camp theatrics. Vance, an early front-runner in the 2028 race to become the next Republican nominee for president, offers one possible vision for his party post-Trump: MAGA without its verbal sequins and six-inch stilettos.

Then again, Trump hardly pioneered bizarre far-right homoeroticism, which flourishes in the discourse of Nick Fuentes, among the groypers and similar online communities, and in the gay-gooner-adjacent feed of the manosphere personality Bronze Age Pervert. Perhaps the future of the party will be decided in a bleak struggle over who can best own and adapt Trump’s ersatz homosexuality: the real freaks on the fringes or the normie assimilationists.

The Trump-Husted affair, for all its weird comedy, has quickly become tiresome. It is a phenomenon best discovered on a feed, passed around group chats, and rapidly forgotten amid the deluge of information bloodying our eyes. But the president is, as is his wont, wearing out his latest hit at speed, retelling the story of how and why he examined Husted’s ass almost daily and adding little grace notes and follow-up bits about other men at his pleasure. One of those follow-ups led the Democratic Party’s X account to post a still from a video in which Trump appears to mime sucking, and perhaps gagging, on a massive piece of meat. The performance captured in the video took place at a rally in Texas and was Trump’s clever way of insinuating that James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for Senate in that state, doesn’t like barbecue and is secretly gay and thus unfit for high office. It is my duty to wearily tut-tut the casual homophobia of the liberal party’s unmoving rejoinder, which amounts to “No, you’re gay.”

There’s also the fact that Trump’s approval numbers have tanked and many election forecasters predict his party will cede one or both houses of Congress to the Democrats in the midterms. The gay stuff has produced what qualifies under the circumstances as a positive press minicycle, a quaint and presumably ineffective distraction for an administration facing intense voter anger for presiding over an affordability crisis, data-center expansionism, a hot-and-cold war with Iran, and so on. But on another level it has allowed the strongman to tacitly remind the masses that in fearful times their only hope is strong men and hard-asses, a point that the novelist and gay guy Daniel Lefferts made to me in an email.

“Trump has always had an intuitive understanding of — and a talent for harnessing — the country’s libidinal energies, and what he understands (again, if only intuitively) is that the muscular, bulging, grabbable male body is the primary sex object of our moment,” Lefferts wrote. “We’re in a state of perpetual, ambient crisis — economic, political, military, technological — and when we’re in a state of crisis, when we’re afraid, we reach for and valorize the strong male body: ‘Daddy will protect me.’” Some among us long for supermen; Trump serves us one, or attempts to. (Husted is a fairly normal-looking guy, from where I’m standing.)

Trump and the White House’s social media accounts have also served us an image of Trump as Superman himself, as well as illustrations of the octogenarian with rippling bikes and trikes and a shimmering six pack. On one level these images are merely a comically vulgar contemporary rendition on the ancient practice by which political leaders circulate idealized depictions of themselves; they’re gauche, mildly amusing propaganda, in other words. But they also underscore the gaudy intensity of his manifestation of that disorder as often associated with homosexuals as with Trump: narcissism. In light of all this, the question that Trump’s recent examinations of men asks — and what this latest episode in his ongoing project of absolute linguistic freedom puts to his audiences — is: Don’t you still want me, or the man I wish I was? Isn’t there another man on the dais we all admire? Isn’t it me?

Alessi is expanding its celebrated kitchen range with this screw-themed moka pot, which takes inspiration from machinery in the company’s factory.

London-based designer Philippe Malouin worked with Italian brand Alessi to create this take on the stovetop moka pot. The piece draws inspiration from the threads of screws, with its spiral ridges and grooves referencing the twisting motion used to assemble the pot – making aesthetics part of the pot’s intuitive use. Its lower chamber is made from die-cast aluminium and its upper section features a heat-resistant thermoplastic-resin handle. Its colours are taken from the surfaces of machinery inside the Alessi factory. Adding to its appeal is the fact that it features a magnetic steel base that works on induction, gas and electric stoves.
Rediscover the joy of traditional film photography with this revamped camera design.

Kodak has provided an upgrade to the traditional plastic disposable camera with its new 35mm film model, the Snapic A1. It features a sharp three-element glass lens for crisp images, a two-zone focus (which allows you to switch quickly between close-up portraits and wide landscape shots) and a built-in flash. It also has a wide focal length that keeps scenes sharp: perfect for everything from travel and street photography to casual indoor shoots. The main appeal, though, is in its simplicity.
Free from distractions such as digital screens or phone apps, the Snapic A1’s pared-back design keeps its user in the moment and on the task.
Fiio CP13 Portable Cassette Player
Chinese brand Fiio plugs into the trend for retro audio players with this superior throwback.

Though China has long been disparaged as the home of cheaply made electronics, its new domestic makers are proving that the country has the manufacturing chops for quality audio. Analogue tapes are enjoying a resurgence in popularity (fans point to the allure of being able to “own” music) and Guangzhou-based Fiio’s CP13 Portable Cassette Player has found its way into New York’s Museum of Modern Art shop. It features old-school physical buttons, while its modern touches include USB-C charging and a 13-hour battery life.
The CP13’s 13 hours of continuous playback marks a significant improvement on the classic Sony Walkman.
Hay Outdoor Market Fire Pit
Light up your garden party or campsite with this versatile portable fireplace and cooker.

Designed in collaboration with Jasper Morrison, this fire pit brings to life the London-based product designer’s “super normal” ethos – an approach that aims to make everyday objects feel essential. Made by Danish brand Hay, its stainless-steel construction is portable, making it equally at home on a terrace or a trail. More than just an outdoor fireplace, it doubles as a cooker, thanks to its removable grill and charcoal basket.
There’s something about a fire pit that lights up our brains. Humans have evolved to associate flames with warmth, nourishment, safety and connection.

items.title: From historic emporiums to literary cafés: Our favourite bookshops in Barcelona
items.description: In a city where tourism is increasingly seen as a threat to local culture, Barcelona’s independent bookshops are thriving. Even as cinemas close and small music venues disappear, the city’s number of bookshops has climbed to 140, a 30 per cent increase since 2
items.author: Julia Webster Ayuso; Tabitha Sipp
paragraphs: In a city where tourism is increasingly seen as a threat to local culture, Barcelona’s independent bookshops are thriving. Even as cinemas close and small music venues disappear, the city’s number of bookshops has climbed to 140, a 30 per cent increase since 2008. According to the Catalan Guild of Booksellers, new openings have far surpassed closures in recent years, though some have struggled to keep their doors open.

In 2024, the threatened closure of the historic Llibreria Sant Jordi triggered weeks of public mobilisation. While it ultimately shut, it reopened a year later with a gastronomic offering. The episode underscored deeper anxieties over skyrocketing rents, the declining use of Catalan and the strain that a tourism-driven economy places on local life. And yet, while more retailers stock titles in English and other languages, Catalan-language publishing is growing too. Barcelona’s new wave of bookshops has become a valuable refuge for locals and foreigners alike.

Since launching as a small shop in Gràcia in 1962, Ona slowly built a reputation for its selection of Catalan literature. A few years ago, second-generation owner Montse Úbeda teamed up with entrepreneur Tatxo Benet to expand the business and, upon opening a 900 sq m space on Carrer Pau Claris in 2020, Ona became the world’s largest bookshop dedicated to Catalan-language books.

The boutique also stocks a selection of Catalan literature translated into 15 languages, from English to Mandarin. “We stock 1,500 references by authors who write in Catalan that have been translated into other languages,” says Ona’s director, Iolanda Batallé. “It’s painstaking work because we have to go publisher to publisher but we’re very proud of it.”

Ona has grown fivefold over the past six years, hosting book clubs, talks and live music in its café space, as well as a busy schedule of events in its vast children’s section. “Most bookshops have only about 30 per cent of books in Catalan because Spanish takes over,” says Batallé. “Shops like Ona are very important for the growth of the Catalan publishing industry.”
- Recommended novel: Ona director Iolanda Batallé is the author of I’ll Do Anything You Want, published in 2013
- Current bestsellers: Death in Spring and In Diamond Square by Mercè Rodoreda

When the longtime owner of Llibreria Sant Jordi, Josep Morales, passed away in 2024, the historic bookshop in Barcelona’s Gothic Quarter announced that it would be closing its doors. After an appeal urging book lovers to buy its remaining stock, hundreds of people turned up to purchase discounted books on art, photography, design and illustration. The event morphed into a spontaneous tribute to a local business which – with its listed 19th-century wooden shopfront – had been a fixture of the street since the early 1980s.

“The neighbours made it clear that they didn’t want yet another shop to close,” says Alba Biliotti, who now helps run the business under a new model. To the delight of locals, Llibreria Sant Jordi reopened its doors in December 2025 with most of its interiors unchanged. In the evenings after shoppers have left, the space transforms into a restaurant that hosts book clubs, literary discussions and dinners with authors. “Most people still come because it’s their local bookshop,” says Billiotti. “But now it has two different atmospheres. Some people come for dinner and walk out with a book, while others come to buy a book and end up staying for a drink.”
- On the menu: Piquillo peppers stuffed with cod brandade and caramelised foie with Kalamata olives and fig jam
- Current bestseller: The Little Frog’s Guide to Self-Care by Maybell Eequay

In 1980, four young women opened the doors of Laie on Barcelona’s Carrer de Pau Claris without much fanfare. “Back then it wasn’t customary to announce the opening of a bookshop; it wasn’t considered particularly newsworthy,” co-founder Conxita Guixà wrote for the shop’s 40th anniversary in 2020. “Perhaps three or four people came in during the first few hours.” Four decades later, Laie runs 35 outposts all over Spain, from Santiago de Compostela to Palma de Mallorca.

Fresh out of university, co-founders Conxita Guixà and Montse Moragas wanted to create a space dedicated to the humanities and critical thinking. It quickly became a meeting point for the city’s intellectuals, who would hide their favourite books in the wrong sections so that they could purchase them later. In the 1990s, a café and restaurant opened on the first floor. On any given day, you can still spot journalists, authors, playwrights and politicians conducting interviews or discussing book deals over a plate of ham croquetas or fish soup. “Gustavo Petro, the president of Colombia, walked in the other day and I had to act normal,” says literary director Damià Gallardo. “Laie has become a nerve centre of Barcelona’s culture; people have made it their own.”
- First book ever sold: An anthology by the Greek poet Giorgos Seferis
- Current bestseller: La Bola by Daniel Verdú, which was recently presented at the bookshop
- Recommended novel by Damià Gallardo: What I Loved by Siri Hustvedt

Huygens, a publisher dedicated to academic and educational titles, was planning to open its first bookshop in April 2020 when the coronavirus pandemic hit. When it finally opened months later, it was welcomed by locals who had rediscovered the pleasure of reading during Spain’s strict lockdowns. Founded by editor Mariana Sarrias and law professor Víctor M. Sánchez, Llibreria Byron – named after the British poet – opened with a café, quiet reading nooks and a space for events, designed with the ambition of giving neighbourhood residents a place to reconnect. “We decided to call it a bookshop but right from the start, we wanted it to be more than that: a place where culture is brought to life, not just sold in the form of books,” says Sarrias.

Byron has a large children’s and young-adult section, and a packed calendar of community events. Every Friday a group of neighbours from El Raval gathers for a philosophical coffee hour to debate a variety of questions from the dangers of consumerism to the role of uncertainty in daily life. These discussions often take place around a walnut-panelled fireplace that Sarrias found in an antiques shop and had restored before placing it at the heart of the shop. Though it’s powered by electricity, it still fulfils its intended purpose: to create a cosy, welcoming atmosphere for people to get lost in a book. In the evenings, Byron makes space for music too. The café’s grand piano is used for everything from jazz performances to renditions of Puccini’s Madama Butterfly.
- Recommended book: A Man Asleep by Georges Perec
- Poetry book-club pick: Hardly Creatures: Poems by Rob Colgate
- Bestselling Spanish-language book: Insular by Franco Chiaravalloti

Llibreria Finestres (Catalan for “windows”) opened in 2021 inside a modernist building by architect Enric Sagnier. Just a few steps from Passeig de Gràcia, the shop was designed by Quintana Partners and is furnished with carpets, sofas, well-lit reading nooks and a fireplace. The retailer describes itself as “a bookshop for reading”, where patrons are invited to curl up with a book inside or linger on the terrace with a glass of vermut.

A second location opened shortly after the first, dedicating its venue to comic books as well as publications on illustration and art. Thanks to its success, the business’s expansion has continued: another outpost arrived in the coastal town of Palamós last summer and in May, Finestres Palestina, an outlet devoted to Palestinian culture and literature, opened in the Gràcia neighbourhood. Designed by Valencia-based Palestinian architect Malek Murad Mateu, the latest addition features bright green sculptural bookshelves, hand-woven rugs and an indoor fountain inlaid with a mosaic map of Palestine.

Run by the Finestres Foundation, the bookshop is also behind several literary awards and writers’ residencies. Its impressively multilingual selection includes titles in English, French, Italian, German, Portuguese, Galician and Basque, alongside Spanish and Catalan.
- Phones off: The poor signal inside the shop serves as an unexpected advantage, stopping notifications and incoming calls from interrupting your browsing session
- A line from its foundational manifesto: “We know that there are a lot of bookshops in the city. We also noticed that there are even more readers than bookshops.”

After several bookshops in Catalonia closed following the 2008 financial crisis, journalist and writer Isabel Sucunza and historian Abel Cutillas teamed up in 2014 to open a space to showcase the work of new small publishing houses. Named after Catalan writer Pere Calders, who lived in the Sant Antoni neighbourhood in his later years, Llibreria Calders occupies a former button factory in a small alley. It has gathered a loyal following for prioritising local authors over bestsellers. “At the time there were very few independent bookshops in Barcelona,” says Sucunza. “There also wasn’t a single one named after an author.”

The space resembles a vast wine cellar, with dark bookcases set against bare stone walls. Customers seek it out for its well-stocked poetry section, as well as its selection of titles on theatre and dramatic theory. “Poetry wasn’t so central to the bookshop at first but as soon as we started hosting recitals, we noticed that there was a huge demand for it,” says Sucunza. Readers can continue to pay homage to one of Catalonia’s most famed writers at the nearby bar, Calders, which serves “dishes of exile” inspired by the author’s banishment to Mexico after the Spanish Civil War.
- Books recently presented at the bookshop: A new Catalan translation of Homer’s Odyssey by Pau Sabaté
- All-time favourite book: The Day of the Watusi by Francisco Casavella, a coming-of-age novel about Barcelona from the Spanish Transition to the eve of the 1992 Olympic Games
- Number of titles in stock: Between 10,000 and 12,000

A bookshop that specialises in art publications occupies a former shoe boutique on the corner of a 19th-century building in Sant Antoni. When the space became available in 2020, it caught the eye of Lucía Bonet and Luis Cerveró, who had long dreamt of opening a dedicated outpost of their publishing house, Terranova.

With the help of furniture design studio Owl, the pair restored the modernist listed building’s original features, including its tall ceilings and white wooden floorboards. The original bookshelves, which once stored shoe boxes, returned to their olive-green colour, while a custom-made central island that sits in the centre of the space was painted the same bright red as the Vico Magistretti Carimate chairs scattered throughout.

The shop features Terranova’s design-focused publications, alongside a broader selection of titles on art, fashion and design. Highlights include Servilletas, a book by photographer Felipe Hernández on napkins gathered from bars across Spain, and Sofia Coppola’s visual history of Chanel’s haute-couture designs.

Rather than sorting books by category, the duo has decided to arrange them randomly for customers to stumble upon as they browse. The shop hosts monthly exhibitions and houses a collection of rare books, which are available to view by appointment.
- Recent exhibitions: Madrid-based photographer Jesús Umbría Brito’s Familia Real, a series focusing on Spanish youth and counterculture
- Period covered by its rare-book collection: More than seven decades, from the 1950s to the present
- Year that publishing house Terranova was founded: 2014

With so many visitors regularly passing through the city, it’s perhaps not surprising that Barcelona is home to Europe’s biggest travel specialist bookshops. In 1979, Pep Bernadas founded Altaïr – named after one of the brightest stars in the night sky – in a small space in Barcelona’s El Raval neighbourhood, where he began to collect guidebooks. It quickly outgrew that first venue and, for the past 20 years, has occupied a vast space spanning three floors in the Eixample, where globetrotters can peruse an unparalleled selection of maps, travel guides and titles that cover every corner of the world. “The only country that we haven’t been able to get any books on is San Marino,” says Altaïr’s director, Helena Bernadas.

Books are organised by country in order of their proximity to Spain, from an extensive selection of publications on Barcelona all the way to a section on Oceania downstairs. Since 1992 the business has also housed a travel agency and an online magazine of the same name, both of which are centred on a “more anthropological than touristic” approach to travel. It is the bookshop, however, that plays the most important role in preparing for any trip. “We like to put together a curated reading list for our customers that includes guides but also fiction or poetry,” says Bernadas. “There are a million different ways to engage with Japanese culture, for example, so we try to find the titles that best reflect our customers’ specific interests.”
- Recommended book: The Innocent Anthropologist by Nigel Barley
- Number of maps in stock: 11,000
- Number of guidebooks in stock: 16,000

During his teenage years, Carles Armengol helped his parents’ business by serving tables at their restaurant in L’Hospitalet de Llobregat. When the establishment eventually closed in 2012 after 80 years in the family, Armengol began to write. His debut book, Collado: La maldición de una casa de comidas (Collado: The Curse of a Diner), was published in 2022 and explores his complicated feelings about the restaurant industry.

Today Armengol has brought his two passions – food and literature – into a single space. After he presented his novel at +Bernat, the bookshop’s owner, Montse Serrano, offered him the opportunity to open a café inside the shop. Today +Bernat describes itself as a place where “literature feeds you”. Walls lined with the latest releases surround tables where Armengol serves a simple lunch menu of classic Catalan dishes, such as fideu casserole or chickpea stew with calamari. He spends the rest of the day assembling sandwiches named after classics made with local produce, from Crime and Punishment (sobressada and Minorcan cheese, roast aubergine and honey) to Il Gattopardo (mortadella from Bologna with cashew pesto, scamorza and spinach). “A café and a bookshop are destined to work well together,” says Fernando Pelayo, who runs the bookshop while Armengol tends the bar. “They make each other stand out.”
- Recommended book: Beginning, Middle, End by Valeria Luiselli
- Bestselling sandwich: The Bikini (Barcelona’s iconic grilled ham-and-cheese sandwich). At +Bernat it is named Collado, after Armengol’s book
- Year that the bookshop first opened: 1978

items.description: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute
paragraphs: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute for Play, explains to us on page 154. Throughout the issue, we explore pathways to play, including expert advice on rediscovering your own play type as a busy adult and, failing that, five games devised and demonstrated by artist Carsten Höller for those who don’t know where to begin.

In a study of architects, psychologist Donald MacKinnon found that those considered most creative by their peers were often those who knew how to play; this is certainly true of John Outram, whose over-the-top masterpiece, Sphinx Hill, we visit on page 70. Painters play with color and line—a type of immersive flow state our fashion editorial explores on page 60. And musicians improvise and experiment, a process familiar to the band Balming Tiger (interviewed on page 78), whose alternative approach to K-pop subverts the genre’s perfectly synchronized image.

items.title: Balming Tiger - Kinfolk
items.description: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
paragraphs: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
- Hair & Makeup Mahito Ohtani

My Zoom interview with Balming Tiger is chaotic. Five of the eleven members are on the call, each in a different location in Seoul. Omega Sapien is at a salon, dyeing his hair green for a music video. Leesuho is munching on a snack with a soda. Unsinkable is strumming a guitar, on mute. bj wnjn is lying in bed in sweatpants. Mudd the Student sits calmly, his long wavy hair dyed like a lion’s mane. There are multiple conversations all happening at once as we wait for the other members, some of whom never show up.

When the interview starts, however, the group is focused and attentive. A self-described “alternative K-pop group” from South Korea, Balming Tiger is composed of two women and nine men. They’ve been described by critics and fans as pioneering, experimental, an artist collective beyond music and, last but not least, “a group of hairstyles that elderly Koreans would definitely hate,” a running joke among fans online. In their two studio albums and a debut mixtape, released in 2018, they sing about alienation, absurdist humor, friendship and love, pigeons and frogs.
“We want Balming Tiger to be its own genre,” says Omega Sapien, a rapper and singer-songwriter, holding up the phone as his hair, now fluorescent green, is being rinsed out in the sink.

Ironically, Balming Tiger’s alternative identity depends on its proximity to South Korea’s best-known cultural export. K-pop, literally Korean popular music, is itself less of a distinctive genre than a cultural phenomenon. Within South Korea, it can refer to a wide variety of styles including ballads, EDM and hip-hop. Abroad, K-pop most often means idols: entertainers whose music and image are strictly produced by massive entertainment conglomerates, such as mega-groups like BTS and Blackpink, or soloists such as Somi and G-Dragon. However you define it, K-pop is a glittering symbol of Korean soft power. The stratospheric success of different Korean musicians in the past decade—especially BTS on the US charts—has catapulted K-pop into a household name everywhere.
“Honestly, we don’t really think about what genre we are, other than during interviews,” says Leesuho, one of Balming Tiger’s producers and video directors.

True as that may be, the label they have chosen—alternative K-pop—is a strategic choice, devised by the group’s founder and creative director, San Yawn. With K-pop’s international popularity, Balming Tiger has smartly positioned themselves as adjacent to something familiar to the global audience—giving themselves a wide playground to try anything and everything.

“It’s always more fun when the possibilities are open,” San Yawn later explains over email. “Whatever we are now won’t be ‘the final version’ of us. We have no idea what we’ll be in the future, but we want to continue to express the little joys of the world in our own language.”

It’s true that the structure of Balming Tiger is wildly different from a conventional K-pop idol act. Idols are usually conceptually defined by an agency, with clear roles differentiating members, for example “lead vocalist” or “lead dancer.” Idol wannabes train, sometimes for years, to audition for a role. Once the group is formed, the performers are the faces of a much larger and more intricate corporate structure.

There were no trainees in Balming Tiger. And no auditions—think more “Wanna join?” conversations at waffle houses and barbecue joints. Nor are all of Balming Tiger’s members performers—their 11 members include producers, photographers, music video directors, A&R managers and DJs. Some faces are more familiar, like those who sing, rap and dance in the music videos (usually Omega Sapien, bj wnjn, Mudd the Student and Sogumm, with cameos by others), but behind the scenes, everything is more collaborative and collective.

Balming Tiger can be seen as less a band with a signature sound than a creative universe, a rainforest of different species colliding and coexisting with each other. From their critically acclaimed debut mixtape, Homie304, to their first studio album in 2023, January Never Dies, to the 2026 album, Gongbu, Balming Tiger’s music defies classification—as does their creative direction. Their videos embrace Hong Kong noir (“SOS”), a ’90s boy band parody (“Big Butt”), and the industrial-era alleyways of the Euljiro neighborhood in Seoul (“Sexy Nukim,” featuring BTS member RM). Their sounds traverse old Korean pop, EDM, psychedelic rock and—of course—hip-hop, many of the members’ first love and forays into music.
“We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

The origins of Balming Tiger can be traced to Itaewon, one of the most culturally diverse neighborhoods in Seoul. It’s a place where the city’s only mosque towers over a hill, next to mom-and-pop stores and cockroach-filled villas, the US military base and ritzy alleyways that are home to the Samsung family and BTS members.

“Balming Tiger is basically a meeting of people that are full of holes,” San Yawn once said on the Korean talk show Moneygraphy. These “holes”—loneliness, for instance, and the desire to fill them through music and art—were what brought together this cacophonous collective through a random series of events starting in 2017, when San Yawn began looking for a crew.

They met at San Yawn’s home in Itaewon and spent much of their time together at Trans 201, on the second floor of a run-down villa in an area popularly known as Transgender Hill. The members started connecting in various ways: through friends of friends, an Instagram message, a chance listening to a future member’s SoundCloud account. “Trans 201 was Omega Sapien and bj wnjn’s house,” recalls Mudd the Student. “The space was very damp and full of dark energy.”

“After a heavy rain, the ceiling in my room was bulging with water, like a giant pimple,” Omega Sapien adds. “We had horrible mold problems. bj wnjn and I split the rent, which was like 600,000 won [approximately $400], and I didn’t even have that money, so my older sister helped pay half of my 300,000. It really was an awful time.”

“Not for me,” says bj wnjn, a vocalist, singer-songwriter and producer. “That space is one of the most memorable moments of my youth. Even with the cockroaches and all that noise from the clubs outside, there was a joy particular to that time.”

Memories like this are specific to Balming Tiger, to Seoul, and permeate their art in ways that can’t be manufactured. The evolving members remain consistently curious about their own experiences and the world around them. There have been some member changes over the years, including the exit of Byung Un, a beloved front man in the early years. But the joy—and the DNA—from that early, formative period is still alive, holding everyone together 10 years later. “There’s a childlike attitude that we never lost as a group,” Sogumm, a singer-songwriter and vocalist, says in an email. “A simplicity that feels honest.”

Often, Balming Tiger’s childlike experiments feel much deeper than mere fun and play, resonating like a sharp resistance against the norms imposed by others. Sometimes this critique feels particularly Korean—like in the 2023 music video of “Kamehameha,” where exhausted office workers are forced to drink with their superiors at a hoesik, an after-work company gathering notorious for heavy alcohol consumption. And at other times it feels fantastically delocalized, like in “UP!” where a cashier at a mega supermarket climbs up the mountain of objects he must clear, reaching for the sky.

“It’s different for me,” says Omega Sapien, who grew up in Korea, China, Japan and the US. “I’m not trying to be rebellious. But I do like provoking a sense of discomfort in others. I like creating differences of opinion through what we do.”

“I’m less interested in making others uncomfortable than in creating a sense of wonder,” says Mudd the Student, who is from Busan, down south. “I love art that makes me feel things for the first time. I suppose that can sometimes make people uncomfortable.”

Despite their almost tongue-in-cheek label as alternative K-pop, Balming Tiger is grateful to the K-pop industry for opening doors for other Korean musicians. The group has performed at major music festivals including SXSW in the US, Primavera Sound in Spain and Fuji Rock Festival in Japan. Their creative orbit is similarly wide-ranging: they’ve collaborated with artists including Japanese girl group ATARASHII GAKKO! and RM of BTS, while independently creating content celebrating figures they admire, such as Korean artist Lee Bul and Thai filmmaker Apichatpong Weerasethakul. Their music video with RM, “Sexy Nukim,” remains Balming Tiger’s most viewed, with 20 million views.

“People often think of idols as these puppets, who only do what they’re told,” says Omega Sapien. “But creative languages within the idol industry are changing too. I really love groups like CORTIS. I think their work is raw and fantastic.”

“I’m really interested in girl groups,” says Unsinkable, a producer and DJ. “These days we see groups that are more like crews, with more creative independence from their company. I sometimes wonder if new idol acts are inspired by what we do.”

In Gongbu, Balming Tiger explores themes of Korean and Asian identity. The single “Home” is absurdist and nostalgic, evoking Korean folk music while mixing synthesizers, rap and ritualistic chants. The music video is black and white, reminiscent of a Park Chan-wook film or a Lee Gap-chul photo. It’s inspired by the architecture of Kim Chung-up and the traditional marriage ritual hamjinabi.

“What does it mean to be Korean? To be Asian? When we were younger, we looked up to American hip-hop,” says Omega Sapien. “I wanted to be like J. Cole. But now I see that that’s his thing. We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

items.title: Taking Play Seriously - Kinfolk
items.description: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
paragraphs: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
A conversation with the National Institute for Play.

In 1966, psychiatrist Dr. Stuart Brown was appointed by the governor of Texas to investigate a mass shooting at the state university—at the time the deadliest in American history. Brown realized there could be a connection between the gunman’s actions and his oppressive childhood, which had been dominated by his controlling father. He would go on to spend the following decades showing that the need for play is biologically hardwired into the brain stem—the part of the nervous system that governs our essential functions like breathing and heart rate.

“When we’re deprived of play, it can be similar to being deprived of sleep and nutrition and connection—the things that fundamentally make us human,” explains Mia Sundstrom, Dr. Brown’s granddaughter and the CEO of the National Institute for Play—a nonprofit organization Brown established in 1994 to champion play as a public health necessity. “I grew up through play,” she says, “and have firsthand seen the benefits of it.”
Appointed to her role earlier this year, her mission at the institute is to show “how people can incorporate play into their lives to promote cognitive, social, emotional and physical health.”
Ellen Peirson-Hagger: Why is play important?

Mia Sundstrom: Here’s the paradox—and it’s why it’s so difficult to convince people that play matters: One of the core definitions of play is that it’s purposeless, that it’s not done for any specific outcome. Yet there’s a ton of purpose in the outcomes we get. We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.
EPH: What are the benefits of play?

MS: When we are in a state of play, it boosts the production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which is the neuroplasticity protein that helps to create new neural connections and strengthen existing pathways. Play also calms down our amygdala—our emotional processing center—meaning it takes us out of a stress response, which is great for emotional regulation. And in the case of social play, our mirror neurons—which light up when we observe the motor activity of someone else—allow us to develop the basic foundation of attunement, which is the first seedling of connection with another human being, and which in time leads to trust, to community, to belonging. So on a neurobiological level, play promotes our cognitive health, our emotional resilience and our social competence.

Physical play is obviously good for us: Exercise is healthy, whether we enjoy it or not. But we’re a lot more likely to sustain it when it’s something we enjoy, so we might as well try and find a form of physical exercise that feels like play.
EPH: If we don’t play, are those things lost?

MS: When we’re play-deprived, there can be really severe consequences. It can lead to cognitive rigidity, which is when you can’t think outside the box and solve problems creatively. We have seen that a lack of play can lead to susceptibility for anxiety and depression, and toward addictive behaviors, because we try to find those things that we need from play in other forms—alcohol, drugs, social media, sugar—all these things that offer short-term relief rather than long-term benefit.

And then there’s social incompetence: As my grandpa’s research showed, when we don’t play it’s hard to build tolerance and empathy for each other because we miss that fundamental level of attunement. This leads to diminished well-being.
EPH: How does our need for play change as we become adults?

MS: There’s a misconception that it has to change like crazy, that what you do as a kid is not what you should do as an adult. But we don’t ever lose the desire to play, we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways. For example, as you go through grade school, the playgrounds change—there is no longer the opportunity to go down a slide at recess—and then all of a sudden you forget that you love to do that, and you might never do it again.

I don’t think adults should stop swinging, or playing at parks, or jumping on a trampoline in the backyard. We often think that we outgrow these things, but we really shouldn’t. Lego is a breaker of this rule: Lego adult sets are selling so well right now because of their connection to nostalgia and childhood. And what’s great about moving from childhood to adulthood is that the possibilities to play open up significantly: Instead of exploring your backyard with a stick and turning your cardboard box into a rocket ship, you have access to a car and a plane.
EPH: Is play different to different people?

MS: Everyone is born with a deep natural predilection for play, but that looks different for each of us. There are people who love to make things—art, music, building, tinkering with objects. There are people who love to dream or get lost in a book or movie and create imaginary worlds in their mind. There are people who love to compete, who play through mastering. There are people who love to organize—collecting new things, arranging social gatherings, even cleaning out a junk drawer. These are all different play styles, and one of the greatest gifts you can give a child is to notice what those natural tendencies are and help nourish them.
EPH: Do you think we need to take a broader view of what play is or can be?

MS: Yes! Most of the time, when I ask people “What is play to you?” they say “a board game” or “my kid’s sport.” We have confined play to this really narrow scope, when actually play is any activity that brings us into the play state, which is an altered state of being, almost dreamlike, that takes us out of the usual experience of time and space and evokes positive emotions like joy and awe. It is intrinsically motivated, not coerced, so it’s done for its own sake, and it’s self-reinforcing, so the benefits of a play state last beyond the time we’re playing.

Any activity that meets that criteria can be play—that could mean coding for someone who loves to code, or cooking for someone who loves to cook. Heck, that could even be cleaning if you put on a great song and you turn your broom into a microphone.
EPH: Why is society so resistant to play?

MS: Well, the psychologist and play researcher Peter Gray would answer by taking us back to the 16th century, when the Protestant Reformation taught us to believe in the moral virtue of work and that play, by contrast, is the breeding ground of sin. And then you throw capitalism into the mix which calls for more production, more consumption: that’s what defines success in the capitalist dream, right? Then you add in the compounding effects of automation and AI. Of course play isn’t celebrated in a world that prioritizes those things.
EPH: Has digitization played a role?

MS: We can’t prove causation, but our screens do seem to be factor in why we’re not playing. Scrolling on your screen disguises itself as play because you lose track of time, and it feels fun in the moment. But it has long-term detriments in terms of our attention span and our loneliness. If we’re scrolling, we’re not connecting with each other on a human level.
EPH: What kind of society would we have if we all played more?

MS: Play dissolves our differences and reminds us of what we have in common. Our world is so polarized, but play brings us together and is one of the most powerful ways to create a better society. Play lowers our inhibitions—I want to shout that from the rooftops. If you disagree with someone and go play with them, you’ll see the humanity in one other. It can also help combat the trends that we’re talking so much about right now—loneliness, disengagement, burnout—because play brings us back to that deep intrinsic drive to do something for a sustained period of time that makes the time pass more quickly.
EPH: What should adults do to help recover their love of play?

MS: We help adults rediscover their natural spark—their thing that makes them most curious and fully alive—and then think about small ways to reintegrate that into their life. The first step is to think back to your earliest memory of play: What was that thing you loved to do before the world told you who to be? Second, based on that, what do you love to do now—is there something that you’ve forgotten about and haven’t done for ages? Third, nothing ever works when we try to create massive changes all at once. So we say that 30 seconds is enough. See if you can add a burst of play into your morning or evening routine, based on those two things you reflected on. What’s great about play is that it’s self-reinforcing, so as soon as you give yourself that permission, it will keep you coming back for more.
“We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.”

items.title: Kyle Kuzma - Kinfolk
items.description: The NBA forward is playing the long game.
paragraphs: The NBA forward is playing the long game.

Kyle Kuzma is enjoying himself. He’s about to catch a flight for the south of France, where he’ll be attending the Cannes Film Festival, and is midway through the long, complex and, for him, extremely pleasurable process, of picking out what to wear. “If I’m going somewhere in three days, I may already be in my closet, just trying on clothes, seeing what I want to wear, thinking about what type of events I’m going to,” he says over a video call from his home in Miami. He’s planning ahead for the films, parties and red carpet events.

If a lot of this sounds like fun, Kuzma thinks so too. “Everything is play—unless, you know, it’s your profession,” he says. This is the challenge because Kuzma’s job is, after all, a form of play. He is in his 10th year in the NBA. A first-round draft pick in 2017, he’s currently a power forward for the Milwaukee Bucks; in 2020 he won the NBA national championship with the Los Angeles Lakers in only his third year in the league.
