items.title: Exclusive: Lisa Rinna's No. 1 Holiday Party Survival Tip: "I Don't Say Goodbye"
items.description: Lisa Rinna’s Unapologetic Guide To Surviving Holiday Party Season
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: Lisa Rinna’s Unapologetic Guide To Surviving Holiday Party Season
The Bravo legend is serving up her best winter style tips — with a side of exit strategy.
This holiday season, Lisa Rinna is trading Beverly Hills for Manhattan. And she’s *very* excited. “It’s going to be our first Christmas in New York,” she gushes over Zoom.

With a new ZIP code comes a whole new set of holiday plans, which so far include watching the Thanksgiving Day parade from her apartment and leaning into her signature main-character dressing — but for the winter chill. “You feel more elevated here for Christmas than you do on the West Coast. We have 80-degree Christmases in L.A.,” says the Real Housewives of Beverly Hills alum, who’s tapped to star in the upcoming Off-Broadway revival of Neil Simon’s Rumors from Jan. 9 through Feb. 28. “New York just makes you want to up the ante.”

Rinna is already ahead of schedule. In her new campaign for Express, “Holiday, Hamlin Style,” launching today, she test-drives festive classics like high-shine sequins, glamorous Santa-red gowns, and cozy knits. The shoot was a full family affair, featuring her husband, Harry Hamlin; daughter Delilah Belle Hamlin; and Delilah’s boyfriend, Mick Maio. “To get to work with your family, pinch me,” she says of the shoot. She’s especially thrilled about sharing the lens with her partner: “A couple of weeks ago, I was like, ‘We need to make Harry into a supermodel now.’ Everybody else is. I literally put that out in the universe.”

Naturally, working alongside her loved ones sparked a little holiday nostalgia. The project took her back to her own traditions, particularly matching with her family in Christmas sweaters. (As true Bravo fans know, Rinna loves a matching moment — whether they’re in red flannel pajamas or Santa hats.) It even inspired a possible outfit idea for this year.

Ahead, the reality-TV icon shares her one foolproof holiday ’fit, her secret to tricking everyone into matching, and how to navigate awkward party small talk (and when to deploy the perfect Irish exit).
How To Feel Festive In 2 Seconds

Holiday dressing practically comes with its own maximalist dress code — think sequins; velvets; bows; and enough reds, greens, and metallic golds to make you look like you’re twinning with the tree. But according to Rinna, getting into the holiday spirit doesn’t require a head-to-toe disco ball look. All it takes is a cozy knit to pull off an instant seasonal vibe shift.

“When I was with Delilah, we were wearing the sweaters — laughing and dancing around,” she says of her favorite piece from the campaign. “You put on a Christmas sweater — a cute one — and it makes you feel like Christmas.”
How To Get Your Entire Crew To Match

With a household full of working models — daughters Amelia and Delilah, plus husband Harry — getting everyone to agree on a single style aesthetic can be a challenge. But individual tastes go out the window in December.

“Because [the girls are] three years apart, I never matched them except for Christmas,” says Rinna, adding, “As long as it’s not really a really, really bad Christmas sweater — which is a funny idea actually now that I think about it — they’ll pretty much wear whatever I bring to the table.”
How To Guarantee A Major Style Moment

Finding a bold way to make a statement in the winter is easy. But if she had to pick her go-to festive uniform, it would be a sharp pantsuit. “I love a red suit, a green suit, a holiday-inspired gold suit,” she says. Her only rule? Make sure it fits right. “If it’s tailored properly, everybody looks great in it,” she promises.

On the flip side, there is one style choice she’d encourage everyone to ditch this season. “Unless it’s soft and cozy, anything that’s an uncomfortable fabric, we can retire it,” she says. Consider this your permission to permanently shelf any scratchy sequins or stiff velvets.
How To Trust Your Own Fashion Instincts

While Rinna is a legendary tastemaker, she’s no longer the only fashionista in the family. To say her daughters have an impact on her wardrobe would be an understatement. “A thousand bajillion percent,” she says of how much they inspire her.

Because her daughters have completely different styles — Delilah loves vintage, shopping for bold patterns and jewelry at flea markets; Amelia prefers classic, opting for more tomboyish choices and very few prints and accessories — Rinna has plenty of fresh mood board ideas to draw from.

But there’s a difference between borrowing ideas from her kids and asking them for validation. When it’s time to actually pull together a look, she shuts out the noise and trusts her own gut (and her stylist’s expertise). “I don’t ever show anybody [my outfits],” Rinna says. “I don’t think you need anybody’s opinion.”
How To Master The Party Exit Strategy

Between the endless small talk and the risk of bumping into a frenemy, holiday parties can be a lot. Luckily, Rinna has a straightforward approach to getting through them. Her first rule is basic: Know when to leave. And when you’re ready, you just... go. “I don’t say goodbye,” she says. “I just slip out.”
How To Survive The Social Drama

And if you bump into someone wearing the exact same ’fit? Embrace it. “I like to accidentally match with somebody else. I think that’s fun,” she says. What she won’t do, though, is suffer through an uncomfortable conversation just for the sake of being polite. She’d rather skip out on an event entirely than sit there faking niceties.
She also has one major rule passed down to her daughters: Keep it cute. “Don’t drink too much. Ever,” she explains. “Don’t get sloppy. Don’t get messy.”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Here’s Your November Horoscope
items.description: November opens in the deep end. The new moon rises in uncompromising Scorpio on Nov. 9. Prepare to get real about what you want. What are you finally ready to release in order to get it? This isn’t the time for half-measures or surface-level intentions. The ch
items.author: Alexandria Lettman
paragraphs: November opens in the deep end. The new moon rises in uncompromising Scorpio on Nov. 9. Prepare to get real about what you want. What are you finally ready to release in order to get it? This isn’t the time for half-measures or surface-level intentions. The choices you make now carry a lasting weight, so consider them carefully.
The fog finally lifts on Nov. 13, when Mercury retrograde ends in Scorpio. It may feel easier to pick up the thread of a conversation, decision, or idea you have been circling since late October.

The next day, Venus follows suit when it stations direct in Libra. The culmination of this retrograde is the exhale you’ve been waiting for. Notice what has changed about what you are willing to give and receive to sustain a relationship.

After all of Scorpio season’s intensity, the sun’s ingress into Sagittarius on Nov. 22 swings open a window and lets the light back in. Adventure and hope are back on the table. Look forward and aim high.

Electric energy buzzes around the full moon in Gemini on Nov. 24. Uranus, the planet of innovation and change, links up with the bright supermoon. A breakthrough could be on the horizon, the kind that leads you to finally share what’s on your mind. However, one thing remains uncertain: how other people will respond. Don’t let this stop you from speaking your truth.

When motivated Mars enters precise Virgo on Nov. 25, effort, discipline, and methodical action beat impulsivity. The goals that have been gaining momentum now require focus and a plan of execution. Roll up your sleeves and dive into the real, productive work — then relax the next day with some turkey and cranberry sauce.
Happy birthday, Sagittarius!

Good news, Aries! The words you couldn’t find in October may spring to mind with clarity this month. That conversation you’ve been dreading could turn out to be the one that actually frees you. Don’t be afraid to revisit a situation that has tested your honesty, trust, and ability to be vulnerable.

Whether you are hashing out a shared financial burden or getting intimate with a partner, you could walk into Sagittarius season (beginning on Nov. 22) feeling optimistic about what lies ahead. Rather than letting your thoughts fester, speak up in the moment. Luck is on your side.

All relationships have ups and downs, but they shouldn’t feel permanently exhausting. After the intimate Scorpio new moon on Nov. 9, you may have a clearer idea of what’s worth fighting for. How can you turn over a new leaf?

By mid-month, complicated issues at work can be resolved through stronger collaboration. Remember your worth and think twice before you pick up other people’s responsibilities again. In late November, a breakthrough might inspire you to reallocate your time, energy, money, and resources. This is your green light to invest in your creative side hustle or a promising romantic connection.

For you, the whole month is building toward the full moon in your sign on Nov. 24. But first, you should lay the groundwork. In early November, you need to adjust your priorities. Cut out whatever’s been draining your energy, and focus on habits and activities that fill your cup.
An old passion project or romantic connection could find its worth again ahead of Sagittarius season (beginning on Nov. 22). If you feel hopeful, dive in.

Finally, the full moon brings surprising clarity on what needs to change within in order for you to manifest the life you really want. Don’t underestimate what can click into place when you let go. Only worry about what you can control.

Don’t be surprised when the passion, connection, and spark you thought was lost makes a dramatic return. The Scorpio new moon on Nov. 9 creates space for you to get clear on your values, hidden desires, and what will truly make you happy. This kind of self-reflection could be a powerful magnet for love.

However, don’t expect to figure out all the answers at once. Clarity will come gradually and certain outcomes will remain uncertain. On Nov. 24, try not to worry about the missing pieces when the full moon lights up your psychological sector. Choose your next step and see it through.

Unresolved feelings have been churning in the background, creating a moody start to the month. However, when you are committed to building bridges — not burning them — you may finally make progress. Lead with honesty and speak with care.

The second half of the month revives the fire in your social life, but concerns about your budget and schedule could hinder your ability to live in the moment. Don’t be irresponsible, but stay as flexible as possible. Your friendships are worth their weight in gold.

Confusion turns into clarity this month. Mark your calendar for Nov. 13, when Mercury retrograde switches gears, alleviating the pressure you feel to dissect the subliminal meaning of every text or email. In order to get conversations moving again, you don’t necessarily need to find the perfect words for expressing yourself. Start by recognizing that your voice has value, even if others disagree with your perspective.

Around mid-month, your focus shifts toward pursuing your life’s purpose. On Nov. 25, calculating Mars enters your sign, boosting your energy, discipline, and drive. Forge your own way rather than adhering to other people’s standards. Your journey is yours alone.

Venus, your ruling planet, is in retrograde from Oct. 3 - Nov. 14. Your attention has been focused on the hard work of examining who you are, what you want, and whether you’re willing to ask for it. However, don’t expect immediate progress once this phase wraps up. Acknowledge where self-doubt still keeps you stuck.

A deep hunger for meaningful conversation kicks in during the second half of the month. Whether you engage in thoughtful debates, pick up a new book, or listen to a podcast that blows your mind, prepare for your outlook to radically change — or at least you’ll plant new seeds.

November opens with a deep personal reset. The new moon rises in your sign on Nov. 9, setting the stage for new goals, intentions, and ideas around how you want to show up in the world. You can reinvent yourself at any moment, even on a random Wednesday, if you’re tired of holding back.

Your self-awareness sharpens on Nov. 13. Mercury travels forward in your sign, dissolving the intense air of mystery you’ve been projecting that’s kept some people at arm’s length. If you are emerging from an extended period of solitude, be wary of rushing into trust, consistency, and comfort. Nothing worth having is built overnight. People will treat you more warmly if you act with confidence and generosity.
Sagittarius (Nov. 21-Dec. 20)
You’ve been bravely confronting your fears for months, and you’ve finally earned a break. Relax and release the negativity!

The real shift comes on Nov. 22, when the sun reinvigorates your sign. Suddenly, you’re back to your best self. You don’t need to force optimism, and adventures seem to be looking for you, not the other way around. Pursue what makes you feel alive. That said, your partner may ask where they fit into your solo exploration.
If relationships don’t steal your focus at the end of the month, your career might take to the spotlight. Move with a plan.
Capricorn (Dec. 21-Jan. 18)

Any uncertainty surrounding your career or public image will resolve in the first two weeks of the month. A relationship with a boss or mentor may move in a positive new direction, or you might find yourself getting involved with a community that shares your values. Either way, welcome the support!

As a hard-working Capricorn, you struggle to accept that rest can be productive. Everyone needs to recharge, and when Sagittarius season begins on Nov. 22, it’s your turn. Use introspection as a healing practice. As a result of your quiet time, you may be inspired to make a change in your lifestyle. Once your energy returns, set things into motion as soon as possible.
Aquarius (Jan. 19-Feb. 17)

It’s difficult to plan your life when you are questioning the very principles that have long underpinned your definition of success. Give yourself grace for the slow progress made this autumn. You may be stumbling toward something more valuable than you realize: a renewed sense of passion and purpose. Once Mercury and Venus station direct on Nov. 13 and 14, follow your heart with unwavering loyalty. Share your inspiration and the ideas that have motivated you with your friends or followers.

If you’re single or casually dating, a sudden peak in your love life could coincide with the flirtatious Gemini full moon on Nov. 24. Just keep in mind that you are in an important season of building. Enjoy what feels light and playful, but be cautious of entering a serious commitment until you are more certain of what you are able to invest.

If a new course of study or philosophical idea calls your name, go all in. You may discover a belief or intellectual field that resonates with where you are now rather than who you used to be. Before you hand over your credit card, however, wait for the hazy retrograde energy to settle around Nov. 14.

If you are itching for a bigger life during the second half of the month, the right move is to follow your feelings rather than your fears. Be discerning about who you team up with this month. Make sure they share your enthusiasm and seriousness about building in a new direction.
For more, check out your tarot reading.

items.title: Glow Recipe's Blur Balm, Tate McRae's First Perfume, & 21 More October Beauty Drops
items.description: October might just be the perfect month. It’s not too hot, not too cold (all you need is a light jacket), the foliage is pretty enough to make an eyeshadow palette jealous, and you can finally wear your emotional support blazer again. And making this already p
items.author: Rachel Lapidos
paragraphs: October might just be the perfect month. It’s not too hot, not too cold (all you need is a light jacket), the foliage is pretty enough to make an eyeshadow palette jealous, and you can finally wear your emotional support blazer again. And making this already picturesque month even better? The best beauty launches hitting shelves are just as good as the scenery.

Haus Labs, for one, introduced a liquid bronzer that delivers a summer glow in a tube. Celebrity dermatologist Dr. Sheila Farhang, M.D., also ventured into cosmetics with a line designed to deliver color and coverage to post-treatment skin. And for smoky-eye season, Anastasia Beverly Hills dropped a neutral eyeshadow palette that serves as an all-in-one toolkit.

As you transition your perfume wardrobe for fall, you'll appreciate this month's new releases — like Merit’s New Wave L’Extrait de Parfum, a spicy aroma that takes the floral fragrance category into a decidedly moodier realm. Korean brand Elorea, meanwhile, debuted a honeyed fragrance that's equal parts warm and sweet. And Joonbyrd entered the category with its own take on functional fragrance.
Keep scrolling to shop October 2026’s best beauty launches, as curated by Bustle’s beauty team.

“I recently learned that wearing perfume to the office is a faux pas, and ever since, I’ve been on the hunt for one I can get away with. Elorea’s Quiet Trace is my pick. As the name implies, it stays close to the skin rather than announcing itself to the entire room. The combination of honey and floral notes reminds me of Phlur’s Honey Moon — but if you found that one a little too sweet, this might be more your speed. At first spritz, you get the soapiness of gardenia before it settles into something warmer and muskier. I’m happily wearing it on weekends, too.” – Emma Stout, beauty writer

“I’m convinced that I look better with a tan, but until I can go on a beach vacation, this Haus Labs liquid bronzer will do the trick. It’s sheer enough that I don’t have to worry about going overboard, but still delivers enough pigment to add some much-needed color back to my complexion. Even better, it leaves behind a hydrated finish — courtesy of its 70% skin care ingredients — that makes everything look much more believable. Call me a catfish, but I’ll be faking my summer glow until further notice.” – ES

“Dewsy has always been about high-quality body care, and its latest retinol-infused cream is giving my skin a serious upgrade. The formula is powered by 0.1% retinol, copper peptides, and ceramides — a combination that hydrates, smooths, and brightens. I’ve been using it after showering for the past few weeks, and my skin looks noticeably brighter, feels more hydrated, and is smoother to the touch. Even my husband has commented on the difference. And that’s when you know it’s good — that man notices nothing.” — Shyema Azam, beauty director, branded content

“With all the red light therapy masks hitting the market, it takes a lot to make one stand out — but JOVS’ latest makes a compelling case for the splurge. Unlike traditional LED masks, it combines laser light therapy with a 10-electrode EMS system designed to stimulate facial muscles, essentially bringing two treatments together in one. Its multi-wavelength light technology and customizable settings let you tailor each session, whether you’re looking to boost radiance, support collagen, or target the appearance of sagging and loss of definition. I love how comfortably snug the mask feels, and the attached remote makes it easy to switch between treatment modes and seven EMS intensity levels. After my first week of use, my skin looked and felt more refreshed, and after a month, I noticed it looked slightly firmer, too. It's definitely a luxury purchase, but for anyone looking to level up their at-home skin care routine, this offers more than your average light therapy mask.” — SA

“I will tell people until I’m blue in the face that they need to try Makeup By Mario’s lip pencils, so naturally, I couldn’t get my hands on the new Lip Trip Gift Set fast enough. Featuring minis of three bestselling shades — Toasty, Smokey Pink, and Travis — the full-coverage matte pencils create the perfect lip base, while the brand’s lip-lock technology helps keep your look in place through every holiday party, cocktail hour, and festive gathering to come.” — SA

“I may have found my dream fall eyeshadow palette, and I haven’t been able to put it down since it landed on my vanity. With 12 shades spanning taupe, brown, and mauve, plus a mix of velvety mattes and light-catching shimmers, there's something for every mood. The formulas blend effortlessly, making it easy to create everything from a soft, lived-in wash of color to the smokiest, most sultry eye look.” — SA

“If you love a dark, moody fragrance for fall, Arabian Mate is worth a sniff. It opens with bright bergamot and lemon before giving way to spiced pear and cardamom, followed by a floral heart of rose, jasmine, and saffron. The dry-down, though, is where it gets particularly interesting: Oud, sandalwood, vanilla, and amber give it a cozy, subtly sweet finish that smells utterly rich.” — Rachel Lapidos, deputy beauty editor

“The industry-beloved LED mask just got an upgrade with the launch of Series 3. It retains the same comfortable silicone design and six clinically backed wavelengths, but now comes with a companion MyDose app that lets you track and customize your treatments. It's a smarter, more personalized way to get your red light therapy at home.” — RL

“With the Joonbyrd Mood Jelly sticks, fragrance application is a little more fun. The solid perfume delivers a mood boost through its feel-good scent and satisfyingly squishy jelly texture — perfect for tossing in your bag for an easy swipe-and-sniff self-care moment.” — RL

“La Roche-Posay is among the first brands to bring BEMT, the first new sunscreen filter approved by the FDA in more than 25 years, to the U.S. market. The innovative filter is now part of the brand’s cult-favorite Anthelios formula, giving you the same hydrating sun protection you know and love with an upgrade in UV-filter technology.” — RL

“My first impression of Merit’s second fragrance? Incredibly sexy. Its sensual blend of incense, woods, and green aromatics is softened by a touch of vanilla, creating a scent that feels unexpected and a little addictive. It's the kind of fragrance that leaves you wanting another sniff.” — RL

“I don’t love overly sweet gourmands in perfume form, but when it comes to body care, I’m all about decadence. Enter: e.l.f.’s Spicy Bundt body cream. The deeply hydrating formula melts into skin without feeling heavy, and makes you smell like an irresistible dessert.” — RL

“In case you haven’t heard, Tate McRae has officially joined the celebrity fragrance club. Tate 01 is the pop star’s take on a white floral, but as it wears, notes of amber, sandalwood, and tonka emerge, giving the scent a warmer, more intimate, skin-like quality.” — RL
14The Multifunctional Foundation

“After years of patients asking what makeup they could safely wear after in-office procedures, dermatologist Dr. Sheila Farhang decided to create something herself. Enter Dose of Derm, her take on the skin care-meets-makeup category. The All-in-One Clinical Foundation combines mineral-based sun protection and breathable coverage with longevity-focused ingredients, including exosomes, peptides, and vitamin C — exactly the kind of multitasking formula you'd hope for from a dermatologist-founded makeup line.” — RL

“Leave it to Glow Recipe to create the ultimate blurred lip essential. The soft-matte formula contains vegan PDRN, panthenol, and hyaluronic acid for pillowy-soft hydration — meaning no emphasized lip lines. The tapered tip makes application a breeze, whether you're lining or filling in your pout. It feels like cushiony air on your lips — truly mind-blowingly lightweight. I'm obsessed with every single shade, but Set The Tone, a rosy beige, is my current fave for everyday wear.” — RL
16The Luminizing Body Lotion

“Old Navy Beauty Co. has added another fragrance to its lineup: Shimmer Sparkle, a luxe gourmand with notes of salted caramel, crystallized sugar, and quince. This body lotion lets you wear the scent while delivering lasting hydration and a subtle shimmer — an ideal find for your holiday party circuit.” — RL

“This is the first chocolate-forward fragrance I've fallen in love with. You know that first sip of your latte when it's been made just right? That's the vibe of Mocha Magic. Rich espresso, mocha, biscotti, toffee, vanilla, and bourbon mingle in this creamy gourmand that I simply can't stop talking about.” — RL

“Praise be: Facialist Sofie Pavitt has brought her signature hot-cold therapy treatment from her facial studio to your vanity with the Temp Check mask duo. Start with the warming mask for gentle, enzyme-based exfoliation, then cool things down with the hydrating exosome mask (yes, it actually feels cold). The result? A pro-level glow in just 20 minutes.” — RL

“This limited-edition lip oil from Gisou is the candy-coated gloss of millennial dreams. It appears dark in the tube, but the shade blends into a milky, sheer red for a perfect, on-the-go autumn look — not to mention, the flavor is fabulous.” — Samantha Nik, director of talent relations, BDG
“Meet your new joy stick. With its balmy universal highlighter and rich, smoky eyeliner, this duo is made for your upcoming slate of holiday parties — or just a Tuesday afternoon.” — SN
21The Travel-Friendly Must-Have

“The coquette collab we didn’t know we needed (but most definitely did). Beauty tool guru Lauryn Bosstick and Djerf Avenue founder Matilda Djerf teamed up to give some of their beauty favorites a makeover in the Swedish fashion brand’s Summer Berries print. Each collection also comes with a limited-edition pair of PJs and a matching robe.” — SN

“I’m going to say it how it is: This is a salmon sperm facial in a bottle. After trying the Marini Reboot serum during a treatment, I was immediately sold. Its salmon-derived PDRN helps support collagen production and calm inflammation, while squalane delivers a dose of deep hydration and helps reinforce the skin barrier. Consider it a little post-facial magic for your everyday routine.” — SN

“A supermodel founder’s best-kept beauty secret? This sheet mask. Unwrap the pink packaging to reveal a completely clear jelly mask, then wear it for 15 minutes for skin that looks like you’ve gotten a full eight hours of sleep. Powered by vegan PDRN — aka the California roll version of the salmon sperm facial — plus glycerin, hyaluronic acid, and niacinamide, this pretty little mask leaves skin looking plumper, smoother, and dewier before happy hour.” — SN

items.title: 5 Spicy Friends-To-Lovers Books ‘Nobody Wants This’ Fans Will Swoon Over
items.description: The central love story of Nobody Wants This may be the star-crossed pairing between “hot rabbi” Noah and sex podcaster Joanne, but in Season 3, a new fling enters the chat. And friends-to-lovers fans... this one’s for you.
items.author: Grace Wehniainen
paragraphs: The central love story of Nobody Wants This may be the star-crossed pairing between “hot rabbi” Noah and sex podcaster Joanne, but in Season 3, a new fling enters the chat. And friends-to-lovers fans... this one’s for you.

Brought into each other’s orbit by their respective siblings’ relationship, Morgan and Sasha have spent several seasons developing their own special friendship — one defined by playful banter that even they’re rarely sure is friendly or flirty. (As Morgan told Sasha in Season 1, “Stop saying that it’s not weird when we both know that it kind of is.”)

In the latest entry, they finally hook up, and while fans might debate the specifics of their fling, there’s no denying that the friends-to-lovers trope brings a special kind of buzz. That built-in intimacy can lend itself to sweet, humorous repartee — there’s no need to play brooding or aloof when you know someone that well.
Need some more? Here are seven spicy friends-to-lovers books that echo the playful passion and relationship conundrums of Nobody Wants This.
The Roommate Risk by Talia Hibbert

After sharing a passionate night in college, Jasmine and Rahul decide to be just friends. Best friends. But seven years later, a plumbing emergency forces them into close proximity — leaving them to reckon with feelings that never really went away.
Funny Feelings by Tarah DeWitt

Stand-up comedian Farley is best friends with her manager, Meyer. When a career opportunity prompts them to begin a fake relationship, their closeness takes on a new (and deliciously passionate) form.
When Javi Dumped Mari by Mia Sosa

Though he’s had feelings for her since college, Javi’s insecurities lead him to believe his best friend Mari is unattainable. By the time he feels worthy of her, Mari’s engaged — and he’ll have to make his feelings known before she says “I do” in a countdown to the altar sweetly reminiscent of My Best Friend’s Wedding.
Hook, Line, and Sinker by Tessa Bailey

Much like Morgan in Nobody Wants This, Hannah meets Fox through her sister’s relationship, and the two become good friends. But when actor Hannah moves to Fox’s coastal town to shoot a movie, they discover a romantic tension that’s too reel to ignore.
Romancing Mister Bridgerton by Julia Quinn

There’s a Bridgerton book for every trope, and friends-to-lovers is executed beautifully in Romancing Mister Bridgerton. Penelope has long nursed a crush on her family friend, Colin, and while their union brings some obstacles to work out (including Pen’s secret gig as the ton’s juiciest gossip), all those years of pining have some seriously steamy payoff.

items.title: Exclusive: 'RHOSLC' Star Bronwyn Newport Dishes On The Upcoming 'Traitors' Season
items.description: Bronwyn Newport knows how to make an entrance. The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star has made a name for herself by wearing outfits that test the limits of what might be considered appropriate, normal, or even wearable. (Rainbow feathered Dolce & Gabbana
items.author: Rachel Lapidos
paragraphs: Bronwyn Newport knows how to make an entrance. The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star has made a name for herself by wearing outfits that test the limits of what might be considered appropriate, normal, or even wearable. (Rainbow feathered Dolce & Gabbana coat, anyone?) Her beauty philosophy, however, is a different story. “Beauty-wise, it’s always very, very tried-and-true for me,” she tells Bustle.

Rather than chasing an entirely new look, Newport, 41, focuses on skin health and preserving what makes her feel like herself. “For me, such a big part of beauty is who you naturally are,” she says. “I’ve obviously had a rhinoplasty. But I always want a big, beautiful smile — that’s always the finishing look, where you are yourself.”

It’s why her partnership with Colgate Optic White is such a natural fit. It's part of her everyday getting-ready routine, and she recently appeared at the brand’s activation at Bravo Fan Fest in Charleston, South Carolina. “I always have this big goofy grin everywhere I go,” she says. “I never look like I’ve been there before or I’m used to it or I’m cool. I always look like [I’m] giddy to be invited to the opening of an envelope.” For Newport, it’s about making sure “the health behind my skin and my teeth and my hair is done properly.”

Still, being a Housewife has made her more aware of how her appearance is perceived. Her imperfect teeth became a talking point among viewers early on, for example — but she’s learned to separate other people’s opinions from her own. “It’s hard to put yourself out there in every way on the show, especially your physical self, to be consumed and digested and discussed,” she says. “But I also really live for a woman in the year of our Lord 2026 being like, ‘No, this is what I want to look like, and this is how I want to feel.’”
Ahead, Newport opens up about filming The Traitors, the fan reactions she’s still processing, and why she’s approaching her next chapter with an open mind.
What is your favorite beauty treatment, and what’s the last one you treated yourself to?

It’s always about really great skin prep. I’m a big believer in retinol and lasers. I get a lot of glam done and my hair done, and when I don’t, I really don’t. I’m a ChapStick-and-mascara person. I said this in my first confessional ever that “sexy” is not really my aesthetic.
Your fashion is super adventurous and maximalist. Do you take the same approach to beauty, or do you keep certain parts more classic?

My approach has always been that the clothes are the star of the show. I’m not even the star of the show — it’s the outfits I put together. Beauty-wise, I stick with products that I know and have loved and used forever. It’s about the simplicity of knowing that all of that is taken care of and elevated and fabulous.
There were a lot of comments online about how you reacted in the episode where you took your castmates to San Francisco. How are you handling them?

It’s a lot. It’s so nice when something I do or say resonates with people. I was sharing quite a bit about what it feels like to be in a new chapter. San Francisco was home for me for so long, and so many people were appreciative of what I shared about publicly going through a separation and pending divorce.

One of the beautiful things about sharing my life on the show is getting to physically watch yourself and ask, “Wow, was that a choice that I liked? Was this a way that I responded?” I’ve realized I tend to act a certain way, and I don’t know if I love that.

There was some feedback this week about the way I handled certain things that made me think, “Yeah, that’s fair. I could have handled that better.” I don’t know that I’ll ever get another opportunity to respond to a diss at a party celebrating my separation, but if I do, I’m now armed with all the right ways to do it.
Has the “Hypocrisy & Bulls*it” song grown on you at all?
No. Shockingly enough, it has not. I have a feeling I will never hear the end of it, but it’ll just be one of those earworms that I have to deal with.
What can you say about the Traitors experience, and who were you most surprised to see in the castle?

I was surprised to see everyone because they do such a good job of keeping it quiet. I know that everyone was surprised to see me because I didn’t tell a soul. I was trying to buy things undercover, shopping at all kinds of different places and buying vintage so nobody would think, “Why is Bronwyn buying all this plaid?”

It was so fun. That’s maybe one of the last special things in the world: truly getting to surprise somebody. It’s a beautiful production to work on, and they’ve put together a cool group of people and a fabulous game.

I don’t always smile so much on Housewives. The dinner-party games usually aren’t smile-inducing. But on Traitors, I was grinning the whole time, running through the Scottish Highlands, being like, “I’m at work right now!” as we’re doing a challenge, or I’m wearing some crazy vintage outfit and arguing with somebody about whether I’m a Traitor.
Would you say that being a Housewife has made you better at reading people, or does it make you more suspicious of people?
A little bit of both. I like to think that I can see a train wreck coming now that I’ve been through so many Housewife dinners. I tend to feel the storm building as the entrées are ordered.

But it also makes me a little suspicious. I wanted to be so good at the game aspect of Traitors, but there’s no real way to plan for it. You never know what your role will be, how it will evolve, or who else will be there. The best strategy is to have no strategy. You’ll get to see how that plays out for me — pun intended — as I make a new strategy every day.
What is something you’re excited to explore or embrace in this next chapter of your life that you might not have been ready for a year ago?

Oh my gosh, everything. This was a lot more change and upheaval than I thought it would be. I always like to say that I’m dumb, not stupid, but sometimes I’m like, “Wow, this was very different from what I thought it was going to be.” I thought I really understood what a separation and divorce was going to look like, and I did not.

It’s interesting to sit with the idea that there’s a lot of grief and sadness and closure, which always tend to have a negative connotation, but that it can also bring so much optimism and hope. The dual-edged nature of that is that everything is possible again, and that’s a really beautiful thing to be able to say. I don’t know if I’ll enjoy or stick with everything I try in this new era of my life, but it’s fun to try things out.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: How To Shop Sephora's Holiday Savings Event Like A Beauty Editor
items.description: All linked products are independently selected by our editors. If you purchase any of these products, we may earn a commission.
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa
paragraphs: All linked products are independently selected by our editors. If you purchase any of these products, we may earn a commission.

The holidays have arrived early at Sephora, and by that, we mean the retailer’s highly anticipated savings event is back for 2026. Whether you’re eyeing a bevy of sparkly gift sets or looking to replenish your favorite luxe serum, Sephora’s Holiday Savings Event is the perfect opportunity to do just that.

If you’ve shopped Sephora’s sales before, you probably know the drill: Depending on your Beauty Insider membership tier — Insider, VIB, or Rouge, determined by how much you spend annually — you can score 10%, 15%, or 20% off, respectively. The sale is now open to all Beauty Insider tiers, and new this year, Rouge members can share the love (aka the sale's top discount) with up to five friends, each of whom will receive a one-time-use coupon for 20% off. The event wraps up for everyone on November 9, and to redeem your discount, simply enter promo code ALLONSALE at checkout; your savings will automatically reflect your membership tier. (One more perk worth knowing: All Beauty Insider members get 30% off Sephora Collection products from October 30 through November 9, no code required.)

As with previous years, there are a few exclusions and limits to keep in mind as you plan your Sephora haul. Shoppers are limited to two Dyson items (choose wisely), three Shark Beauty items, and three The Ordinary products.
Now that you know the rules of the road, onto the fun part: Keep scrolling for the most worthwhile items to add to your cart during the sale.

Rhode entered Sephora doors only last year, and you know what that means: All your dewy skincare essentials are available to shop during the Holiday Savings Event. If you can only choose one product, make it the Glazing Milk essence, which is perfect for adding a light veil of hydration as the weather cools down.

This blockbuster advent calendar by Sephora Collection is 30% off during the entire duration of the Holiday Savings Event, bringing the price tag down to just $42. With a value of $190 in products, this is a serious steal that we predict won't stay in stock for long.

We previously reviewed Shark’s FlexFusion styler, and it surpassed our expectations with flying colors. This year, we're eyeing the Glam —Shark's newest hair innovation, which includes curling barrels, a smoothing brush, finishing tool, straightener, and a concentrator nozzle to achieve a variety of looks in a limited edition steel blue colorway.

If we had a beauty crystal ball, we would forecast that this Danessa palette will be quite the hot commodity for holiday makeup looks this season. Create endless dazzling looks using the entire assortment, or pop out each six-pan palette, remove the magnetic logo mirror in the center, and take it on the go. (Genius!)

If you love niche, luxury fragrance, here's a name you've probably never heard of — for now. From the brains of Melanie Bender (whose resume includes executive roles at Rhode, Versed, and Merit) and Joe Cloyes and Greg Gonzalez (founders of Youth To The People) comes Lore. The collection of five hyper-sensorial, unique fragrances ranges from fruity with a hint of smoky mezcal (Disfruta) to Lovely And A Little Twisted, a milky rose that's utterly addictive. Best of all: They all clock in at $92 for a full-size bottle — easily half of comparable designer brands — and that's before your sale discount.

Summer Fridays' hydrating, nonslip hydrogel eye patches are soaked in skin-loving ingredients to soothe and depuff tired eyes, making them a great option to stock up on ahead of the holiday travel season.

There’s stiff competition in the world of tinted lip butters, balms, and treatments, but EADEM has carved out a niche as the ultimate IYKYK status lippie. This cozy set comes with five full-size balms in the brand’s most beloved flavors, working out to just $17.60 each — a steal for a formula that feels a little more special than your everyday lip balm. Consider it the perfect gift to split with your besties (or, you know, keep all to yourself). Shopping on a tighter budget? There’s also a trio of Le Chouchou minis for $39.

Patrick Starrr’s ONE/SIZE setting spray is goated for a reason: It locks makeup in place for hours on end while delivering a soft-matte finish that can withstand even the longest holiday parties. This holiday duo costs the same as the full-size spray alone, so you’re essentially getting the mini for free. Consider it a no-brainer for makeup maximalists and anyone whose glam needs to stay put from morning to midnight.

This time two years ago, celebrity makeup artist Mary Phillips' brand, m.ph, was still waiting in the wings. This year, however, is a different story. The versatile complexion palette is already a Sephora bestseller, and thanks to a recent restock (and long-awaited shade expansion, you can snag yours at a discount during the sale.

items.title: Scorpio Season Is All About Death, Sex & Rebirth. Your Tarotscope Explains Why
items.description: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
items.author: Tatianna Tarot
paragraphs: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
Beautycon is a global platform that brings together beauty enthusiasts, brands, and industry leaders to explore the latest trends, innovations, and conversations shaping the future of beauty.

November opens with the dead, particularly our ancestors and beloved spirit guides. On November 1 and 2, Día de Muertos fills homes with marigolds, candles, and the favorite foods of those who came before us. At the same time, in Haiti and across its diaspora, Fèt Gede honors the Gede, the spirits of death in Haitian Vodou. They’re known for their dark humor, their unapologetic sexuality, and their power to heal. Neither tradition treats death as something to fear. Both treat it as part of life, a doorway, and a reason to celebrate.

This month, we are also deep in Scorpio season, ruled by the very things most people avoid talking about: death, desire, and transformation. Scorpio knows that nothing is reborn without first being let go, and that pleasure and power live in the places we’ve been taught to hide. The New Moon in Scorpio on November 9 plants the seed of who you’re becoming. Meanwhile, on November 13, Venus and Mercury both station direct, ending the review of your love life and your truth that began in October. What you learned in the dark is now ready to be lived.

Death, sex, and rebirth aren’t taboo. They’re sacred themes that help us embrace more life. Something in your life is ending. Something in you is craving more. And someone new is emerging from what you’re finally ready to release. You can’t fully live until you’re willing to let something die.
These tarotscopes will show you what’s ending, what you’re desiring, and who you’re becoming. Read for your sun, moon, and rising.

items.title: That feeling of values crumbling has a name: civic grief | Psyche Ideas
items.description: If reading or watching the news feels less like staying informed and more like a daily horror or heartbreak, you’re not alone. Many of us are carrying a kind of civic homesickness. It’s what happens when the truths we presumed were universal start to crumble.
items.author: Rebecca Lewandowski
paragraphs: If reading or watching the news feels less like staying informed and more like a daily horror or heartbreak, you’re not alone. Many of us are carrying a kind of civic homesickness. It’s what happens when the truths we presumed were universal start to crumble. Sometimes, differences of worldview so profound have emerged that even dinner conversations feel like foreign policy negotiations.

How do we give shape to this disquiet? We might call it fatigue, burnout, or ‘just needing a break from the world’, but often it’s grief – mourning for a faith we once had in fellow citizens to recognise a certain decency or sense of fairness. It isn’t partisan; it’s human, and it has a name. Civic grief doesn’t care which side of the table you sit on. It can visit anyone who has seen their values of citizenship and belonging abandoned or even opposed by their neighbours or friends or country.

If this sounds familiar, take heart. The ache itself is proof of care, a sign that some part of you still believes we can do better. Around the world, survey after survey shows people losing faith in institutions, leaders, and even each other. Freedom House’s 2026 report found that global freedom declined for the 20th consecutive year in 2025, with political rights and civil liberties deteriorating in 54 countries and improving in only 35. Those numbers have lived counterparts: military coups, efforts to weaken constitutional safeguards, violence against peaceful protesters, attacks on courts and journalists, and families increasingly unable to discuss public life without treating one another as hostile witnesses. The grief, in other words, is not floating above reality. It is responding to it. In naming civic grief for what it is, we can find a more honest place to begin, and perhaps a way to see what is still in common even across bitter divides. First, civic grief needs to be understood more clearly.

The first stage is denial, a most civilised coping mechanism. It wears a suit, reads editorials, and insists that things are not as bad as they look. We might remind ourselves that democratic government has survived worse: wars, recessions, demagogues, corruption. We use history like a sedative, and call the system ‘resilient’, confident the pendulum will swing back. We vote and try to convince ourselves that the institutions are working as they should. Denial has its uses, but slowly we begin to absorb the scope of the crisis in small, unavoidable doses.

The trouble comes when denial hardens into complacency. In places where the erosion of our civic life is subtle, it is easy to believe that real breakdowns aren’t a crisis. If we decide events are a ‘temporary disturbance’, nothing fundamental has to change. Scaled up, it turns into a false, reassuring voice saying ‘institutions are basically fine’ long after the evidence disagrees.
The cycle of scandals, polarisation and moral fatigue accumulates until they register as the new reality

When denial cracks, anger usually walks in, puts its feet on the table, and opens a social media account. Biologically, it is the nervous system in fight or flight. The amygdala turns up the volume on threat, stress hormones spike, and attention narrows to villains and blame. It can fix on corrupt officials, apathetic neighbours, ‘elites’ or ‘the media’. In one country, it centres on police violence or election fraud; in another, on inequality or culture wars. It often shows up as indignation at bias, apathy or the endless loop of shouting heads who look like they are debating but are mostly performing disbelief, showing they still care enough to be furious. Algorithms love this, which is why anger is the grief stage most compatible with modern technology. We mistake outrage for engagement, and forget that noise and signal are not the same. Yet anger has a purpose. It is the immune response of conscience. The task is to keep it from turning autoimmune, and to let it fuel stewardship instead of scorched earth.

The next stage of civic grief is bargaining. It sets in once the adrenaline cools. This is the ‘if-then’ logic of the optimist feeling despair. If we educate the next generation better, if more people vote, if we just talk across the aisle, things will get better. Bargaining is democracy’s prayer: let us return to normalcy, and we promise to behave better this time. It is noble but delusional, for it assumes the old ‘normal’ can be restored. Still, bargaining reveals something precious: the refusal to give up. Even naive hope has moral worth. Bargaining may not save democracy, but it prevents cynicism from claiming the soul entirely.

The fourth stage of civic grief is depression, the weight of disillusionment. The cycle of scandals, polarisation and moral fatigue accumulates until they register as the new reality. This is the stage of numbness: when people withdraw from the public sphere not out of apathy, but out of emotional self-preservation. The ballot box feels like theatre. Debate feels like déjà vu. Facts feel negotiable. Philosophically, this is a dangerous moment, when the demos, the people, cease to believe their will matters. This is a kind of soft despotism from long ago: not tyranny of chains, but of indifference. Depression acknowledges that idealism has limits. Here is when people often ask, what if the system is functioning exactly as designed? What if the system is no longer democratic?

Accepting the stages of our civic grief is important and does not mean surrender. It means we can move on to seeing more clearly. It is where citizens begin to understand that democracy was never an inheritance, but an ongoing responsibility and an act of stewardship and creation. Acceptance is where we stop waiting for ‘the adults in the room’ to fix things and recognise that we are the adults. The work of democracy, it turns out, is not glamorous: it’s reading city budgets, attending community meetings, and listening to people who annoy us. It also requires humility. The idea that one political side or ideology can ‘save’ democracy misunderstands it. Democracy, by nature, is a tense structure built to hold disagreement without collapse. The goal was never unanimity, but coexistence. Democracy was never meant to eliminate conflict. It was meant to civilise it, to keep disagreement from becoming dehumanisation, and to turn competing claims into conditions where dignity, security, opportunity, collective wellbeing and belonging remain possible.

Coming through to the other side of civic grief means no more nostalgia for the previous order. Instead, it brings us to reinvention and action. This kind of hope insists that, even when institutions falter, individuals must act to represent democracy and can still support democratic values of curiosity, empathy, courage, restraint. Hope becomes real when it stops being a feeling and becomes a discipline. It means choosing one part of the common life and tending it close to the ground: a school, a library, a neighbourhood association, a local campaign, a food pantry, a veterans’ organisation, an environmental group. Democracy is rebuilt there, through habits that may outlast us: transparency where suspicion could take root, listening where contempt would be easier, and enough restraint to remember that opponents are still people, not symbols arranged for our convenience.

Emotions are not irrational storms; they are intelligence about what we value. Civic grief says that fairness, dignity and shared obligation were precious enough that their loss hurts. In the body, it feels like heaviness or fatigue. In the mind, it becomes questions: who are we if what we were told to trust keeps failing us? What does it mean to be a ‘good citizen’ when the rules feel soft for some and razor sharp for others? How do you keep caring about an ‘us’ that no longer feels shared?

It can be unsettling to realise that the person who seems to live on the other side of every issue may be grieving a different story about what was lost, but they still felt something crack where they thought ‘we’ lived. Calling this civic grief does not erase our differences; it gives us a shared language for the ache and a first step toward something more useful than fighting or shutting down.

items.title: How psychology’s classic studies misled us about the self | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Imagine a creature that is like humans in every way, except that it has no enduring inner self. The behaviour of this hypothetical species – which we will call Homo vacuus – would be driven not by their private beliefs and inclinations, but rather by knee-jerk
items.author: Jack W Klein; William B Swann
paragraphs: Imagine a creature that is like humans in every way, except that it has no enduring inner self. The behaviour of this hypothetical species – which we will call Homo vacuus – would be driven not by their private beliefs and inclinations, but rather by knee-jerk responses to their immediate environment. Lacking an enduring web of preferences, attitudes and proclivities, the contents of the H vacuus character would be filled by whatever situation they find themselves in. As a result, their behaviour would vary dramatically as they moved from one situation to the next.

Scrutiny of H vacuus would reveal a host of curious behaviours. Their attitudes towards others would be shaped by random factors that unconsciously influence their thoughts. They might feel ‘warmer’ toward others when they handle a hot cappuccino, and ‘colder’ when clasping an iced latte. Their political decisions would hinge on seemingly innocuous details. For instance, turnout in their elections would surge if they were affirmed as being ‘voters’, rather than merely people who vote. And on morality, their views on topics from abortion to pornography could depend on something as mundane as whether they had washed their hands, making them feel ‘cleansed’ and in the mood for judging others.

Given the inherent fluidity of H vacuus, trying to predict their behaviour beyond the present moment would be pure folly. H vacuus would be so mercurial that when they wed, they would effectively be marrying a stranger. In the end, being the pawns of powerful environmental forces would compromise their ability to effectively plan and adapt. Others would recognise the impossibility of holding them responsible for their actions, as they could refuse to accept responsibility for their behaviour by claiming: ‘I was just responding to the situation!’ At the end of the day, religious, ethical and judicial systems would be largely irrelevant.

In light of the many challenges facing H vacuus, it may be surprising to learn that this fictitious creature is based on an implicit assumption about human nature suggested by the work of numerous influential behavioural scientists. This assumption is that if you were to peer into the contents of people’s selves, you would discover little that isn’t susceptible to the random influences of the situation. Indeed, the peculiarities of H vacuus life described above – including the ideas about ‘warm’ attitudes, election turnout and moral cleansing – are based on claims that have been made about real humans.

We label this view of human psychology the empty-self metaphor. Although it has fostered an erroneous understanding of human nature, the empty-self metaphor has inspired a large following. These followers embrace an optimistic view in which human foibles can be readily vanquished through systematic manipulation of the social environment. However alluring it may be, we suggest that it is time to replace this Panglossian view with one that acknowledges the importance of enduring psychological structures.

The empty-self view has a long history in psychology, arguably tracing its origins to the behaviourist movement at the beginning of the 20th century. The behaviourists were almost entirely focused on ‘the situation’, eschewing speculation about what they considered the ‘black box’ of the mind. This emphasis on the situation was influential with founding social psychologists, who defined social psychology as the study of how individual thoughts, feelings and behaviours ‘are influenced by the actual, imagined, or implied presence of other human beings’.

An emphasis on the power of the situation, and its propensity to overwhelm or displace personal agency, has dominated social psychology ever since. Examples abound. In the 1970s, the author of self-perception theory argued that, rather than beliefs guiding behaviour (as common sense might imply), situations cause behaviour, and people generally infer their own beliefs by taking note of how they behave. Others made the corollary argument that personalities effectively do not exist. In fact, the term ‘fundamental attribution error’ was coined to describe an allegedly flawed tendency to attribute someone’s behaviour to their personality. Elsewhere, including in sociology, impression management research and the dramaturgical movement suggested that all the world’s a stage, with people portraying whatever character best suits a given scene. This focus on the situation reached a fever pitch with the ‘situationists’, who explicitly placed the influence of the situation on human behaviour far above any possible internal motivations.

Although situationism has lost some of its lustre, the empty-self metaphor has remained at least implicitly popular within certain circles. This is particularly true in the field of social priming, which deals with the impact of seemingly inconsequential environmental cues on human behaviour. In examples of this kind of research, seeing words related to old age seemed to make university students walk more slowly, and plotting dots on paper further apart appeared to make people feel more distant from their family.
Classic evidence for the primacy of the situation has lost force

In recent years, however, the evidential tide has turned against the empty self. Social priming and other areas of social psychology have struggled in the wake of the ‘replication crisis’ – the unfortunate realisation that a surprising number of psychological findings could not be independently replicated. Many such findings are likely to have been false positives, stemming from tendentious statistical decision-making and other questionable research practices. The authors of one report found that when a number of social priming studies were carried out again, only 17 per cent of the findings were successfully replicated. A much smaller proportion of empty-self-style research has been dismissed as simply fraudulent – such as the celebrated finding that people are more honest when filling out forms if they sign at the beginning, rather than at the end.

In our own research, we’ve compared studies that were or were not premised on the empty-self assumption that behaviour is unexpectedly shaped by subtle, seemingly irrelevant environmental factors, as opposed to pre-existing beliefs and dispositions. We found that studies reflecting an empty-self view were far less likely to hold up.

Classic evidence for the primacy of the situation has also lost force. Take, for instance, Stanley Milgram’s obedience studies, in which participants were asked to administer electric shocks to someone until the victim seemed to be unconscious or dead. These classic studies have been taken as evidence that authority can override individual will. However, subsequent research has found that personal traits associated with diligence and helpfulness predicted an increased willingness to administer the electric shocks. This reframes the experiment as demonstrating not mindless obedience, but often wilful collaboration – participants who gave the shocks were ostensibly helping an experimenter in the service of ‘science’.

Consider also the Stanford prison experiment, led by Philip Zimbardo, where students acting as guards in a fake prison (with others acting as prisoners) appeared to succumb to their temporary role, becoming belligerent. Attributing this behaviour to the roles the students were assigned is jeopardised by several design flaws, including a selection bias that likely caused dispositionally authoritarian individuals to be overrepresented in the study. The upshot is that participants’ unique, personal identities seem to have mattered far more than the authors of these classic examples of situational influence would have us believe.

The idea that the human mind is so fickle should have attracted more scepticism than it has often received. First and foremost, it is at odds with other evidence. The entire field of personality psychology – which investigates the unique qualities of people that persist across situations – informs us that the self is not empty at all. Measures of personality such as the Big Five traits (openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism) are remarkably stable and predictive of behaviour and long-term life outcomes. In fact, research suggests that the average effects of personality and situations on behaviour are similar in magnitude. Elsewhere, there is ample evidence for an enduring self: for example, self-esteem is largely steady over the lifespan, and attempts to break habits frequently fail, highlighting that personal tendencies impede many people’s efforts at self-change.

It is not difficult, though, to understand the appeal of the empty-self metaphor. The idea that our thoughts and behaviours are dictated by banal aspects of daily life, such as the temperature of our coffee, offers a tantalising glimpse at ‘hidden’ causes of behaviour. This is probably why social priming occupied a full chapter of Daniel Kahneman’s bestselling book Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), why mentalists like Derren Brown attract large TV audiences by showing how the ‘power of psychology’ can be used to control and befuddle, and why exciting ‘counterintuitive’ findings are published in top journals.

The empty-self metaphor also lends itself to an admittedly admirable progressive agenda (popular among social psychologists) that is focused on addressing inequality in the social environment and avoiding victim-blaming. If the plight of the have-nots is primarily attributable to the harsh social conditions that society unwittingly thrusts upon them, then the obvious solution is to change those social conditions. Ultimately, the empty-self metaphor teases the provocative possibility that society could be righted if only we determine how to control the social environment. But reality is much messier.
There is considerable evidence for human consistency, agency and a remarkable propensity to shape our situations just as they shape us

The good news is that psychology appears to be slowly moving toward increased acceptance of what’s called ‘interactionism’: the view that the person and the situation interactively dictate behaviour. Many people have heard of nudging, in which subtle changes to the presentation of choices can systematically influence behaviour (eg, placing fruits and vegetables more conspicuously, to increase healthy consumption). The idea of nudging has proven enormously popular, with multiple governments around the world setting up ‘nudge units’, but initial results were lacklustre. Happily, research has moved to second-generation, interactionist nudges that tailor the intervention to the beliefs and preferences of the individual. For example, recent research suggests that personalised nudges to make healthier food purchases might be more effective than generic ones.

Interactionism likewise paves a more realistic path forward for social change. Rather than assuming that one size fits all, an interactionist approach acknowledges that individual differences inform the way people respond to social situations. Any social movement to reduce harmful behaviour or improve wellbeing needs to meet people where they are at. That means acknowledging that different individuals will respond to the same policies and political messages differently, and in accordance with their own perspectives.

Rebuking the empty-self view recognises that, far from being the dithering shells that psychology studies have often suggested we are, most of us are loyal to a reasonably clear and coherent self-concept. We do not ‘marry strangers’, nor do our relationships hinge on irrelevant details of the moment. On the contrary, there is considerable evidence for human consistency, agency and a remarkable propensity to shape our situations just as they shape us. Although imputing this degree of agency and stability to the self may lack the intoxicating simplicity of Homo vacuus, we are confident that it will pave the way to a deeper understanding of Homo sapiens.
