There are also many personal secrets tucked away inside the images, where they often look overly sexual – rarely my first thought, if thought about at all. There’s an undercurrent of personal meaning. Some images in the story are overlaid with pictures from my dad’s favourite beach. That’s seaweed. Mother earthing. My dad has Benson’s disease, so he’s not able to communicate any more. But I still want to include him in my life in ways that I can. It’s sad when I think of how good he would have been as a grandfather.
SF This story is so intensely autobiographical. Do you think all of your work is?

HW It is. I graduated from art school in 2010. I loved emotive art and started as a painter, which seemed to be the most primitive and uninteresting trade at the time. There was a bit of a backlash against people like Tracey Emin – who wore their heart on their sleeve. People whose work was too autobiographical, too self-involved. I loved her diary works and felt a kinship to them but my era was having a conceptual moment that I didn’t fit in with. I will always be an artist first but fashion allowed me to continue to use emotive language more freely and the impulse has never left me. There’s a picture of me with a pushchair on fire. I wanted to express the fear of being a bad mother. That’s my neighbour’s shed. It’s like a doll’s house. The dream gone wrong.
SF Very few artists have represented fear in pregnancy. Probably because they are mostly men, so maybe it’s not their place to look at that.
HW Yes, that was nice. They left it for us.
SF But being pregnant can be really frightening at times.

HW Part of the story I wanted to show was my thoughts of, oh God, am I going to be a bad mother? Am I going to drop the baby? Am I not going to love the baby? Am I going to have postpartum depression? What’s amazing is that there is so much information about those things now and people talk about it all the time.
SF That anxiety goes on for ever, I think. Did working with a body double in a mask feel strange to you?

HW So strange. Every time I look in the mirror now, I see the mask. It’s terrifying. When you ordinarily look in the mirror you see what you want to see. You think you look good or you think you look terrible. It doesn’t matter what you actually look like. I asked Chaïm, who made the mask, to get all the bits and bobs in there. Go hard on the skin blemishes. I knew they were there but when you actually see them looking back at you, it’s quite grotesque. My face like a piece of meat, you really see it that way. When I show the photos to people, they can’t understand that it’s not me in those pictures.
SF Did you do it for purely practical reasons?

HW Not only. There is something very laborious about taking a self-portrait, the tripod, the focusing etc, but I also wanted to divide myself – the divided self. She was supposed to be the idealised version of me, unstretched and glossy. It’s a shame we didn’t have more time with Anna, who wore the suffocating mask along with the fake bump and wig. There was so much more fun to be had.
SF The image with the snake is referencing Avedon’s Nastassja Kinski and the Serpent [1981]?
HW Yes. I thought that was funny. It’s my “pregnancy picture”.
SF You know the thematic of this issue of the magazine is cliché?

HW So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask.
That’s a real snake crushing me in the picture. I put make-up on in that one too, to cover the pigmentation on my face, to be the idealised pregnant woman for her pregnancy shoot.
SF And there’s an apple in another image. Eve’s apple.

HW Yes. Purity lost. And for taking the apple we must suffer in childbirth. But I actually feel purer than ever. There’s something in the body becoming so functional, it’s before shame. The instinctiveness and the nakedness of breastfeeding, for example, feels like that moment before the apple when there was no shame attached to the naked body. There’s one really disturbing breastfeeding image, the masked me breastfeeding me, the idea of a mother still needing a mother. There’s also me breastfeeding from John. Which takes the breast even further away from the sexual, because he doesn’t have one. It’s about becoming dependent on each other in a new way as a family and recognising that we all need to be nurtured.

SF You are photographing something that is transient, and by photographing it you’re fixing it in time. I suppose that is what photography is more generally, but it feels somehow more pronounced in this context.

HW The permanence is scary sometimes. I only thought about showing my child these images today. I thought maybe the baby never sees these. It’s very different because it’s still inside me. Baby out, different.
SF Do you think about that often, with explicit imagery?
HW I think about it all the time, but I try to be free. I don’t always get it right and people correct me. I like that conversation though.
SF Do people ever talk about your nudes, or look at your nudes, in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable?

HW It’s hard to put yourself out there and be judged. The real private self isn’t this though. It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait. Looking back, I realised I was trying to seem approachable, not too attractive or too sexy. But I’m obviously aware of the camera and that annoys me. I wanted to catch myself in a real state, but because I’m the one taking the photograph, that’s almost impossible. Some pictures are ugly because I felt I should include them, so I wouldn’t seem vain, which is probably the vainest thing you can do. In one I’m standing nicely, in another I’m slumped and badly postured. Sometimes I feel I can be quite vulgar. That’s part of me, letting people see a little too much. Not necessarily deliberately.

“So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask” – Harley Weir
SF And you don’t lie awake at night thinking about that.

HW Sometimes. You don’t want to read the comments too much. I don’t put much on Instagram for that reason. I would say that I have some boundaries, but the idea of vulgarity is something I subconsciously play with a lot. Or at least it seems my tolerance is higher than most. There is me covered in milk with my legs up. It reeked, because it came from France in a heatwave with Leana the make-up artist. I was trying to photograph what the baby would see coming to get the milk. Unfortunately, I didn’t get a linea nigra, the dark line that can appear when pregnant, apparently as an arrow to direct a new born to the breast.
SF There’s also the cliché of the earth mother, and that huge power, but equal to that is vulnerability.

HW Since I’ve become obviously pregnant, when I’m not with John, I don’t like walking around at nighttime. I want to be with my husband. I know most people are not thinking bad thoughts, but I feel vulnerable. There’s something of the mother earth in the photo of me feeding the fawn. This instinct to nurture, but also suggestive of how exposed motherhood can make you feel. I read that, in England, they used to use puppies to keep the milk supply going if your baby was away from you, fawns or pigs in other countries. And if your milk wasn’t working, they would bring round a donkey or a goat for the baby to suckle from.
SF Some of your self-portrait imagery displays a complete lack of vanity.

HW Art and fashion both rank quite high in the thoughts of the self. Oddly with fashion, being the voyeur that I am, possibly the less self-absorbing of the two. It’s so much about the other. It’s rare to see the photographer. We’re like ghosts haunting the image but we are never really there. I often photograph some of the most attractive people in the world and then sit with retouching comments to make them look even more attractive. So it’s hard to think, damn I look hot here, because in my mind, by comparison, I look like a gremlin. Me looking vain as hell to the public is probably me thinking I look real and unfiltered. It’s hard to be objective when it’s me in front of the lens but I like to think I show both sides. Perfection isn’t interesting.

Styling: Georgia Pendlebury. Hair: Alex Brownsell at Streeters using KEUNE and BLEACH LONDON. Make-up: Leana Ardeleanu at Artlist using MAKE UP FOR EVER. Mask: Chaïm Vischel. Manicure: Lauren Michelle Pires using Le Vernis in Garconne and La Crème Main by CHANEL BEAUTY. Set design: Phoebe Shakespeare. Casting: Gabrielle Lawrence for People-File at MiniTitle. Model: Anna Ramfel. Talent: John Kelleher. Studio manager: Melissa Arras. Lighting director: Jordan Lee. Photographic assistants: Chiara Croserio and JJay Johnson. Styling assistants: Ethan Barbara, Michiel Heemskerk and Stoyan Chuchuranov. Hair assistant: Tommy Stayton. Make-up assistant: Gwen Ryan. Set-design assistants: Freya Purkhardt and Keelin Coyle. Charting fashion from the 19th century to the Nineties to now, the stylist Panos Yiapanis combines garments from his own personal archive with pieces from Pieter Mulier’s five-year tenure at Alaïa. items.title: Has Kim Jones designed the ultimate hotel merch?
items.description: ‘One of the first things I do is go to the hotel shop, and buy everything,’ says the British fashion designer Kim Jones, who – having held roles at Louis Vuitton, Fendi and Dior Men – is well-versed in the business of travel. And, indeed, in the collection of
items.author: Jack Moss
paragraphs: ‘One of the first things I do is go to the hotel shop, and buy everything,’ says the British fashion designer Kim Jones, who – having held roles at Louis Vuitton, Fendi and Dior Men – is well-versed in the business of travel. And, indeed, in the collection of rare and obscure objects: his west London address houses first-edition books and century-spanning artworks; when we meet, in Tokyo, he has spent the day trawling the city’s second-hand shops for research garments to take back to his London studio (he has just announced the launch of an eponymous label, Kim Jones, which will begin with an A/W 2027 collection next year).

We are in the 33rd-floor lobby of Aman Tokyo, the hotel group’s vertiginous outpost in the city, which occupies the upper six floors of the Otemachi Tower in the Chiyoda business neighbourhood (the impressive view stretches across Tokyo, from the imperial gardens at the hotel’s base to the Tokyo Tower in the south, and even – on a clear day – the snow-capped peak of Mount Fuji on the horizon). Jones is what is colloquially known as an ‘Aman junkie’, the name given to those who have visited more than five of Aman’s 36 properties, though he has far overshot this milestone; by his estimate, he has visited ‘about 30’, and is in the top-two worldwide customers.
The story behind Kim Jones’ collaboration with Aman Essentials

‘Every detail is considered and already done before you get there,’ he says of Aman, which was founded by hotelier Adrian Zecha in 1988 as a riposte to the gaudy excesses of other luxury resorts of the era. In the decades since – now led by owner and CEO Vladislav Doronin – Aman, which began with the Ed Tuttle-designed Amanpuri in Phuket, Thailand, has honed a vision of serene minimalism (linear planes of limestone and marble; floor-to-ceiling glass; meditative gardens and pools) and arresting locations (several are in, or in close proximity to, Unesco heritage sites; the Tokyo outpost is a rare city-centre Aman). The name ‘Aman’ itself is derived from the Sanskrit word for ‘peace’.

‘Every Aman that I stay at, I know the people that work there – some of them for ten, 15 years,’ Jones continues. ‘So it’s just like coming home. I have the same room, I have the same set-up, and I can relax. And they are all so beautiful in different ways – here, [in Tokyo], you are looking out to concrete and glass; in Aman-i-Khás a tiger can walk past your tent.’ (The latter is located in Ranthambore National Park in Rajasthan, India and comprises a series of Mughal-inspired canvas tents for guests.)

So when Kristina Romanova, the CEO and creative director of Aman Essentials, the hotel’s lifestyle arm, which spans clothing, leather goods, fragrance and beauty products, approached Jones about a collaboration, it took little soul-searching. ‘We met at a masked ball in Venice, in around 2018,’ says Jones. ‘Kristina knew how much I loved the Aman, so I think she just asked me, and I said yes. It took about a year and a half to get to the point we are now.’ (The collection has now launched in selected Aman outposts and online, as well as at a handful Dover Street Market locations, including Ginza, Tokyo.)
‘It was the first collaboration of this magnitude that we had undertaken,’ adds Romanova. ‘When we started thinking about collaborating with a designer, we were just like: it’s got to be Kim.’

And, while hotel merch is certainly having a moment, Aman x Kim Jones goes far beyond the gift-shop branded caps and tote bags that have become increasingly ubiquitous among the style set. ‘There’s the whole merch aspect of Aman that people love,’ says Jones, referring to collectibles like the leather luggage tag you receive after your stay (they are unique to each property, and have become a subtle status symbol for those in the know). ‘But I was really thinking about what you wear at the Aman – you know, the things that you might have left behind when you packed in a rush, or what you might want when you’ve been at the resort for a while.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
‘I always end up going to the shop and buying stuff, and then just wearing it the whole time,’ he continues. ‘So it all just felt very organic, and real.’

So what are Jones’ travel essentials? There are those items one might expect to be able to purchase at a hotel store: pyjama sets (here constructed from silk in mineral-blue stripes or a deep ‘kombu’ green), swimwear (bikinis edged in woven cord; board-style shorts; sleek swimming costumes with visible zip fastenings), and slippers (ultra-padded with a fleece interior and toggle fastenings). But there are also garments made for traversing a new destination: a series of ‘technical tailoring’ captures Jones’ knack for pragmatic luxury (think: tailored abaca city shorts; zip-up Harrington-style jackets), while activewear comprises base-layer tanks, leggings and bralettes. Completing the line-up is a draped silk dress, should one be without an outfit for an evening at the hotel bar.

‘There’s a functional utilitarianism to the clothes, but there’s also something sexy to the silk story. I was thinking about the Aman couple, and obviously we have one part of the ultimate Aman couple here,’ Jones says, gesturing to Romanova (she is the partner of owner and CEO Vladislav Doronin). ‘I was talking to Vlad, and I was talking to you, and thinking about how we could make [these pieces] become reality.’
‘It’s got to be versatile, functional, but it has to have this understated elegance, and I think that’s what Kim is very well known for,’ says Romanova. ‘He is the master of that.’

The accompanying campaign was photographed in Aman Tokyo and across the city, with the launch marked by a sprawling eight-course dinner in the hotel’s restaurant (local attendees included rapper Verbal and designer Yoon; international guests were shuttled in by Japan Airlines’ luxurious new flagship vessel, the Airbus A350-1000). ‘I’ve been staying here since before it was open, it just feels like being in the future,’ says Jones about the choice of location. ‘Then you go up to the rooms, and they are so beautiful and spacious. And the baths – [I love] getting in that bath and just staring out at all of the lights.’

‘Tokyo was our first urban destination for Aman, and it was the first place I stayed in the city,’ adds Romanova. ‘I came for the opening, and it was such a defining moment for my personal taste to experience Japan and all the attention to detail. Everything has its purpose, and I think it really defined the way that I look at things.’

Aman Essentials launched in 2022, after an initial beauty line revealed a desire among guests for items they could take home with them to remember their stay (or, indeed, for those yet to spend a night but simply wishing to indulge in the lifestyle). ‘When we were going through options for names, we were like: what do we call it? It had to capture that essence of what we represent, and it’s really the essentials on your trip, or on your holidays, and this [is the thinking] behind every product,’ says Romanova. ‘Like, what do I need during my stay? Whether it’s a piece of clothing, pyjamas, a hat, a perfume, or a face mask, we are basically building that perfect traveller’s wardrobe.’
The collection is available at selected Aman resorts, and on Aman’s website, and selected Dover Street Market locations.

Jack Moss is the Fashion & Beauty Features Director at Wallpaper*, having joined the team in 2022 as Fashion Features Editor. Previously the digital features editor at AnOther and digital editor at 10 Magazine, he has also contributed to numerous international publications and featured in ‘Dazed: 32 Years Confused: The Covers’, published by Rizzoli. He is particularly interested in the moments when fashion intersects with other creative disciplines – notably art and design – as well as championing a new generation of international talent and reporting from international fashion weeks. Across his career, he has interviewed the fashion industry’s leading figures, including Rick Owens, Pieter Mulier, Jonathan Anderson, Grace Wales Bonner, Christian Lacroix, Kate Moss and Manolo Blahnik.

items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: A couple of decades ago, in a world before pandemics and video calls, the now achingly Gen X phrase ‘road warrior’ was coined to apply to the new breed of perpetually mobile workers. Enabled and emboldened by tech – both in terms of gadgets and the soaring scope of the industry itself – road warriors saw themselves at the vanguard of the new post-office landscape.

The pandemic put paid to any lingering glamour and the vast majority of modern remote workers have swapped the road for the kitchen table, with the occasional coffee shop if funds allow. But the idea of being rootless and restless, whilst remained tethered to co-workers and a career is still an attractive one, even if it often comes out of necessity rather than desire.

We’ve scoured the stores to find the best tech accessories for keeping up to date and on the ball when you’re out and about, whether it’s the perennial problem of having enough battery life on hand, or the myriad promises of AI-powered productivity boosts. Here’s our guide to gear for running an office on the move.

One of the thinnest and lightest laptops on the market, the new Acer Swift Blade 14 weighs in at just 799 grams. With a 14” OLED screen, 50Wh battery and Intel Core Series 3 processors (up to the Core 7 processor 350), along with 512GB of storage and 12GB of memory, the Swift Blade 14 is our choice of ultra-lite, providing you’re able to live with one of the two finishes, Marshmallow White and Marshmallow Blue.
There’s also four-speaker audio, three USB-C connectors and an easily switchable webcam. The 14’s overall thickness of just 12.9 mm makes this an easy addition to the smallest of bags.
Acer Swift Blade 14, from £1,049.99, Store.Acer.com

Pairing well with the Swift Blade 14 is the Krafted Edge, an ultra-slim laptop powerbank designed to slot beneath the device itself. Just 12mm thick, the Edge has 20,000mAh capability, enough for up to three full laptop charges or four phone charges. Charging the Edge itself should take around two hours and there are two USB-C slots and two USB-A slots for simultaneous device charging.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

The battery itself is modular and replaceable, while the casing combines an aluminium alloy base with a top panel made from OBP-certified ocean-plastic (i.e. waste that would otherwise have been ‘Ocean Bound Plastic’). The design cleverly incorporates a braided USB-C cable that slots into one end of the case so you’re never without a means of charging. Perfectly shaped to slot into a laptop sleeve alongside your computer, you won’t even know that it’s there.
Krafted Edge power bank, £149.99, Kraftedtech.com
Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD

The new Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD from Lexar is designed to bulk up the data capability of your smartphone. Described as the world's thinnest portable SSD, this pocketable storage measures just 8cm by 4.8cm by 3.8mm – it’s only 1 mm thick at some points). Available in 512GB and 1TB sizes, it weighs in at 26.5g and there’s a magnetic sleeve accessory for clipping it to the back of your phone.
Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD, available soon, Lexar.com

Timekettle have a pair of AI-equipped earbuds out in the wild, the W4 Plus and the LiveTalk. The former more focused on translation, while the LiveTalk is the choice for everyday translation and conversation summaries. Like all products of this ilk – and there are now a lot of them – there’s a certain amount of commitment required to get the best performance. LiveTalk consists of a pair of 6.9g open-ear earbuds that offer real-time AI translation, along with with AI-powered conversation summaries.

They do work, after a fashion, although the system struggles to keep up with the speed of casual conversation and works best when translating a piece of recorded speech. The sci-fi dreams of genuine real-time, UN-grade machine-driven simultaneous translation are not here yet, but they will be. LiveTalk can be used via your phone’s microphone or by joining in on a phone call.

Battery life is an impressive 35 hours (with the relatively hefty case) and as always there’s a subscription service for heavy users who need more than the basic 200 free minutes a month. Occasional travellers will find the LiveTalk’s arsenal of 54 languages (all European languages along with including Chinese, Japanese and Hindi and many more) spans most of the globe.
Timekettle LiveTalk AI Translation Earbuds, $109, Timekettle.co

Adopting a new workflow doesn’t always feel intuitive, plus there’s the very real danger of switching over to a system or technology that flails, fails or gradually fades into obsolescence. That’s why we’re only giving a cautious nod to the new Flowtica Folio, a luxury notebook folder designed to be used with the Flowtica Scribe AI note-taking pen. We can already sense your hesitation.

Essentially, the Scribe is another form factor for the increasingly common AI-driven Dictaphone model, a pen that contains a microphone, 32GB of onboard storage and the ability to export recordings to the Flowtica app, where they’re automatically transcribed.

There’s no additional trickery, save for a button that adds a bookmarklet into the recording when you want something highlighted. The Folio simply acts as a smart way of combining the pen with your favourite notebook. In this age of E-ink tablets and hyper-capable smartphones, Flowtica’s set-up feels like a step too far, and having a relatively discrete recording device in meetings, etc., is a potential legal red flag.

The company’s newest product, the Verso, is a more practical piece of portable technology. Superficially similar in function – it’s an AI notetaker – the Verso clips on the back of a Smartphone and has its own E-ink touchscreen, so memos and notes can be read straight away. Orders are open now.
Flowtica Scribe Field Kit (Pen + Folio Notebook), £144, Flowtica.ai
Flowtica Verso E-ink AI notetaker, more information at Flowtica.ai

If you’re the kind of person who can keep hold of a travel adaptor for more than one trip, it’s worth splashing out on a quality unit that does it all. That’s certainly the case for Anker’s newest 4-in-1 universal charger, a hefty but compact travel accessory with inbuilt UK, US, and EU plugs - Type G, Type A and Type C, for those keeping track. With enough sockets to charge up to four devices at once – and 100W power for laptops – it’s a one-plug solution to almost every travel and remote working use case.
Anker Universal Charger, £69.99, Anker.com

The Power Keyboard from Clicks is a really truly tiny, tiny keyboard. Those with long memories will remember the Blackberry, once heralded as the ultimate device (peak road warrior, in fact), but somewhat elevated in status by the passing of time. The Blackberry had a physical keyboard, you see, something that Steve Jobs’s new-fangled touchscreen couldn’t hope to surpass.

You’d be hard-pressed to find a modern human being who isn’t well-versed in high-speed smartphone text input, and even harder pressed to find someone who still uses their Blackberry. Clicks reckon there’s enough enthusiasm out there for their Power Keyboard, however, a battery pack combined with a slide out keyboard that adds power, bulk and the delight of tapping away on tiny little keys. The large fingered need not apply.
Clicks Power Keyboard, £109, Clicks.tech
ProtoArc XK01 Foldable Keyboard

Another way of transforming a tablet or smartphone into something a little more practical is a folding keyboard. We particularly like ProtoArc’s tri-fold XK01 unit, which offers a full-size 105-key layout, including a host of multimedia keys and a number pad, and an onboard battery for up to 120 days of standby power. The company also offers a version with an onboard trackpad.
ProtoArc XK01 Foldable Keyboard, £44.99, ProtoArc.com

items.title: Zaha Hadid built just two private houses; one’s now for sale
items.description: It's exactly ten years since Dame Zaha Hadid passed away unexpectedly at the age of 65, leaving an unassailable legacy in her Issey Miyake-clad wake. In a strange piece of synchronicity, there’s now an incredibly rare chance to own one of her buildings in the
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: It's exactly ten years since Dame Zaha Hadid passed away unexpectedly at the age of 65, leaving an unassailable legacy in her Issey Miyake-clad wake. In a strange piece of synchronicity, there’s now an incredibly rare chance to own one of her buildings in the heart of London.

Constructed from 2014 onwards, this house in Belgravia’s Grosvenor Crescent Mews has the distinction of being one of only two private residential projects completed by the studio (the other being the Capital Hill Residence outside Moscow).

A unicorn in the London property market, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews isn’t just a rare example of Hadid’s work but it’s also a 3,980 sq ft house with integral garage just a stone’s throw from Hyde Park Corner, located in what is Belgravia's only private gated mews.

Gaining permission for such an avant-garde structure in the midst of a thicket of Conservation Areas and listed buildings was no mean feat, even for an architecture of the calibre of Zaha Hadid. The site had boundaries with no fewer than nine different neighbours, placed in such a way that the only public-facing façade was just six metres in width.
That element, a rippling curtain of back-lit brickwork lattices and patterned glass, belies the scale of the house behind it, which extends over four generous 1,000 sq ft floorplans.
Basement kitchen, dining and living area
Basement kitchen, dining and living area

The garage was a planning condition, but it was fitted out to a residential specification so that it can be used as a study area if needed. It adjoins the main reception room, a space bounded by the curved interventions of the polished balustrade rail and the custom-designed staircase, formed from polished concrete and shaped to wind sinuously between the floors.
Atrium views from the lower ground floor
Atrium views from the lower ground floor
Atrium views from the lower ground floor

Like many London mews and conversion projects, the house goes down as well as up, with a kitchen and sitting room located in the basement, beneath a double height space which in itself is topped by a glazed terrace at first floor level. With windows, parapets, courtyards and walls arranged so as to avoid overlooking from surrounding properties, the entire house is cleverly folded into its site, making the most from the available space.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Utility, plant and stores are tucked away in the basement behind the kitchen, another area that is defined by a trademark Hadidian swoop, this time in the form of a polished kitchen counter that projects out from the wall like a geological form.

From here, the two-storey atrium rises up to the gauzy light that filters through the glass roof, with the polished balustrade playing off the curved concrete stair risers contained behind a glazed wall.

The first floor houses the principal bedroom suite, complete with curved glass and sole access to the terrace. A living wall flanks the perimeter of the property (it’s joined by a brown roof system designed to improve the house’s insulation), while the glazed stair tower rises up beneath the fluted forms of another skylight. On the second floor there are two further ensuite bedrooms, each winding around a central dressing room space.
The artistry and style of 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews is sadly unrepeatable, making this project a rare opportunity to acquire a functional work of art in the heart of London.

In the decade since her death, the firm Hadid established in Studio 9 of a former school on Bowling Green Lane in Clerkenwell has gone all out into making her wildly exuberant approach into a clearly defined architectural style, Parametricism, translating Hadid’s wild, analogue forms into a heady, AI-infused cocktail of data-shaped aesthetic adventures.
Design details, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews
Design details, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews
Design details, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews
Design details, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews
Design details, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews
If you can ignore the Succession-like shenanigans that have swirled around ZHA in the years that followed, the Zaha Hadid Foundation holds a fascinating archive of her work.
6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews, London SW1X is for sale at £11.95m through Forbes Gilbert-Green, ForbesGilbertGreen.com

items.title: This winter’s menswear is all about ‘crafting characters’
items.description: The changing of the fashion seasons gives one a chance to craft a new persona. For winter, menswear designers posited their own takes on character dressing, one which riffed on the tenets of traditional sartorialism with a preppy, sporty – and oftentimes colou
items.author: Jack Moss
paragraphs: The changing of the fashion seasons gives one a chance to craft a new persona. For winter, menswear designers posited their own takes on character dressing, one which riffed on the tenets of traditional sartorialism with a preppy, sporty – and oftentimes colourful – twist.

Such was the starting point of our November 2026 menswear fashion story, which saw London- and Paris-based photographer Luke Gooden and stylist Guy Miller capture A/W 2026’s spirit of easy elegance – where classic tailoring and outerwear meets elements of utility, from toggle fastenings and parka-style hoods, to a proliferation of pockets.
A/W 2026’s menswear is all about character dressing

Through it all, elements of colour and play: the vivid red of a Dries Van Noten overcoat, cut with oversized storm flaps; the exaggerated cuff of a Prada shirt, peeking out from beneath the sleeve of a technical parka; or the easy, sporty cut of tailored trousers from Loro Piana and Wooyoungmi, the latter featuring the kind of zip pockets one might find on track pants.

Gooden, who says he uses ‘the shapes, sounds and conversations’ to influence his photography, says the story was about ‘crafting characters and narratives’. ‘It’s all part of the act,’ he says. ‘The images are the final result of a built up symphony, orchestrated long before they reach the pages, and sung once seen.’

Models: Gideon Adeniyi at Next London, Arthur Vaughan at Elite. Casting: Concorde Casting. Hair: Michael Harding using Bumble & Bumble. Make-up: Sarah Edenborough. Photography assistants: Sam Robbins, Tommy Aucott. Fashion assistants: Minna de Bagota, Leonie Dennett. Production assistant: Danielle Quigley.

A version of this article appears in the November 2026 Art Issue of Wallpaper*, available from 8 October in print on newsstands, on the Wallpaper* app on Apple iOS, and to subscribers of Apple News +. Subscribe to Wallpaper* today

Jack Moss is the Fashion & Beauty Features Director at Wallpaper*, having joined the team in 2022 as Fashion Features Editor. Previously the digital features editor at AnOther and digital editor at 10 Magazine, he has also contributed to numerous international publications and featured in ‘Dazed: 32 Years Confused: The Covers’, published by Rizzoli. He is particularly interested in the moments when fashion intersects with other creative disciplines – notably art and design – as well as championing a new generation of international talent and reporting from international fashion weeks. Across his career, he has interviewed the fashion industry’s leading figures, including Rick Owens, Pieter Mulier, Jonathan Anderson, Grace Wales Bonner, Christian Lacroix, Kate Moss and Manolo Blahnik.

items.title: Discover Ellis King, the artist making sense of women's experiences
items.description: ‘I became a parent and had a really difficult journey getting there,’ says British painter Ellis King, who is examining the quiet spaces where unresolved trauma lives in her debut exhibition at London’s SQFT: Space Gallery.
items.author: Hannah Silver
paragraphs: ‘I became a parent and had a really difficult journey getting there,’ says British painter Ellis King, who is examining the quiet spaces where unresolved trauma lives in her debut exhibition at London’s SQFT: Space Gallery.

It makes sense that King turned inwards when creating her paintings, which are both deeply autobiographical and highly charged. Her scenes capture the mundanity of existence, yet sizzle with the tension inherent in a moment when experience briefly catches up with you, unawares – in King’s paintings, women freeze at the sink, or in the bath, lost in a recollection.

‘It changes something inside you when you have a baby, and I think that, coupled with the stress of my experience, switched something in me that I hadn't been aware of before,’ King says. ‘It was a bit like the blinkers were removed and I suddenly saw, on a small scale, how many women experience these huge, life-changing things, and then you're just kind of left to crack on. It was all of that we go through that's just never seen or heard.’

King’s distinctive style sits somewhere between reality and abstraction, her self-portraiture a foil rooted in realism, jarring against the sharp graphics and flat planes upon which she sits. ‘Working in self-portraiture meant I could be honest about the emotions I'd actually felt – disgust, shame, pity, exhaustion – rather than softening them,’ says King. ‘Those quieter moments are so often set at home, too. It holds some of the best and worst moments of our lives, and yet so much of what happens there stays unseen. A lone figure in a domestic space can carry a huge amount without anything dramatic happening at all. The quiet moments are where so much of women's private experience lives, unremarked on, easy to miss, but often where the real weight sits.’

For King, the paintings become a way to explore and consider her own anger, at a system which lets women down, and at the expectations women are held to. Ultimately, though, she wants the works to begin a conversation, rather than an argument. By rooting these scenes in her personal experience, King opens the doors for a dialogue in a new medium. ‘Quite honestly, I think I came back to painting partly out of rage at the system, and partly because I needed somewhere for all of that experience to go. I'd always painted portraiture, so it was the natural language for me to return to. I didn't fully realise it at the time, but painting became a way of processing what had happened. That experience has stayed at the centre of my practice. It's what made me interested in the things women carry quietly.’
Spilt Milk at SQFT: Space Gallery until 5 November

Hannah Silver is Head of Art & Culture at Wallpaper*. A writer, editor and author with over 20 years of experience in journalism, spanning national newspapers and independent magazines, she has overseen offbeat art trends and conducted in-depth profiles for print and digital, as well as writing and commissioning extensively across the worlds of culture and luxury since joining in 2019.

Apartamento was founded in Barcelona in 2008. Its namesake magazine, published twice yearly and widely considered one of the most influential interiors publications of the past two decades, is rooted in how people actually live: the spaces they inhabit, the food they cook, the work they make, and the conviction with which they build their lives. Known for its unfiltered, human approach, each issue brings long-form conversations with artists, writers, designers, and thinkers across disciplines, accompanied by photography that unsettles conventional categories.

The values of the magazine extend beyond print. Through events, collaborations, exhibitions, design objects, and a growing body of short and documentary films, Apartamento builds community in real spaces around the world.

Since 2015, Apartamento has published books across a range of formats: monographs, cookbooks, photobooks, architecture series, artist books, and even a graphic novel. The publishing programme extends the editorial curiosity of the magazine into longer, more sustained forms, spanning art, design, architecture, food, and visual culture.

Members receive each issue of Apartamento magazine at a special 20% discount, plus unlimited access to our digital archive—including every interview, essay, and story ever published in our previous issues. In addition, members receive an automatic 10% discount in our Shop, as well as a free Apartamento Tote Bag and one 60-day trial for MUBI.

Current issues of Apartamento magazine tend to sell out quickly, and all earlier issues are sold out and can be hard to find. Our digital archive preserves each and every issue of the magazine on our website, a place where members can read every interview, essay, and story ever published!
The exact cost of shipping each issue express to your home is calculated at check out, according to the competive rates our courier partners offer us.

items.title: A conversation with Eileen Myles for Apartamento magazine issue #37
items.description: Marfa: ‘For a time I / stole trays / from hotels / & now I steal / cups’ writes Eileen Myles in ‘Göteborg’, a poem which becomes a love letter to desire itself. I wonder if any of the stolen objects exist in Eileen’s real world: ‘Yeah, and it was a beautiful w
items.author: Valeria Tusquets
paragraphs: Marfa: ‘For a time I / stole trays / from hotels / & now I steal / cups’ writes Eileen Myles in ‘Göteborg’, a poem which becomes a love letter to desire itself. I wonder if any of the stolen objects exist in Eileen’s real world: ‘Yeah, and it was a beautiful wooden tray. That lives here’. Despite famously moving to New York City to become a poet in 1974, a metropolis which serves as the backdrop for much of their work, in this instance, ‘here’ is Marfa, Texas. Situated in North America’s largest desert with a population currently under 2,000, Marfa became a magnet for creatives after the artist Donald Judd moved there from New York in the ‘70s, and there has been an uneasy truce between outsiders and locals since then. Jokingly referred to as their ‘fortress of solitude’, Eileen’s Marfa home looks like many on their street, with a pickup truck parked outside a chain-link fence and little city blocks of prickly pear cactus dotted around their lot.

Eileen’s work has been translated into dozens of languages, and they have published more than 20 books across poetry, fiction, and nonfiction, earning them a Guggenheim Fellowship and an Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant. One of Eileen’s many superpowers as a writer is their ability to marry first-person narrative with more ephemeral truths, or, as they say, ‘trusting the mechanism of desire…[the] desire for certain language to sit over some curve of a moment’. This realness, coupled with writing about a character named ‘Eileen Myles’, has also led to being flattened by labels—another Charles Bukowski or Patti Smith—as they slid between poetry and prose. ‘I have a specific system that downplays grammar in a lot of ways’, they say, but their system of delaying any easy resolution is also grammatical; there’s a really tight thought, but they don’t let it resolve immediately. We are taken away, shown something new. The action is deferred until the text realises its necessary climax.

Inside their home, cut-outs between rooms create a flow where kitchen peeks into office peeks into bedroom peeks into living room. A big picture window in their office, paid for when the show Transparent bought some of Eileen’s poems and based a poet character on them, looks out into the yard towards their ‘writing shack’ which sports a clawfoot bathtub, a bench press and weights, and a desk facing double sliding doors out onto the porch where we sit and sip Topo Chico. While access to DC Comics’ original Fortress of Solitude is controlled by a key carved from super-dense dwarf star material weighing half a million tonnes—imagine lifting 100 elephants or the weight of a small cloud—Eileen’s own abode is guarded by three desert-coloured pups who sound an imposing alarm when we pull up.

items.title: PRE-ORDER: Written at Night, Ettore Sottsass
items.description: The third in our reading series, Written at Night is the fragmented autobiography of Ettore Sottsass, one of the most seminal figures of 20th-century radical design. Originally written in Italian and published posthumously in 2010 as Scritto di notte, it now a
paragraphs: The third in our reading series, Written at Night is the fragmented autobiography of Ettore Sottsass, one of the most seminal figures of 20th-century radical design. Originally written in Italian and published posthumously in 2010 as Scritto di notte, it now arrives in English for the first time, translated by one of the most distinguished translators of Italian literature into English, Alastair McEwen.

As he recounts his upbringing in Trento and Turin, his conscription in WWII, his Milan debut, his dance with poverty, and his travels—from Cuba with Hemingway to a snowy Italian night drive with Ginsberg to the fever of India—Written at Night begins as a slow tide into the mind of one of radical design’s greatest figures, only to sweep you up in its storm. Digging through the debris of memory, he finds the precious metals of people and places, so that what he’s writing in the dark is a sweeping blueprint of love, lust, and survival. In his attempts to start from childhood and climb forwards, Sottsass produces a piece of art in and of itself—self-interrupting, self-critical, self-affirming, self-annihilating.
Written at Night joins our growing reading book series, following Essential and The Unimportance of Form.

Ettore Sottsass (1917–2007) was an Austrian-born Italian postmodernist designer and architect, considered one of the most seminal figures in 20th design, and hailed for co-founding the design collective known as the Memphis Group. Considered a polymath by many, he moved freely between furniture, glass, lamps, jewellery, objects for the home and office, as well as the design of many buildings and interiors, magazines, and publications. Alongside a significant canon of published books, his contribution to design has earned him four Compassi d’Oro. His works are exhibited in the permanent collections of museums around the world, such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the Centre Pompidou in Paris, and the Victoria & Albert Museum in London.

Alastair McEwen is considered to be one of the most distinguished translators of Italian literature into English. To date, he has published over 100 book-length translations, essays, articles, and poems, plus several feature film scripts and operatic librettos. He has translated some of the most important Italian writers of our time: Umberto Eco, Roberto Calasso, Antonio Tabucchi, Fleur Jaeggy, Alessandro Baricco, Aldo Busi, and many others.
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
Release date: November 16, 2026

items.title: Making a Show, Sabine Marcelis
items.description: Making a Show is a photobook with Dutch artist and designer Sabine Marcelis, published on the occasion of her first museum exhibition at Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, Sabine Marcelis—Light and Color, on view from October 30, 2026 to April 4, 2027. Photographed
paragraphs: Making a Show is a photobook with Dutch artist and designer Sabine Marcelis, published on the occasion of her first museum exhibition at Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, Sabine Marcelis—Light and Color, on view from October 30, 2026 to April 4, 2027. Photographed by Mattia Balsamini inside Sabine’s Rotterdam studio in the months before the opening, the book documents an exhibition in transit: light, colour, and material stretched, poured, altered, and refined until they reach the simplicity that is Sabine’s fingerprint. Smashed mirrors, pink resin slabs, perfect droplets—all part of a symbiotic world, where the work produced inside the studio is in constant conversation with the hands that supply it from outside. Alongside, curator Damian Fopp grounds the book with a written introspection on living inside her universe as the show took shape, declaring by the end that ‘what appears effortless is anything but’. Punctuated by WhatsApp messages and email snapshots between Sabine’s team and the museum’s, Making a Show distils the incantatory movement of an exhibition in the making and the infrastructure of people behind it.

Sabine Marcelis is a Dutch artist and designer based in Rotterdam. Working across installations, objects, and spatial projects, she explores light, colour, and material, collaborating closely with a network of local manufacturers to push each to its limits. For the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival 2026, Sabine designed one of the headlining large-scale art installations, an immersive temporary installation titled Maze. She has also received multiple Designer of the Year honours (2020–2024) and her works are part of permanent museum collections worldwide, including MoMA, the Stedelijk Museum, and the Vitra Design Museum. Sabine Marcelis was previously featured in Apartamento magazine issue #21. Find her story from our digital archive here.

Mattia Balsamini is an Italian photographer based between London and Milan. After joining David LaChapelle’s studio in 2010 as a studio assistant and archivist, Mattia went on to develop personal and editorial projects through collaborations with institutions including MIT and NASA. His work has been exhibited at the Triennale di Milano, MAXXI, the Sandretto Re Rebaudengo Foundation, and the Italian Cultural Institute in San Francisco.

items.title: ADRIEN BRODY - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star
paragraphs: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star

Twenty-two years after he became the youngest ever winner of a best actor Oscar, for ‘The Pianist’, Adrien Brody has gone and done it again, this time taking home an Academy Award for his deeply moving performance as Hungarian architect László Toth in ‘The Brutalist’. What makes it all the more remarkable is that only a few years ago Adrien had all but given up acting. The awards are much deserved, of course. Adrien, 52, is an intense and uniquely gifted actor, which also makes him entertaining company. He doesn’t do things in half measures. He’s all in, all the time, and not afraid to speak his mind. In the following story Adrien engages in some energetic verbal ping-pong and gets dressed up in fashion by his friend Thom Browne. It captures some of the essence of what makes him such an incredible performer.
From Fantastic Man n° 40 – 2025
Photography by ILYA LIPKIN

The instant Adrien Brody sweeps into the room, he begins to express what I will soon come to think of as his resting affect: a kind of intense but fuzzy gratitude. “I just got back from London yesterday night,” he tells me. “Feeling very blessed with all the love that’s been coming my way. It’s a really special moment. It really is.” Maybe it’s just for now, in these hectic weeks promoting ‘The Brutalist’ ahead of the Academy Awards, but it’s with words like these that Brody seems at his most comfortable, and throughout our conversation he will periodically return to similar sentiments, restating and expanding upon them with evident sincerity.

With other kinds of words, though, it will often come to feel as though there are fault lines everywhere. Seconds after this initial declaration, I ask Brody – my question intended as little more than small talk to fill the empty space between us as we greet each other and take our seats – whether it feels like he’s being carried away in a whirlwind. He responds – not just in his words but in his body language too – as though he’s being somehow misunderstood or as though something wonderful is at risk of being spoiled.

“No, it’s not that at all,” he says, correcting me firmly. “No, my feet are on the ground. I’m ultra-present. I’m ultra-present and able to reciprocate the love. It’s different. Being older gives you a degree of perspective. It’s been a very long time since I’ve had an opportunity to do the work that I’m yearning to do. And the work is completed. So this is just something magical.”

Brody will prove to be engaging, fascinating company, and a man with plenty to say. In our conversation there will also be moments where he exudes a sense – verbally, but also through a repertoire of expressions that seem to hover between saddened and harried – that the world doesn’t quite get him.

What I then find myself wondering is whether such a sensibility might be a consequence of setbacks and reversals he has faced along his idiosyncratic chosen path, or whether it’s such a sensibility which sends you down that path in the first place. Conversely, I also find myself wondering whether it’s exactly this kind of off-kilter mindset which, when everything comes together in just the right way, somehow fuels Brody’s singular ability to inhabit and transmit a role like ‘The Brutalist’s’ László Toth with such compelling, all-consuming mastery.

It was back in 2019 when Adrien Brody was first given the script of ‘The Brutalist’, the expansive tale of a visionary Hungarian architect who escapes the Holocaust and makes his way to America, where he finds a new life – one of opportunity, but also one with horrors all of its own. Brody read it in the apartment he and his partner, fashion designer Georgina Chapman, then had in Manhattan. “I found myself very moved by the writing and the breadth of the storytelling, the complexity, the flaws of the character,” he remembers. “The opportunity for me to play someone that is experiencing so much and contending so much in life [was] wonderful. And I did consider parallels of László’s lived experience with my mother’s and my grandparents’ journey.” Brody’s mother, whose maternal grandparents were rounded up and taken to Auschwitz, survived the war in Budapest. She escaped in 1956, at the age of 13, buried under corn in a horse-drawn cart as she and her parents crossed the Austrian border. In New York, Brody grew up around his Hungarian grandparents. “So that, too, definitely is evident to me in reading it – saying: ‘Wow, I’m quite right to play this character.’”

After reading, Brody met with the director, Brady Corbet, who had written the script with his professional and personal partner, the filmmaker and actor Mona Fastvold, for brunch downtown. “A very long meeting – conversed a lot about lots of things,” Brody recalls. Nonetheless, he learned in due course that another actor had been chosen. “The message comes from your agent,” he says. “It’s either you get the message or they hope you’ve forgotten.” That’s the pattern. “I mourned the loss of this one,” he says. “I did not have expectations that it would be what it is today – I still mourned the creative loss of what I wanted to pour into it.”

Brody makes clear that over his career he has learned that this will happen, and maybe even why. “As an actor, you may be right for certain roles and you’re not necessarily eligible for them,” he says. “Even if you are quite a well-known actor and quite a successful actor. Because there are all these factors that are out of your control. You know, there are lists, and lists are based on a number of things that one might deem as an indication of success. Right? You know, consistent box office earnings are the primary reason you would be on the top of a list. But if you do make experimental choices and interesting choices in an artistic pursuit in a business, it’s not met with the same appreciation as, you know, your mother might have for your varied tastes.”

Brody points out that he’s balanced experimentation with “big blockbuster movies,” and that he enjoys those too. “But I like the range,” he says, and his suggestion seems to be that too much range has consequences. “I’m aware of how it has made certain things, such as this even, challenging,” he says. “Where I’m probably the most right performer for the role, but I wasn’t deemed valuable enough.”

This time, thankfully, everything eventually worked out. The film’s shoot was delayed several times, in part because of Covid, and by the time the project fell back in place the actor previously scheduled to play László Toth, Joel Edgerton, was no longer available. Brody heard from his agent that the role was back in play. Even then, it wasn’t as though Brody simply got a call saying the part was his. “No, not at all,” he says. “Not at all.” In the end, though, it was. Finally given the chance, he threw himself into it. “I knew we were making something special,” he says. “I wish I knew why things come when they do. This moment is because we’re very fortunate – all of us who have been involved in this project – that every collaborative creative element lifted up the other.”

It’s around now, a few minutes into our meeting, when another question seems to throw Brody, though this time the person asking is not me. It is the waiter, asking what Brody might like to eat or drink. From Brody’s reaction, you could easily think that he finds such an inquiry – at a pre-booked table by the window in a high-end New York hotel bar – somewhat perplexing. He talks aloud through this latest dilemma. “I’m not sure what I’m needing,” he says, then considers one kind of option. “I’m happy to have a drink,” he weighs, “but I’m also not needing it just yet.” He expands this thought. “I don’t really need anything.”
After vacillating further, he orders an oak milk decaf latte.
“Not too much milk,” he adds. “Just nice and strong.”

That ‘The Brutalist’ would allow Brody such a remarkable professional and creative renaissance is all the more marked given the place he has described finding himself in in recent years: sufficiently dejected by the opportunities coming his way that he had, unannounced, more or less turned his back on movies. As he recently put it, “I didn’t announce I was retiring, but I stepped back.” For a time, he concentrated on other artistic pursuits that he found more fulfilling, principally painting.

“I’ve been doing this so long, since I was a boy,” he says when I ask about that period. “There’s an ebb and flow in everything, in your own creative connections and personally, professionally in life, right? So I also was not under any illusion that it should just flow. But I found it oddly challenging to be up against things like this. I feel that I’ve proven my range. I’ve worked. The reason it seems inconsistent is I’ve been consistent in trying to break out of the box of subjective perception of what I am capable of doing, or what I represent for a character, or physically. Whatever it is. Too specific, often. And they find that…” He pauses, considering his words. “There’s a safer option, basically.”
“It wasn’t being reciprocated, for whatever reason,” he says. “It wasn’t. What I had to give was somehow not understood or not of value. I didn’t feel that I was of service and of value.”
How did that lack of reciprocation make him feel?

“I didn’t feel like I needed to prove that I was worth it. If I wasn’t, I’m going to go do something else that makes me feel good. I work primarily to feel connected and to feel immersed in something creative. And I handle my side of the bargain.”
I ask him whether he feels like he does all this for the same reasons as his peers do it.

“I mean, I would think so,” he says. “Like what? Like what reason?” Then he supplies his own answer. “I think anybody who cares about what they’re doing, which is such personal work – you have to embody the role. You have to ingest it and live it and feel it and be it. And you can only do that well if you feel it and believe in it.”
But, I put to him, my gut feeling is that a lot of actors, including some very talented people, may have a slightly more detached or casual relationship with their work.
“Yeah,” acknowledges Brody, and he laughs in a way that’s tricky to read. “I’m not detached enough. Or casual, I guess.”
I point out that, although I’ve only known him for 20 minutes, my sense is that he doesn’t want to be.
When I further echo this – suggesting out loud that he wants to be like he is – the notion seems to spark something in Brody, this time in a more helpful way.

“You know, it’s funny,” he says. “When I was young, there were a lot of tough kids in my neighbourhood, and I was always very sensitive. I was always amazed at how certain ones weren’t empathetic. You know, how they would torture ants and things when we would play, and how they got pleasure out of that. I was littler than them, and I didn’t really want to say all the time, like, ‘Why are you going to hurt…?’ because they’ll just pick on me. And I was always kind of aware that it was harder. It was harder to be more sensitive.”

From the age of four, Brody grew up in the New York suburb of Woodhaven, Queens, and he has occasionally alluded over the years to various rough aspects around the edges of this experience of growing up in a neighbourhood suffering from high levels of drug and gun crime. He compares it in general terms to his life these days: “Now, I have no one in my life that isn’t on the path that I feel we should all be on. But I think growing up in Queens I didn’t know anyone, really, who was on the path.”
And yet, I point out to him, it sounds as though while he’s grateful for what he didn’t end up doing, he still feels slightly romantic about that world.

“I am a little nostalgic for it,” he agrees. “It wasn’t terrible. It was also another time. Like, the whole world was different, let alone New York City. It was different. There were no [mobile] phones. I was on the street very young. I was taking the train. I was riding bikes with a bunch of kids around the neighbourhood. I was getting into trouble. I was kind of left on my own. I didn’t have a pager or a phone with a tracker on it. I wasn’t seeing what kids were doing on social media and living a better life, and ‘Why don’t I have these sneakers?’ I just lived. Lived.”

Following up on what he’d just said, I ask him what trouble he was getting into; this will be another of those moments where the mood shifts. “Here we go…” he says. But he nonetheless offers a response.
“I was around a lot of…yeah, a lot of stuff,” he says. “It was a lot of hardship…and there was a lot of… It was wild. It was just a wild time. You know, I was a good kid…but I was around a lot.”

There are a lot of long pauses in this answer, and as he speaks I feel like I can almost see all the things Brody is remembering but not saying flashing across his eyes and around the edges of his mouth. It’s quite a show. If I could transcribe everything he thought of between those sentences, I suggest to him, it would be quite a paragraph, wouldn’t it?

“It would be,” he confirms, and his laugh seems one of genuine shared amusement. “Yes. It sure would. And I’d love to share wonderful stories with you. Just somehow things always get taken out of context. I never would brag about doing things that…you know, whatever.”

We leave that there, but one of his mother’s books offers a fascinating snapshot into a different side of Brody’s childhood. His mother, Sylvia Plachy, is an acclaimed documentary photographer. ‘Unguided Tour’ was published in 1990, the year Brody turned 17. It’s far from a family album – it contains a dizzying variety of evocative photos, many taken around New York and quite a few in Eastern Europe, alongside occasional portraits of interesting notables (amongst them William S. Burroughs, Louise Bourgeois, Jorge Luis Borges, Claude Lanzmann, Hubert Selby Jr. and Tom Waits) – though there is one image of a joyous young Brody in a pool with his grandfather. But there are occasional pieces of text placed next to photographs, and several images are accompanied by words Brody apparently said to his mother when he was very young. (Brody is referred to throughout as Mishi, the name his mother used to call him.)

This, for instance, is from 1977, when he was four years old: “Mommy, I had a very sad dream. I was in a restaurant with a grown-up girl and I really liked her. She even bought me ice cream. But when we came out she just crossed the street and left me, and I’m not allowed to cross the street by myself. She just said good-bye and I don’t know why she left me. I loved her even more than I love you. I’m going to sing a song about it: ‘She left me and I don’t know why she left me, I really loved her.’”

And this is from the following year, when he was five: “Mommy, I had a bad dream; men made out of metal were after me with their metal ray guns. But then my nose started bleeding, I shouted ‘Time Out!’ and they all stopped.”
When I mention these to Brody, I comment that it sounds like he was a strange kid.
“I don’t think it was that strange,” he counters. “It was imaginative.”
What kind of four-year-old, I ask him, tells a fully realised story about a girl not being in love with him, or a five-year-old about men of metal coming at him?
“I don’t know,” he says. “This one.”
I reiterate: Not everyone, I promise you.

“But you think it’s strange?” he says. I point out that I like that he said those things. “Okay, good. It’s unusual – I don’t disagree. Yeah, it’s something.” After we talk a little more, he adds: “They sound like me. It sounds like something I would come up with.”
And that, I point out, is what I’m trying to understand.

“You can see that I’m an actor,” he reflects, “and that was her intuition.” He seems to be casting forward from age five to a famous pivot point in his life: when he was eleven, his mother was sent on assignment to the American Academy of Dramatic Arts, and when she saw their young people’s programme she thought it might suit her son. That’s how Brody started acting. He talks more about those qualities he had as a child. “I can see a lot of things, and I can see circumstances – imagine them fully,” he says. “Quite fully in emotion. I think those are qualities that are necessary to inhabit others. I am quite empathetic, and I think that’s been cultivated through that process.”
But it’s interesting, I say, that he was like this when he hadn’t yet had any training.

So where do you think it comes from? “No idea,” he says. “Just there.” But then he offers what seems like a suggestion. “My parents treated me with respect as a child. They didn’t treat me like a child.”

Brody has said that his parents saw acting as a way of keeping him out of the trouble that might have subsumed him in the neighbourhood. When I ask whether this was a big impulse, he says no at first but then offers up a surprising detail. “My dad considered me going to a military academy at one point. He knew what was around. Both of them understood that I needed some kind of creative outlet, that I was very creative. And that’s what’s evident in those things: that I had a very imaginative mind, a very curious mind. And hanging out on the block wouldn’t have given me a leg up in that space. It would suppress it, ultimately.”

Brody enjoyed some success right from the start. Aged 14, he was a lead in a TV movie, ‘Home at Last’, playing a New York orphan shipped out west. The following year, he was cast, if only for a day, by Francis Ford Coppola in his portion of ‘New York Stories’. A variety of roles followed before, at 23, he landed a wonderful, improbable opportunity. The director Terrence Malick was a legend, partly because 20 years earlier he had stopped making movies. The filmmaking world was abuzz with news that Malick was planning to return with an adaptation of James Jones’s World War II novel about combat in the Pacific, ‘The Thin Red Line’. It seemed as if the whole of Hollywood wanted to be in the movie. After Brody met with Malick – they talked for two hours in a hotel near where we are now, looking down at the skaters in Central Park – he was cast as one of the leads.

There’s a version of the script online, apparently close to the one Malick used when they all headed off to Australia to shoot for half a year. Brody’s character’s name, Corporal Fife, appears in the script 315 times. Fife speaks on 127 separate occasions. “We shot six months,” Brody recalls, “and we did many embellishments.”

In the lead-up to the release of a film Malick was yet to show to anybody, Brody did press interviews as the hot new young star he now was presumed to be. Malick did call him at one point and mentioned that his role had been “reduced,” but nothing even slightly prepared him for the truth. Just before the film’s release – still a grand secret – Brody was invited to what he was told was a private screening in New York. He took his parents. It wasn’t a private screening – selected press were there too – and as the film’s nearly three hours unspooled in front of everyone, Brody discovered that Malick had completely changed his movie in editing. Brody’s character appeared on screen for only a few minutes, and you could count the fleeting lines he spoke on one hand.

Brody has often talked about this as a formative experience and a key moment in his story, but today he seems less willing to reflect on it. “You want to get into all the past and the hardships. I don’t think about them. I don’t harp on them. You can reference them all you like, but I don’t harp on them,” he says.

I point out that the whole point of talking about any of this is to provide context to his role in ‘The Brutalist’ being such a triumph. And though it’s a little awkward to raise, I feel like he should know that I’ve spent much of the last eight years writing a book about events during the Holocaust in Lithuania and how one deals with the aftermath (the recently published ‘No Road Leading Back’), which, in a very different way, processes some of the same themes that lie at the heart of ‘The Brutalist’. We talk about that for a while. “It’s good to represent these stories,” he says respectfully.

Eventually I tell him that I should ask him some more annoying questions about his past. “It’s not annoying – it’s really not,” he says, and returns to the subject of ‘The Thin Red Line’. “It’s just, to then read it again – this moment, this terrible situation…” Even so, whether or not because of the break we have had, Brody addresses the situation with some thoughtfulness. “I do feel like you asked me why and how things happen,” he says. “And I don’t know, but that happened for a reason. You know what I mean? And that shaped me. It shaped my journey. It gave me a great understanding of loss as it pertains to my work. And had potential to be very detrimental to my future and the work that I’ve dedicated my whole life to. I gave everything to that project, too. Unquestioningly.”
It could have broken you, I point out.

“Yes,” he exclaims. “I was 23! But my dad always has a really great perspective of it.” (Brody’s father, Elliot, is a retired history teacher.) “He said: ‘That movie, as painful as it was for you, made a lot of people know about you in your business. Whether they saw your work or not, they knew about you.’ And he’s right. But I was concerned one could make the assumption that I must not have been good enough for the part. You have this iconic filmmaker who hasn’t made a movie in all these years, and then you have an actor who out of nowhere gets this thing – he must not have been good enough. And that’s what I felt. Like, I had no way to prove my side of this.”

Thankfully, at least through the lens of history, not too long a time passed between what could have been a debilitating humiliation and Brody’s first unequivocal triumph: playing the central figure in Roman Polanski’s ‘The Pianist’, based on the true story of a Polish-Jewish musician, Władysław Szpilman, and his desperate struggles to survive in the Warsaw ghetto during World War II. “It was profound – and also out of nowhere, you know,” Brody says. “It was only a few years from where I thought: ‘I may never work again.’”

To me, Brody seems like the kind of high-wire actor who, in a film that works less well, can sometimes appear stranded; you can almost viscerally feel the disconnect between the film he’s imagined and the film that is. But when everything works it’s the opposite: he entirely inhabits a character in a way which is mesmerising without being showy. So it is in ‘The Brutalist’; so it was in ‘The Pianist’. “It was nothing I had experienced,” he reminisces. “You know, I had such a responsibility throughout the making of it, saddled with the need to faithfully represent a survivor’s story and what it speaks to of the enormity of loss. And [as] a young man, I had to deeply immerse and understand that level of loss that was so profound that I didn’t have an understanding, really. I opened up a portal to a depravity and the horror and cruelty that exists. My association to darkness was very different prior to that. So that was a big shift. Darkness and light. And finding light through darkness…”

At this very moment, something remarkable happens. Presumably in response to the dwindling daylight outside, just as Brody says the phrase “light through darkness,” the lighting in the hotel bar suddenly surges to about twice its previous level of brightness.
“See!” he declares. “I have a way about me!” He looks delighted. “If we did that on the take,” he says, “that would be in the movie!”

For his role in ‘The Pianist’, Brody was nominated for an Oscar for the first time. The other four nominees – Jack Nicholson, Michael Caine, Daniel Day-Lewis and Nicolas Cage – had all previously won Oscars, and in the weeks beforehand, as the major precursor awards were announced, Brody won none of them.
But on the evening, it was his name that was read out. He became – and to this day remains – the youngest winner of the best actor trophy.

“Time did slow down,” he says. “I remember that. I remember that feeling where it literally warped down to something. It was enormous. It was enormous. And it was a real outpouring of love. That room lit up. And there I was, surrounded by so many people I admire, and all the influential people in my industry. And I just… I was plucked from obscurity. I had been working and toiling away as an actor for 17 years. And overnight” – he laughs – “I was now successful. In the world’s eyes.”

‘The Brutalist’ is now on the same awards circuit. So far, it is going well. A couple of weeks before we met, Brody gave an emotional speech after winning best actor at the Golden Globes. It is, of course, a strange quirk that the two roles towering above all others in his career, as different as they are in most respects other than the commitment and intensity he brings to them, are both connected to the Holocaust.

It’s also the kind of low-hanging fruit ready-made for awards show hosts, and in the first few minutes of the Golden Globes, during comedian Nikki Glaser’s opening monologue, she said, “Oh, look! It’s two-time Holocaust survivor Adrien Brody.” As the camera fixed on his face, Brody gamely grinned and blew Glaser a kiss.
As I watched, I tell him, I wondered whether he was wincing slightly inside.

“Of course,” he says. “Of course. You know the nature of her humour. Of course. I feel very privileged to have been able to speak to this horrific time in my work. Such great depths. And there’s been a lot of ancestral loss and struggles, and I don’t take it lightly, obviously.”
Not long before Brody leaves the bar, I ask him what he thinks his talent is. He takes some time before he starts to speak.

“I’ve managed to not lose the imaginative quality of my youth through my experiences in life,” he tells me. “And I can apply that similar curiosity and enthusiasm to my work, and my encounters with others. And it gives me a sense of freedom. And I can incorporate that into my work, and the process of doing my work. I can find, I can access, things that I find quite fulfilling and real, that shed light on lots of things in my work and in life. So that is what I’m most grateful for.”
I ask him when he’s happiest.
“When I’m working,” he says. “When I’m immersed in something creative. The most alive, yes. Definitely not on vacation or something. I don’t know. I’m more happy working.”

He says he doesn’t yet know what he will do next. “There are a few things that are interesting,” he says. (Naturally, those lists will be looking much better for him right now.) Even aside from ‘The Brutalist’, in recent times Brody’s world seems to have opened up a little. When he renewed his focus on acting after his unannounced break (he has credited Chapman with nudging him in that direction), he began to make distinctive contributions to TV shows, most notably ‘Peaky Blinders’, ‘Succession’ and ‘Poker Face’, and renewed his ongoing relationship with Wes Anderson, now five films deep. Brody also co-wrote, produced and starred in a dark revenge movie, ‘Clean’, and wrote its music. (He has been making beats for many years.) There’s another script he’s writing, inspired by a painting he saw in Madrid’s Prado museum. And, for that matter, he wants to get back to his own painting. “I have no time to do anything at the moment, unfortunately,” he says ruefully. “Like, literally no time. I would like a window to paint a little.”

Brody made a documentary, too, several years back: ‘Stone Barn Castle’, about the seven-year renovation of a building he owns in upstate New York. He showed the film once at the SXSW festival, but it hasn’t been seen since, and he tells me he wants to redo it sometime, change the structure and the storytelling. “I envision another iteration before it’s something to share publicly,” he explains. “But I have an enormous amount of footage.” And, like so many things, it may have already found its worth in another way.

“It’s fascinating,” he says of the documentary, “especially in context of me playing an architect, having spent a good seven years toiling away and trying to bring a building back to life and integrate all these architectural elements. And my aesthetic, which is quite unique, influenced from Eastern sources and modern things – that, too, probably informed some connection with my character.”

As he further explains the connection between the renovation and his most recent landmark character, I realise that Adrien Brody could just as much be talking about his life. And maybe that’s the point.
“The need to complete it,” he says. “And not letting it get the best of me. And all of the stuff you have to overcome to get there.”

Chris Heath, as mentioned in the preceding interview, is the author of the recently published book ‘No Road Leading Back: An Improbable Escape from the Nazis and the Tangled Way We Tell the Story of the Holocaust’. It was voted a 2024 book of the year by ‘The Washington Post’.

items.title: AI WEIWEI - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: The extraordinary artist makes monumental installations of a radical and provocative nature, telling the truth about China and putting his very life in danger
paragraphs: The extraordinary artist makes monumental installations of a radical and provocative nature, telling the truth about China and putting his very life in danger

The Turbine Hall at London’s Tate Modern is one of the world’s most coveted exhibition spaces, and the next artist to fill it is Ai Weiwei. Although a veteran of major art events such as Documenta 12 and the 48th Venice Biennale, in his home country of China Ai Weiwei is as much known for his activism as he is for his aesthetics. Based in Beijing, where he is under constant surveillance, the artist brazenly flouts the law to bring his view on modern day China to the rest of the world. He is an avid user of fashionable social networking sites, and on an average day he tweets approximately 107 times.
From Fantastic Man n° 12 — 2010
“Okay, let’s start,” says the artist Ai Weiwei, greeting me with a wide smile.

It’s 9am on a sunny Beijing morning – so much for creative types sleeping late – and Ai Weiwei has already been up and at it for several hours. Given his reputation, I assume he’s been irritating the Chinese government and tickling his legions of followers by way of his famously acerbic Twitter feeds. (Consider: “The system doesn’t follow the law. The people don’t believe in the law. So who’s out of luck?”)

I have made what’s been called the ‘ritual pilgrimage’ to the compound Ai designed and built for himself in the city’s northeast outskirts. It’s a journey previously taken by the likes of Gerhard Schröder, Diane von Furstenberg and countless others who fancy themselves sophisticated and international. From the centre of town, you go past unremarkable high rises and light industry zones, beneath highway overpasses and railroad tracks and, finally, along a quiet, gingko-lined road. A blue metal door marks the entrance to Ai’s fabled home and studio, which he shares with his wife, the artist Lu Qing, and which these days also happens to be under surveillance by Chinese authorities.

Inside, the word FUCK is mounted on a garden wall in big neon letters. Otherwise, the scene is quite tranquil. Ai is sitting next to a pleasant, grassy lawn framed by cypress trees, antique stone fragments and thickets of bamboo. He’s accompanied by a member of his 30-or-so-person studio – a young woman, Germanic, I’d say, possibly Scandinavian – and several of his unconfirmed number of cats and dogs. (“We don’t really know how many we have,” he admits.) Ai has close-cropped hair, an unruly beard and an ample belly that together define what you might call the Ai Weiwei look.
