And I remember that after a couple washes and a couple of gestures, it felt finished a lot quicker, and in New York, it felt finished only after days of just pushing through it.
Then the hibiscus flower itself, it’s from the Caribbean, right? Is it associated with one of the other places you’ve lived in, aside from those two cities?

Yeah, although the first hibiscus I drew was in New York, because it was by the playground by my parents’ house, next to a mural of Marcus Garvey. I remember painting it and bringing it to my stepdad because they had these hibiscus flowers in their garden as well. And so even though I really first met it in the Caribbean, the first time I engaged with it in a real way was in New York.
14. BREAKFAST AT TIFFANY’S

As a kind of appendix to the Pantin show, Alvaro created a playlist of 45 songs which, thanks to the underrated magic of QR codes, was available to listen to as visitors pondered the work in situ or as they reflected on it afterwards. Various hip-hop artists are present in the playlist, which includes two tracks by DMX (‘How’s it Goin’ Down’ and ‘Slippin’’) and ‘Jesus Walks’ from Kanye West’s 2004 album ‘The College Dropout’, for example.

Perhaps most characteristically, it begins with three separate interpretations of the same pop-cultural artefact, namely ‘Moon River’, a song whose overfamiliarity never seems to nullify its impact of making the listener temporarily imagine themselves as the star of a movie. There’s the sparkling original by Audrey Hepburn from the soundtrack to the film ‘Breakfast at Tiffany’s’; there’s Frank Sinatra’s crooned one; and there’s Frank Ocean’s rendition, released as a single on Valentine’s Day 2018, turning an otherwise wistful and nostalgic number into something more assertive and forward-looking.

It’s the Hepburn, says Alvaro, that really moves him, and indeed the show took its inspiration from Truman Capote’s novel: “One day I picked up ‘Breakfast at Tiffany’s’ at Strand Book Store in Union Square and I realised the NYC I was experiencing in the ’90/2000s was what Truman Capote wrote about in ‘Breakfast at Tiffany’s’.”

That’s from a statement Alvaro released with the exhibition. Can he elaborate? “It was mostly about what I thought of as an end of a New York that I think of as being between ‘Breakfast at Tiffany’s’ and ‘Sex and the City’. It’s a very particular New York. How do you go from being a gay guy in the middle of Pennsylvania who’s deeply religious, socially awkward at best, and imagine yourself to be Andy Warhol? Or your Notorious B.I.G. or your Jay-Z? There was a New York that was about how — no matter where you started — you could get to this impossible thing that was only limited by your imagination.”

The Duveen Galleries at Tate Britain are 300 feet long. Over a million people pass through them each year. The most recent commission to fill the galleries was by Hew Locke and was called ‘The Procession’, back in 2022. Alvaro Barrington’s project will run from 29 May until 26 January 2025.
Styling by Stuart Williamson. Fashion by Bottega Veneta. Photographic assistance by Andy Moores. Styling assistance by Helly Pringle. Production by Fiona Percival and Phoebe Clothier.

items.title: The Gentlewoman – Autumn Durald Arkapaw
items.description: Autumn Durald Arkapaw was destined to be in the movies. Her parents named her after Cheyenne Autumn, John Ford's 1964 epic Western. It was at university and through watching films such as Trainspotting and Heat that Autumn found her calling as a cinematographe
paragraphs: Autumn Durald Arkapaw was destined to be in the movies. Her parents named her after Cheyenne Autumn, John Ford's 1964 epic Western. It was at university and through watching films such as Trainspotting and Heat that Autumn found her calling as a cinematographer. Forty-two projects later, in March this year, Autumn, 46, became the first woman to win the Academy Award for best cinematography, for her work on Ryan Coogler's Sinners. She shot it on a 30-kilogram IMAX camera, which she nicknamed her “little refrigerator”, and a rare Ultra Panavision 70, both hauled through the sweltering heat of Louisiana to sun-drenched, shadow-thick effect. She and her cinematographer husband are bringing up their 10-year-old in Los Angeles, not far from where she's shooting Marvel's and Coogler's next Black Panther instalment. Autumn, evidently, is just beginning.

Seated in the Dolby Theatre for the Academy Awards in March, Autumn Durald Arkapaw was scanning everything in her glimmering orbit for signs. Would she be taking home the statue for best cinematography for Sinners, or would it slip away? On the one hand, her assigned aisle seat boded well; on the other, the primary predictor of Oscar success, the American Society of Cinematographers award, had gone to Michael Bauman the week before for One Battle After Another. As the evening progressed and few of the 16 record-breaking nominations for Sinners panned out, she resigned herself to simply enjoying the show.

Then she discreetly texted her publicist to ask who would be presenting the award. The answer: Demi Moore. “All of a sudden, I became really, really positive,” Autumn tells me months later when we meet at an outdoor cafe in Eagle Rock, a north-east Los Angeles neighbourhood not far from the home she shares with her husband, Adam Arkapaw, also a cinematographer, and their 10-year-old son, Aedan.

This is the first time she has told the Oscar story, and the electricity of the moment burns brightly. “If this actually happens, I’m going to thank every woman in the room,” Autumn remembers telling herself. The thought “just popped in my mind.” After Moore said her name and Ryan Coogler, the director of Sinners, rocketed out of his seat, Autumn took to the stage in her custom-made Thom Browne ensemble: silk skirt, organza shirt, black tie and lace-embroidered overcoat.

At first, she says, she stuck to her speech, naming the women who directly inspired her: Ellen Kuras, the first female cinematographer Autumn knew of as a college student, and Rachel Morrison, her friend and the first woman to be nominated for best cinematography, for Mudbound in 2018. Then, in a moment that would go viral, Autumn, in her soft, commanding voice, asked all the women in the room to stand up. “I feel like I don’t get here without you guys,” she said, a slight quiver hinting at the emotion. As performers, directors, make-up artists and others rose to their feet, the rest of the audience cheered raucously. Morrison, who was watching with friends in Mexico, tells me she “was moved to tears, because it represented so much more than her singular journey. It’s been nearly a century, and she finally broke through the glass ceiling.”

Autumn was the first woman (and the first person of colour) to win for best cinematography; after Morrison, Ari Wegner was nominated in 2021 for The Power of the Dog, and Mandy Walker in 2022 for Elvis. She is also the first female cinematographer to shoot on IMAX 65-millimetre and Ultra Panavision 70, two grand-scale film formats. (Shooting in the steamy heat of Louisiana, she carried the 30-kilogram IMAX camera on her shoulder, affectionately referring to it as her “little refrigerator”.)

At a time when AI threatens to destroy the humanity of the creative process, Autumn wants “to make sure every single moment is good, that it’s all emotionally and cinematically felt. I love movies that give you scope,” she says. “I want it to feel like a movie, and like you’re watching a movie because it’s giving you a view that’s wider than what you normally see. It feels like you’re right in the landscape.” The decision to shoot Sinners, set in the Jim Crow era of harsh racial segregation, on large format was important. “Ryan would always say, ‘We haven’t seen these characters with these faces on formats like this ever.’ It really elevates those people and their culture.”

Autumn is still benefiting from the Oscar bump with more work, and unimagined opportunities such as throwing out the first pitch for the LA Dodgers on their Black Heritage Night. But most important for Autumn is that “it just gave hope to so many women,” she says, telling me about a flight attendant of Asian descent who congratulated her at the airport recently. Her victory has shown people “that we can make a change. Women can be strong, and we can do things in this industry and beyond.”

Women have yanked open plenty of doors in Hollywood, but the one to cinematography has been jammed shut more tightly than most. The heavy equipment alone, the old saw went, would make success near-impossible for them. Autumn labels that “a farce”, with amusement rather than anger. “They were saying it just to keep us out. After being pregnant, going through childbirth, raising a child – there’s no bigger strength than that. Like, a 35-pound camera?” she says. “Or heavier, like I operated? You find the strength within you to make it happen.”

Autumn seemed predestined for cinema – the romantic adventure of it and the myriad challenges. Her parents named her after their favourite western, John Ford’s 1964 epic Cheyenne Autumn, shot in (wait for it) 65-millimetre. She was born in Oxnard, LA, but after her parents separated when she was two, she and her Filipina mother moved north to San Leandro, in the San Francisco Bay Area. “I had my family so close. My mom has six brothers, so I had a lot of cousins.” Hours were spent at the local cinema or gazing at her grandparents’ photos of their travels in America and England.

Then, when she was eight, Autumn and her mother moved to suburban Danville so Autumn could attend a better school. At the time the area wasn’t very diverse. “I never felt like an outsider,” Autumn says, “because my mom worked so hard. She’s an entrepreneur and has worked in global trade for 35 years. It was true that we had less than other people. We were in smaller homes, but my mom always made them beautiful.”

By the age of 20 she was cutting iMovies of her friends hanging out and soundtracking them herself, hinting at her future making music videos for Rihanna, Solange, Haim and others. “But my whole thing was being a photographer,” she says. “I never put my finger on it that I wanted to be a filmmaker.” Instead, she followed her interests in photography and fashion and studied art history at Loyola Marymount University.

At university she took a mandatory film genres course, and in the black-and-white glow of Raging Bull and Broadway Danny Rose, “I wanted to know everything. Who’s shooting it? Who’s making these things? What is that job like?” Those questions eventually led her to look into cinematography, and specifically to look for a woman cinematographer. It was only when she checked the credits on Blow, one of her favourite films as a teenager, and saw that Ellen Kuras was the director of photography that she thought, “Oh, there’s a girl. Great, I can do it! In my mind, if you’re raised by a single mom and you’re looking up to her, watching her do stuff, that’s it. There’s one, and so there can be two.”

The reality proved less straightforward. After graduating in 2002, Autumn spent three years at AOL, in a “nice job”. Her boss paid for a one-night-a-week UCLA extension course in cinematography. In 2005, Autumn applied to the prestigious American Film Institute (AFI) Conservatory and didn’t get a place. But she made the alternate list, and the head of cinematography encouraged her to get more experience and reapply. “I got a wonderful job as a first assistant camera on the documentary series On the Road in America and travelled across the US and eventually to the Middle East.” Autumn did reapply to the AFI cinematography course and was accepted.

Her fellow students would become her constant collaborators, her on-the-run teachers. Between her first and second years, she shot the mumblecore drama Macho for her classmate Rafael Palacio Illingworth. The 35-millimetre film won the award for best micro-budget feature at the indie Raindance festival in London in 2009. After graduation came another low-budget indie, Guadalupe the Virgin, directed by Victoria Giordana.

Then, in 2011, another AFI student introduced her to Gia Coppola. Coppola was looking for a fill-in DP for a test shoot for her first feature, Palo Alto, based on James Franco’s short stories. That day yielded one of Autumn’s most fruitful relationships. “I love working with her,” Autumn says. “We have that trust because we’ve worked together our whole careers.” After doing fashion shorts together, she and Coppola built the visual language for Palo Alto. “She’ll send me these references, and I’ll know exactly what she’s after.” Think landmark teen movies like The Last Picture Show, Dazed and Confused and, from the Coppola family canon, The Outsiders and The Virgin Suicides; Instagram images of messy teenage bedrooms; and the photography of William Eggleston and Stephen Shore. Coppola and Autumn’s collaborations are all stylised play.
“I love movies that give you scope, like you're right in the landscape.”

It was AFI, where she now guest-lectures, that taught Autumn “how important it is who you’re working with, especially for someone like me who doesn’t come from a film family.” So when the time came to find the right look for Palo Alto, she contacted Panavision, which she’d worked with as a student. It was the beginning of a lasting association with the company. To help her achieve the nostalgic 35-millimetre look she wanted on digital video, Panavision provided Zeiss Super Speed lenses, which delivered a saturated, grainy softness. Palo Alto led the director Max Minghella to ask her to shoot a music video, and later his first feature, 2018’s Teen Spirit. Autumn also caught the attention of the legendary director Spike Jonze, who hired her as his cinematographer on the Netflix comedy special Aziz Ansari: Right Now (2019) and later for Apple TV+’s Beastie Boys Story (2020). Before long, Kate Herron, the director of the first season of the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s TV series Loki, had drafted her in. Autumn received her first Primetime Emmy Award nomination for her work on episode 3, “Lamentis”.

In January 2024, she was reunited with Gia Coppola for The Last Showgirl, starring Pamela Anderson as a performer whose Vegas revue is ending after 30 years. They were shooting on 16-millimetre, and Autumn asked Panavision to create a lens especially for her. “I wanted to make an anamorphic lens that I could shoot Super 16-millimetre with and get a 2.39:1 aspect ratio,” she says. “There’s a lot of softness on the edge of the frame, but you have the women clear in the centre. It’s just a beautiful format.” Panavision’s bespoke lens captured a fishbowl feeling reflective of the story’s undertones of desperation and faded glamour. In the back of her mind, Autumn tells me, she was thinking she would use this lens for Ryan Coogler’s next project, code-named Grilled Cheese, on which they were going to collaborate. “Ryan envisioned it in 16-millimetre, something with this grittier feel. But then Sinners changed completely,” she says.

Autumn and Coogler met when Rachel Morrison, his cinematographer for Black Panther, was unavailable for the follow-up, Wakanda Forever. Morrison had a hunch that the two would hit it off. “Ryan surrounds himself with others who share a sense of empathy and intrigue,” she tells me by email. “He’s also incredibly thorough and believes in pushing the boundaries. Autumn invests and pushes herself.” Autumn tells me that at work she is “very dialled in, very serious. But I also laugh a lot because I’m working with friends.”

Morrison’s hunch was correct. Working with Coogler felt immediately familiar, Autumn says. Along with Gia Coppola, he’s become “like family” to her. “I want to work with people I believe in, that I enjoy being around and who I care about, and that’s Ryan.” After Wakanda Forever’s complicated year-long shoot, their working relationship became so strong that Coogler described it to The New York Times as “like gravity”.

For Sinners, the challenge was in shooting Michael B Jordan playing identical twins, the hustler brothers Smoke and Stack. Coogler and Autumn found inspiration in Eudora Welty’s photographs of daily life in Depression-era Mississippi and the Farm Security Administration’s Kodachrome slides held in the Library of Congress – along with Quentin Tarantino’s The Hateful Eight. “I wanted to show the land,” Autumn says. “I wanted to show the distance and that flat horizon.” After some test shoots in the California desert there was no going back: they embraced the texture and richness of extra-large film stock.

Though she has shot digitally to acclaim, namely for Palo Alto, Autumn prefers anamorphic lenses, which squeeze the image horizontally, allowing for a wider field of view, better vertical resolution and less grain. She likens the effect to looking through old glass, which “has texture and nostalgia. It’s worked in, like an old photograph. I want something to feel like it’s from the past, to get you emotional, because that’s what it’s all about.”

The anamorphic lens is part of US cinematic history. In the early 1950s, by which time more than half of US families owned TVs, Paramount and 20th Century Fox developed a widescreen filmmaking process called CinemaScope to lure viewers back to the movies. Anamorphic took over and continued to reign in the kinds of 1970s and 1980s auteur movies that inspired Autumn in her early days at university: Chinatown, Apocalypse Now, The Empire Strikes Back. In a sense, Sinners took her back to the beginning. The film reverberated into her family life as well: she reconnected with her father’s Louisiana family on the shoot. One of her paternal aunts, Janis, can be seen in the grocery store scene.

Autumn has just wrapped the pilot for Coogler’s X-Files reboot in Vancouver when we meet, and they’ll be collaborating again on the next Panther instalment, scheduled to shoot in 2027. Asked about it, she says only that “people should be excited. He’s such an exciting filmmaker that when he’s excited his team gets excited.”

Filming is a physically demanding job, and Autumn conditions her body by doing Pilates and playing tennis. “My coach is the loveliest, and I always enjoy learning the game,” she says. At home in Los Angeles, where she has lived since moving there for university in 2000, she and Aedan watch the Netflix show Formula 1: Drive to Survive. They used to see films at the Cinerama Dome on Sunset Boulevard (“I’m a sucker for popcorn and Raisinets”), fittingly, as it was designed to show extra-widescreen Cinerama films, until it closed in 2020. “But they recently announced that the Alamo Drafthouse Cinema will replace it,” she says.

Autumn’s success is an American story. The Oscar for Sinners didn’t come her way simply because it was high time to recognise a woman. Her work shines with a confidence that says: We belong here. There’s the all-too-singular joy of being on a set brimming with people of colour. But the message of belonging is most clarified in how she lights non-white skin.

“I won’t name names,” she says, “but when something’s being overlit, you can tell that that photographer is afraid a little bit, so they want to ‘make sure’. I feel like what’s cool about working with Ryan is that we’re very brave. We want to do what’s right emotionally for the character and for the story. It’s not about being afraid that someone is coming in and out of darkness, or being afraid of someone who has a very dark skin tone. There’s beauty in that, and there’s a way to light that. It’s just a trust.” Blowing out skin tones and facial expressions with too much light also screams that the camera is right there, breaking the spell. By letting faces fall into shadow, eyes eclipsed by darkness, Autumn is foregrounding a different truth. “It’s about beauty, really,” she says, as the late afternoon sun burnishes us gold. “This is why finding the right people to work with is so important. Culturally, you’re on the same page. You ask them, ‘What do you find beautiful?’ Some people will criticise letting an actor’s face go dark, but I’m OK with it and Ryan is OK with it. This is what’s going to be most beautiful, because it’s real.”

Margaret WapplerMargaret Wappler is a writer based in Los Angeles. She has interviewed the likes of Serena Williams, Margaret Atwood and Amy Adams and has written about arts and culture for the New York Times, Rolling Stone, Los Angeles Times and Washington Post, amongst others. Margaret is also the author of Neon Green,…read more Portraits by

Angalis FieldAngalis Field is a photographer, screenwriter and director based in New York City. Known for his intimate portraiture, Angalis’s work has appeared in magazines such as i-D, The New York Times and HommeGirls. His short films, The Dalles, a queer coming of age neo-Western, and Bust, a political thriller…read more

items.title: The Gentlewoman – Club
items.description: Welcome to The Gentlewoman Club. Join up to receive our fortnightly newsletter and invitations to fabulous Club get-togethers.
paragraphs: Welcome to The Gentlewoman Club. Join up to receive our fortnightly newsletter and invitations to fabulous Club get-togethers.
Northbound Outbound Unbound with Canada GooseJuly 2026, Aberdeenshire

Gentlewoman Club members headed over the Cairn o’ Mount and into Glen Dye, 15,000 acres of working Aberdeenshire land, to test the contention that nature remains our trustiest operating system. Annie Armstrong of Wild Braemar led a bracing swim in the River Dye, the piper Julie Brinklow called the group to a Woodshed lunch and the forest-bathing guide Jules Mckinnon led a serene session among the pines, and in the shadow of Clachnaben. Bliss. Photography by Murray Orr.
Wardrobe optimism with MissoniJune 2026, London

The Gentlewoman Club convened on the Georgian Terrace at Harrods for a breakfast co-hosted with the magnificent Missoni — a morning given over to the specific sartorial joys of summer dressing, the art of the zigzag and the eternal optimism of colour. The writer and Gentlewoman contributor Otegha Uwagba delivered a tableside mini-lecture. “I want clothes that match my mood,” she told us, “joyful, spontaneous, with a propensity to say yes instead of no.” The motion passed with flying colours. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
The Gentlewoman Club T-shirt arrivesApril 2026, London

Pow! The Gentlewoman Club T-shirt is out in the world. Our covetable boxy-fit tee got its IRL welcome in London via a festive gathering hosted by our friends at magCulture, with Issue nº 33 of The Gentlewoman in the window. Spun from 100 per cent cotton, The Gentlewoman Club T-shirt is a heavyweight hitter at 205gsm. See it in the magazine. Snap it up on the website. Wear it at many happy Gentlewoman Club events to come. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
The joy of joining in with TOASTOctober 2025, New York

Clubbable? You bet. The Gentlewoman Club and TOAST took to Nine Orchard in the Big Apple for a rollicking evening devoted to the joy of joining in. The politics and pleasures of membership were brought to life by the panellists Natasha Pickowicz of Never Ending Taste, Lucy Yu of Yu & Me Books and Suzie de Rohan Willner, the CEO of TOAST, in a discussion led by The Gentlewoman’s Editor in Chief, Penny Martin. There followed questions and insights from a floor of Gentlewoman Club members that included the astrologer Susan Miller and the filmmaker Jeannie Sui Wonders. Then, a spirited mixer abuzz with new connections. Photography by Noa Griffel.
The Gentlewoman nº 32 launch do with Miu MiuSeptember 2025, London

The festive unveiling of Issue nº 32 of The Gentlewoman took place in the splendid surroundings of the Miu Miu flagship on London’s New Bond Street. Snazzy! Friends from far and wide converged for champagne and conversation. Cheers to you all. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
London to Oxfordshire and back again with Bicester VillageMay 2025, Oxfordshire

It was all aboard the 10.40 express from Marylebone as The Gentlewoman Club tripped from London to Bicester Village and back again for an anniversary celebration of the luxury shopping destination and the momentous year of its arrival. Penny Martin cut the ribbon on the Village News Kiosk, our print-packed pitstop whose merchandise includes the limited-edition publication 1995, a gentlewomanly look back at three phenomenal decades. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
The Gentlewoman nº 31 launch do with Dear FrancesMarch 2025, London

Auspiciously coinciding with the spring equinox, Issue nº 31 was launched at Shreeji Newsagents in London. Thanks to Dear Frances — whose fab mesh flats and signature loafers are famed in discerning circles — for their largesse in co-hosting, and to our dear readers, too, who always bring the zing. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
Softness in the city with VINCEOctober 2024, London

The Gentlewoman Club convened in autumnal splendour for a special tour of the Chelsea Physic Garden, London’s riverside cornucopia of healing plants. Then, it was on to the VINCE store on Draycott Avenue, where the brand’s creative director Caroline Belhumeur talked us through the outdoorsy Future Heritage collection over a seasonal brunch by Violet. All marvellously mellow. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
The Gentlewoman nº 29 launch do at Margaret HowellMarch 2024, London

Hooray! Issue nº 29 received an impeccable welcome chez Margaret Howell on London’s Wigmore Street, with special copies of the magazine featuring a cool A2 poster with artwork by Scheltens & Abbenes. Thanks to our ever-engaging readers for making it a cracking shivoo. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
Tour de force at the V&A with ChanelDecember 2023, London

The Gentlewoman Club’s 10th anniversary celebrations culminated in high style in London with our special members’ tour of the V&A’s Gabrielle Chanel. Fashion Manifesto exhibition — the hottest ticket in town — led by none other than its curator Oriole Cullen, who wowed us all with her knowledge of all things Coco. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
A legendary lunch with Versace IconsDecember 2023, London

How better to toast the glamour and ambition of Versace Icons than with a Gentlewoman Club feast along a Medusa-bedecked table? Guests from the worlds of film, fashion and music convened at Cromwell Place in London for a lunchtime lecture by Susan Irvine exploring the mythic tendrils of the Italian house’s definitive iconography. Bellissima! Photography by Holly Whittaker.
An Evening with Chaka KhanNovember 2023, New York

On the eve of Chaka Khan’s induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, The Gentlewoman hosted an evening with the singing superstar at the Times Square EDITION in New York City, where, for one night only she answered all our burning questions. Photography by Adam Slama.
The Gentlewoman Club turns 10October 2023, London

It was all round to Cromwell Place to celebrate 10 years of The Gentlewoman Club and the launch of the Gentlewoman T-shirt, made in collaboration with our friends at Arket. As the champagne flowed, guests enjoyed a special performance by Florence Shaw of Dry Cleaning. What a laugh! Photography by Dunja Opalko.
Sarah Lucas: Happy Gas with BurberrySeptember 2023, London

Art, fashion and rip-roaring cab rides through central London were the order of the day as The Gentlewoman Club and Burberry hosted friends new and familiar for a private view of Sarah Lucas: Happy Gas at Tate Britain. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
A Denim Masterclass with Levi’sJuly 2023, London

The Gentlewoman Club discovered the secrets to the perfect fitting jeans in a denim masterclass by the expert makers at Levi’s, as together we celebrated 150 years of the iconic Levi’s 501. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
The Gentlewoman nº 27 launch do at magCultureMarch 2023, London

Issue nº 27 was ushered in with a jovial evening at magCulture — thanks to our dear readers for turning out. And a special word of gratitude for our friends at Veuve Clicquot for keeping everyone refreshed. Cheers! Photography by Adam Slama.
Fresh air with Loro PianaDecember 2022, London

The Gentlewoman Club took a breather with Loro Piana to enjoy the outdoor vitality of the Italian house of sensuous apparel’s Holiday Collection, exploring London’s clean-air pathways, followed by a deep-breathing workshop and a seasonal lunch prepared by Laura Jackson of the al fresco cafe Towpath. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
Modern Manners Live!July 2022, London

Modern Manners: Instructions for living fabulously well was live at the Twenty Two in London’s Grosvenor Square, with special guest readings from our esteemed contributors Caroline Roux, Joan Juliet Buck, Otegha Uwagba and Susan Irvine. Sincerest thanks to our hosts at the Twenty Two and to Equiano Rum for the delicious refreshments. Photography by Adam Slama.
Celebrating Sonia BoyceMay 2022, London

In honour of Radio Ballads featuring Sonia Boyce at Serpentine, Bettina Korek, Hans Ulrich Obrist and Penny Martin hosted a special tour of the exhibition for members of The Gentlewoman Club in the company of Sonia herself. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
A London launch at CASA LOEWEApril 2022, London

Issue n° 25 was welcomed by readers, friends, well-wishers, and the iconic Dame Zandra Rhodes, one of the fabulous gentlewomen gracing its 304 pages this season. Enjoy these photographs from the launch do at CASA LOEWE London. Photography by Adama Slama.
In Milan with Fondazione PradaNovember 2021, Milan

The Gentlewoman Club made a thrilling return to Milan with our friends from Fondazione Prada. Club members enjoyed private tours of Sturm&Drang at the Osservatorio Fondazione Prada, the Domenico Gnoli retrospective, and the Atlas exhibition, as well as the hearty fare of Pasticceria Marchesi and Restaurant Torre. Oh, Milano! Photography by Adam Slama.
A marvellous mini-book signing in LondonFebruary 2020, London
It was mini books and max jollification on the Mall for The Mini Magazine festivities at the Institute of Contemporary Arts in St. James’s, London. Photography by Adam Slama.
The Gentlewoman Tour: BraemarNovember 2019, Braemar

The Highlands called as The Gentlewoman Tour ventured to the Fife Arms in Braemar with Begg & Co, where Club members enjoyed rambling and revelry amidst the majesty of the Scottish outdoors, along with the festive unveiling of Touring blanket.
The Gentlewoman Tour: StockholmNovember 2019, Stockholm

To celebrate 10 years of fabulousness in print, The Gentlewoman hit the road with an anniversary tour. First stop: Stockholm, for an urban expedition with ARKET exploring the Swedish home and the women redefining it. The outing concluded with a hearty feast at Rosendals Trädgård in the jovial company of our newest and fondest friends. Skål!
Celebrating Issue nº 20 at Hauser & WirthSeptember 2019, London

The 20th issue of The Gentlewoman magazine, marking a decade of style and purpose in print, was welcomed in a fabulous flurry of friends, well-wishers, gentlewomen of past and present and tasty tequila cocktails by Casamigos. The dear Xavior sizzled on the baby grand, while La Grotta Ices ensured everyone kept their cool. Here’s to 20! Photography by Marco Torri.
A night of cards at Isabel with Salvatore FerragamoSeptember 2019, London
A season in fashion and a fabulous new bag by Salvatore Ferragamo, the BOXYZ, were toasted with a glamorous cards night at Isabel in Mayfair, London. Photography by Adama Slama.
A very private view with Christian DiorMay 2019, London

The hottest ticket in London town this summer is Christian Dior: Designer of Dreams at the Victoria & Albert Museum. Club members were treated to a dreamy, early-morning private view courtesy of our friends at Dior. Photography by Kasia Bobula.
A vinyl love-in at 5 Carlos PlaceApril 2019, London

It was Bring-Your-Own-Vinyl as The Gentlewoman Club and MATCHESFASHION.COM got together to compile the ultimate gentlewoman playlist at a disco-down in Mayfair. On the wheels of steel was the heavenly Hanna Hanra, while the incomparable Kate Tempest captivated with a performance of new, as of yet unreleased, work.
Enjoy the evening’s playlist in full, here, on Spotify.
In Firenze with GucciNovember 2018, London

The Gentlewoman Club spent an autumn afternoon in Florence with our friends from Gucci, enjoying the wonders of the Boboli Gardens, a five-course luncheon at Gucci Osteria da Massimo Bottura and an exclusive tour of the Gucci Garden led by curator Maria Luisa Frisa. Photography by Adam Slama.
A night at the pictures with Agnès VardaSeptember 2018, London

The eighteenth edition of The Gentlewoman arrived in spectacular style with an exclusive screening of the film Faces Places in the company of its director and issue cover star, Agnès Varda. Special thanks to our friends at Curzon for their wonderful hospitality. Photography by Holly Whittaker.
A lively life drawing with Giorgio Armani, Julie Verhoeven and Studio VoltaireJuly 2018, London

Giorgio Armani and The Gentlewoman Club got together at the Royal Academy of Arts for an exuberant life drawing class led by the artist Julie Verhoeven, with special guest sitter Anna Calvi. Sincerest thanks to our friends at Studio Voltaire and to Armit Wines for the delicious refreshment on a balmy evening. Photography by Kasia Bobula.
Stepping out in BrooklynMay 2018, New York City
McNally Jackson were our gracious hosts on the occasion of The Gentlewoman Club's first outing in the Big Apple. Photography by Adam Slama.
A summer supper with Tory BurchMay 2018, New York City
To welcome forth a new season, Tory Burch and Penny Martin fêted the wild and wondrous women of New York City at the designer's Manhattan home. Photography by Adam Slama.
A gentlewomanly get-together at TenderbooksFebruary 2018, London
A festive unveiling of The Gentlewoman nº 17 at Tenderbooks in Covent Garden, London.
Photography by Adam Slama.
Cocktail Hour at BlacksNovember 2017, London

An evening of delicious Martinis at Blacks Club in London's Soho district on the occasion of the launch of The Cocktail Needle by The Gentlewoman and Delfina Delettrez — the exquisite pick of the divine and the dissolute. Cheers! Photography by Adam Slama.
Glimpses of the Future: LondonSeptember 2017, London

The second leg of the Glimpses of the Future international architecture tour by COS and The Gentlewoman saw Club members journey through 100 years of the Big Smoke's modernist dream. Photography by Adam Slama.
Glimpses of the Future: Los AngelesSeptember 2017, Los Angeles
COS and The Gentlewoman Club travelled through the architectural highlights of Los Angeles on the first stop of the Glimpses of the Future international architectural tour. Photography by Adam Slama.
Ciao, Milano!March 2017, Milano
The Gentlewoman welcomed its fifteenth edition with a sublime get-together in Milan at Pasticceria Marchesi. Special thanks to our friends at Prada – sweet dreams, indeed!
Cards night at The Savile Club with BrownsOctober 2016, London
It was an evening of high jinks and high stakes as The Gentlewoman and Browns hosted a glamorous night of cards at the Savile Club in London's Mayfair. Photography by Adam Slama.
An intimate dinner in honour of Lauren CollinsOctober 2016, London

The Gentlewoman assembled some the magazine's nearest and dearest for a charming dinner in celebration of contributing writer Lauren Collins' new book When in French: Love in a Second Language, published by 4th Estate. Photography by Adam Slama.
A sumptuous soirée with Filippa KSeptember 2016, London
The Gentlewoman and Fantastic Man co-hosted a grand celebration of fashion in print with our friends at Filippa K, with performances by Xavior and Lung Dart. Photography by Adam Slama.
Day trip to Durslade FarmJune 2016, Somerset

In the jovial company of Paul Smith, The Gentlewoman Club headed west for a countryside jaunt to Durslade Farm, Hauser & Wirth's Somerset art complex. There, we revelled in bucolic splendour with a sumptuous summer picnic by the Roth Bar & Grill. Photography by Adam Slama.
B.Y.O.V.April 2016, London

The Gentlewoman Club celebrated Record Store Day with a Bring-Your-Own-Vinyl shindig at Alleycat on London’s famous Tin Pan Alley, aka Denmark Street. Beloved post-punk prima donna Brix Smith Start also regaled with tales from rock ’n’ roll's frontline in a reading from her memoir, The Rise, The Fall, And The Rise. Photography by Adam Slama.
A springtime celebrationFebruary 2016, London
An evening with friends and well-wishers on the occasion of the launch of The Gentlewoman No. 13 and a smashing sartorial collaboration with Sunspel. Photography by Adam Slama.
A literary soiréeJanuary 2016, London

Bookish banter abounded at the Club's reading group with Sonia Rykiel featuring "Dangerous Liaisons" by Choderlos de Laclos. An animated discussion was led Dr Ann Lewis, specialist in 18th century French literature, and Marketa Uhlirova, director of Fashion in Film. Dramatic readings from the book were courtesy of actor Stacy Martin. Photography by Adam Slama.
A guided tour by Es DevlinOctober 2015, London

The Gentlewoman Club was treated to a very special tour of the exhibition Louis Vuitton Series 3 – Past, Present, Future by the award-winning stage designer Es Devlin. Please enjoy these photographs from the evening's festivities. Photography by Adam Slama.
The Gentlewoman Running Club: Summer 2015Summer 2015, London
A jolly do at The Millinery WorksJune 2015, London

To celebrate the enduring brilliance of Arts and Crafts furniture, The Gentlewoman Club co-hosted a jolly do with the antique traders at heart of its renaissance: those fabulous fellows at The Millinery Works. Photography by Kasia Bobula.
The Gentlewoman in SohoFebruary 2015, London
The Gentlewoman No.11 was ushered in for spring and summer two thousand and fifteen with a sublime party at Claire de Rouen books in London's Soho. Photography by Fernando Uceda.
Christmas Ghost WalkDecember 2014, London

The Gentlewoman Club hosted its first Christmas Ghost Walk on a chilly December evening with a terrifying exploration of Soho and Covent Garden convening at Sunspel on Old Compton Street for warming post-walk drinks. Photography by Danny J Peace.
The Gentlewoman keeps shop at House of VoltaireDecember 2014, London

It was a jovial evening of affordable art, drinks and shopping as The Gentlewoman played shop with special guest gentlewoman shopkeeper actor Maddy Hill at House of Voltaire. Photographs by Kareem Abdul.
An intimate screening with Anne CollierOctober 2014, London

The Gentlewoman Club hosted a film screening with Studio Voltaire and the artist Anne Collier at The Club at Café Royal. Anne selected the cult classic “Eyes of Laura Mars”. Photography by Danny J Peace.
A super-duper party in BerlinOctober 2014, Berlin

To Berlin! The Gentlewoman and Fantastic Man caught up with old friends and made some new at Voo Store in Kreuzberg, who hosted a super-duper party in honour of the new issues of both magazines. The evening also featured a special live performance by Heatsick. Wunderbar!
A glamorous night at Hotel Café RoyalSeptember 2014, London
It was a scintillating evening of disco-dancing with Swedish pop superstar Robyn, the face of The Gentlewoman nº 10. Photography by Ivan Ruberto and George Harvey.
A tour of Bridget Riley’s show at David Zwirner LondonJuly 2014, London

To celebrate Bridget Riley: The Stripe Paintings 1961-2014 at David Zwirner London, friends and members of The Gentlewoman Club were treated to a special tour of the exhibition by Angela Choon, senior partner at David Zwirner. Photography by Ivan Ruberto.

items.title: The Gentlewoman – nº 34
items.description: Slam! Issue n° 34 of The Gentlewoman is fronted by Coco Gauff, the 22-year-old American champion reshaping women’s tennis. Two majors in, and with her game rebuilt from scratch, Coco is playing the best tennis of her life, resplendent in her signature kit and
paragraphs: Slam! Issue n° 34 of The Gentlewoman is fronted by Coco Gauff, the 22-year-old American champion reshaping women’s tennis. Two majors in, and with her game rebuilt from scratch, Coco is playing the best tennis of her life, resplendent in her signature kit and making sure the game’s Black pioneers are not forgotten. She’s a joy to behold, readers.

Joining Coco are the reunited Sugababes — Mutya, Keisha and Siobhán — who talk candidly about maintaining harmony; Autumn Durald Arkapaw, the first woman to win the Oscar for best cinematography, on shooting Sinners; and the architect Sophie Hicks on four decades of building for Chloé, Acne and herself. The oceanic pioneer Sylvia Earle, 91, shares tales of days and nights living underwater. Fashions-wise, colour-drenched knitwear takes to the South Downs, and rugged shearling and rubber pitch up for autumn.

There’s writing addiction with the musician and poet John Glacier, and a sporting death stare with Hollie Davidson, who referees men’s top-flight rugby. We meet Vivien Wong, the mochi mastermind behind Little Moons, and Lira Valencia, the birdwatcher on a mission to get Londoners looking up. Plus: Celia Celebrity Traitors Imrie on becoming a youth sensation after 60 years in showbiz, and the screenwriting duo behind KPop Demon Hunters: Danya Jimenez and Hannah McMechan. Elsewhere, a forensic ode to peeling, and the case for multilingualism. Lots to talk about, then!

The Gentlewoman celebrates modern women of style and purpose. Its fabulous biannual magazine offers a fresh and intelligent perspective on fashion that’s focused on personal style – the way women actually look, think and dress. Featuring ambitious journalism and photography of the highest quality, it showcases inspirational women through its distinctive combination of glamour, personality and warmth. These qualities are also at the heart of its website, thegentlewoman.com, a virtual place where real women, real events and real things are enjoyed.

items.title: The Gentlewoman – Privacy Policy
items.description: At The Gentlewoman we are committed to respecting your privacy. This policy explains when and why we collect personal information about the people who visit our website, sign up to The Gentlewoman Club and receive our mailings, how we use this data and keep it
paragraphs: At The Gentlewoman we are committed to respecting your privacy. This policy explains when and why we collect personal information about the people who visit our website, sign up to The Gentlewoman Club and receive our mailings, how we use this data and keep it secure.

When you sign up to The Gentlewoman Club on our website to receive newsletters or invitations to Club socialities and when you RSVP to attend one of these events, we collect your data to allow us to carry out this request. This information will typically include your name, email address, age and location. You are also invited to submit additional information about yourself, but this is always completely at your discretion.

We use this information to pursue our legitimate interests in a way which might reasonably be expected as part of running our business and which does not materially impact your rights, freedom or interests.
UK Data Protection laws allow the following as part of our legitimate interest in understanding our Club members and providing the most relevant levels of service:
• to contact you about events that we think might be of interest to you;
• to assess your eligibility for an event;
• to communicate with you;
• for marketing purposes; or
• to analyse your behaviour, activities, preferences and needs in order to send relevant and tailored promotional communications to you.
We will store your information either until you unsubscribe (there will always be an option to opt-out in every email we send) or if you have not opened an email from us over the past year.

We use third-party software (Campaign Monitor) to help us process your data.  All this is either registered with the EU-US Privacy Shield programme or will have entered into model EU clauses with any sub-processor it uses and is based outside the EEA or has established a set of binding corporate rules with its foreign subsidiaries who are based outside the EEA or the Information Commissioner has made a positive finding of adequacy in relation to the territory in which the sub-processor is based and to which your information may be transferred.

We collect information about traffic to thegentlewoman.co.uk using Google Analytics, a web analytics tool that helps us understand how visitors engage with our website. We use this information to help us improve our website and your experience of it. This information is aggregated and anonymised so that we cannot access personal information such as IP addresses.

thegentlewoman.co.uk uses essential cookies to improve its functionality. Cookies contain information that is transferred to your computer’s hard drive and are used by us to store information such as the time the visit occurred, whether users have visited the site previously and what site referred them to the web page. For your protection, The Gentlewoman’s website is SSL certified.
The Gentlewoman will never share or sell your information to a third party.

items.title: The cinematic universe of María Zardoya - A Rabbit's Foot
items.description: With albums such as Hable con Ella and Cinema, The Marias frontwoman María Zardoya has established herself as one of LA’s most visionary musicians, finally earning her accolades with a Grammy nomination for The Marías early this year. But there’s no time to re
items.author: Kitty Grady
paragraphs: With albums such as Hable con Ella and Cinema, The Marias frontwoman María Zardoya has established herself as one of LA’s most visionary musicians, finally earning her accolades with a Grammy nomination for The Marías early this year. But there’s no time to rest on her laurels. The show must go on, she tells Chris Cotonou, even if it means creating in subversive new ways.

María Zardoya came to Los Angeles by accident. That’s what the frontwoman for the supercool Grammy-nominated band The Marías tells me: that she headed out West after earning some money from a Halloween contest and on the behest of a friend.

Serendipitous accident: Since forming The Marías in 2016 with Josh Conway, Jesse Perlman, and Edward James, Zardoya has become one of the most alluring singers of her generation, crooning meaningful, dreamy indie ballads in both English and in Spanish (she was born, after all, in Puerto Rico).

Ten years later, the band is one of the groups that most defines modern America—with millions of fans the world over. When I met Zardoya, a week after her Grammy performance, and following our striking photoshoot—which you can discover in these pages—it’s evident that so much of her success is because of her charisma and vision as a performer; but also as an obsessive “builder of worlds,” she explains. Everything is still rooted in a universe Zardoya and her bandmates created for themselves ten years ago; irrespective of all of the fame.

Their album Cinema (2021) should have given away just how much the movies inspire The Marías’ world. But even more recently, with nods to Three Colours: Blue (1993) on the cover of Submarine (2024) and hints at Pedro Almodóvar in song titles. What I especially like about Zardoya is her vision: every album, every show, is a chance to experiment with references and ideas, and like many of the best artists, she moves on to new ideas without much issue. Her solo project Not For Radio (2025) went on tour in January and paid homage to the Swan Lake, in part because her audience may never have had the chance to see the ballet. So why not at her show?

It’s a mission for true, real, high-culture art that makes everything Zardoya does so engaging. The following is a conversation that spanned her roots, bilingual music, Almodóvar, Bad Bunny, and California.
A Rabbit’s Foot: As a Puerto Rican and someone who’s been playing with bilingual music for a long time, what did you make of Bad Bunny’s recent performance at the Super Bowl?
María Zardoya: It felt, more than anything, like a celebration of the culture. My best friend is Puerto Rican and she was texting me, “I’m in tears. This feels like a love letter to Puerto Rico.”

Seeing him on that massive stage, especially with all the political turmoil around him being the performer, was really powerful. There were so many little references to Puerto Rican culture. Representation is extremely important in the media, and he represented Puerto Rico beautifully—also the wider Latin community with that nod at the end to all the Latin American countries. I’m really proud to know him, to collaborate with him, and to be from the little island of Puerto Rico.
ARF: How has the music industry changed around bilingual music since you started, and how do you see your place in that?

MZ: The landscape has definitely expanded. You can thank artists like Bad Bunny for bringing those sounds and that language to the mainstream. For me, it was never a strategy. I grew up bilingual and bicultural, speaking both languages and listening to music in both. The first song I wrote was in Spanish, the second in English, then another in Spanish, then English, then mixed—it was just natural.

What I discovered was how many people in the US shared that bicultural experience and gravitated toward it. A big moment was a festival in Jakarta, where people were singing every word in English and Spanish—even though Spanish isn’t their language. That really showed me music can transcend language.
ARF: You left Georgia for California at a very young age. Why California instead of, say, New York?
MZ: Honestly, one friend. She was also from Georgia, had moved to California to pursue music, and kept calling me saying, “If you want to do music, you need to be here.”

I was saving money, figuring out where I’d live. Then she called: one of her roommates had moved out. Around then I won a Halloween costume contest at the agency I worked at—five grand—so I thought, “Okay, I can do this.” I bought a car and drove to California knowing only her. That was it.
ARF: Did California—and especially Los Angeles—shape the music you made with The Marías?

MZ: I think so. All the guys in the band are born and raised in California. When I started writing with Josh [Conway], he had this psych-rock, California vibe. Our music became this mesh of his California upbringing and my bicultural, bilingual, small-town upbringing. It just worked.
ARF: Your music feels very cinematic. What film or visual references feed into your work?
MZ: Early on I was extremely inspired by Pedro Almodóvar. He’s one of my all-time favourite directors. My dad is from Spain, so I grew up watching his films.

When we were discovering our visual identity, I watched a lot of his movies and took notes on his use of colour, especially red. If you look at our early visuals and videos, there’s always a pop of red, and that carried into the EPs and our first album, Cinema (2021). I even named two songs after Hable con ella (2002)—“Hable Con Ella” and “Talk to Her.” Later, for Submarine (2024), I was inspired by [Krzysztof] Kieślowski’s Three Colours trilogy (1993–94). He did an ode to the French flag; I wanted to do something similar for the Puerto Rican flag. So the second album is blue—Submarine—and now people are expecting the next to be white. Film is a huge part of how I think about albums and visuals.
ARF: How do you separate ideas between The Marías and your solo project, Not for Radio?

MZ: The challenge is keeping things distinct, because I spearhead the visuals for both. With The Marías, I’m also considering the guys—they have this 90s, edgy, Thom Yorke/Radiohead-inspired thing. With Not for Radio the solo project is very inspired by nature and the underworld. It’s a “green” album. For the next Marías project, the “white” one, I’m thinking more Three Colours: White (1994), Trainspotting (1996), 90s freshness. I literally see the guys as Ewan McGregor in Trainspotting—playful and edgy. So The Marías lean more into that energy; Not for Radio is more romantic and connected to nature.
ARF: You speak about albums like films—with colour, character, and arcs. Do you see them as one big story?

MZ: Yeah. From Superclean (2017) and Cinema—the red, romantic period when Josh and I were in a relationship—to Submarine, blue, which symbolises solitude and the breakup. Not for Radio is green, a rebirth for me individually, like a seed being watered and growing into myself. The next “white” album feels like a rediscovery of who we are as a band after that rupture—coming up from underwater and seeing the light. So it’s all one story, but I also get obsessively lost in each album’s visual world while I’m making it.
I was inspired by [Krzysztof] Kieślowski’s Three Colours trilogy (1993–94). He did an ode to the French flag; I wanted to do something similar for the Puerto Rican flag.
ARF: As the band has become more visible, has your willingness to be vulnerable in your lyrics changed?

MZ: I definitely have moments of, “Did I say too much?” But those thoughts come after the song is written. The way I write is very subconscious, like free-writing or journaling, so what comes out is honest. Before releasing Not for Radio, I texted my manager, freaking out, like, “I think I was too honest—people are going to speculate.” She told me, “If you’re living in your integrity and being as honest as you can, that’s what matters.” People will make up their own stories anyway. That really grounded me.
ARF: You’ve mentioned being obsessive. What are you most particular about in the studio?

MZ: Everything. I obsess over a drum sound, the tone of a synth, tiny details in the mix. Mixing is when my brain really loops, because it feels like the last chance to get it right. I’ll suddenly hear some high-pitched thing in the snare and can’t unhear it.
But I’m learning to let go. The solo project helped because it came together so fast I didn’t have time to obsess over every detail. I just had to follow the energy.
ARF: Do you have ways of leaving one project behind and moving into the next?
MZ: Being completely in the moment helps. That’s something I always encourage fans to do at shows—lose themselves in that moment.

On the Not for Radio tour, with the Swan Lake (1875–76) references, I started the show as this delicate swan, then, after the “death” of the white swan, leaned in to the grittier, darker black-swan energy. Women are conditioned to always be beautiful and delicate, but there’s a darkness and “ugliness” I wanted to show.
To move on, I leave that version of me in that moment. Now I’m in a different one. The past is what it is; the future isn’t here yet.
ARF: It feels like the more visible you get, the more you push against mainstream norms. Is that deliberate?

MZ: Yeah. As The Marías got bigger and reached a more mainstream audience—partly through things like TikTok—there was a part of me that didn’t want to go further into that; I wanted to go more inward and against the grain.

I wanted to make songs over four minutes, without obvious internet hooks; shows that weren’t just about screaming along to big drops. I wanted to invite people to put on headphones, sit under a tree, and really listen.

Calling the project Not for Radio gave me the confidence to be unconventional—to do a more theatrical production, with people sitting down, and to bring them into a different kind of world. I’m grateful the team saw that vision.
ARF: Where did this love of cinema start?

MZ: At home. My dad went to the store and asked for the biggest TV they had. This was pre-flatscreen, so we ended up with this giant 88-inch tube TV and surround sound in the living room, just for watching movies.

Whenever guests came over, he’d play Twister (1996) to show off the rumble. That family movie time really started it. The first film that really shook me was Alfonso Cuarón’s A Little Princess (1995). I watched it over and over. I spoke to him a few months ago about it.
I studied film in high school and college, and when I chose music, it felt like the perfect bridge: I could be a filmmaker through our videos and visuals.
ARF: It’s a bit of a random question. But I’m curious. If you could spend an evening with three people from cinema, dead or alive, who would they be?
MZ: Pedro Almodóvar, Guillermo del Toro, and Alfonso Cuarón. Having all three of them in the same room, sitting by a fire, asking each other questions—that would be the dream.
ARF: Would you ever want to direct a film yourself?

MZ: Maybe one day. I love putting worlds together visually. A couple of years ago I went down a Sofia Coppola rabbit hole after watching Marie Antoinette (2006) for the first time. I was like, “I want to make a movie like this.”

She captures femininity and the female perspective in such a beautiful way. I watched all her films, bought her book, and just flipped through the images, totally inspired. So maybe after my next Sofia Coppola rabbit hole, I’ll finally make a movie.
ARF: And your favourite Guillermo del Toro? Say Pan’s Labyrinth (2006)…
Pan’s Labyrinth, for sure. And The Shape of Water (2017)—I’ve seen that so many times. It’s so, so good.

items.title: The awesome ascent of Archie Madekwe - A Rabbit's Foot
items.description: Following breakout roles in Emerald Fennell’s Saltburn and popstar Oliver in Alex Russell’s noirish Lurker, the London-born actor is getting his flowers. As he is nominated for a BAFTA EE Rising Star Award, Madekwe—our February digital cover star—speaks to Han
items.author: Kitty Grady
paragraphs: Following breakout roles in Emerald Fennell’s Saltburn and popstar Oliver in Alex Russell’s noirish Lurker, the London-born actor is getting his flowers. As he is nominated for a BAFTA EE Rising Star Award, Madekwe—our February digital cover star—speaks to Hanna Flint about his background at the BRIT school, diversity in casting and what his mum will be wearing to the ceremony this Sunday.

When Archie Madekwe goes to the cinema, he wants to feel transported. He wants to feel challenged. He wants to feel uncomfortable. He wants to feel alive. That emphatic appreciation of the arts was nourished early on in life, growing up in South London. The actor’s father–a plumber by trade, a film fan at heart–and his fitness instructor mother would rent videos from their local Blockbuster every weekend and take him on trips to see various plays and movies. He vividly recalls seeing Black Swan (2010) on the big screen with his dad, where his eyes flooded with tears as the climactic ending crescendoed into white.

“We just sat in silence as the credits rolled,” he tells me on a rainy afternoon in Shoreditch at a studio where A Rabbit’s Foot is shooting with the star. In an hour, he’ll be heading back to his East London home to get suited and booted for the premiere of Wuthering Heights. Right now, he’s in a faded T-shirt and jeans, grinning as he leans back into the memory of that formative cinema trip. “That moment has stayed with me because it did something to both us and the whole audience. I remember thinking, how amazing it is that you can watch a film, and it can move you to the point where you’re frozen in your seat—there are no words, but we all shared that experience.”

Fifteen years later, the 31-year-old is committed to that same cathartic feeling. Whether it be in Ari Aster’s visceral folk horror Midsommar (2019), Emerald Fennell’s pitch black class comedy Saltburn (2023) or most recently Lurker, Alex Russell’s suffocating portrait of fan obsession and modern celebrity, Madekwe is choosing roles that confront both himself and the audience–especially when it comes to “seeing characters that look like me in spaces that we don’t typically see them.”

As a biracial actor of Nigerian, Swiss and English descent, Madekwe has long been cognisant of how race influences casting. When studying at both the BRIT School and the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art, Madekwe has spoken of how he was duly informed that he looked too “urban,” the baritone timbre of his South London accent too “street,” for the likes of Shakespeare and Chekhov.

Still, Madekwe values his time at the BRIT school and is supportive of the next generation. He did a Q&A with students the morning of the shoot and celebrated the achievements of fellow alumni FKA Twigs, Lola Young, Olivia Dean and RAYE at the Grammys a few days earlier. He himself has earned a BAFTA Rising Star nomination at the upcoming awards ceremony. Together, they prove artists of colour can garner universal appeal by being unapologetically themselves, where their race doesn’t have to be the sole focus of their art or the stories they tell. A point that Madekwe is passionate about when choosing his roles. “Can they just be heartbroken? Can they have just lost their job?” he asks, with the fervour of an actor who knows too often that they can’t. “We all experience heartbreak and love and fear and happiness and joy and firsts.”

With films like Teen Spirit (2018) and Gran Turismo (2023), plus his latest crime thriller series Steal, in which Madekwe plays a trade processor at a pension management fund embroiled in an armed heist, the actor has relished exploring characters where the central conflict isn’t linked to heritage. Yet he does value colour-conscious casting, whereby a role is shaped to the actor portraying it. “I’ve worked with lots of directors who have been so open to collaboration and made it so I’m not scared to bring my full self to these characters,” he tells me. “It can be something as small as he should be wearing a headscarf in a scene when he goes to bed. It’s a subtle and easy tweak to make that person’s life feel richer and actually more relatable on screen.”

Madekwe’s breakthrough came with his role in Saltburn as Farleigh, a mixed-race cousin of Jacob Elordi’s elitist lead, and an antagonistic character precariously negotiating the upper echelons of a white family estate. “She’s a person of colour and has been so great at finding interesting ways of telling stories with people from everywhere in the world,” he says of casting director Kharmel Cochrane, noting her conversation with Fennell about the casting of the film’s footmen. “They became people of colour, and that added so much to the wider questions of Farleigh–his way of looking inward and projecting.”

I mention an underlying racial tension I observed in Lurker, a sharply tuned film in which Madekwe plays Oliver, a musical artist on the precipice of superstardom, but whose inner circle is infiltrated by Matthew (Théodore Pellerin), a parasitic fan seeking obsessive control over the star. I point to the history of black artists having their careers puppeteered by white men. He takes a moment to consider this.

“That’s such an interesting way to look at it, but to be honest, I wasn’t thinking about that,” he answers. “Partly because Oliver’s in a place in his career where he is so new, and we were telling Oliver’s story just before that [puppeteering] started to happen.”

Brimming with the psychosexual tension of films such as Single White Female (1992) and The Talented Mr Ripley (1999) but attuned to the contemporary pop culture lens of Ingrid Goes West (2017), Madekwe and Pellerin exude a disquieting chemistry, where the push and pull of power simmers with foreboding realism. “The relationship between Matthew and Oliver is dark,” he says. “Oliver is fighting to stay afloat, and we’re seeing him in a dangerous place, working out this weird intersection of: Do I want to be famous? Do I want to make good art? How do both of those things intersect, and do I want to keep this person around if it means I get those things?”

One might glean some overlap between the creative choices of Oliver and Madekwe, who has had to make smart choices about his career trajectory. He’s had to say ‘no’ to a lot of offers to play dark-skinned American historical figures: “I would never want to play those parts, I’d be setting myself up—it’s absolute crucifixion.” He’s also had to delete a few reviews from his Letterboxd account after a follow from Charli XCX put avid users of the platform in his direction. “They were screenshotting my reviews real quick, because I was really giving reviews,” he laughs. “I was like, Okay, time to think—no more fun.”
“We’re not afraid to show the bumps and the bruises and the grey areas.”
Archie Madekwe – on British cinema

No more fun on Letterboxd, maybe, but there’s tons more to be had in Madekwe’s future. He’ll soon start shooting in his hometown for Bijan Sheibani’s feature debut, The Arrival, playing long-lost brothers with Kingsley Ben-Adir. “We’re not afraid to show the bumps and the bruises and the grey areas,” Madekwe, who hints to developing his own projects, says of British Cinema. “I remember watching [Steve McQueen’s] Hunger, and Shame and a lot of Andrea Arnold and feeling we’re not afraid to look at what’s happening around us and say, ‘this story’s worth telling.’”

First, however, there’s the BAFTAs, where he’ll be competing against Robert Aramayo, Miles Caton, Chase Infiniti and Posy Sterling for the Rising Star title of 2026. “It’s beyond words,” he says of the nomination, but whether he wins or loses is less of a concern than his mum having a good time. “I get a text probably every 10 minutes about what she’s gonna wear,” he laughs. “It’s a very surreal time for everybody. When I was younger, I was dictating to my parents what I was going to do, auditioning for the BRIT School, the National Youth Theatre. This was not the world that I grew up in, but they just supported me throughout, so it’s a special thing for them to see it happening.”
No matter what goes down on February 22nd, one thing is for sure: Madekwe is a star on the rise—and he’s ready for even more close-ups.
