He’s almost got a work vibe, even socially,” says a close friend of Porch’s. “When we all met Robert, we thought, This is amazing, because Robert is not a filtered, edited guy. We were all just so happy for Charles that he could have that joy of life and the extravagance.”

Denning first heard of Porch on a group chat with a bunch of gay men from Stanford business school. “I’m a reject of one of his friends,” Porch tells me. One person in the chat wrote that he’d been told to go on a date with Porch — and he followed this announcement with multiple vomit emoji. Denning looked up Porch to find him chatting with Gayle King on CBS This Morning about onboarding the pope to Instagram. Says Porch, “He’s like, ‘I think he’s cute. Can I go out with him?’ The friend says ‘no.’ So then Robert’s like, ‘Now I have to go on this date.’”

Denning went on Instagram and found a mutual follower he knew from business school and Porch knew through Randi Zuckerberg. “And he DMs his friend and says, ‘Becca, I’m sorry for not RSVP-ing to your wedding ten years ago or acknowledging your two children, but I need you to do something for me,’” Porch says. “And she writes back right away and she’s like, ‘I don’t know him that well, but I’ll try.’” The next day, Denning and Porch got drinks at Temple Bar. “Becca had a place of honor at our wedding, but we both barely know her,” says Porch.

Denning had just moved to New York. He was recently sober and, following the fire sale of his luxury-eyewear start-up, trying to figure out what to do next. His father, Steve Denning, sat on several boards; as Steve’s health declined, Robert started filling in for him, and his philanthropic career took off from there. In 2024, Denning became the then-youngest member of the board of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. “He’s great on a board,” Porch says.

By December 2022, they had made the relationship Instagram official, hard-launching with a photo in front of Joe Biden’s White House (Denning is a big Democratic donor). And the following October, they were engaged. Denning thought they were going to a dinner at the Met in honor of an exhibit opening, but really they had the entire museum to themselves. Porch got down on one knee in the Greek and Roman wing.

In the spring of 2025, Amy Griffin, Foster and her two sisters, Naomi Gleit, and Meyer threw Porch a Charlie’s Angels–themed bachelor party at the ultraluxury Amangiri resort, all of which was documented on Instagram. For the wedding, Porch and Denning hosted roughly 400 guests at Le Bristol, renting out the luxury hotel for the first time in its 100-year history. They paid for everyone’s room as well as their room service. Night one was a party in the hotel courtyard; night two was the ceremony, held in the sculpture garden of the Rodin Museum. Ten minutes before the ceremony was to begin, the sky opened to a downpour, only to clear suddenly to an amber light. First came the bridal party, a group of six children — godchildren and spawn of close friends — outfitted by Thom Browne in seersucker suits, ties, and knee socks (Porch’s idea). Then came the grooms, who walked down the aisle to the Jurassic Park theme (Denning’s idea). Foster officiated. Barbara Bush gave the first reading, Griffin the last. The couple encouraged women to repurpose their old wedding dresses for the event; seemingly the only one who did was Real Housewife Carole Radziwill.

Then it was off to the Hôtel de la Marine for a reception and dinner. Before the guests sat down, Denning gave a vaguely political speech calling attention to the fact that this was a gay wedding and urging the roomful of people with lots of resources and power to take care of those whose rights they were celebrating. At the after-party, French drag queen Nicky Doll performed. The fairy-tale weekend ended with a black-tie affair at Château de Villette on the last Saturday of summer with the couple in custom midnight-blue Hermès tuxedos.

The pair have been well received in New York in part because they’re so happy to be here. “Anna loved him because she could invite him to any dinner party and sit him next to any annoying or difficult person and he knew how to show up, lift the conversation, and never complain,” one fashion editor recalls of Porch. “He’s just very kind and normal and unassuming,” says Wes Gordon, the creative director of Carolina Herrera and a friend of Porch’s. “It’s easy to forget he was a very senior person at Meta and now OpenAI.”

Porch and Denning are tight with theater producers, fashion designers, art curators, and socialites such as Lauren Santo Domingo, Jenna Lyons, and Derek Blasberg. “They were two separately quiet people in different realms and then when they came together, they started making a splash,” says one journalist. “A lot of people will make names for themselves in San Francisco and L.A. and then they come to New York and it’s like being shot out of a cannon into other worlds.”

A couple of months after the wedding, Porch was at Instagram HQ in Menlo Park when Altman’s call came through. They discussed how “everyone’s talking about AI and productivity and that’s great, but no one’s talking about AI and culture,” Porch recalls. “And those two things are going to come together, and culture is run by all these creative industries, and question mark on what that’s going to look like.”

There were more conversations, with Altman and Fidji Simo, Altman’s then-No. 2, with whom Porch worked for more than a decade at Meta. “I think what Fidji really realized is there was an enterprise-and-sales arm that was being built for it, but there wasn’t anyone to work on the talent side,” Porch tells me. “That is where there was an obvious opening for me to come in.” Still, he had just gotten married, and he politely declined. When Simo came calling again in January, Porch was more receptive. “It was like, ‘New Year, new me.’ Time to jump to the next frontier,” he says. “Sam, I feel, is the same person I met socially years ago in San Francisco. And it’s kind of fun to work for a gay guy.”

He started in March, spending his first few months on a listening tour, mostly in New York and L.A., meeting with everyone from the Council of Fashion Designers of America to HBO showrunners. “I ran around and went to a bunch of people I knew would have strong opinions on it, good or bad,” says Porch. He went to the Cannes Film Festival, meeting with directors and hearing their feedback on the technology. “There was way more openness because directors have been using AI forever,” says Porch. He also went to San Francisco — “a lot,” he says, stressing the t — “to bond with the product folks and the researchers and try to get a sense of what they’re really interested in. I don’t have that many mathematicians on speed dial.”

Then he brought people together for intimate events — “just a lot of relationship building for the company,” says Porch. At Paris Fashion Week, he hosted a dinner at Sushi Park with Joopiter, Pharrell Williams’s digital-first auction house, for various French creators. “It wasn’t heavy programming, and it wasn’t branded,” Porch says. “It was just a collab with Joopiter to get people talking.” He has also hosted dinners for TBPN, the daily tech-industry podcast OpenAI acquired in April to help bolster positive conversation around AI. The first TBPN dinner was held in L.A. and attended by the Foster sisters, Monica Lewinsky, Crazy Rich Asians director John Chu, and manager turned tech-investor Guy Oseary. They replicated it in New York a few months later at the downtown restaurant Kiko, where TBPN president Dylan Abruscato was seated next to SNL’s Chloe Fineman and Kareem Rahma of “Subway Takes.” Vogue head of editorial content Chloe Malle and Vanity Fair editorial director Mark Guiducci were also in attendance. “He has been very instrumental in helping TBPN deepen our relationships with Condé Nast,” says Abruscato.

A few days before our interview, I attended one such event, a dinner Porch co-hosted at the subterranean members’ club Chez Margaux. In celebration of influencer Serena Kerrigan’s new book, the gathering was attended by a mix of podcasters, creators, and Real Housewives, but, I noted to Porch, I didn’t hear any discussion about AI. “That was a personal dinner, just so you understand. My personal and professional kind of blend,” he says. “But what’ll happen from that dinner is Serena’s probably going to call me in two months and be like, ‘Wait, I have this idea. I love Chat for this. Do you wanna do this thing with me?’ So there’s a nice cadence of how that happens. But also, you know, there were three Real Housewives there. If an AI model comes up on the show, it might be Chat because we have this nice drumbeat. This is what I’ve been trying to explain to folks: It’s not about deals; it’s about relationships.”

Still, it’s hard to say what exactly is supposed to result from this strategy. The idea appears to be that all this social lubrication will pay off and that Altman and his ilk will one day be seen less as freakish world destroyers than as parts of a broader mosaic of American celebrity. Familiarity, even at an elite level, tends to trickle down.

So far, though, things look decisively less glamorous than they did at Instagram. Aside from Lionel Messi’s ChatGPT World Cup partnership, the most prominent celebrities working with the company have been rookie NFL quarterback Fernando Mendoza, who recently spoke to GQ about using ChatGPT for meal planning and nutrition, and designer Francesco Risso, who discussed the role of Astra in his creative process in an OpenAI-sponsored video on Vogue’s YouTube channel. “There might come a day when I get a call from Charles about doing something, and I’ll navigate that in real time, but I recognize this brand has very bad PR right now,” says one creative professional. They add, “If you’re someone who doesn’t like where things are headed, anyone affiliated with this world is going to be seen as part of the problem.”

“When Kevin Systrom or Adam Mosseri were having events with celebrities, people wanted their leverage to help them grow their account, grow their influence,” says one media executive. Instagram is inherently about marketing yourself; OpenAI’s main product isn’t yet public facing. “Aligning yourself with OpenAI, every star has to ask, ‘What’s in it for me?’ — except for potentially a big check and a lot of blowback,” says the media executive. Skepticism around technology has only grown since Hollywood cashed in on the NFT and crypto crazes, resulting in embarrassing commercials and promotions that blew up in many high-profile faces. And the threat AI poses to cultural fields also seems to be putting a higher premium on good old-fashioned human creativity and originality. “I don’t care how cute you make Waymo look: This autonomous-AI-powered life is not warm and cuddly,” says the media executive. “There’s not a cool factor.”

At the same time, many in the entertainment industry are desperate. “Right now in Hollywood, only the top people are working,” the executive says. “It’s why Robert Pattinson is in every project or why Nicole Kidman is literally in everything you watch on TV. The next tier down is not getting jobs.” According to Porch, when he joined OpenAI, there was a backlog of inquiries from various celebrities looking for an endorsement deal, production studios wanting to become more AI focused, fashion houses trying to figure out e-commerce, and sports teams and leagues looking to integrate more AI. It’s possible that we will look back at this moment as we do at musicians who wouldn’t give their songs to iTunes. “Now, it’s like, ‘I can’t believe you would have turned down the check,’” one journalist says.

Some people roll their eyes at Porch, dismissing him as someone whose job is to be friends with famous people and questioning whether he has any expertise at all. “He’s a super-wily leverager of social relationships, but it helps when you have multimillion-dollar marketing budgets to get people what they want,” says a tech adviser. Another media executive sees what Porch has done as a kind of surfing: You choose your wave, start paddling at the right time, and rise at the perfect moment. It’d be fair to say Porch is a good surfer, they note. And now people are watching to see if he can stay up. “He sits in the middle of the convergence of media, culture, and tech, but he’s also right at the changing of the tide,” says the tech adviser, noting that Porch embodies a certain older-millennial brand that may be going out of fashion. “How much longer does someone like him maintain clout when it may be based on an outdated model of how those worlds interact?”

Porch insists he’s not worried. “What I keep coming back to is, I think, the usefulness of AI,” he says. “What it’s transforming for people is undeniable. And the more conversations I have, I just — I feel it coming, people being able to talk about it more.” He adds, “Everything moves faster in AI.”
*A previous version of this story misstated Eva Chen’s role at Meta.

items.title: The Future of AI Will Be Shaped by an Astonishingly Small Number of People
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: The Editors
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

AI has minted a new power structure. A handful of private companies command the might and wealth of small nation-states and are mostly left to self-govern. A few dozen employees are on the brink of becoming centimillionaires and considering which causes and presidential candidates they will funnel their vast resources toward. The industry is perpetually one breakthrough away from a step change in capability or public adoption, the question of who gets there first dependent on the specific expertise and visions of a handful of engineers.

One way to tell the story of how AI is changing our world is through some newly familiar names. Sam Altman and Dario Amodei are locked in a race to build AGI and persuade President Donald Trump to regulate the technology to their liking. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and venture capitalist David Sacks are advocating for the president to take a light touch, concerned about how regulation might jeopardize America’s dominance. As these figures have scaled their public influence, their surrogates and spokespeople (OpenAI president Greg Brockman, top OpenAI lobbyist Chris Lehane, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark) have populated news stories, too.

But an astonishing amount of power rests in the hands of a few dozen other people, none particularly well known, some virtually anonymous. So New York Magazine has dedicated this year’s annual “Power” issue to surfacing 26 people whose influence on the AI landscape far outstrips their fame. To assemble the list, we partnered with Transformer, a small but impressive publication with a command of the politics within transformative AI. The Transformer team drew on its years of reporting, as well as new interviews with more than 50 high-ranking industry leaders, to help articulate what makes these people powerful. We then commissioned multi-media artist Simon Denny to create images of each.

Despite the hundreds of billions in capex and upcoming IPOs, many parts of the field are immature, which means those who decide how AI is built, adopted, and controlled can quickly become among the most influential people in the world. A few on this list, for example, are tasked with shaping how the public, or a company, thinks about the technology — a high-leverage role for a field where everyone’s views are still being formed. (This is, in part, why AI has such an “essay”-driven culture — a blog post really can cause a seismic change.) Some will invent entirely new product categories, reimagining how we interact with AI, while others can spin up new industries or advocacy groups with a single check. Who is ahead and who is behind can change almost overnight (just look at Microsoft), which helps explain why a legacy tech CEO could have less sway over what Altman thinks than a 26-year-old with a podcast and why an engineer who runs a new critical function may appear on this list instead of a colleague who sits several rungs higher in their org chart. (Relatedly, the list’s average age is 36. It is also overwhelmingly male.)

The AI scene is still small. The 26 individuals on our “Power List” are remarkably intertwined, some even sharing offices, homes, or funding. (Transformer receives funding from an organization run by Alexander Berger, who appears on this list — and he in turn has ties to many of the other people cited.) The widespread societal impact of AI led us to include names from both private and public sectors, so you’ll find founders and engineers as well as lawmakers and regulators. Most important, they still have everything to play for. The new power brokers will decide how it all shakes out, refashioning the world for the rest of us in the process.
Logan Graham Stands Between Us and the Next Rogue AI Model
Head of the Frontier Red Team at Anthropic | Age: 32

As the leader of Anthropic’s frontier “red teaming” efforts — a Cold War–inspired practice of playing the villain to find holes in your own defenses — Logan Graham has the job of pushing AI models to do terrifying things. This may mean persuading models to run cyberattacks or explain how to build a bioweapon. If the model then behaves dangerously, Graham’s Frontier Red Team is in charge of warning both company leadership and the public. So far, that’s happened at least twice, and each time Anthropic has pointed to Graham’s work as evidence. On April 7, the Frontier Red Team announced that Claude Mythos Preview had surpassed the usual cybersecurity benchmarks — tests designed to measure how good models are at hacking — and had to be tested on real-world security tasks instead. It found that the model could locate and exploit security bugs in every major operating system and web browser, potentially empowering nonexperts to run major cyberattacks. The company withheld Mythos from the public but granted limited access to a few dozen big-tech companies, including Amazon Web Services, JPMorgan Chase, Microsoft, and Google. Graham became the public face of this decision, which critics called a marketing strategy or elitist with Anthropic unilaterally determining whose cyberinfrastructure was worth defending first.

Graham joined Anthropic part time in 2022. That November, Graham “started red teaming LLMs for biorisks/weapons risks in my bedroom,” according to his subsequent tweet. Back then, frontier models couldn’t reliably do math or count the number of r’s in strawberry, but Graham still persuaded his bosses to dedicate resources to figuring out what AI could do at its worst. The Frontier Red Team he built would be one of the first in-house research groups of its kind.

“Some people’s intuition from growing up in a peaceful world is that somewhere there’s a room full of adults who know how to fix it,” Graham told Time earlier this year. “There are no groups of adults. There is no room in the first place … You are responsible.” Despite the nature of his work, a colleague described Graham as “very chipper.” Once, when asked what quality he most sought in red teamers, he responded “craftiness.”
Paul Christiano Is One of the Few People Who Can Slow Down OpenAI From the Inside
Founder of Alignment Research Center | Age: 37

Over the past 15 years, Paul Christiano has helped pioneer the AI-safety movement, converting the mostly theoretical concerns of figures like Eliezer Yudkowsky into hands-on research and seeding the ideas and frameworks — documented in papers, blog posts, and comment threads — that have become the air the whole field breathes. But as an early researcher at OpenAI, he was integral to inventing the technique that helped make the company’s products commercially viable, kicking off the AI arms race.

As an undergraduate at MIT, Christiano read LessWrong, the online forum co-founded by Yudkowsky that helped birth today’s AI-safety world. Christiano was studying math and quantum computing but gradually turned his attention to alignment, the challenge of creating AI systems that do what human users want them to do. A blog post of his, titled “What Failure Looks Like,” laid out what have become the two dominant visions of AI’s worst-case scenarios: one, which Christiano calls “going out with a whimper,” where humans gradually render themselves irrelevant; another, “going out with a bang,” where AI-controlled critical infrastructure breaks down, leading to societal collapse. When doomers talk about “doom,” they’re often picturing Christiano’s nightmare.

In 2017, Christiano joined OpenAI, where he led the development of reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF, a method that turns raw language models into helpful, instruction-following assistants. RLHF is one of the biggest differences between Sydney — an unhinged Microsoft chatbot rumored to be an early version of OpenAI’s GPT-4 — and today’s polite, helpful chatbots. It’s now a crucial part of all frontier AI-training pipelines and may have done more to unlock the technology’s mass-commercialization potential than almost anything else.

Around the time Dario Amodei, Christiano’s co-author of the paper that helped introduce RLHF, exited OpenAI, Christiano left, too, founding a research nonprofit called the Alignment Research Center. In the spring of 2024, the Biden administration brought him on as the AI Safety Institute’s head of AI safety, where he would be in charge of testing frontier AI models. Government staffers threatened to quit over his ties to effective altruism before his first day on the job. But through widespread DOGE-era cuts and institutional overhauls, Christiano somehow stayed put — he still works part time as a special government employee. In September, the day after Jacob Coxon’s viral Anthropic resignation tweet, Christiano announced that he was joining OpenAI’s nonprofit board to serve on its Safety and Security Committee. The five-person committee, at least on paper, has the power to delay OpenAI’s model releases, giving Christiano the chance to wrangle his former employer into controlling its AI risks before it’s too late.
Dylan Patel’s Analyses Can Spook Even Nvidia’s CEO
Founder and CEO of SemiAnalysis | Age: 30

Jensen Huang runs the world’s most valuable company. Even he cares what Dylan Patel, founder of the research-and-consulting firm SemiAnalysis, thinks: At the company’s conference this year, Huang took a moment to say that Nvidia’s chips are good because SemiAnalysis says they are. Since Patel launched it six years ago as an anonymous blog about semiconductors and hardware, SemiAnalysis has quickly become one of the industry’s leading sources of research and analysis of the chips, data centers, and power that AI runs on. When SemiAnalysis said AMD’s chips were being held back by poor software, CEO Lisa Su met with Patel the next day. The company publicly acknowledged the critique and set up a developer-relations team seemingly as a result.

Patel has been obsessed with the technical nuances of silicon since he was a teen lurking on chip sub-Reddits and has a talent for networking that feeds him a steady stream of gossip. In 2023, when everyone was reporting that TSMC’s limited chip-packaging capacity was curtailing the supply of Nvidia chips, SemiAnalysis mapped the upstream suppliers, showing how long the bottleneck would last and who would profit. “There were a bunch of people doing technical research” when SemiAnalysis launched, according to Sequoia’s Shaun Maguire, “but no one that could combine the technical breakthroughs with the business impact.” (Sequoia has invested in SemiAnalysis.) When the AI boom started, Patel and his team “were the first to really understand the whole systems math,” says Maguire, building complex models that linked the cost of chips to AI companies’ margins — and selling them to hedge funds, AI companies, and semiconductor giants.

SemiAnalysis reportedly expects $100 million in revenue this year. It recently acquired Citrini Research and raised $500 million for a fund investing in AI infrastructure and chip companies. Critics note that could create serious conflicts of interest — something Patel has brushed off.
Every Silicon Valley CEO Is Listening to Dwarkesh Patel
Host of ‘Dwarkesh Podcast’ | Age: 26

Top episodes of Dwarkesh Podcast, where guests talk unabashedly about “the parallelization penalty” and “the Schwarzschild metric,” often for well over 90 minutes, can attract some 2 million views. But the scale of the audience matters less than its composition: It has become required listening for Silicon Valley’s top AI researchers and executives. Big industry names like Jane Street and SpaceXAI’s Grok Bot have sponsored the show, knowing they’ll get in front of nearly every AI executive in the Bay Area. And while many of the guests — which include Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk — might be unavailable to most reporters, they’ll agree to be interviewed by Patel. One top tech PR representative told us that clients would rather be on his podcast than 60 Minutes.

Patel’s show sets the agenda for what the industry thinks about. Take his November 2025 interview with Ilya Sutskever, the tight-lipped co-founder of Safe Superintelligence Inc. Sutskever — who, while working at OpenAI, correctly foresaw that training bigger AI models on more data with more computing power would reliably make them smarter — told Patel, “Now that compute is big, we are back to the age of research.” Sutskever was predicting that we’d hit the limits of what increased computing power alone could do and sparked fierce debate about whether AI progress was about to hit a wall. Through essays and interviews, Patel also seeds his own point of view — that AI will be a big deal, but truly transformative models will come slower than companies have promised because they haven’t yet achieved continual learning, or the ability to learn independently in real time. While “people were aware of it as a problem,” Anthropic’s Sholto Douglas said in an interview earlier this year, “a lot of the AI labs started talking about it publicly after Dwarkesh raised its public prominence.”

Patel isn’t exactly a journalist, and what might qualify as egregious conflicts of interest in legacy media give him a leg up in tech podcasting, where busy researchers tend to distrust reporters and lack the patience for surface-level conversations. His interview with Mechanize founders Ege Erdil and Tamay Besiroglu, whose stated mission is the “full automation of the economy,” dropped the day the company launched; Patel disclosed himself as an angel investor in Mechanize as well as several other companies whose founders he’s interviewed. A friend of Patel’s says they “would go as far as saying that if he wasn’t an insider, the researchers wouldn’t trust him.”
Thibault Sottiaux Is Deciding How You, Your Boss, and Your Employee Use AI at Work
Head of core products at OpenAI | Age: 34

In the two years since he joined OpenAI, Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux has become one of its top executives, overseeing ChatGPT, Codex, and the company’s API platform. His decisions affect all 1.2 billion weekly users of ChatGPT and the future of work as we know it.

Anthropic originally had the advantage in the coding market with a cultlike following among developers for Claude Code. OpenAI’s competing product, Codex, was faltering. That changed once Sottiaux took over the team last year. At the time, coding agents were mostly used via developers’ “terminal” apps — a clunky, text-only command-line interface that scared off the average user. Sottiaux, who has a background building internal tools for researchers, realized that this wouldn’t work, especially once users’ interactions with agents became more complex and they began to run multiple agents simultaneously and work on longer tasks. So he pivoted the team to building a native desktop app, a simple interface that would let nontechnical people direct AI agents for office work (sifting through emails, handling spreadsheets, writing memos). It was a “contrarian bet,” says Dan Shipper, a founder and AI commentator who recently wrote a lengthy history of Codex. But the team yielded to Sottiaux’s “sense of focus,” an OpenAI colleague says.

The Codex app was released in February, and Codex had 2 million weekly users by March 19. In May, Sottiaux was promoted to head of core products, reporting directly to president of OpenAI Greg Brockman. Two months later, ChatGPT’s desktop app was rebuilt around Codex. Sottiaux’s “little backwater … became the foundation of ChatGPT, and their leaders became the people who run the whole of the ChatGPT org,” Shipper says. It helped that Sottiaux had become something of a personality among the AI crowd, thanks to his remarkably accessible X presence and his habit of frequently and publicly resetting people’s usage limits, handing out tokens as freely as Oprah once did cars.

Sottiaux, who deploys Codex as a “little chief of staff,” now has his sights set on something bigger. In a recent podcast interview, he described wanting to build a “permanent active intelligence that knows everything it needs to do and is available through any client, any screen”: something similar to the omnipresent AIs of Star Trek. Dots, a personal assistant slowly rolling out to ChatGPT’s billion-plus users, is a step in that direction.
Nat Friedman Put Back in the AI Race
Head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs | Age: 49

In the spring and summer of 2025, Meta’s AI strategy looked desperate and lost. The latest version of its open-weight Llama model had been a bit of a bust, so Mark Zuckerberg went on a spending spree to lure the world’s best AI researchers and executives. Two of the pickups were Scale AI co-founder Alexandr Wang and former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman.

Things were tumultuous for a bit. Legacy AI talent headed out, Meta cut about 600 jobs in its AI division, and some new hires left, some almost immediately. This past June, when Meta delayed its new AI model Muse Spark, the division looked dead on arrival.

In September, the company released Muse, an agentic AI assistant that can book flights, organize your inbox, and discover money that you may be owed. Although it arrived amid a wave of agents released by tech companies — SpaceXAI, OpenAI, and Instinct — Muse, powered by Spark, rose to the top of the app charts. Wang has been the face of Muse, appearing onstage at the annual Meta developer conference and turning his X account into a flow of memes featuring the app’s fuzzy mascot. But sources close to Meta’s AI team say the credit for the app’s success belongs to Friedman. While Wang is head of Superintelligence Labs, the AI division responsible for developing the models, Friedman is tasked with Muse’s product development. He technically reports to Wang, but sources say they’re valued equally in Zuck’s eyes. It’s still unclear how big AI agents will get, but Muse is best positioned to market itself on the back of Meta’s billion-plus-user platforms.

Friedman has made a career of taking open-source software that only programmers could love and making it publicly accessible. He co-founded a company in the late 1990s that tried to make the free Linux operating system friendly for ordinary computer users. He later went on to run GitHub, the Microsoft-owned site where millions of software developers store and share their code. On his watch, GitHub released Copilot, the first AI coding assistant to really catch on. Likewise, Friedman said Muse was heavily inspired by OpenClaw, a free AI assistant that went viral with programmers earlier this year but was too technical for the average person to use.
Sarah Guo Might Pick the Next Baby Billionaire
Founder and partner of Conviction | Age: 37

In June, the venture capitalist Sarah Guo published a blog post about an “AI psychosis” that had consumed her fellow investors across the Valley. It was characterized, she wrote, by “a despair that nothing is investible, that we should put all our money into Anthropic and Nvidia and go home.” But that “psychosis,” she says, didn’t reach her. “I have never felt it,” Guo wrote.

Guo is the founder of Conviction, one of the biggest AI-native VC funds to emerge from the post-generative AI era. She started it in 2022 after leaving Greylock, where she’d become its youngest partner at 28. Her thesis: Capital won’t just flow to a small number of vertically integrated frontier labs but to a whole ecosystem of AI: AI-native software companies, data-serving providers, chip manufacturers, and scientific researchers. Her first investment, the then-little-known legal start-up Harvey, is now valued at $15.5 billion. She followed with early-stage investments in European lab Mistral, AI-assisted medical-search engine OpenEvidence, and coding tool Cognition. OpenEvidence, or “ChatGPT for doctors,” has become so popular OpenAI is competing with its own copycat product, while Cognition has started to raise at the dollar amounts of frontier AI companies (it is reportedly pursuing a $1 billion raise).

On the podcast she co-hosts, Guo has interviewed industry veterans like Jensen Huang as well as founders she’s invested in, building hype for follow-on funding rounds and attracting customers. Critics may say she is too gauche, too flashy — the type of investor who makes a celebrity of themself with vinyl outfits and a podcast. But a peer investor says Guo has a knack for making the founders best suited to build ecosystem projects eager for her coaching. The child of two engineers, Guo tends to zero in on technical people, whom she invests in at the Series A or seed stage, or even earlier, incubating start-ups in their infancy. Her investments sometimes act as a signal to other venture capitalists as to where to invest and trigger trends in and of themselves. “I love killer nerds,” she says.
Karol Hausman and His Team Could Break AI’s Physical-World
CEO of Physical Intelligence | Age: 38

AI may be on its way to automating knowledge work, but it still can’t interact with the real world, leaving large swaths of the economy mostly off-limits. Many companies are squaring up to the challenge of building AI for robotics, but Physical Intelligence, a start-up led by former Google researcher Karol Hausman, has set itself apart by trying to solve one very fundamental part of the problem: It is trying to design AI models to build a universal robot brain.

In November 2024, Physical Intelligence, also known as Pi, announced it had received $400 million in funding from the likes of Jeff Bezos, OpenAI, and Thrive Capital. Another $600 million followed in November 2025, and a further $1 billion earlier this year — all for a company with no commercial product and no revenue. The start-up reportedly held discussions with Anthropic about a potential acquisition, too. (A representative for Pi declined to comment.) Making its financials more mind-boggling is that the company has made no promise to investors about selling products.

Hausman left his role leading research into robot manipulation at Google to start the company. Also on the founding team: Sergey Levine, who is a professor at UC Berkeley and, by some metrics, the most-cited researcher in robotics; Chelsea Finn, whose Ph.D. was co-advised by Levine and whom former colleagues call a “robot whisperer” and who is a professor at Stanford, where her lab masterminded the low-cost two-armed-robot setups that many serious robotics labs now use. Together, the three helped lead a project at Google that’s broadly thought to have parlayed the transformer architecture of LLMs into robotics by adding images and motion to the training data to create vision-language-action models, or VLAs. Two of the other co-founders, Brian Ichter and Quan Vuong, also worked on that project. Adnan Esmail, another technical co-founder, was previously SVP of engineering at Anduril Industries. On the business side is Lachy Groom, an early employee at Stripe, when he was just 18, and a solo VC who invested in Figma, Notion Labs, and Ramp.

Already, Pi has managed to show progress on the fundamental problems that still puzzle flashier companies. Most humanoid robots have yet to live up to the hype of their developers. Tesla’s Optimus has faced criticism for reliance on remote controls during presentations; the AI robotics company Figure has reportedly exaggerated the scope and scale of its deployments; the home helper of rival company 1X requires a remote operator to do anything that could count as useful. But Physical Intelligence’s latest model, π0.7, eventually worked out how to cook a sweet potato in an air fryer it had barely seen in training. Critics contend, with no agreed benchmarks in robotics, it’s hard to say if the progress it has made is particularly meaningful. Proponents argue that it’s a glimmer of what researchers call compositional generalization, the ability of a model to stitch together snippets of what it knows into a bigger, more complex task.
Beth Could Force the Industry’s Secrets Into the Open
Founder and CEO of METR | Age: 29

On September 16, in the middle of apocalyptic statements from industry defectors and polarized calls for regulation, the New York Post published a cover story: “The Woke Wizards of A.I.” Its subject was METR, a nonprofit that tests AI models before they’re released. The previous week, Dario Amodei had named METR a potential “embedded third-party evaluator” meant to monitor his and other labs. Now the Post was painting Beth Barnes as the leader of a band of “globalists” who believe in “genderless pronoun[s]” and the impending AI apocalypse.

Barnes spent three years at OpenAI researching how to stop AI models from going rogue or otherwise acting against human intentions but lost confidence in anyone’s ability to change the industry from the inside. (“I think I am a very open and honest person,” she told Time in 2024. “I am not very good at navigating political things and not making disagreements pretty obvious.”) Founded in 2022, METR has positioned itself as a small team of trusted technical experts, more resourced and bullish on AGI than existing academic labs. The first of its kind, it used its ties with industry researchers to gain early access to OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Anthropic’s Claude, pioneering the practice of third-party model evaluations in the world of AI safety. It would be another year until peer-auditing organizations like Apollo Research and the U.K.’s AI Security Institute came along. METR’s “time horizon” chart — a curve illustrating the exponential growth in the difficulty of tasks models are capable of — has become one of the most-cited charts in AI. It’s what people point to as a sign the singularity is coming.

Barnes, a scrupulous technical researcher, has managed to earn the trust of nearly everyone in and around major AI companies. Today, METR shares a building with a number of AI-safety nonprofits, funders, and industry research fellows, providing “lots of opportunities to interact directly with people at the AI companies,” said David Krueger, former research director at the U.K.’s AI Security Institute. That, on top of Barnes’s long-standing connections to OpenAI, gives METR rare access into otherwise-impenetrable companies. And while METR doesn’t take money from AI companies or individuals working at them, it uses their free tokens and relies on the continued goodwill of industry researchers, who can revoke METR’s access anytime they’d like. Anthropic recently gave six METR staffers “employee-like access” to its office, including hardware and tools normally hidden far from outsiders.
Brendan Foody Might Be the Reason Your Job Gets Automated
Co-founder of Mercor | Age: 23

If AI comes for your job, there’s a good chance it’ll be because of Mercor. The early years of hiring thousands of people to prod, test, and train AI models mostly focused on cheaper labor, but Mercor, founded in 2023 by Brendan Foody and his high-school debate friends Adarsh Hiremath and Surya Midha, recruits doctors, bankers, academics, and even poets.

These highly skilled employees are paid to help train AI models to do their jobs. They evaluate how good models are already, develop rubrics to measure what “good” looks like, and rate models’ outputs to help train them. Mercor’s AI Productivity Index (APEX) has become a core standard against which models are judged, feeding into predictions about how much of the knowledge economy AI will eat and letting companies know where they are falling short. “When a gap shows up in APEX, it tends to become what the whole industry works to hill-climb next,” says Foody. But the longer-term goal is to use that data to make those workers replaceable by turning their knowledge of their own jobs into training environments for AI. (A spokesperson for Mercor says the goal is for AI to take on “more of the routine tasks, and professionals move up the value chain to focus on higher-order work.”) As Foody told economist Tyler Cowen last year, “We’ll move toward these fixed-cost investments of teaching an agent how to do something … then being able to use agents as many times as we want.”

The focus on the premium end of the economy has already borne fruit, making the founders, all college dropouts, the world’s youngest self-made billionaires. As of last October, Mercor was valued at $10 billion and was reportedly in talks over a $20 billion valuation in July 2026. It sells its data and training environments to all the leading AI companies, and the valuations reflect how central Mercor’s approach may be to breaking down the barriers currently stopping AI models from becoming workers.

Mercor’s next step is to become indispensable to everyday businesses running AI agents and getting employees to improve their own employer’s AIs. “Companies are deploying agents without knowing whether they work,” says Foody. “The people who know what good work looks like are their own employees. In five years, Mercor will be the infrastructure every company and every lab uses to measure and improve how AI performs on real work.”
Dean Ball Is Nudging OpenAI to Embrace Regulation
Head of strategic futures at OpenAI | Age: 34

Earlier this year, OpenAI employees became increasingly upset with the company’s global-affairs team. Under Chris Lehane, OpenAI had taken a more reserved approach to AI regulation — one at odds with its engineers, many of whom had AI-safety concerns. The problem, some thought, was that the lobbyists thought of AI as a normal technology (Lehane had a background at Airbnb and in crypto) rather than the world-changing, godlike technology its staff were trying to build. The employee uproar seems to have worked: OpenAI’s policy stances have grown more pro-regulation in recent months. Perhaps more importantly, it hired Dean Ball.
Ball reports to chief strategy officer

items.title: Caviar and Caged Zebra: Inside Trump’s Halloween Bash For ‘Rich Friends’
items.description: Donald Trump has never been shy about showing off his wealth, even when it’s not politically prudent. During the 2025 government shutdown, he threw a Great Gatsby–themed Halloween party, mingling with Mar-a-Lago members dressed in glittering 1920s getups hours
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Donald Trump has never been shy about showing off his wealth, even when it’s not politically prudent. During the 2025 government shutdown, he threw a Great Gatsby–themed Halloween party, mingling with Mar-a-Lago members dressed in glittering 1920s getups hours before SNAP funding lapsed. In the months leading up to the midterms, Trump has repeatedly called Americans’ affordability concerns a “hoax” and made no secret of his focus on building himself a ballroom and gilding every available surface of the White House.

Still, Trump’s decision to host another ostentatious Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago just days before an election focused on voters’ economic concerns was really something. Here are some of the wildest details from Trump’s 2026 Halloween bacchanal.
Trump kept talking about his “rich friends.”

The president did not wear a Halloween costume; he showed up to the party in his usual red tie and navy suit. He noted that a lot of the “rich people” in attendance had spent far more time and money on their look.
“I came as Donald Trump,” he said. “I didn’t have time to get — people spent a lot of time and money. Rich people. They spent nine hours getting ready. I had ten minutes, so I came as Donald Trump.”

Membership to Mar-a-Lago is believe to be at least $200,000 a year, and at the party, Trump kept pointing out that his pals are quite wealthy. According to the New York Times, he repeatedly referred to attendees as his “rich friends.”
“Look at all my rich members,” Trump said. “They spent all day getting ready. Look at these guys.” He added, “These are the biggest guys on Wall Street.”

While most Americans served pizza and bowls of “fun size” candy at their Halloween parties, Trump’s bash featured Alaskan king crab and a caviar bar. The Daily Beast noted that Golden Goat Caviar tagged Mar-a-Lago in an Instagram story showing its products, and one partygoer posted this photo of the spread:

Diverging again from the typical October 31 bash, the theme of the party wasn’t simply “Halloween.” The Mar-a-Lago ballroom was transformed with green lighting, elaborate centerpieces, and a leafy archway with a sign that read “Jungle Cirque Adventure.” The Times noted:
There were cheetah and zebra stripes on the walls and tables. Women wore sequined leotards and elaborate headdresses, and one couple flocked around in bright-feathered costumes of jungle birds.

Many of the partygoers wore elaborate, skin-tight costumes and body paint that appeared to be custom-made for the event. Aside from the one guy in a rubber Joe Biden mask, no one was wearing some old costume they pulled out of the back of their closet:
A live zebra and a miniature pony were used as décor.

If you scrolled through those last few Instagram posts and thought, “Wait … is that a real zebra?” your eyes were not deceiving you. Multiple party photos posted to Instagram show people posing in front of a caged zebra. According to the Times there was also a miniature pony, but it seems he managed to avoid the shame of being caught at this tacky soirée:
Trump invited Speaker Mike Johnson.
And surprisingly, the Speaker didn’t think attending this ostentatious party just days before the midterms might be a bad idea. The Times spotted Johnson in an extremely sad VIP section:
There was Speaker Mike Johnson and Sergio Gor, the U.S. ambassador to India, in the cordoned-off section of the ballroom.
MAGA influencer Michael Solakiewicz also posted footage of Johnson mingling with Trump as a very on-the-nose remix of “Everybody Wants to Rule the World” plays in the background:
The Times noted Attorney General Todd Blanche was also supposed to attend the party, but it seems he thought better of it:

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who traveled with Mr. Trump on Air Force One on Friday, told reporters that he planned to wear an astronaut suit to the party. (On Sunday, a spokeswoman for Mr. Blanche said he neither attended the party nor intended to.)
Trump also invited the press.

How do we know exactly what went down at this party for extremely wealthy Trump fanatics? It’s not because some clever journalist snuck in disguised as the miniature horse. The president invited a gaggle of reporters into the event, and he spent about ten minutes gabbing with them on the dance floor as Secret Service agents kept people in parrot and safari costumes at bay. Trump answered questions on a variety of topics, from terrorism to the Iran war to why he doesn’t want his former lawyer Alina Habba Mildon to be paid $50 million for helping someone seek a pardon (unless she gives him a cut):

So there’s Trump’s closing midterms message: I’m eating caviar with my rich friends at a tacky Halloween party rather than doing anything to help everyday Americans — but at least I’m transparent about it!
It’s not great, but it does beat Damn, Jon Husted’s got a beautiful ass!

items.title: Prosecutors Intend to Retry Lindsay Clancy for Deaths of Her Three Children
items.description: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her three children to death in 2023 whose trial ended in a hung jury on Sept. 4, will likely be retried, prosecutors said on Monday.
items.author: Althea Legaspi
paragraphs: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her three children to death in 2023 whose trial ended in a hung jury on Sept. 4, will likely be retried, prosecutors said on Monday.
During a hearing on Monday, Clancy returned to court for a motion to dismiss the charges that she murdered her children. It was the second time she’s headed to court following her first trial.

On Monday, the defense argued to dismiss the charges citing double jeopardy, a legal rule that protects an accused person against being prosecuted by the state twice for the same crime. Prosecutors argued that double jeopardy “does not bar the Commonwealth from seeking justice on behalf of the three victims.”

According to Associated Press, Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington asked the judge to investigate the sole holdout juror, Michael P. Desronvil, bringing into question the juror’s use of a cell phone while the jury deliberated, alleging the juror researched terms related to the case. He also questioned if the juror had been telling the truth during jury selection in terms of disclosing previous criminal history that may have affected whether he would be selected, which if true would be a “fatal infection of the independence, the honesty and the integrity of this juror.”

Heather O’Connor, an attorney for Desronvil, said the defense were able to question the juror prior to the trial, accepted him, and only began to challenge his credibility once he became a holdout. She also disputed the cellphone allegation.

Things became heated between Judge William Sullivan and Reddington after Reddington publicly identified the holdout juror, with Sullivan alleging this was potentially confidential information. Reddington claimed the name was already “all over the internet,” but then acquiesced and stopped using the name.
Sullivan also heard arguments from the prosecution’s request for a gag order to restrict public statements from the attorneys involved, which could affect future court proceedings.

Clancy’s triple-murder trial ended in a mistrial after jurors said they were deadlocked and a higher court rejected the defense’s bid to intervene in the deliberations. The jury could not reach a unanimous verdict with the vote remaining 11-1 for at least two days.

Clancy had admitted to strangling her three children to death in January 2023, with her defense lawyers arguing she was in the throes of psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible. Meanwhile, prosecutors argued that while Clancy was deeply troubled, she understood that what she was doing was wrong. They asked the jurors to convict her of three counts of first-degree murder.

At the hearing on Monday, Sullivan did not immediately rule on the motion to dismiss. Prosecutors said they plan to retry Clancy if the case proceeds, but they have not identified if they would pursue the same charges. The next hearing is scheduled for Nov. 16, and if there is a retrial it could begin in March.

items.title: Timbaland Sues Ex-Managers for $15 Million, Fires Back at Claim He Blew Fortune
items.description: Timbaland, the Grammy-winning producer known for smash hits including Justin Timberlake’s “Sexy Back” and Missy Elliott’s “Get Ur Freak On,” is suing his ex-managers for $15 million and blasting claims by one of the managers, Gary Marella, that the hitmaker is
items.author: Nancy Dillon
paragraphs: Timbaland, the Grammy-winning producer known for smash hits including Justin Timberlake’s “Sexy Back” and Missy Elliott’s “Get Ur Freak On,” is suing his ex-managers for $15 million and blasting claims by one of the managers, Gary Marella, that the hitmaker is trying “to shift responsibility for his own overspending.”

“Mr. Marella is the one attempting to shift responsibility here,” the producer’s lawyer, Tynia Coats, says in a new statement sent to Rolling Stone on Monday. “Timbaland hired him to manage his business affairs and protect his interests. Holding someone accountable for the responsibilities they were hired and paid to perform is not shifting blame.”

Timbaland, whose legal name is Timothy Mosley, filed his lawsuit Friday in Los Angeles County Superior Court. It alleges Marella, along with Mosley’s business manager, Bruce Seckendorf, took over his finances in 2016 after the musician uncovered alleged misconduct by a prior management team. Rather than look after his interests, the lawsuit claims, the new managers used “their entrusted authority to enrich themselves and others, conceal financial misconduct, and deplete Timbaland’s valuable assets.”

According to the new lawsuit, obtained by Rolling Stone, Marella took at least $2.5 million in “excessive or unauthorized” commissions and saddled Mosley with fees, reimbursements, and “undisclosed American Express cards” that Marella allegedly used for groceries, cosmetic medical procedures, family vacations, and other personal expenses.

Mosley alleges that when he received two $5 million payments in 2021 from the Verzuz platform he created with Swizz Beatz, Marella was entitled to $1 million in commissions but took two payments of $750,000. He claims Marella and his company also “took $775,000 more than their authorized 10 percent commission” from his 2019 Hipgnosis catalog sale and that Marella “grossly mismanaged” their Beatclub venture, treating it like “a piggy bank to repair the problems he created.”

Mosley accused Seckendorf of facilitating the unauthorized payments, failing to disclose irregularities, failing to pay his taxes and mortgage, and taking a cut of sale proceeds without transparent accounting. He says the “scheme began to unravel in March 2025,” when a foreclosure notice arrived at his home.
In a statement sent to The Hollywood Reporter, Marella said Mosley was to blame for his financial issues.

“Unfortunately, Tim is attempting to shift responsibility for his own overspending and financial decisions onto someone else (again) as he did before we managed him,” Marella told the outlet, which first reported the new lawsuit. He claimed Mosley “had spent all of his money and was living in a rental,” and that over nine years, they generated about $75 million in business together. “Despite that, Tim continued spending beyond his means, ultimately having to sell his home last year due to his actions and move into a rental in Coral Gables. Those were the consequences of his own financial decisions, no one else.”
On Monday, Mosley and his lawyer said the issue isn’t “a problem with the artist’s spending.” They said they would “welcome a full accounting” showing how Mosley allegedly spent the $75 million.

In their response, Mosley and Coats alleged that beyond missing money, they have evidence that financial records were falsified to show that a third-party consultant was paid $16,000 when he actually received $165,000. They further claimed emails were altered to make it appear that Mosley approved paying an attorney $250,000 instead of $100,000.

Seckendorf did not immediately respond to requests for comment, but Marella sent an email statement to Rolling Stone claiming Mosley “was already in a bad financial place” when they started working together.

“The allegation that I paid myself without his knowledge is not possible. His business manager handled his finances and paid management commissions along with every other payment on Tim’s behalf, which Tim was aware of,” he said. Regarding Beatclub, he said, “Tim and I come from the music business, not the technology area.” He blamed Beatclub’s problems on an employee who allegedly “failed to build the platform properly.” Marella also claimed he and Mosley took out a joint $1 million loan and used $980,000 to cover outstanding company obligations.

Mosley’s new 75-page lawsuit includes claims for breach of fiduciary duty, fraudulent concealment, breach of contract, and civil theft. It alleges Mosley suffered damages estimated to exceed $15 million and asks for a jury trial.

items.title: War Recap: Stars — They’re Just Like Us
items.description: Here are some questions I asked myself as Carla Duval walked on to the set of the Jack Jeffreys Show in the opening sequence of this week’s episode: Where is Jeremy, Carla’s obnoxious co-star who appeared a few times in the season premiere and never again? Why
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: Here are some questions I asked myself as Carla Duval walked on to the set of the Jack Jeffreys Show in the opening sequence of this week’s episode: Where is Jeremy, Carla’s obnoxious co-star who appeared a few times in the season premiere and never again? Why is Serena there? (Answer: To remind Carla not to mention “the D-word,” the first instruction from Serena that Carla has ever had the courage to disobey.) Shouldn’t Carla’s publicist be there? Where is Carla’s publicist?

However relevant that question may be for the rest of the episode, it was especially pressing in the beginning, given that Carla bombs her late-night appearance. She looks nervous even before starting, but making the fake-nice chitchat required of talk-show interviews while host and audience fawn over that picture of herself with Morgan — the one taken on the red carpet shortly after she was served divorce papers — proves to be impossible. Carla goes rogue. Seething through her teeth, she says that Morgan is a “bullshitter” who wants a divorce. At the suggestion of his producer, Jack Jeffreys (Danny Sapani) tries to take a commercial break, but Carla apparently wants to talk, though she doesn’t say much. She only manages to tell the audience to “shut the fuck up” when they start heckling. In the wings, Serena makes a face like she knew this was coming.

This sequence, which kicks off the rest of the episode’s events, would have been a great opportunity for Sienna Miller to invest Carla with some intensity beyond her three established registers — compliant, angry, and horny; she’ll hit them all by the end of the episode — but Carla’s meltdown isn’t convincing, especially not when television history is littered with the minds celebrities lost during late-night interviews. Later, an incredulous Bella insists the whole thing is clearly a bad PR stunt. But this theory also puzzled me. What good would it do Carla to act contemptuously toward the public, when she needs their favor as she heads to court?

Almost no good, which to a capable publicist, is good enough. Serena summons Grace Hopper (Katherine Kingsley) to mitigate the crisis, which again brings up the question of where Carla’s own publicist is hiding. I’m not a stickler for details like these. I’m not a lawyer or a celebrity or a tech mogul; I hope to never be too familiar with the proceedings of a divorce; and as long as a show builds a consistent, compelling world, I’ll believe pretty much anything. But the fact that Carla doesn’t have her own publicist undermines the world-building — who, if not a publicist, would have booked her on the Jack Jeffreys Show? — and cheapens the plot. I want to sink into this fictional world, not question it.

What I do buy is that Cathcarts is happy with Carla’s disastrous public appearance. As the Taylor & Byrne office stresses over the interview, Cathcarts surveys the several tabloid stories that have come out about it while practically licking their lips. Both teams know that the viral interview has no legal bearing, but it does have the potential to shift public opinion, which matters for litigation. Carla’s major, and perhaps only, advantage over Morgan’s wealth was the favor of the public, which she compromised when she swore at an unsuspecting audience. In the immediate aftermath, a wreath of flowers arrives for Nick and Serena, along with a card that reads, simply, “R.I.P.”

Cathcarts’ next move is to stall the litigation process as much as possible. They know, from the financial statements that Johnny sent to Schill, that Taylor & Byrne is broke, so the longer the process takes, the worse it will be for them. Beatrice calls it “the march of the snails.” When Taylor & Byrne request a statement of interests for the past six months, Cathcarts sends dozens of boxes of documents, any of which could contain the single relevant file. Except, as Schill tells Johnny over the phone, Cathcarts “forgot” to send the right box, which will only arrive the next day, via “London’s slowest courier.” It’s a dirty trick familiar to anyone who has watched a legal drama or two.

While the overworked and probably underpaid Taylor & Byrne associates sort through the boxes, Michael and Nora go over Carla’s personal assets with her while Saeed takes notes. Carla is despondent and distracted, scrolling Zephyr while they talk, but she is soon warmed by Nora and Michael’s kindness. She jokes that the only thing they’re missing is her Ferrari Testarossa, which the equally distracted Saeed puts down as an asset, right under “two horses.” He asks Molly to type up the notes for Serena, so it’s Molly who gets chewed out when Serena points out that neither Carla nor Morgan own a Ferrari. Molly retypes the list, as instructed, but when Johnny snoops around Serena’s office later that night, after everyone has left, he takes a picture of the uncorrected asset list — the one that includes the Ferrari — and sends it over to Schill. That’s how the Ferrari reappears on Cathcarts’ asset list. When they finally get a hold of it, Molly and Saeed are befuddled: How could Cathcarts possibly know about the imaginary Ferrari? Cut to Johnny looking nervous.

Meanwhile, Carla drowns in paparazzi. They mob her house and yell out cruel things about Gabe, making it “impossible” for Carla to go anywhere, including theater rehearsals. Not even Johnny’s charm can make her feel better — he offers to take her out for a drink, but she snaps at him that she’s not exactly in a position to be seen out and about.

When she enters the stage, Grace — the crisis-PR expert summoned by Serena — immediately brings up that old showbiz adage: There’s no such thing as bad publicity. It’s good that people are talking, because it means they care; and as long as they care, things can still change for Carla. And change they do, when a singer named Tamara Chong (Mei Mac) appears on a chat-cast called “Every Little Thing She Does” and encourages the public to take Carla’s anger seriously. Surely, she must have a reason. Social-media sentiment consequently shifts, and suddenly Carla’s high placement on Zephyr’s trending topics is not such a bad thing. Seizing the moment, Grace and Serena book Carla to go on the podcast that same day. Carla worries about the impact of this continued exposure on Gabe, but Serena assures her that they’ll be able to “control everything.”

Famous last words, I thought, but as it turns out, Carla is better at guesting on a podcast than on a late-night show. Looking strong and a little bit tired, as Grace advised, Carla avoids speaking too explicitly about the details of the divorce — she doesn’t bring up the cheating — and clarifies the reason for her angry outburst on the Jack Jeffreys Show: She was served divorce papers at her own premiere.

It’s the most listened-to podcast episode in the country, Smallwood tells Morgan, as well as the show’s most popular interview. Morgan resents the fact that he’s being made to look like a villain when the real villain is Smallwood. Besides, he was honey-trapped! But Cathcarts can’t use the Flora stuff because they’re not supposed to know about the honey trap, not that Morgan knows that he is not supposed to know. Thought You Can See Everything is the only thing out right now that raises questions about truth and deceit? Think again! Now I’m getting distracted imagining St. John Smallwood and Billy Evans going head to head in a court of law.

Smallwood’s advice to Morgan is that he call Gabe — who has been sending him “vicious messages” — to try to mend their relationship. For such a smart and powerful man, Morgan continues to be extremely gullible when it comes to Smallwood’s machinations. Morgan has a nice, conciliatory dinner with Gabe, which leads to a hug outside the restaurant, where Smallwood has some paparazzi strategically waiting. They snap a picture, which undoes all the healing Gabe and Morgan had just been through; Gabe immediately identifies their dinner as a PR move. The puppeteering incenses Morgan, who storms into Cathcarts to demand his lawyers quit playing games and get on with litigation already.

Then again, when has Morgan ever successfully put his foot down? Even Zephyr’s executives distrust his authority. At a meeting with seemingly every senior-plus employee of the company, Gillian and Eric address Morgan with open hostility. Guy (Olivier Sublet), a creative director who Morgan doesn’t even remember hiring, points out that the outcome of Morgan’s divorce could affect the whole company. Morgan defensively reminds the room that he is the founder, and as such, he gets to call the shots. Yet later, after he has tried to impose himself much in the same way at Cathcarts, he arrives at the Zephyr offices to discover that the board meeting he thought he was heading into is, in fact, a meeting with Michael Ancker (David Menkin), who finally comes with an offer to buy Zephyr. When Morgan says that such a transaction is impossible because of the freezing order, Michael offers to send him £2 billion through a “safe” account neither Carla nor her lawyers will be able to reach (sounds illegal). Morgan refuses Ancker’s offer outright and stops just short of spitting in the man’s face.

Whether or not the picture the Daily Mail publishes under the headline “Son Sides With Step-Father” will impact the positive sentiment toward Carla is to be determined, but it’s immediately effective in making Carla feel horrible. She was feeling better after giving in to Johnny’s “anything you need, call me X” text and inviting him to sneak into her house through the back door. They spend the whole night together, which means Johnny wakes up to several texts and missed calls from Bella. Seeing the tabloid story in the morning makes Carla reconsider the exposure litigation will bring. At the Taylor & Byrne offices, she tells Nick and Serena that she doesn’t want to go to court because of the public scrutiny it will invite into her and Gabe’s lives. Wondering how things got so vicious between her and Morgan — ahem, lady, you asked your friend to seduce him? — she remembers how at that idyllic, beloved cottage in Normandy, Morgan didn’t even know what “zephyr” meant. She is the one who named the company, after a poem she was fond of reading to Morgan. Pause: Carla came up with the name Zephyr? Nick says that if they take this simple fact to court, they could stand to win as much as half of Morgan’s money. It’ll be enough to take care of Carla and Gabe forever.

Carla immediately changes her mind and agrees to go to court after all, as she has done every time Nick and Serena have advanced their agenda, even though they have promised her this same outcome before. In War, the lawyers are more powerful than their clients, and if this makes for compelling drama, it can also lead to inconsistent characters. Morgan is wealthy and powerful, in theory, but seemingly helpless to enact any influence; Carla is “difficult,” in theory, but compliant with her lawyers. Now in the back half of its first season, War is at a loss as to how to answer a simple governing question: Who is the boss here?
Representations and Acknowledgments

• In this episode, asking for Johnny’s attention and expediency as he helps Cathcarts make the most out of chaos, David Schill quotes Keanu Reeves for the second time in the show. Loving this bit; would welcome more.
• I would also love to see a special episode that follows the theater group having to deal with Carla’s diva antics. She simply never showed up to rehearsal!

• The Ferrari Testarossa slipup is the first mistake Johnny makes as a mole, but there doesn’t seem to be much that can trace it back to him. As far as we know, he was alone in the office when he snapped the picture of the document. What it could potentially do is incriminate Serena, or at least make her look inattentive. Maybe in the end it will be Molly taking the heat, since she was the one to mistype the note, which might create some compelling drama — Molly has been watching Johnny like a hawk. I’m starting to think she’s going to be the first person to sniff him out.

• Speaking of the asset list mix-up, one thing confused me. Why is the photo Johnny sent even valuable to Cathcarts? Isn’t the whole point of the list that Taylor & Byrne would have sent it to them, anyway? Why would Cathcarts base their documents on the picture Johnny sent, rather than the list they got through Taylor & Byrne, when it doesn’t put them at any explicit advantage? It’s not like Johnny was giving them any information they weren’t guaranteed to have?

items.title: Druski Sets Netflix Series ‘Collect & Praise’ Based on Megachurch Sketch, Signs Multi-Year Deal With Streamer
items.description: Druski is bringing his money-hungry megachurch pastor character to Netflix.
items.author: Ethan Shanfeld
paragraphs: Druski is bringing his money-hungry megachurch pastor character to Netflix.

The comedian will star opposite Mike Epps in a new, semi-scripted comedy series titled “Collect & Praise,” premiering on the streamer on Dec. 1. The show is based on a character made viral by Druski in an internet sketch and at the BET Awards. Epps will play the pastor’s deacon as they “scheme their way through scandal, chaos and controversy,” according to the logline.

“Collect & Praise” is the first project to be produced as part of a multi-year deal Druski signed with Netflix to create original content exclusively for the streamer through his 4Lifers Entertainment company.

The series marks the first time the 32-year-old, born Drew Desbordes, will adapt one of his popular internet personas into a longform television production. The comedian, who became famous by self-financing his content and distributing it independently on social media, now forms his first major partnership within the Hollywood studio system.

As part of the deal, Netflix will license select content from Druski’s existing catalog, including “Coulda Been Love,” “Coulda Been Daddy,” “Coulda Been Records Auditions” and his comedic skits. These series, posted directly to YouTube, have generated more than 1 billion views collectively.

“I’ve built my platform by creating characters and comedy that resonate with people,” Druski said in a statement. “This partnership with Netflix will give me the resources to build on that comedy foundation and bring my work to a new global audience. It’s a tremendous opportunity for our team at 4Lifers Entertainment to expand our reach, develop original programming for the masses and take our creativity to new heights.”

“Druski has a gift for building characters that people can’t stop talking about,” said John Derderian, who oversees Next Gen Content at Netflix. “We want the best talent in the world to bring us their most ambitious work, reach new audiences and build their brands. ‘Collect & Praise’ is just the beginning, and we welcome Druski to Netflix.”

Druski is one of comedy’s most exciting and fast-growing voices in recent years. Earlier this year, the Atlanta native became the youngest-ever host of the BET Awards, and he joined Emma Stone and Chris Pine in the cast of upcoming rom-com “The Catch.” His other credits include Prime Video’s “Livestream From Hell,” “Praise This” and the “House Party” reboot. This weekend, he will host “Saturday Night Live,” becoming the first true digital creator to do so.

items.title: HBO Renews Sharon Horgan Comedy ‘Youth’ For a Season 2
items.description: HBO has given a Season 2 order to “Youth,” the latest series from Peabody and BAFTA winner Sharon Horgan. The series’ Season 1 is currently streaming on HBO Max.
items.author: Michael Schneider
paragraphs: HBO has given a Season 2 order to “Youth,” the latest series from Peabody and BAFTA winner Sharon Horgan. The series’ Season 1 is currently streaming on HBO Max.
In the show, Horgan plays a 50-year-old divorcee navigating relationships, her ailing parents and her troubled son, who isn’t quite gelling at his new college.
Horgan plays Alex in the series, which also stars Rupert Friend (Patrick), Sharlene Whyte (Sam), Aran Murphy (Ruari), and Robbie Gee (Frank). Season 1 consisted of eight episodes.

“I’m so happy to get another opportunity to live out my emotional and biological crises on HBO,” Horgan said in a statement. “I can’t think of a better platform to air my UTI problems on. The response to ‘Youth’ has been beyond what I could have hoped for. I’m so grateful for the response and the chance to work with this incredible cast and creative team once more.”

According to HBO, “Youth” ranks “among the top five HBO comedy launches globally.” The show has a 97% score on Rotten Tomatoes, and critics have been positive — including Variety, which lauded Horgan for her “magnetic screen presence” and as “a sharp comic writer.”

“In a way that only she can, Sharon has created a show that makes us howl with laughter and with tears — often in the same moment,” said Amy Gravitt, the exec VP of HBO Programming and head of HBO & HBO Max comedy series. “Each performance in ‘Youth’ is more delightful than the next. Along with our partners at Merman, we are so thrilled to have this brilliant ensemble back for another season.”

Merman (“Amandaland,” “Bad Sisters,” “Vladimir”) is behind “Youth.” Sharon Horgan stars in, writes and executive produces the series. Additional executive producers are Faye Dorn for Merman, Jim Kleverweis and Dawn Shadforth, who also directs.

items.title: Former ‘Ellen’ Executive Producer Matthew Wright Dies as Ellen DeGeneres Posts Tearful Video Calling Him “The Glue to Our Entire Family”
items.description: Former The Ellen DeGeneres Show executive producer Matthew Wright died Friday in what a GoFundMe campaign for his family calls an “unfathomable tragedy.” He was 52, according to reports.
items.author: Hilary Lewis
paragraphs: Former The Ellen DeGeneres Show executive producer Matthew Wright died Friday in what a GoFundMe campaign for his family calls an “unfathomable tragedy.” He was 52, according to reports.
Wright died while working remotely in Los Angeles, according to the GoFundMe, while his family is in New York. Both Wright and his husband were “laid off this summer,” the GoFundMe states.

“And the unexpected costs of getting Matt home, a funeral and a memorial are impossible for the family to bear,” the GoFundMe reads. “If Matt has ever made you laugh, said an encouraging word right when you needed it or ordered one too many appetizers for the enjoyment of the whole table, now is the time to repay the favor. Please donate what you can and share this with anyone who’s been in the orbit of Matt’s huge heart. And when you’re at dinner and see a sunset, know that Matt is looking down, loving you, but wildly disappointed in what you ordered.”
DeGeneres posted a tearful video on Instagram Monday remembering Wright, who worked on her show from 2006 to its finale in 2022.

“He was an amazing guy. He was funny. God, he made me laugh. He would surprise me with things that he did all the time. He was smart. He was kind. He was the part of our show that — I mean, everyone loved him. I loved him. And it’s just shocking — it’s shocking. We’re gonna miss him. He is and always will be the glue to our entire family at The Ellen Show.”
DeGeneres also noted that Wright was close with former Ellen DJ Stephen “tWitch” Boss, who died in 2022, saying she believes the two are now reunited in the afterlife, “dancing and laughing.”

DeGeneres ended her tribute with a compilation of some of Wright’s funniest moments on her show, including a video of him jokingly admonishing restaurants for bringing too many appetizers to the table at once in a segment called “Strong Opinions With Matt.”

Fellow former Ellen executive producer Andy Lassner also took to Instagram to remember Wright, sharing photos of himself with Wright on the set of The Jennifer Hudson Show on Thursday, where Lassner now works as a executive producer, which Lassner said were taken “hours” before Wright died.

“We are all in shock. He was a brilliant producer and an even better human being,” Lassner wrote in the caption. “The way he looked after his mom, flying back and forth from Los Angeles to New York practically every weekend before she died, showed what an incredible son he was. He gave that same depth of love to his friendships. My heart breaks for his husband, Justin, his family, and all of us who loved him. I was so lucky to work beside Matt for so many years and to call him my friend. We should have had so much more time with him.”
Former The Real co-host Loni Love also paid tribute to Wright, writing on Facebook that she was “devastated and heartbroken” to hear that he died.

“He was such a talented, sweet man and always game for anything. I cannot believe he’s gone,” she wrote. “What a pleasure it was to have known him. Sending love and heartfelt condolences to his husband, family and all who loved him.”
The fundraising post, which sought to raise $50,000 for a funeral and memorial as well as a trust for his niece, had already surpassed its goal by Monday afternoon.

items.title: Inside CNN’s Tech-Forward Midterm Election Set
items.description: Multiple magic walls. New forms of data. And a decision desk that will be front and center are among the plans CNN has up its sleeve for Tuesday’s midterm elections.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: Multiple magic walls. New forms of data. And a decision desk that will be front and center are among the plans CNN has up its sleeve for Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Abigail Crutchfield, senior VP of Washington programming & special events programming for CNN, gave a walkthrough of the set for The Hollywood Reporter, showing off the walls of screens, the new Magic Wall displays that John King will hold forth at, and sections of the set and decision desk that will allow for more conversations between anchors and experts.

“We are making choices about what is the thing that we want to talk about and show you at any given moment,” Crutchfield says. “Obviously we don’t want chaos, and we don’t want it to just be a flood of information that nobody can understand. But we do want to be able to connect the dots between the different pieces.”

As with past elections, the anchors will serve as the masters of ceremonies, so to speak, calling the races, asking the analysts and correspondents for their thoughts, and throwing to reporters in the field. But this year data will be a supporting character too, and not just on King’s Magic Wall (though they will have that too).
