“I view myself as something of a conductor on election night,” says Jake Tapper, who will co-anchor coverage alongside Anderson Cooper. “I’m surrounded by people who are really, really good at what they do, and part of my job is knowing when to bring each of them in. Let’s say John King at the Magic Wall is the horn section, and our analysts and commentators are the strings. It’s a team effort, and you’re trying to bring all of those voices and all of that information together in a way that makes sense for the viewer.”

“If you’ve ever been in a control room on election night, you have so much data and information at your fingertips, and then usually it’s the control room that is really picking ‘okay, what are we going to show viewers? What are we going to talk about on air?’ And a lot of that is about just having clarity and storytelling,” Crutchfield says. “But we live in an age now where people can be looking at results online, and there’s things that they’re getting on social media. So, a lot of what we wanted to do is just put some of that information that we have always looked at on election night, and put it front and center for our viewers and for our talent … we wanted them to be able to see everything real time, like we are as it’s coming in, so that we can all help interpret it and bring it to viewers together.”

Viewers will notice that many of the anchors, correspondents and analysts will all be on the set together, a change from recent elections where multiple sets and multiple cities were the norm. It’s part of the larger goal of taking viewers behind the scenes to understand how the sausage gets made.

“What’s exciting about this set is that more of that team is going to be in the room with us,” says Jake Tapper. “There will be more people, more information and more tools at our fingertips, so viewers will really get a sense of the full operation behind an election night.”
And King’s Magic Wall will get its multi-screen upgrade, which Crutchfield says will be distinct from previous efforts in that the data will all be connected.

“What we’re what we’re able to do this year is they’re all connected. So when John is digging into a particular county on his wall, he gets he gets data that’s connected to that county, whether it’s demographics or history,” she says. “There’s different options that he can choose, but it all comes up simultaneously to help with his storytelling. And then it also has a dynamic leaderboard so that he can see at any given moment where the races are for the Senate, House, or governors, and then where the possible flips are.”

But it is the decision desk, led by Jennifer Agiesta, that will play a more prominent role in coverage, with the anchors expected to turn to them to really explain why they are making the calls that they are.

“It’s basically giving viewers a sense of what are the indicators, and sometimes the indicators are not pointing the same direction, and that’s when it gets really interesting,” Crutchfield says, noting the “confusing” nature of midterm elections. “It’s giving people a sense of where the race is going, and then it’s explaining to them why we think that, and that’s obviously all real time data.”

“I’ve been covering elections since 2000, and there’s still nothing quite like them,” Tapper says. “You can prepare for every scenario, but the night ultimately takes you where it takes you. After months if not years of polls and pundits and predictions what’s exciting about election night is it’s entirely up to the voters. It’s entirely in their hands. That lack of control and excitement about the unknown makes it so fun to anchor.”

items.title: Ezra Frech on Tackling ‘DWTS’ Season 35 With Amber Glenn as “Teammates” and What Becoming the Show’s First Amputee Winner Would Mean
items.description: Like any athlete, Ezra Frech is in it to win it on Dancing With the Stars. And there’s a real chance he could be the celebrity walking away with the mirrorball on the show’s Nov. 24 finale.
items.author: McKinley Franklin
paragraphs: Like any athlete, Ezra Frech is in it to win it on Dancing With the Stars. And there’s a real chance he could be the celebrity walking away with the mirrorball on the show’s Nov. 24 finale.
Frech doesn’t want to look too far ahead, though. “You can’t think too far ahead on a show like Dancing With the Stars. Anything could happen at any week,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter.

The Paralympic gold medalist has consistently scored well on the competition dance series, and is an even bigger hit with fans online. He has particularly inspired a younger generation of viewers, many who seem themselves represented in Frech’s journey as an amputee.

“Our grounding, stabilizing force is the love and support that we receive from the fans,” he says, adding that his “motivation” for doing the show was to represent the disabled community and “all people with disabilities.”
Many athletes have competed on DWTS, and the track and field star is not left lonesome this year, as he’s also dancing against fellow Olympic gold medalist Amber Glenn.

Their castings as the sole athletes on this season of the show was further winked at with the professional dancers they’re partnered with; Frech dances with Daniella Karagach, and Amber is with Pasha Pashkov, the two of whom are married.
“This journey feels like we’re on the same team together,” Frech says of navigating season 35 with Karagach, Glenn and Pashkov. “Amber and I are teammates in this.”

When asked about how fans believe the season 35 Len Goodman mirrorball trophy may end up in the Pashkov-Karagach household, Frech still doesn’t want to look too far ahead in the competition, but admits it “would be really special” if they all made it to finale night.

Below, Frech opens up about why he felt “called” to partake in season 35 of DWTS; the Hunger Games fan theory he saw fans say he and Glenn should implement so they can “split the trophy”; what being the first amputee to win DWTS would mean; and working with Karagach.
Tell me a little bit about your knowledge of Dancing With the Stars prior and how the opportunity came about for you.

I’ve watched Dancing With the Stars for a long time. I have had friends who have been on the show. There’s been a lot of amazing disability representation on Dancing With the Stars. Amy Purdy, Daniel Durant, Noah Galloway: They’ve done a fantastic job of making people with disabilities feel seen through dance. It’s always been something that was in the back of my mind as a dream. Then in more recent years, it looked like it could potentially become a reality, and then it ended up working out really well this year.

[Season 35] falls perfectly in my off season. From a track and field standpoint, my season ends, and I have three months of an off season, and it happened to fall right in the Dancing With the Stars season. It just felt like the perfect timing. It felt like the perfect moment, and sometimes you can’t explain it, but you feel called to things, and I felt very called to to do this.
Are you doing any training right now for track and field, or are you fully focused on Dancing With the Stars?

I am weightlifting a little bit, but honestly, I had a mentor [Heinrich Popow] who was on the German version of Dancing With the Stars. He was an amputee and was also a former gold medalist in my same event. He told me, “Be very careful how much work you do outside of the dance studio, because you’re going to be putting so much stress on your body. You don’t want to risk injury.” We’re being pretty strategic to not do too much outside of the rehearsal studio right now. I’m all in on dance.

You’ve been in the spotlight as an athlete, and you’ve also done advocacy work throughout your adolescence. What has it been like being introduced to this new level of exposure that comes with Dancing With the Stars?

I mean, Dancing With the Stars is another level. The fanbase is so amazing and massive, and it is so beautiful to see the love and support. Honestly, this is definitely a journey that is a roller coaster of emotions. There’s so much going on, and the support I’ve felt, it’s just so special. I’m beyond grateful.
How do you think your background, not only as an athlete, but somebody who has been in the public eye has been helpful during your time on the show?

When I step into the ballroom, it feels the same way I’ve always felt my whole life when I step onto the track and I’m about to compete. That has been helpful just in the athlete mentality, of course, that Amber and I have, and it translates in a different way. Of course, I’m not necessarily running full speed for 100 meters when I’m on the dance floor. It’s a little bit more intricate, delicate, artistic.

You are partnered with Daniella and Amber is with Pasha. A lot of fans think the mirrorball might end up in the Pashkov-Karagach household. With that expectation and how great you both have done, does that put an added level of pressure on your couples, or do you think being partnered with somebody who has a husband competing on the show has allowed for more collaboration between your couples?

Definitely more collaboration. It feels like we’re going through this side by side. Of course, you know, everyone’s super excited for us on social media, and it means a lot to Amber and I. I saw a couple funny videos of people saying that we need to do what they did in the Hunger Games, and like eat the berries and split the trophy. But no, Amber and I are teammates in this, and she’s so amazing. And Pasha and Dani collaborate obviously with each other all the time; they are married, they are each other’s rocks, so Amber and I have become really, really close throughout this experience.

It’s cool because in an experience that can super easily feel overwhelming to have so many eyes on you at all times and we’re doing this thing that is out of our comfort zone in some ways, to have somebody who you feel like is on the same team with you, navigating with you, it’s really special. I really cherish Amber and I’s friendship. And you know, we take it one week at a time. We have to dance every week like it’s our last. We focus one week at a time, but of course it would be really special if we had the opportunity to get to the finale together.
If you did win the show, you would be the first amputee to ever win Dancing With the Stars. What would winning the show mean to you?

Of course, getting the opportunity to make the finale, to win the show, to get to represent the disabled community in that way and become the first amputee to win Dancing With the Stars would be very, very special, and would mean a lot to myself and hopefully to all people with disabilities and the community as a whole. That’s the motivating factor; is representing my people well, representing this contingent of the population that I feel hasn’t had proper representation in mainstream media and doesn’t feel maybe properly included in society. That’s the motivation for even being on the show in the first place, is [to] represent them well. And then hopefully in the process, if I can go out there and do some fun dances, maybe people all over America, their perception of disability will change ever so slightly. That’s really important to me.
I’ve seen videos of young kids watching you dance and being inspired by you. How does that feel to know that you are inspiring such a vast majority of people as you take on Dancing With the Stars?
So so so special. I watch those videos all the time —
You’re always in the comments.

I try to be. First of all, watching videos where I get to see people with disabilities cheering me on is so special for me. But then also, if I get to send a little bit of love back and respond and say how appreciative I am for them, [that] takes two, three seconds out of my day. It just creates a beautiful love and energy back and forth, so I feel like it’s always worth it. I try to respond every time I see a video or something like that.

But seeing those videos and the support from all over social media, I mean, I just watched this video recently of this little kid who has a hand difference and he’s jumping up and down on his couch and watching me, and that warms my heart. That’s the type of stuff that brings a tear to my eye, and that’s the motivator. That’s what’s fueling my fire.
What do you and Dani have planned for Disney Night?

We are dancing a samba to The Little Mermaid, which will be a lot of fun. Everybody online, one of the weeks earlier in the season, said I look like Prince Eric all over social media because I slick my hair back (laughs). And so now we’re doing a samba to Little Mermaid “Under the Sea,” and it’ll be a lot of fun. It’s a classic, so gotta do it right.
Was this already picked out for you to do a Little Mermaid inspired number, or did that spark after the social media of it all?
I honestly think we were back and forth between a couple options, but the social media love around Prince Eric, I think, guided us in the right direction.
What is your favorite part of the full week process of Dancing With the Stars?
Live show day, 100 percent.
What has been your favorite dance so far that you’ve performed?
What has been the hardest dance style to learn so far?
Our salsa was probably the hardest, but now it’s going to be the samba (laughs.)
What is the greatest piece of advice that somebody has given you that you’ve applied and taken into Dancing With the Stars?
Be as present as humanly possible.
What is the number one thing you have learned from your partnership with Dani?

Oh, I’ve learned so much from my partnership with Dani. She is a special, special human being. The main thing that I’ve learned is her motto is trust the process. So we put a lot of work in, we trust the process. We work as hard as possible, and then we go out there and give it our all. But definitely trusting the process, trusting our work has been a great lesson.
Describe season 35 of Dancing With the Stars in one word.
You’re in the Dancing With the Stars world right now. You’re also training for the next Paralympics. Is there anything else that you want to tease for your future?

We have a nonprofit, Angel City Sports. We do sports for people with physical disabilities in Southern California. So anybody that has a physical disability and wants to come out and try sport. Also we have a documentary called Adaptive, which aired after the last Paralympics in Paris, and we’re in the process of filming season two to L.A. 2028, and that will eventually air at some point. But fun things in the pipeline, and obviously focused on dancing right now.
Season 35 of DWTS airs Tuesdays at 8 p.m., simulcasting across ABC and Disney+, and streaming the next day on Hulu. Read all of THR‘s DWTS coverage here.

items.title: Young Men of Cornell Want to Talk. Why Are Older Men So Quiet?
items.description: Read the rest of GQ’s special report on Cornell here and here.
items.author: Savannah Sobrevilla; Bowen Fernie
paragraphs: Read the rest of GQ’s special report on Cornell here and here.

One night in early October, activists broke a glass door at the entrance of Cornell University’s Day Hall, an administrative building that houses the office of president Michael Kotlikoff. They also vandalized its façade with the messages “Smash the patriarchy” and “At Cornell rapists are protected, protesters are expelled.” The next day, thousands of students and faculty gathered in Cornell’s Ho Plaza. When I stood in front of Day Hall, 36 hours later, much of the evidence had been erased. College life seemed to carry on as normal. Midterms, or “prelims,” were underway; students zoomed stoically past on electric scooters. The shattered panels had been replaced with planks and a sign directing visitors to an alternate entrance, and the graffiti had been power-washed to dark-gray smudges.

Cornell is situated among the gorges of Ithaca, New York, and I drove up from New York City to understand how men were making sense of a civil suit brought in September by an anonymous accuser, called Jane Doe in legal documents and media reports, alleging that she was plied with ketamine and sexually assaulted by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024. All the men have denied wrongdoing. Jane Doe’s suit also alleges that Cornell failed to appropriately safeguard her from sexual assault. University administrators acknowledged that they had “fallen short and [are] taking meaningful action.”

According to punishment summaries obtained by The New York Times, Cornell had conducted a Title IX investigation, which resulted in the expulsion of two fraternity brothers and suspension of two others. The Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office declined to pursue criminal charges. (New York governor Kathy Hochul criticized the Cornell police and the Tompkins County DA for their handling of the allegations and appointed attorney general Letitia James as a special prosecutor to investigate.) Among the materials included in Jane Doe’s suit was a photograph of a phone displaying a Chi Phi group chat, with reportedly more than 50 people, in which one of the men advertised Jane Doe’s “free pussy.” Some cheered. One asked if “the shop” was still open. In the screenshot, not a single voice raised an objection.

Men’s perspectives have been underreported during past sexual assault crises, perhaps out of the well-intentioned belief that we should prioritize listening to women. But when such moments to object to a woman’s dehumanization arrive, I wanted to know, why do men so often stay quiet?

Several people told me that my trip coincided with Ithaca’s most beautiful season, and, in person, the landscape did indeed look quintessentially autumnal. (My visit also coincided with the time of year in 2024 that Jane Doe alleges her assault in the Chi Phi house took place.) In the Arts Quad, Oscar, 21, was on his way to class, although he didn’t seem to have anything with him besides his phone. He was dressed in sweats and a boxy yellow tee, and he told me that he had joined a fraternity because he wanted to make friends. He had just left a Sexual Assault Prevention and Safety Club meeting for members of sororities and fraternities, where he and other students had discussed how the Greek system can develop stronger guardrails. One promising approach, he told me, was to delegate prominent members of frats to speak up about sexual assault. “It’s a scary and really hard conversation to have with your friend, especially somebody you think wouldn’t do something like that,” he said. “That’s what our meeting is about: How can we try to make these conversations more normal, more open?” Oscar was generous with his thoughts but grew reserved on the topic of fraternity culture.

Over by the Library or “Libe” Slope, an idyllic stretch of lawn on a rolling hillside, two guys tossed a Frisbee. I sat on the bench next to theirs while they hydrated. “A lot of people are saying, ‘If you were in that group chat, you should have said something,’ which I agree with,” said Hudson Tumey, who graduated last year. “You absolutely should have.” Tumey is a member of Cru, a Christian ministry on campus, and was visiting with William Canlis, a sophomore, who is also involved in Cru. “If I was in that group chat, I would’ve hoped with all my might that I would’ve said something,” Tumey said. “But I think I’d be lying to say that I would’ve for sure said something.” Tumey and Canlis explained that their faith offers them a man to emulate in Jesus Christ. “If a man doesn’t have that standard to look up to, that’s where bad things happen,” Canlis said. “If you don’t have Him, then what role model is left? The world? Look how broken the world is.”

I started looking around for other male role models. Near Sage Chapel, a non-sectarian church on campus, two clergymen visiting the campus said they hadn’t known about the Chi Phi case until that morning. One of them told me he preferred to stay out of it. Just outside Schoellkopf Field, an associate basketball coach asked me to email him. At the ROTC offices in Barton Hall, an Army poster read “Sexual assault. Sexual harassment. Not in our army.” A master sergeant paused his lunch to talk with me. He sat for a moment, then left to call his superior. After five minutes he returned and, with a half-apologetic inhale, said that he couldn’t speak with me until it’s brought up the chain of command and that I should email him. A roving police officer said that the only person on the force approved to speak with the press was Eric Stickel, Cornell University Police Department’s recently appointed chief of police, and I should email him. Ultimately, I approached almost two dozen non-student men associated with the town or the school and only one talked to me on the record.

At the Morrison Dining Hall, a seven-hour sit-in was underway, roughly matching the length of time Jane Doe spent in the Chi Phi house until she lost consciousness, according to the lawsuit. One of the sit-in’s appointed press contacts was John Hartnett, a 19-year-old sophomore representing Students for a Democratic Cornell, a group that had also helped organize the protest earlier in the week. He was proud of that turnout, as it was one of the largest protests at Cornell since the Vietnam War, but incensed by the irony of the school’s history of suspending students involved in other protests. He was also taking inventory of how he and his peers influence each other.

“It’s a difficult thing because you have to realize that some of your past actions—not sexual assault—perpetuated these things,” he said. “It’s something that men have to ask themselves: What am I not doing in terms of not holding the people around me accountable?” My phone rang. Someone from Cornell’s media-relations team informed me that the school was aware of my presence on campus and that none of the administrators were available for comment.

Reporters from Telemundo, The Ithaca Voice, and Reuters descended on Hartnett, and the sheer number of us bombarding him cast the reticence I encountered from his elders in a new light. While an inevitable chorus rose up to defend fraternities or disparage Jane Doe, some young men on campus seemed to be earnestly reckoning with the case or struggling to find their voice. But their community leaders appeared, at most, disconcerted. Perhaps those older men were grappling internally or opting for silent solidarity; whatever their reasons, I was struck by the persistence of their absence.

Later in the evening, I attended a Common Council meeting downtown at Ithaca City Hall. More than 50 people squeezed into a room set up for half that number. Ithaca mayor Robert G. Cantelmo oversaw the proceedings. A dozen or so students found spots on the floor; the local television station was filming. There were complaints regarding the closure of a parking garage, concerns about winter snow plowing, and, eventually, a proposed moratorium on some of Cornell’s event and noise permits, which was put forth as an effort to limit Greek-life activities. The floor was then opened for public comment, but only to those who had filed a slip.

“I think sacrificing some of the fun is more than justified by protecting people from these heinous crimes until the university gets off its rear,” John King, an Ithaca resident, said in support of the moratorium. “I applaud the city government for being willing to do so instead.” Sam Poole was a freshman when Jane Doe first reported her assault to the Cornell police. “I live in a Cornell co-op,” he said. “Co-ops host parties just like fraternities do, plenty of student organizations do, but we decided we’re not going to host parties until the moratorium is over.” Almost a week after the meeting, Cornell banned frat parties for the current academic year.

A few rows behind me, a man in a C-SPAN hoodie and tech pants was growing agitated that he had not been called on. “Michael Tracey,” he called out repeatedly. Mayor Cantelmo explained that Tracey’s name was not among the comment slips given to him by the clerk. “Motion to reconsider,” Tracey yelled out. “You’re definitely not eligible to make motions, because you’re not a member of this body,” Cantelmo replied. Tracey alleged his slip was thrown in the trash. “You should be ashamed for using the power of your office to conclusorily [sic] declare that any American citizen has committed crimes as heinous as gang rape before any semblance of adjudicative process,” he said as he walked out. I passed him my number.

Tracey asked to meet in the lobby of the Canopy Hotel. On my way there I learned that he is a contrarian Substack journalist, known for social media provocation; recently he argued that aspects of the Jeffrey Epstein case were overblown. He’s made multiple trips to Ithaca, where he’s filmed himself cross-examining students and faculty and showing up to public gatherings. He told me that he had driven from Jersey City to Ithaca to report on the Cornell case, motivated by his belief that Jane Doe’s identity should be made public. The previous week, he tweeted out her name before deleting the post. Internet sleuths published her address online. Then, according to Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, on the night before the meeting at City Hall, Jane Doe was swatted—that is, someone made a call to the police reporting invented violence at her home, prompting a large-scale police response. Giuffra told CNN that his client has been “terrified.”

Plaintiff anonymity is “used to manipulate the court system and thereby the public as a PR tactic to create pressure,” Tracey told me. “I have nothing against Jane Doe. She seems kind of cool, actually.” He showed me a text he sent to a number he claims belongs to her: “Given that settlement funds are being sought, especially considering that criminal investigations have been triggered, I consider it in the public interest to report on your identity.” When I pointed out that anonymity enables sexual assault victims to come forward with less fear of vitriol and death threats, he described the death threats he has received. This is what one of the loudest male voices I encountered in Ithaca sounds like.

I walked down Ithaca Commons to peer into Moonies, the bar Jane Doe visited before the alleged assault, but it was closed for the night. On Instagram, it appeared to be business as usual, with promotions for “Flash Friday” and “Saturday Surge” parties. In the suit, Jane Doe says she left a sorority event at this bar, went to another bar, and then “stumbled alone” to a party at the Chi Phi house. (Moonies is named in Jane Doe’s suit and its owners have denied that it illegally served alcohol to the underage Jane Doe.) I got into my car and headed to the frat. Even from the cozy confines of my rented Toyota Corolla, that path seemed uninviting. There’s a brick-and-stone charm to downtown Ithaca that dissolves once you cross over the gorges and onto frat row. Flashy trucks and clusters of mega-mansions run by very young adults bordered the drive. I spotted a handful of bongs resting on windowsills. For a minute, I couldn’t find the actual Chi Phi house and when I finally spotted it—massive, menacing—I was nearly relieved.

The next morning, campus cleared out for fall break. Visiting faculty member Mark Brown Jr. sat on the steps of Goldwin Smith Hall and finished a game of virtual chess before speaking with me. “I think frat culture is incredibly toxic,” he said. Some undergraduates in his art classes preferred to discuss the subject in a “roundabout” way. The potential of repercussions, he said, may be deterring open discussion.

I approached two students sitting under a statue of Andrew Dickson White, Cornell’s first president. “All men are honestly guilty for this,” said Daniel Suh, a junior studying public policy. “You ask any man if rape is okay and they’re going to tell you no. But men expect a perfect victim.” His friend, Anand Patel, also a junior, sat next to him. With their baggy pants and gleaming sneakers, Patel and Suh seemed so sweetly boyish, young, and on the brink of adulthood. But also fed up. While Suh felt regulating frat parties wouldn’t directly address the issue of college sexual assault, Patel was much more critical of frat culture. “Where the true issue lies is what happens when you have a friend who does it, or someone you know. Are you going to act like nothing happened? Are you going to support him, or are you going to cut him off? Because that’s ultimately what happens in these frats,” Patel said. “These men don’t draw a line in the sand saying, ‘Okay, you’re out now.’ ”

These students offered a stark contrast with the many older men I had tried to speak to, on and off campus, who couldn’t or wouldn’t add their voices to the conversation. For Patel and the other students I spoke to on campus, things seemed so clear: We should all call out bad behavior when we see it, because we know what bad behavior looks like. When did that get so complicated? ◼︎
Fraternities control access to coveted resources. They use humiliating rituals to bond with each other, enforce hierarchy, and belittle outsiders. Sound familiar?

items.title: Can the Brooklyn Nets Convert a Generation of Newly Minted Knicks Fans?
items.description: At the Brooklyn Nets’ home opener against the Charlotte Hornets last week, one longtime fan pointed out the strange dynamic inherent to New York City basketball fandom. He was jealous of places like Boston and Philadelphia, he said, because the entire city org
items.author: Cam Wolf
paragraphs: At the Brooklyn Nets’ home opener against the Charlotte Hornets last week, one longtime fan pointed out the strange dynamic inherent to New York City basketball fandom. He was jealous of places like Boston and Philadelphia, he said, because the entire city organizes itself around one team. Sports franchises, after all, are avatars of civic pride, and the very best organizations come to reflect the values of the cities they represent. (Think the Showtime Lakers or the Grit-and-Grind Memphis Grizzlies.) But in New York, home to both the Nets and the Knicks, fan bases are pitted against each other by fans, media, and sometimes even franchise leaders.

For a long time, the Nets could take solace in their cross rivals' decades-long stretch of ineptitude. That vanished when Jalen Brunson and company lifted the Larry O’Brien in June, leaving Brooklyn with some soul searching to do. “It doesn't make us feel very good,” Nets owner Joe Tsai told NetsDaily over the summer. “It irates our fan base and it is embarrassing.” As The Ringer’s Zach Lowe pointed out on his recently launched Substack, the Knicks’ title cost the Nets “an entire generation of fans.”

I, for one, have never understood why commentators are so obsessed with the size of Brooklyn’s fanbase. I am, obviously, a hugely biased homer, but you don’t hear the same concerns when it comes to other little-brother teams like the Clippers or teams, like Wizards, whose games are sparsely attended. Even as they’ve tanked these past couple of years, the Nets have maintained a 99% attendance rate and are the eighth most-valuable franchise in the entire league. Still, I have to hear talking heads argue that the team should move back to New Jersey? I might be salty, but that’s stupid.

Nevertheless, there is clearly angst about building up a coalition of Nets faithful. On his podcast Curious Mike, where I wish he would be less curious, the team’s star forward Michael Porter Jr. recently said, “When we play Knicks, Celtics, Philly, Lakers, it's mostly their fans. It's crazy.” And he’s not wrong: it's a weird time to be a fan of the Brooklyn Nets—the team’s fallen twice in the lottery and is trying to kickstart a rebuild in the shadow of one of the most storied franchises in the NBA. So I made my way over to the team’s training facility in Sunset Park to see how the Nets are tackling this problem with pillars of the present and future.

“I don't give a shit,” says Julius Randle, tucked into a glass room in the corner of the Nets’ famously photogenic training facility, when I ask him about the invasion of opposing fans at Barclays. “I've been on teams that weren't good and didn’t have the excitement around them. Then you start winning and the whole arena is there to see your team and cheer. So I think that's just part of being a fan. For us as a team, we got to give them something to root for.”

Randle, who played an integral role in the Knicks rebuild before being shipped off to the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2024, has seen New York City basketball fandom from both sides of the river. “It doesn't really matter what team I play for. I was at my son's basketball game yesterday and it was like, Man, I'm a Nets fan. You’re going to kill it this year. Then I get on the other side and it's, Thank you for everything you've done for the Knicks."

Randle, now on his fifth team in 13 seasons, also downplayed the idea that the Nets-Knicks intercity rivalry mattered all that much to players. “From the locker room, basketball is basketball,” he insists. “It's not like college or high school where we play our rival on Friday or whatever. You play 82 games a year. You feel the energy during the game, but I definitely think it's a bigger deal from a fan perspective than it is from a player's perspective.”
I can’t even finish my next question before he cuts me off. Do you see part of your role as growing this next generation of fans or are you just here to—

“No, hell no,” Randle says. “I definitely want to be a part of establishing a culture and giving the city of Brooklyn something to be proud of. I'm not here just to come out and get my numbers or whatever it is. I'm here to win a championship. I'm here to help these young guys excel and speed up their growth process.”

One of those young guys is the anointed prince of the franchise, Mikel Brown Jr., the Orlando-born point guard the Nets took sixth overall in this year’s draft and who fans are already calling “the best prospect in franchise history” (I agree.) Another prominent member of Nets Twitter, moved by preseason action, described him as a mix of CJ McCollum and All-NBA regulars Tyrese Haliburton and Kyrie Irving. (I love that tweet, and I love this fanbase.)

With the Nets, Brown came into a peculiar situation. Not only does the future of the franchise’s success hinge on whether he can reach his star potential—so does the team’s ability to cultivate a new generation of fans. It’s a challenge Brown recognizes and embraces. Many fans, myself included, took note of a phrase he kept repeating on draft night: “I’m home.” It felt like a full-throated endorsement of the franchise and its mission. “Most of the [Nets] fans are there in the arena for a draft night,” Brown says when I ask him what he meant. “So to hear the crowd pop and just to see the energy, it brought me a whole bunch of joy.”

Brown is 20 years old, and looks even younger, but he understands just how much is riding on his rookie season. “I embrace it,” he says. “At the end of the day, we're just kind of focusing on what we can control and then let everything else play on. Whatever happens after that and whoever comes along with us, enjoy the ride because we're going to go to war.”

Everyone I talked to believes Brown has the goods to deliver on both his promises and his potential. Randle, too, told me he’s been texting his friends back home to tell them how gifted Brown is. “I've been thoroughly, thoroughly impressed with not just his talent level, but his maturity and his IQ at such a young age is really, really impressive.” Typically, Randle continues, young players are single-mindedly focused on scoring. But Brown understands that there’s more than one way to contribute. “He just knows how to make the right play every single time. He just knows how to play good basketball.”

Brown is the type of prospect us Nets fans have been waiting to call our own. I loved rooting for every iteration of this team, but what the franchise’s best players—Jason Kidd, Deron Williams, Joe Johnson, Kyrie Irving, and Kevin Durant—have in common is that none of them were drafted by the Nets. Developing a homegrown star is a different task altogether, and the Nets have solid reason to believe they've found one.

On Wednesday night against the Boston Celtics, we caught a glimpse of what Brown can do . The 20 year-old was “not human,” as Nets longtime commentator Ian Eagle likes to say, in the fourth quarter. After pouring in several clutch baskets, he sent the game to overtime with a falling-to-the-side three with just 0.2 seconds left. Brooklyn lost the game, but if Brown’s development keeps trending in this direction, maybe we can win the war.

My Nets fandom is the result of perfect timing. I mostly grew up in California but spent my formative sports-team-choosing years in New Jersey when my family and I moved across the country for my dad’s job. After moving back to the Bay Area halfway through elementary school, I clung even more tightly to the Nets to stay connected with the friends and the place I left behind: the Snoopy fishing rod I used at the local lake, the fireflies in my New Jersey-sized backyard, the cul-de-sac that seemed to have a friend in every neighboring house.

During the Nets home opener, with the team wearing their excellent ABA-inspired red-and-blue jerseys, the game seemed all but decided as the Charlotte Hornets started to pull away at the end of the fourth. But with just over a minute left, the crowd started to pop as Randle bullied his way into an and-one layup and starting center Day'Ron Sharpe blocked a shot at the other end.

I thought back to the simple philosophy both Randle and Brown echoed: just win, and people will show up. The Nets eventually lost that game against Charlotte, and a few other heartbreakers since (against very tough competition, for what it’s worth). It’s unclear whether the Nets will ever convert a generation of fans spellbound by the Knicks, or even win the Finals. But I know I’ll be there.

items.title: Every Guy Needs a Gnarly Work Jacket
items.description: For better or worse, the best work jackets for men are no longer associated with garages, factory floors, and loading docks. Instead, as the likes of Paul Mescal and Austin Butler (who told GQ he wore his for a year straight) continue to fly their flag, a grea
items.author: Ben Kriz
paragraphs: For better or worse, the best work jackets for men are no longer associated with garages, factory floors, and loading docks. Instead, as the likes of Paul Mescal and Austin Butler (who told GQ he wore his for a year straight) continue to fly their flag, a great work jacket has become every guy's fastest route to semi-rugged heartthrob style.

Honestly, they make looking good almost too easy. First, they inject your fits with casual, weekend tough-guy energy. (This, to be clear, is a plus.) Second, they flatter you in all the right places, framing your shoulders and neatening up your waistline whether you’re pairing them with jeans or the kinds of wide, puddling trousers we've long been yapping about.

Better still, you don’t have to spend a fortune. The classics from Dickies and Carhartt are as dependable as ever, and even the independent designer options are within reach of your budget—this is a cotton-forward option, after all. Here are 14 of our favorites, all of which will only look better after a few years (and a few scuffs) of real wear.
The Best Men’s Work Jackets, According to GQ
Best Work Jacket Overall: Carhartt Blanket-Lined Detroit Jacket

The Carhartt Detroit work jacket is the classic for a reason. It’s been around for more than 70 years—not quite as old as blue jeans or cowboy boots, but easily in the upper echelon of American fashion’s great exports. So much so that today, luxury brands are riffing on it, even selling pre-distressed, washed-down versions at triple the price. (And yes, this is also the work jacket that Austin Butler told us he wears.)

Cut to the waist, and built from thick, stiff canvas with three perfectly placed front pockets, the Detroit is an Eisenhower-style silhouette (during WWII, the then-Army General overhauled U.S. military dress and introduced the cropped, boxy jacket to American forces). Its insulated blanket lining and corduroy collar also make it one of the few true year-round, toasty work jackets out there. Simply put, this is a real piece of clothing for real life. (Though if it's not fancy enough for you, there’s always the street-ready, slimmer, unlined Carhartt WIP version.)
Best Budget Work Jacket: Dickies Insulated Eisenhower Jacket

Just like Dickies' iconic 874 work pants, the brand's insulated Eisenhower jacket (there he is again) is a hard-wearing, warm, wallet-friendly piece of gear that fits incredibly well. Nearly as old as the Detroit Jacket above, it doesn’t always get the same respect. But maybe that's just because it flies a little more under the radar, with its logo patch tucked discreetly near the hem. Decades in, it remains a low-key, low-cost icon—less shouty than its Carhartt cousin, but every bit as authentic.
Best Upgrade Work Jacket: Wallace & Barnes Lined Canvas Work Jacket

Wallace & Barnes, J.Crew's workwear line, is back with tough fabrics, heritage details, and a big hit of #menswear-era nostalgia—and this wool-lined work jacket shows exactly why folks missed it so much. It has all of the heartthrob-coded details you probably had in mind when you decided to look for a jacket like this: Corduroy collar, zippered chest pocket, slightly cropped fit. But it isn't just good-looking. It also has a wool-blend blanket lining, for superior warmth to help you enjoy it even if the depths of winter. And that, if cost-per-wear logic still applies, makes it more than worth its slightly higher price point.
Best Work Jacket for Cold Weather: Filson Mackinaw Wool Work Jacket

Welcome to the world of truly warm fabrics, and actually glove-friendly pockets. Filson’s been mastering cold-weather gear since your great-great-grandfather was in short pants, and this work jacket continues that legacy. Based on the brand’s original 1914 Cruiser, it’s cut from 24-ounce Mackinaw wool — a tightly woven twill that truly blocks wind, sheds rain, and stays warm even when wet. Without being mean, it’s built to outlast even you. Pricey? Sure. But it’s the kind of thing your kids will remember you by (and fight for) someday.
Best Fancy Work Jacket: Buck Mason Italian Doeskin Station Jacket

Buck Mason’s archive is full to bursting with vintage pieces from decades past, which explains why its collections are filled with absolute bangers these days. Here the brand has taken a mid-century work jacket and remade it, tweaking the fit to make it a touch more relaxed, and using a soft Italian doeskin cotton fabric that’s more plush than anything a worksite would have issued back in the day. There's even more to love in the details: Shoulder pleats for easy movement, real horn buttons on the chest pockets, and a dressy point collar.
Best Lightweight Work Jacket: Polo Ralph Lauren Bayport Poplin Jacket

For Lo-heads, Polo Ralph Lauren's hard-wearing zipper jackets are the stuff of legend. And while you might have grown up with an inherited cotton example from your dad, in the last decade of so, Polo has been pushing its ‘Bi-Swing’ polyester and/or nylon takes instead. That's fine, but some of us aren't so willing to trade in the soft, rugged comfort of a full-cotton jacket. That's where the rarer Bayport Poplin jacket comes in. A work jacket with no delusions, it’s not stealing the working man’s valor — it knows exactly what it is. It’s Ralph Lauren, and it knows you’re working hard at hardly working. But it's also strong enough to handle whatever activities you throw at it, leisure or otherwise.
What to Look for in a Great Work Jacket

These days, work jackets seem to have an undeniable stranglehold on the imagination of guys who spend all day staring at their keyboards. (There’s a political element to this, of course. Whether or not you act in solidarity with your fellow laborers under capitalism, a work jacket allows you to look the part of the everyman.) But also, they’re just a great jacket for busy lives! There’s a generally accommodating cut that doesn’t restrict your movement, plenty of pockets, and hardy materials that can easily handle a snag, or sudden shower.
How We Test and Review Products

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.
We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.
Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

items.title: What Writing a Book About JFK Jr. Taught Me About Personal Style
items.description: John F. Kennedy Jr. wasn’t the first guy to ride a bike wearing a suit. Likewise, the presidential scion and People’s 1988 Sexiest Man Alive didn’t invent the backward Kangol cap, the pinstriped suit, or wearing a waistcoat with jeans—he just did it better tha
items.author: Jeremy Freed
paragraphs: John F. Kennedy Jr. wasn’t the first guy to ride a bike wearing a suit. Likewise, the presidential scion and People’s 1988 Sexiest Man Alive didn’t invent the backward Kangol cap, the pinstriped suit, or wearing a waistcoat with jeans—he just did it better than pretty much anybody else. That’s a big part of why he was one of the most photographed men on the planet in the 1990s, and why he remains a menswear moodboard staple today, nearly 30 years after his untimely death. Still, no matter how hard you try, and no matter how closely you hew to the source material, all attempts to replicate JFK Jr.’s style are destined to leave you looking like a runner-up in a Washington Square Park lookalike contest.

Ask anyone who encountered John-John in his prime—which, in my experience, is virtually everyone who lived in Manhattan in the 1990s—and the first thing they’ll mention is his magnetism, his charm, and the fact that, against all odds, he was actually better-looking in person. I know this because, having recently written a book about JFK Jr.’s style, I’ve spent a good part of the last year poring over photos, reading biographies, speaking to people who knew him, and otherwise immersing myself in his world. Among the conclusions I’ve come to is that you probably won’t look as cool as JFK Jr. did wearing rollerblades, but there are a few style moves you can borrow from his playbook without resorting to full Kennedy cosplay.

JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was built on four pillars: tailoring, preppy basics, workwear, and sportswear. But it was the idiosyncratic way he combined them (i.e., a backward baseball cap with a suit, a polo neck sweater under a tweed blazer, hiking boots with tailored trousers) that resulted in some of his most memorable looks. Surprisingly, while the combination of straight-leg jeans, a button-up dress shirt, and a blazer has become shorthand for JFK Jr.’s style, I’ve never seen any evidence of him wearing it. In fact, he seldom wore jeans at all (some speculate his mother thought they looked shabby, while others told me that jeans didn’t complement his active lifestyle). That said, plenty of other ’90s style icons, from Ralph Lauren to Jerry Seinfeld, rocked this particular look, and it’s a pretty easy one to pull off. As with everything about JFK Jr.’s style, it’s not about lifting these combinations wholesale, but understanding the precise balance of contrast that makes them work.

One of the most consistent elements of JFK Jr.’s style was his love of discordant accessories, from his collection of flat caps to his ever-present wallet chain to his Oakley Eye Jacket shades. Some of these were practical—he was so prone to misplacing his wallet and keys that he needed to chain them to his pants—but others reflected his love of color (funky knit caps), his enthusiasm for skiing (fleece headbands), and his passion for travel (various hats picked up on trips to India and Thailand). Some accessories will suit you better than others, but if you have a personal connection to it, all the better. And most importantly, limit yourself to one standout add-on per outfit.

Speaking of accessories: JFK Jr. was a dedicated scarf guy, and he’d pair one with everything from joggers and sneakers to his best navy blue suit. Rather than draping a scarf loosely around his neck, he tended to tie it in either a dressy overhand or classic Parisian knot, both of which lend a more formal look. He also loved wearing a thick scarf as outerwear, throwing it over a sweatshirt on a chilly day instead of a coat, often paired with a knit cap. For best results, don’t pick a scarf that matches the rest of your outfit too closely.

Among the most surprising things I discovered about JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was his watch collection. I wasn’t able to uncover any evidence of him wearing the long-lost Rolex Daytona given to him by Aristotle Onassis (a watch that, if ever found, would give Paul Newman a run for his money), but I did identify an unusually wide range of other pieces in his collection, from a Victorinox Swiss Army field watch to a Swatch chronograph to a vintage Rolex Oyster Perpetual. This is of a piece with everything else we know about JFK Jr.: he wasn’t bound by any single style, brand, or price point, and got just as much enjoyment out of a cheap quartz watch as a luxury mechanical one.

As a rich kid raised on the Upper East Side, JFK Jr.’s closet included plenty of blazers, chinos, and polos. He was a gym rat who loved playing sports, so he also had a lot of sweats, tees, and sneakers. He was a downtown socialite, so he owned a lot of nice suits and tuxes, too. He also had an enviable collection of graphic tees from NYC institutions like the Russian & Turkish Baths in the East Village and the New York Athletic Club, as well as some commemorating events like the 1984 NYC Fresh Festival, a seminal moment in hip-hop history. What stands out to me—and what I believe makes his style so distinctive—is that JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was an authentic reflection of who he was, where he came from, and what he loved. This might be the most important style lesson any of us can learn from him: Great personal style is less about clothes than wearing them in a way that expresses your individuality.

items.title: This Is What the GOP’s Final Midterms Push Looks Like
items.description: Republicans are spending the final week ahead of the midterm elections defending historically red Senate seats that have suddenly become competitive, according to federal filings and sources familiar with the matter.
items.author: Hugo Lowell
paragraphs: Republicans are spending the final week ahead of the midterm elections defending historically red Senate seats that have suddenly become competitive, according to federal filings and sources familiar with the matter.

A significant focus is now on four Senate races in Kansas, South Carolina, Nebraska, and even Mississippi, all traditionally red seats, in what’s an ominous development for Republicans in their effort to at least keep control of the upper chamber.

Trump operatives tell Inner Loop that they do not expect Democrats to win those Senate seats and that they have mainly directed GOP outside groups to spend there to help boost incumbents that only have a narrow lead.

But the operatives also concede that they are having to divert an increasing amount of resources to those states—states that president Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024 and where Republicans never dreamed of having to spend tens of millions of dollars.

In total, in the penultimate week of the campaign, the Senate Republican–aligned Senate Leadership Fund spent $14 million across those four states, according to a WIRED review of federal filings. The biggest spend has been in Kansas, where SLF has abruptly dumped more than $5 million.

Trump operatives say Kansas has been a major headache since the start of October, when Trafalgar Group, a GOP pollster, found Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton one point ahead of incumbent GOP senator Roger Marshall.

Marshall, a doctor, has had an unusually tough race following a slew of negative stories about how he pursued legal action against his patients with unpaid bills and how much time he spends in Florida. Some political operatives have also complained that he has not taken his race seriously, sources say.

But the last-minute spending is also coming in places like South Carolina, where SLF spent another roughly $5 million to help incumbent Darline Graham, who has struggled to galvanize Trump's base despite having the president’s endorsement that propelled her to victory in the primary.

SLF also spent nearly $3 million in Nebraska to help Republican incumbent senator Pete Ricketts, who has been behind in some polls, and in Mississippi, the fund put just under $1 million toward Republican incumbent senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The final sprint has highlighted the fraught predicament for Republicans, who are having to patch a seemingly ever-growing number of vulnerabilities.

Trump's campaign schedule has also added several deep-red states that are flashing warning signs, in addition to the expected campaign stops in battleground states. Last week, Trump went to Kansas and South Carolina. This week, he has been in Mississippi and will return to Kansas and South Carolina, as well.

Still, several Trump operatives tell Inner Loop they have been encouraged by the fact that Democratic candidates lately have not expanded their leads in several key Senate races—a concern that has cropped up among some Senate Democratic leadership aides.

Chief among their concerns is Michigan, the best GOP pickup opportunity. Many of the most viable paths to Democrats taking the Senate majority pass through the state, but Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has suffered lingering issues with key voting blocs.

Black voters turned out in droves to help Barack Obama carry the state in 2008 and 2012, and the conventional wisdom in Washington is that El-Sayed will need similar support in order to keep the seat blue, one of the Democratic aides tells Inner Loop.

But the trouble for El-Sayed, they add, has been the decades-long animosity between Arab and Black communities in Michigan, a divide that was further strained during the primary when supporters of his challenger, Haley Stevens, ran ads featuring Barack Obama praising her earlier work during the financial crisis.

In an effort to rebuild at least part of that coalition, Obama held a joint rally with El-Sayed in Detroit over the weekend, which aides are hoping could persuade some voters. Operatives aren’t sure if it’ll be enough.
We will have to see how it pans out. See you next week, on the other side!
This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

items.title: I Put a Bunch of AI Agents in Charge of a Fantasy Soccer Team. They’re Not Better Than Humans—Yet
items.description: I have consulted my AI-powered crystal ball, and it’s telling me that frontier models are going to get a lot better at making predictions in the near future. Just ask my Premier League fantasy team.
items.author: Will Knight
paragraphs: I have consulted my AI-powered crystal ball, and it’s telling me that frontier models are going to get a lot better at making predictions in the near future. Just ask my Premier League fantasy team.

A few weeks ago, I deployed a small horde of AI agents to craft and manage an experimental roster. Given the proliferation of AI agents into pretty much every aspect of our lives, I wanted to know if a swarm of bots could put together a winning team.

I first looked at the potential for AI here a few years ago, playing around with a tool from the UK’s Turing Institute that selected teams after modeling previous fantasy league data. Its suggestions were remarkably bonkers—it didn’t incorporate real-world information, like a player’s injury or a team’s change in management.

This time, while on a flight to visit family, I asked Codex for help. First, I fed the model a couple of relevant research papers. Then, I asked it to build a harness—instructions and code that guides different agents through various steps—that would check recent news and run a model to make predictions.

It quickly came up with a setup that seemed to collate and analyze way more information than I ever would have. And yet I was surprised by how dumb the initial team suggestions were. Leaving Erling Haaland on the bench? Really, Codex?

I then asked Codex to create a team of agents that did different things: several that read news and blog posts; others that analyzed recent results; more that ran models; and a bunch that critiqued suggestions. This seemed to significantly improve the suggestions. I tried increasing the number of agents to more than 100, hoping this would make the system smarter still, but it didn’t change much besides running up my API bill.

Still, the improvement from a few years ago was striking. According to Haifeng Xu, a computer scientist at the University of Chicago who studies the uses of AI in market situations, newer models may be even better at making predictions because they’re able to consume and analyze huge amounts of real-world information, and they’re able to orchestrate more complex systems for their guesses.
“AI is just getting smarter in understanding the world—I feel like that's the fundamental reason they’re improving,” Xu tells me.

Late last year, Xu was marveling at the growing popularity of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket. He wondered how the best commercial models might fare on those markets, so alongside several colleagues, he began testing their forecasting skills.
They had models guess, for example, who would win the NBA Championship and who President Trump would meet with.

“Very quickly we started to realize that models did really well,” Xu tells me. The models were sometimes able to do better than the average person without any special instructions or guidance, he says. In their testing, GPT-5 was the best at making predictions, followed by Grok 4, Claude Sonnet, Gemini, and Llama.

The team went on to develop Prophet Arena, a benchmark that measures a model’s ability to make predictions. It’s one of a number of benchmarks designed to test AI’s future-gazing capabilities; another, Prediction Arena, from researchers at Harvard University and a company called Arcada Labs, recently gave frontier models $10,000 to wager on prediction markets over 57 days. The models consistently lost money in their experiment, but the researchers saw evidence of them improving consistently over time.

Xu tells me that AI can most effectively make predictions using a custom harness, and notes that having agents with unique tasks—reading the news, collecting other data, and analyzing the whole system, for instance—seems to be the most effective approach.

Interestingly, AI still often lags behind very skilled experts known as superforecasters. Xu explains that, although humans cannot consume as much information, their understanding of the real world—that is, of the dynamics behind a news story—is deeper.

That said, there’s growing evidence that the human superforecaster’s edge is eroding. A contest called the Metaculus Cup recently showed that AI can sometimes beat even the best human predictors. And a benchmark called ForecastBench could provide further evidence that AI can match human skills when the results of an ongoing contest conclude soon. In fact, I think we can expect the big labs to turn their attention to future-gazing as a powerful new way to measure progress in machine intelligence.

All of these predictive experiments seem to suggest that, like math, coding, and law, industries predicated on trading may soon be upended by AI. Perhaps the best human traders will take on a new kind of role: supervising and orchestrating AI agents capable of divining the future far better than they can.

For the time being, my AI’s suggestions still don’t seem all that impressive. Its team hasn’t outscored the average over the past weeks. I certainly won’t be using any of its suggestions in my own selections.

But AI will no doubt get better, perhaps making it all too easy to dominate fantasy league pretty soon. I’m kind of hoping it won’t, though, as it would spoil the fun of trying to earn bragging rights by winning all by yourself.
This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

items.title: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable
items.description: Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
items.author: Lily Hay Newman; Matt Burgess
paragraphs: Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

As security teams and web admins scrambled this week to patch newly public PHP bugs, criminal hackers quickly attempted to exploit the flaws in the wild. Millions of exploitation attempts hit within hours of the vulnerabilities being published, according to analysis from Cloudflare—unsurprising given broad access to AI tools that can make it easier for attackers to quickly exploit flaws.

So far, the nightmare scenario of mass victim takeovers and breaches hasn’t come to pass. The PHP Foundation says it hasn’t seen any successful exploitation of the bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, and many publicly circulating potential exploits appear to be ineffective. However, perhaps the most interesting role of AI amid the chaos this week is how advanced models helped researchers uncover practical exploitations for the vulnerabilities, which were known about, at least in part, for years. In other words, AI helped turn historic vulnerability into a current crisis.
So are we all about to be walloped by a wave of critical vulnerabilities that have been kicking around for decades?

Researchers at security company Calif were the first to identify the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and create exploits in early August—partially using frontier AI tools as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program, but also using expert human knowledge of PHP, its dynamics, and its weaknesses. Some of the underlying issues were identified in 2024 but were deemed too complex to exploit at the time. Following Calif’s discovery, researchers at OpenAI and the Google-owned security firm Wiz independently discovered PHP2Shell flaws using AI tools.

“The vulnerability had been known to the PHP team for years, but because it could not be leveraged by an attacker—at least, not a human one—it was not addressed,” says Sagi Tzadik, a security researcher at Wiz.

No software is perfect. There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially exploit vulnerabilities. This puts even more pressure on under-resourced IT teams, developers, and admins to keep up. Microsoft’s security updates included a record 1,453 security vulnerabilities this month alone. Meanwhile, Bank of America recently hired 1,000 consultants to fix flaws discovered by Anthropic’s Mythos. Security researchers emphasize, though, that AI is ultimately not doing anything new, but rather magnifying existing dynamics of vulnerability discovery and coordinated disclosure.

“We'll definitely see more of these long-life bugs that are in every version of the software for the last decade or whatever,” says Jake Williams, vice president of research and development at Hunter Strategy and a former NSA hacker. “But I think there’s only so much of this low-hanging fruit. There isn’t much else that has the specific reach of PHP. It’s a pretty wild attack surface—most other tools aren’t exposed to the internet by design.”

Researchers note, too, that even with frontier models, most examples of sophisticated AI-aided hacking also involve human expertise. As Ryan Austin, the Calif researcher who first discovered the PHP flaws, wrote this week, “No model is simply capable of unearthing ‘all bugs’ with simple prompts. At least for now.”

In short, security engineer and researcher Niels Provos says, everyone can dial back their freak-outs, at least a bit. “To be honest, I am not really worried,” he says, about AI finding an overwhelming number of historic bugs that are newly exploitable—or new vulnerabilities that couldn’t have been practically exploited without AI. “People have now been looking with AI for over a year, and it required a highly skilled team to find this one. I guess we will see whether I am completely wrong, but I doubt it.”

items.title: What Democrats Can Learn From New York’s Data Center Moratorium
items.description: Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them s
items.author: Molly Taft
paragraphs: Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.

When New York became the first state in the country to enact a moratorium on data center development, Adrienne Yocina was excited. For the past two years, the mom of three has been organizing in western Genesee County to stop a 600-megawatt data center from coming to a site close to the Tonawanda Seneca Nation’s reservation and a federal wildlife refuge.

But almost four months after the one-year moratorium began, Yocina tells me that she’s “getting nervous.” She’s worried that Democratic governor Kathy Hochul won’t sign a stronger bill to impose a stricter moratorium, and is concerned that the state Department of Environmental Conservation is not adequately involved in the process of evaluating data centers in New York.
“I feel like she’s just trying to shut us up,” she says of Hochul.

Data centers are at the center of midterm races across the country, with politicians of both parties making promises to enact regulations or moratoriums on development. After next week comes the tough part: Newly elected officials must either break their word or follow through on those promises as they weigh large infrastructure projects coming to their states and residents who say they’ll reject data centers no matter what.
How will those compromises go—and will they appease voters? New York’s moratorium, and the continued opposition from some groups, may offer clues.

In July, just two months after dismissing the idea of a data center moratorium, Hochul signed the nation’s first executive order to put a pause on development. Her order was a compromise. Just weeks prior, the state legislature had passed an omnibus bill that would have implemented a one-year moratorium throughout New York. The bill contained several provisions that made it more aggressive than Hochul’s moratorium, including stricter limits on the size of data centers and a mandate that the Department of Environmental Conservation conduct a thorough environmental impact review of data center operations. Rather than sign the bill, Hochul issued her own order. (The governor has until the end of the year to sign that bill, and her office says they are still looking at it.)

One of the bill’s State Senate sponsors, Democrat Kristen Gonzalez, has been publicly supportive of Hochul’s moratorium. The governor’s office, Gonzalez says, proactively reached out to her after her bill passed to help design the moratorium for more immediate relief for New Yorkers.

Gonzalez went on a data center tour of New York at the end of the summer, talking to residents around the state about their concerns. She told me that the people she talked to overwhelmingly wanted Hochul to go further and implement more aggressive measures to protect communities from data centers.

“There are local communities statewide that are living near existing data centers, dealing with significant air pollution and noise pollution, who are struggling with rising utility bills and rising water bills,” she told me. “We see the moratorium as a first step, but it can’t be the last.”

Hochul has a comfortable lead over Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman ahead of Tuesday’s election—something that may have been helped by the moratorium’s passing. In a recent Quinnipiac poll of New York voters, 53 percent of respondents said they trusted Hochul to do a better job in handling AI and data centers, compared to just 31 percent trusting Blakeman. Blakeman, who has voiced support for data centers, called Hochul’s moratorium “crazy” when it was passed in July. His campaign didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Hochul has also touted her tough-on-data-center bona fides on the campaign trail. Early last month, she hosted a roundtable discussion on data centers with agricultural, environmental, and business leaders at a farm in the Hudson Valley. There, she told reporters that she wanted to work with the state legislature to implement more aggressive protections, including banning tax breaks for data centers. At the event, Hochul was flanked by Gonzalez and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, one of Washington’s most prominent data center critics.

I asked Hochul at the event how she anticipates handling continued opposition after her moratorium ends. How does New York balance economic development with community opposition if some people don’t want data centers in their backyards under any circumstances, even with the assurances from the state that Hochul’s office is working to create?

The purpose of her pause, she said, was that communities should be able to choose. “This is democracy in action,” she said. “If you want it, it should come with all kinds of guardrails and restraints, but if you don’t want it, it doesn’t come.”

More New Yorkers may end up choosing the latter option. A Siena poll from September found that 63 percent of New Yorkers would oppose data centers being built in their area even after Hochul’s moratorium expires. (It’s even higher for New York Democrats, with 75 percent saying they’d remain opposed to data center development post-moratorium.)

Many newly elected (or reelected) governors will face a similar dynamic: At least 20 gubernatorial candidates have promised a data center moratorium or pause, according to research compiled by government relations company MultiState. Even more have promised to regulate the industry more tightly. Formerly data-center-friendly incumbents like Texas’s Greg Abbott and Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro have also made pledges to be stricter on their development.

Come January, new governors will face highly engaged constituents who are finding a political home for the first time in the fight against data centers. That includes Yocina, who says she had never voted in a local election before.

She says she understands the need for industries and jobs in upstate New York: Her youngest son decided to join the Army after a fruitless job search and is about to be deployed. Now, her organizing group is moving from focusing on just stopping the data center to brainstorming new ideas for the site.
“We’re trying to figure out what we can say yes to that’s not a data center,” she says.

Buried in Anthropic’s IPO documents filed last week was a startling admission. The tech giant’s plan to develop its own data centers exposes it to financial risk, thanks to its projected reliance on natural gas. Of course, Anthropic isn’t alone in its reliance on gas, and the filing acknowledges that’s a real problem. The heavy demand could “drive up the price of natural gas” and make it harder to purchase. I took a look at Anthropic’s plans for data centers and the brewing competition between data centers over natural gas supply in the US.

- The Verge’s Gaby Del Valle takes readers out west for a deep dive on data centers’ water woes in Arizona—and why a massive and thirsty chip manufacturing plant seems to have escaped the public’s ire.
- New findings from Pew Research Center show that advertisers spent $12 million on political ads mentioning data centers in a 90-day period leading up to the midterms.

- Two professors who study real estate and urban economics write in The Conversation about their most recent research on data centers and job creation. Their findings: Data centers lead to modest job growth in certain sectors like transportation and warehousing, but not in local services like restaurants and retail.

items.title: Elon Musk’s Ties to Texas Republicans Go Much Deeper Than the Midterms
items.description: Elon Musk has enjoyed a cozy relationship with top Texas brass for years. And in recent weeks, as the midterm elections approach and Musk’s financial support of the Texas GOP has become virtually limitless, that relationship has gone under the microscope.
items.author: Tess Owen
paragraphs: Elon Musk has enjoyed a cozy relationship with top Texas brass for years. And in recent weeks, as the midterm elections approach and Musk’s financial support of the Texas GOP has become virtually limitless, that relationship has gone under the microscope.

While polls suggest that a number of races in deep-red Texas are looking dizzyingly close, Federal Election Commission filings show that Musk has given at least $158 million to super PACs supporting Texas attorney general Ken Paxton’s bid for Senate, and last week Musk explicitly endorsed him in a post on X. “The fate of Texas and America is at stake,” Musk wrote. “Vote for @KenPaxtonTX today.”
Newly released state campaign filings also show that Musk also donated $5,000,000 to Governor Greg Abbott’s bid for reelection, making him his single largest donor.

Abbott’s relationship with Musk has been the subject of public interest for years. State representative Gina Hinojosa, who is running against Abbott, recently sued to view, in full, 1,400 pages of the governor’s correspondences with Musk. Abbott has been trying to block their release for some time; his office has described the communications as too “intimate and embarrassing” to be made public. This week, a judge ruled that Abbott had illegally “obstructed and continues to obstruct” Hinojosa’s right to inspect the documents in her capacity as a state lawmaker and ordered their release to her. Abbott has since appealed; a hearing is scheduled for November 2, one day before the election.

State representative James Talarico, who is running against Paxton for Senate, has campaigned on his opponents’ checkered past. As attorney general, Paxton has been indicted on felony securities fraud charges (which he settled without a plea), was accused by whistleblowers of using his office to benefit the financial interests of a political donor, and was impeached (though later acquitted).

And at a campaign event on Monday in El Paso, Talarico raised questions about Paxton and Musk’s relationship. “Ken Paxton has the ultimate megadonor,” Talarico said. “Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat.”

But Musk’s business dealings in Texas politics didn’t start with the midterms. For years, he has enjoyed lucrative state contacts, tax breaks, and allyship from Texas leaders. In 2021, Musk moved Tesla’s corporate headquarters from Palo Alto, California, to Austin, and SpaceX’s headquarters from Hawthorne, California, to Starbase, Texas, in 2024.

Musk’s initial relocation to Texas coincided with a shift in operations inside the Texas Attorney General’s office. In the past, lawyers would prepare notices of investigation (administrative subpoenas known as CIDs) based on public complaints or evidence collected, then send them up the chain for approval.

Sources tell WIRED that from about 2021 onward, lawyers were increasingly instructed by Texas’ executive branch—which included Paxton and Abbott—who and what they were going to investigate, despite internal efforts to steer resources toward more “legitimate” issues. For example, in 2022, eyebrows were raised internally when, the same day Musk sent a letter to Twitter threatening to abandon a $44 billion acquisition agreement over Twitter’s alleged misrepresentation of the number of bots on the platform, Paxton’s office issued a statement asserting that his office would be launching its own investigation against Twitter.

A year later, Paxton once again appeared to use his office to benefit Musk. Musk sued the progressive watchdog Media Matters for defamation after it published an investigation showing that X, under Musk’s ownership, had been placing ads from major brands next to white-nationalist content. Moments after he filed his suit, Paxton’s office announced its own investigation into Media Matters. (Media Matters sued Paxton, asserting that his investigation was brought out of retaliation for its coverage of Musk and X.)
