items.title: The 13 Governor’s Races Worth Watching on Election Night
items.description: While the battle for control of Congress has received the lion’s share of national-media midterms attention, there’s obviously a lot going on downballot, too — particularly across the governors’ races.
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: While the battle for control of Congress has received the lion’s share of national-media midterms attention, there’s obviously a lot going on downballot, too — particularly across the governors’ races.

This year, 36 gubernatorial contests will help determine the direction of many states and perhaps create future candidates for the U.S. Senate or president (25 major-party presidential nominees have been former governors, including 17 who became president). Currently, there are 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors. The governorships up for grabs this year are now split down the middle with 18 from each party.

The odds are high if not prohibitive that Democrats will hold a majority of these positions after the midterms (Silver Bulletin’s FLIPR forecasting model gives Democrats 85 percent odds of a gubernatorial majority and predicts one that would put roughly two out of three Americans in the 27 states governed by Democrats).

But there are a lot of close gubernatorial races — 13 competitive contests, according to the wizards at the Cook Political Report. Six (Alaska, Arizona, Iowa, Michigan, Ohio, and Oregon) lean Democratic, and three (Florida, Nebraska, and Texas) lean Republican. Four (Georgia, Kansas, Nevada, and Wisconsin) are rated as toss-ups. Here’s what to know about those contests.
Where Democrats are Favored

This contest is complicated by Alaska’s unique electoral system, in which the top-four finishers in a nonpartisan primary proceed to a general election that is determined via ranked-choice voting. In the primary, two Democrats finished first and second: former state legislators Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich (scion of a famous political family and uncle of Alaska’s current Republican congressman). But Begich promptly dropped out and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, which put three Republicans in the general election, including Trump endorsee and conservative ideologue Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage mayor Dave Bronson, and former attorney general Treg Taylor. The divided GOP and a united Democratic Party guaranteed Kreiss-Tomkins the lead and probably first place in the general-election balloting. According to Silver Bulletin’s polling averages, Kreiss-Tomkins has a steady 20-point lead over Wilson, the top-polling Republican, and is within striking distance of the majority that would make RCV irrelevant.

A late development in the race was the endorsement of Kreiss-Tomkins by Republican U.S. senator Lisa Murkowski, who has crossed party lines before (notably in backing Mary Peltola against Sarah Palin for the House in 2022; she’s not backing Peltola’s Senate bid this year, though). If, as appears increasingly probable, Kreiss-Tomkins wins, it will represent a Democratic gain (GOP governor Mike Dunleavy was term-limited). At the moment, both chambers of Alaska’s legislature are controlled by a bipartisan and independent coalition; that isn’t expected to change.

Incumbent Democratic governor Katie Hobbs has been expected to face a tough challenge after very narrowly defeating Kari Lake in 2022; Donald Trump carried the state by a surprisingly large margin (5+ percent) in 2024. But aside from a national Democratic wave, Hobbs caught a break when the GOP nomination was won by conservative congressional ideologue Andy Biggs. It says a lot about Biggs’s viability that the normally very aggressive Republican Governors Association hasn’t put any money into the race. Silver Bulletin polling averages show Hobbs ahead by 9.4 points.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both state legislative chambers in Arizona, but Democrats are optimistic about flipping both and giving Hobbs trifecta control of state government.

Iowa’s two-term Republican governor Kim Reynolds has been regularly labeled “America’s most unpopular governor” in the past two years, and that along with a strong anti-Trump wave in recently red Iowa has long made Democrats optimistic about a 2026 win for State Auditor Rob Sand (the only statewide elected Democrat in Iowa). Then, the Trump-endorsed favorite for the GOP nomination, congressman Randy Feenstra, was upset in the primary by “outsider” Zach Lahn, who ran an anti-Establishment but pro-Trump campaign. It was subsequently learned that Lahn had not severed his strong ties to neighboring Kansas and was still spending a lot of time in Wichita while running for governor of Iowa. This easily mocked habit gave Sand’s already strong candidacy a boost, and in the Silver Bulletin polling averages Sand leads by 7.3 points.

In contrast with the state’s red-hot U.S. Senate race, the contest to succeed term-limited Democratic governor Gretchen Whitmer has been relatively calm and steady, with two very well-known pols facing each other and the midterm blue breeze clearly giving the Democrat an edge. Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson has held a steady lead over congressman (and unsuccessful 2018 and 2020 U.S. Senate candidate) John James. Any traction James has obtained by urging a change from the status quo in Lansing has clearly been offset by unhappiness with Trump. In the Silver Bulletin polling averages, Benson leads by 7.9 percentage points, and the spotlight remains on the Senate contest.

Further downballot, both chambers of the Michigan legislature are battlegrounds, with Larry Sabato’s Crystal Ball rating the fights for both the Democratic-controlled Senate and the Republican-controlled House as toss-ups. A stronger Democratic tide could not only lift Benson to an easy win but give her a trifecta.

In a close and expensive contest that has garnered immense national attention of late, Democratic gubernatorial candidate and former state health director Amy Acton is now favored over Republican billionaire (and 2024 presidential candidate) Vivek Ramaswamy in what would represent a Democratic gain in a state thought to be safely red. This contest was very close for months, with Acton benefiting from a Democratic tailwind (and perhaps some right-wing uneasiness with the GOP candidate’s race and background) and Ramaswamy outspending her massively and trying to exploit anti-vaxx unhappiness with her pandemic record in Ohio. Then Ramaswamy rolled the dice with a nasty ad featuring Acton’s disreputable mother (from whom she was long-estranged after alleging rape by her late stepfather). His campaign has now yanked the ad after internal GOP polling showed a major backlash that burnished the Republican’s already significant reputation for unlikeability. While Acton’s lead is 3.1 points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages, there’s a sense Ramaswamy’s campaign could be imploding.

Oregon is the odd blue state with an incumbent Democratic governor who is vulnerable thanks to generally low favorability. Tina Kotek is weathering a surprisingly strong challenge from her 2022 opponent, state senator Christine Drazan, despite outspending her and tying her to the very unpopular president. In 2022 Kotek benefited from a late surge, and her camp is hoping for that again. She leads Drazan by 1.5 points in the Silver Bulletin averages.
Where Republicans are Favored

In 2022 and 2024, the Republican advantage in what had been the close battleground of Florida blossomed, with Governor Ron DeSantis being reelected by a 19 percent margin and Trump carrying his new home state by 13 percent. Now there are signs that in this wave election the GOP edge has shrunk significantly. Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds, a Black GOP congressman and close Trump ally who had a relatively easy road to the general-election ballot, is facing a tougher than expected challenge from Republican turned Democrat David Jolly. Florida Republicans have been tripping over one another to ravage the state’s tax base, and their attention has mostly been focused on gerrymander-driven House races. But Donalds has a significant financial advantage and leads Jolly by 4.6 percentage points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages.

Nebraska is a very red state (Trump carried it by 20 percent in 2024), but GOP governor Jim Pillen isn’t very popular. He drew flak earlier in his first term for proposing sales-tax increases to pay for the elimination of property taxes. And he drew negative attention from national media reports that he has hired lots of undocumented immigrants for his family’s hog farm. He’s also on a ballot with two minor candidates, including someone claiming to represent the America First Party and a pro-marijuana-legalization advocate. All this has given Democratic legislator Lynne Walz some traction, and she actually led the incumbent in one October poll. Overall, though, Pillen leads Walz by 3.3 points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages, and between that and the state’s partisan character, Pillen is expected to survive.

It has been overshadowed by the insanely expensive Senate race in the state, but Republican Greg Abbott’s bid for a fourth term as Texas governor has run into unexpected trouble. Among other things, GOP gains among Hispanic voters appear to have been sharply reversed this year, and Abbott has also aligned himself pretty closely not only to an unpopular president but to his state party’s extremist MAGA wing with its abrasive views on immigration, public education, and Christian nationalism. Democratic nominee Gina Hinojosa has run a shrewd, middle-of-the-road campaign, and has hammered Abbott for his avid promotion of data centers in Texas (which he has tried hard to reverse this year with regulatory proposals). Abbott unsurprisingly has at least a two-to-one financial advantage over his opponent and is benefiting, like all other Texas Republicans, from Elon Musk’s massive last-minute spending on their behalf.

Abbott leads Hinojosa by just 2.4 percentage points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages, but his past electoral record and perhaps a desire for some ticket splitting by Republicans convinced to vote against Ken Paxton in the Senate race could help him in the end.

No Democrat has won a gubernatorial race in Georgia since 1998, but the state has remained competitive in presidential races and has two Democratic U.S. senators. One of them, Jon Ossoff, is up for reelection this year and by all accounts is likely to easily win a second term. He has been campaigning jointly with Democratic gubernatorial nominee and former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, and the big question is whether he can help her win a close race over billionaire Republican nominee Rick Jackson.

Jackson came out of nowhere this year with a huge bankroll and defeated Trump’s endorsed gubernatorial candidate. But while campaigning as an “outsider,” he has managed to hang on to support from both the unpopular Trump and the very popular term-limited incumbent, Brian Kemp. Bottoms, meanwhile, easily won a majority against a large primary field and is running a moderate campaign focused on expanding Medicaid and legalizing casino gambling. But she faces a vast financial disadvantage against Jackson and perhaps some temptation among anti-Trump Republicans and independents backing Ossoff to split their tickets, particularly those put off by her race and gender (she would be the first Black or female governor of this state) or her association with an unpopular Atlanta city government. So far, though, Bottoms has held her own in the polls: She leads Jackson by an eyelash in the Silver Bulletin polling averages. It really could go either way, though the evidence of strong early voting by Black voters is a good sign for Bottoms.

Deep-red Kansas has a recent history of electing Democratic governors when Republican voters split, but current governor Laura Kelly is term limited and Republicans are united behind their nominee, state legislative leader Ty Masterson. However, the strong anti-Trump wave, which in Kansas has helped produce a very strong Senate candidate in Adam Hamilton, is also giving a late lift to Democratic gubernatorial nominee Cindy Holscher, who is running a strong campaign against data-center expansion and other corporate subsidies. Masterson leads by 4.5 points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages, but internal polling from the Holscher camp convinced Cook Political Report to shift this contest to a toss-up.

This very closely divided state, where 2028 presidential contestants are already spending time and money, is featuring a classic pick-’em gubernatorial race between incumbent Republican Joe Lombardo and Democratic attorney general Aaron Ford. Lombardo, whose base is in normally Democratic-leaning Las Vegas, had an early lead and has outspent Ford significantly. But the national breeze is affecting Nevada, too, and Ford seems to have caught up, though Lombardo still has a 0.5-point lead in the Silver Bulletin polling averages. Republicans have to worry about the sizable anti-Trump trend among the state’s abundant Latino population, and it’s not great to be an incumbent in the current sour public mood.

Wisconsin has long been one of the country’s most intensely competitive states, and a chaotic Democratic primary to succeed retiring two-term Democratic governor Tony Evers gave the GOP, united around congressman Tom Tiffany, some real hope. After a wild series of scandals and candidate withdrawals, Milwaukee county executive David Crowley, who had folded but then reopened his candidacy, upset democratic socialist state legislator Francesca Hong in a relatively late (August) primary. So far, Crowley has managed to keep Democrats united, but he has suffered from a more than two-to-one financial deficit against Tiffany. The Democrat has maintained a fragile lead in the polls but got some good news when the final edition of the highly regarded Marquette Law School survey showed him expanding his margin over Tiffany to 7 percentage points. Crowley now leads by 5.6 points in the Silver Bulletin polling averages.
