Anyone can run to the store and grab a gift card, but the best gift givers know that the most-appreciated presents start with giving it some real thought. Whether you’re shopping for your bestie who’s been checking in with FaceTime calls every week or that special somebody you gave your number to while leaving the gym, gifts that come with intention are always the winners of the holiday season.

Of course, you could spend hours opening a million tabs just to find the right item. Or you could get a lil’ advice from a veteran shopping director (hi, it’s me!). I’ve been on the search for the most thoughtful finds this entire year, so the holidays are like my Super Bowl. I get joy out of people asking me, “Where can I find the best personalized gifts?” or “What are some impressive finds that won’t blow my budget?” So, ahead I’m breaking down the meaningful, fun finds that deserve to be wrapped this season. And because we’re always going to be financially smart sirens, start with what you’re comfortable spending, then find something that feels just right for your person. Each item is available for purchase with Affirm, you can pay over time with no late or hidden fees—and keep the surprises where they belong: in the gift giving. It doesn’t matter if you’re giving the gift of a fancy beauty product you discovered at Neiman Marcus, a unique trinket from an Etsy seller, or a hero home essential on Wayfair, Affirm makes checking everyone off your nice list easy peasy.
Take our holiday quiz to find your gifting match or keep scrolling for the Refinery29 edit of thoughtful presents.

She has impeccable taste, sends you links before you’ve even heard of the brand, and somehow already owns everything you were considering. The move? Get personal. An embroidered zebra-print pouch with her name on it gives her everyday essentials a very cute home, while a photo jewelry dish turns that picture of you two into something she’ll actually use. Yes, the one from the night you still talk about. If she loves a beauty treat, Dior lip oil or a bottle of one of Tom Ford’s fragrances brings a little luxury to her getting-ready routine. You know your friend. Pick the gift that proves it.

You’ve seen their kitchen. You’ve admired their table settings. You’ve wondered whether you should start bringing your own containers because even the leftovers leave looking chic. Pink checkered canisters from Wayfair make keeping the counter tidy considerably more fun, and Jonathan Adler’s lip-motif coasters give guests something to comment on between sips. An olive oil gift set from Williams Sonoma is another good call: they can taste their way through it, then casually make you the best salad of your life. And for the host who does all that cooking and washing up? A Jo Malone hand cream trio feels like a little thank-you for their hands.

Maybe they’ve had a year. Maybe they always take care of everyone else. Maybe you simply love watching them open something they would have talked themselves out of buying. Here’s your chance. A Saint Laurent card case makes even pulling out a loyalty card feel a little fancy, while a Dyson Supersonic Nural is a generous upgrade for someone who takes their hair routine seriously. For the person whose signature scent is practically part of their introduction, the Parfums De Marly’s viral perfume puts a favorite fragrance within reach. Start with something you know they’ll love, then give them the version they’ve been eyeing.

“We should do that” has been sitting in the group chat for six months. Let’s give it a little momentum. A pasta basket packed with gourmet treats makes choosing a Saturday very doable, while a personalized passport holder and luggage tag give your buddy something to unwrap before you two settle on a destination. For the friend who keeps promising cocktail night, a gold bar-tool set from Wayfair says, “Great, I’ll bring the limes.” Add a travel journal for the person who wants to remember every meal, wrong turn, and surprisingly good hotel recommendation. You may still have to send the calendar invite, but at least you've got an opening.

Your gift budget also has rent, groceries, and your own holiday travel to consider. Fair enough. A personalized hairbrush feels chosen just for them, and colorful stemware can make their usual Friday-night pour feel like an occasion. For your friend who treasures a good night in, consider a checked pajama piece or a candle in a playful, colorful vessel. Just think about the small pleasures they return to every day, then find something that makes one of those moments a little sweeter.

items.title: Your Horoscope This Week: November 1 To 7
items.description: R29 babes, November begins with a much-needed cosmic breather. With no major planetary shifts this week, we have room to recalibrate while Mercury retrograde in Scorpio and Venus retrograde in Libra continue encouraging us to review our relationships, finances
items.author: Dossé-Via Trenou
paragraphs: R29 babes, November begins with a much-needed cosmic breather. With no major planetary shifts this week, we have room to recalibrate while Mercury retrograde in Scorpio and Venus retrograde in Libra continue encouraging us to review our relationships, finances, and emotional patterns. The Scorpio New Moon arrives November 9th, so consider this week your chance to get grounded before the momentum picks up. We start with the Moon in Leo joining forces with Mars and Jupiter, boosting our confidence and reminding us to align our actions with our bigger vision. Less talking about it, more being about it.

On November 3rd, the moon enters Virgo for two and a half days, helping us get down to the nitty-gritty of what needs to be handled. This is the perfect time to tackle your to-do list, organize your budget, clean up your environment, or address the responsibilities that have been piling up while you’ve been busy processing life’s bigger questions. Sure, it may not be the sexiest cosmic energy, but sometimes paying that overdue bill or finally sending that email can feel just as satisfying as a major breakthrough. The trick is to avoid filling your schedule with busywork just so you can feel productive. Ask yourself which tasks will genuinely move the needle toward the goals you’re setting for November, and give those your attention first.

Then, from November 5th through much of the 7th, the moon moves through Libra, bringing out our more social, flirtatious, and pleasure-seeking sides. After a few days of Virgo-inspired productivity, you may feel ready to dress up, spend time with friends, go on a date, browse your favorite shops, or simply surround yourself with beautiful things. With Venus retrograde in Libra, you might even find yourself rediscovering pleasures, places, or connections that once made you feel especially good. Just be mindful of impulsive spending or romantic decisions you haven’t fully thought through. This week is a reminder that even during Scorpio and retrograde season we’re allowed to lighten up and enjoy being alive. Follow the moon’s rhythm this week: dream boldly, handle your business, and give yourself something to smile about.
Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

Aries, November begins with the Last Quarter Moon in Leo activating your romance, fame, and inner-child healing zone. A week after the Taurus Full Moon brought revelations about your money and self-worth, you may be realizing that certain pleasures, passions, or relationships deserve more of your energy, while others have become expensive distractions. Leo energy encourages you to take pride in your talents and remember what makes you feel alive. If you've been waiting for external validation before pursuing something you love, this lunation could help you release that hesitation. Your happiness deserves to be part of your game plan, too.

On November 3rd, the moon enters Virgo, bringing your attention to work, wellness, and the little habits that keep your life running smoothly. You may feel motivated to get organized, catch up on appointments, or make your schedule more manageable. Then, as the moon enters Libra on the 5th, your relationships take center stage. With Venus retrograde still unfolding in this part of your chart, a conversation with a partner or close friend could help you understand where more balance is needed. Handle your  responsibilities early in the week so you can actually enjoy connecting with people this weekend.

Taurus, the Last Quarter Moon in Leo on November 1st draws your attention toward  home and the emotional foundation you're building for yourself. After last week's Full  Moon in your sign brought certain personal revelations to the surface, you may feel ready to make changes in your private life that reflect how much you've grown. Perhaps your living space needs a refresh, a family dynamic needs healthier boundaries, or you've simply outgrown the expectation that you should always be available to everyone. Leo energy encourages you to take ownership of your happiness. You deserve a space where you can fully be yourself, without feeling like you're constantly performing for others.

By November 3rd, the Virgo Moon lights up your romance, creativity, and pleasure zone, making the middle of the week ideal for enjoying the little things that make life sweet. You could feel inspired to revisit a creative hobby, plan a date, or spend quality time with your children or loved ones. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, shifting your focus toward wellness and daily routines. Since your ruling planet Venus is still retrograde in Libra, pay attention to which habits genuinely make your life easier and  which ones you've maintained out of obligation. A little more balance in your schedule could make your weekend feel surprisingly restorative.

Gemini, November kicks off with the Last Quarter Moon in Leo activating your communication zone and immediate environment. A week after the Taurus Full Moon illuminated your subconscious and brought hidden emotions to the surface, you may finally be ready to put some of those revelations into words. Perhaps there's a conversation you've been rehearsing in your head, an idea you've been sitting on, or a belief about yourself that you're ready to challenge. Leo energy encourages you to speak with confidence, while the waning moon helps you release the need to explain yourself to everyone. Sometimes saying less, but meaning every word, is the real power move.

On November 3rd, the moon enters Virgo, bringing your attention toward home, family, and getting your personal environment in order. You may feel like decluttering, handling household responsibilities, or spending more time in your own company. But by the 5th, the Libra Moon activates your romance, creativity, and pleasure zone, and suddenly staying home folding laundry may sound a lot less appealing. With Venus retrograde here, an old crush, creative passion, or favorite pastime could catch your attention again. Enjoy the nostalgia without feeling pressured to recreate the past. This weekend is about remembering what makes you happy and giving yourself permission to have a little fun.

Cancer, November begins with you being ready to secure the bag, but the Last Quarter  Moon in Leo on the 1st may have you reconsidering what you’re spending it on. After last week’s Taurus Full Moon brought revelations about your friendships, community, and future goals, you may be realizing that some of your financial priorities need to shift. Perhaps you’ve been investing too much money into keeping up socially, or you’re ready to put more resources toward a dream that actually excites you. Leo energy encourages you to recognize your talents and stop undervaluing what you bring to the table. This is a great time to release spending habits or scarcity mindsets that  have been holding you back.

On November 3rd, the moon enters Virgo, activating your communication zone. You may feel inspired to catch up on emails, organize your thoughts, or finally have a conversation you’ve been putting off. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, shifting your attention toward home, family, and your emotional well-being. With Venus still retrograde in Libra, you may feel more nostalgic than usual or find yourself revisiting a family matter that needs some tenderness. Keep your weekend plans flexible, Cancer. A cozy evening at home, a home-cooked meal, or quality time with people who make you feel safe could be exactly what you need.

Leo, are you ready to stop carrying around a version of yourself that you’ve already outgrown? The Last Quarter Moon in your sign on November 1st encourages you to release outdated expectations about who you should be and how others perceive you. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have brought a professional milestone or a realization about your career direction, and now you’re being asked to consider how that evolution is changing you personally. Perhaps you’ve been putting pressure on yourself to maintain a certain image, even when it no longer feels authentic. Give yourself permission to change your mind, your appearance, or your priorities. You don’t owe anyone a permanent version of yourself.

By November 3rd, the Virgo Moon turns your attention toward money, security, and self-worth, making the middle of the week ideal for reviewing your budget, organizing your finances, or getting clearer about what your work is worth. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, bringing a more social and communicative energy into your weekend. You may feel inspired to reconnect with siblings, catch up with friends, or explore your neighborhood. With Venus retrograde in Libra, an old conversation or  connection could resurface, but you don’t have to respond to every message just because someone remembers your number. Choose the exchanges that actually leave you feeling good.

Virgo, your mind may have approximately 37 tabs open as November begins, and the Last Quarter Moon in Leo wants you to close a few. This lunation activates your spirituality, solitude, and subconscious realm, encouraging you to release mental clutter and emotional baggage that’s been quietly draining your energy. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have brought a breakthrough involving travel, education, or your bigger vision for the future, and now you need some space to process what that means. You may feel more introspective, sensitive, or aware of old fears that tend to surface whenever you’re preparing for a new chapter. Give yourself permission to unplug and let your imagination wander without needing to turn every thought into a plan.

Then on November 3rd, the moon enters your sign, and you may feel your motivation returning almost overnight. This is your opportunity to prioritize your personal needs, refresh your appearance, or tackle something you’ve been putting off. By the 5th, the Libra Moon shifts your focus toward money and self-worth, making the weekend a good time to review your spending and enjoy a few affordable pleasures. With Venus retrograde in Libra, you may be reconsidering what you value and whether certain purchases are actually worth it. Treat yourself if you feel inspired, Virgo, but remember that a little financial breathing room can be its own form of luxury.

Libra, how much longer are you going to let other people’s expectations dictate your  dreams? The Last Quarter Moon in Leo on November 1st activates your friendship,  community, and future-goals zone, encouraging you to reconsider which connections and ambitions still feel aligned with who you’re becoming. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have brought revelations about intimacy, trust, or shared finances, and now  you’re seeing how those realizations affect the people you want in your corner. Perhaps you’ve been staying loyal to a social circle you’ve outgrown, or putting a personal dream on hold because nobody else seems to understand it. Leo energy encourages you to take pride in your individuality and trust that the right people will appreciate your vision, even if they don’t fully understand it yet.

On November 3rd, the moon enters Virgo, activating your solitude and spirituality realm. You may crave more privacy, rest, or time away from the group chat to process everything that’s been happening lately. Then, on the 5th, the moon enters your sign,  bringing a welcome boost of confidence, charm, and emotional clarity. With your ruling  planet Venus still retrograde in Libra, you may feel inspired to revisit your personal style, reconnect with an old passion, or simply spend more time doing things that make you feel beautiful and appreciated. Plan something enjoyable for yourself this weekend, Libra. Your happiness deserves some attention, too.

Scorpio, your birthday season is officially underway, but are you still chasing a version of success that you’ve already outgrown? The Last Quarter Moon in Leo on November 1st illuminates your career and public-image zone, encouraging you to release professional pressures or expectations that no longer reflect your priorities. Perhaps you’ve been trying to prove yourself to someone whose approval no longer matters, or you’re realizing that a certain career path has lost its appeal. With the sun in your sign, you have every reason to feel excited about your next chapter. Let this lunation help  you clear space for the opportunities that genuinely deserve your energy.

By November 3rd, the Virgo Moon activates your friendship, community, and future goals realm, making the middle of the week ideal for reconnecting with supportive people or getting organized around a long-term dream. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, drawing you into a more introspective mood as it moves through your solitude and spirituality zone. With Venus retrograde here, you may find yourself revisiting  memories, old attachments, or emotions you’ve been privately processing. Give yourself permission to slow down this weekend, Scorpio. Your birthday season doesn’t have to be one nonstop celebration. Sometimes the best gift you can give yourself is a little peace, a good night’s sleep, and freedom from unnecessary drama.

Sag, your next adventure is calling, but first you may need to stop carrying around beliefs that belong to an older version of yourself. The Last Quarter Moon in Leo on November 1st activates your travel, education, spirituality, and expansion realm,  encouraging you to release limiting perspectives that have been keeping your world smaller than it needs to be. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have revealed where your work, health, or daily routines need adjusting, and now you’re seeing how those changes could create more freedom in your life. Perhaps a dream you’ve been postponing suddenly feels possible, or you’re realizing that a certain path no longer excites you. With your birthday season approaching, this is a powerful time to question what you’ve been telling yourself is realistic. You might be ready for more than you’ve been allowing yourself to imagine.

On November 3rd, the Virgo Moon lights up your career and reputation zone, helping you channel that inspiration into practical professional moves. You may feel motivated to organize a project, follow up on an opportunity, or get serious about a goal you’d like to accomplish before your birthday. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, shifting your attention toward friendship, community, and social connections. With Venus retrograde in Libra, an old friend or former collaborator could resurface, or you may feel inspired to reconnect with people you’ve missed. Enjoy the social energy this weekend, Sag, but be selective about where you invest your time. Your next chapter deserves a circle that genuinely wants to see you thrive.

Capricorn, November begins with the Last Quarter Moon in Leo asking you to loosen your grip on something you’ve been trying to control. This lunation activates your intimacy and transformation zone, bringing up questions around trust, emotional vulnerability, and financial obligations. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have revealed something important about your romantic life or creative passions, and now you’re considering what you’re willing to invest in those areas. If a financial agreement or emotional attachment has become one-sided, this is a good time to reconsider its terms. You can be deeply committed to someone without taking responsibility for everything they carry.

On November 3rd, the Virgo Moon shifts your attention toward travel, education, and bigger-picture plans. You may feel motivated to research a destination, revisit a course you’ve been considering, or map out your next professional move. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, illuminating your career and public image. With Venus retrograde in this part of your chart, an old professional opportunity or unfinished project could resurface. Take the weekend to assess whether it still aligns with your  ambitions before committing to anything. Your definition of success may have changed considerably since you first pursued it.

Aquarius, who’s meeting you halfway these days? The Last Quarter Moon in Leo on  November 1st activates your partnership realm, encouraging you to release relationship expectations that have become unrealistic or exhausting. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have brought a turning point involving home, family, or your emotional security, and now you’re noticing how your closest relationships contribute to that sense of stability. Perhaps you’ve been accommodating someone’s needs at the expense of your own, or expecting a partner to understand feelings you haven’t clearly expressed. This lunation favors honest conversations and a willingness to let old dynamics evolve.

By November 3rd, the Virgo Moon brings your attention to shared finances, intimacy, and practical agreements. It’s a useful time to review expenses, settle an outstanding obligation, or clarify responsibilities with someone you trust. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, activating your travel, education, and expansion zone. With Venus retrograde here, you may find yourself reconsidering a trip, reconnecting with an old mentor, or revisiting a subject that once fascinated you. Give yourself something intellectually stimulating to look forward to this weekend, Aquarius. A change of scenery or perspective could be exactly what you need.

Pisces, that never-ending to-do list isn’t going to complete itself, but does everything on it actually need your attention? The Last Quarter Moon in Leo on November 1st  activates your work, health, and daily-routine zone, encouraging you to eliminate habits and responsibilities that are making life unnecessarily complicated. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have brought clarity through an important conversation or realization, and now it’s time to apply what you’ve learned. Perhaps you’ve been saying yes to too  many requests, neglecting your own appointments, or maintaining a routine that leaves you exhausted. Leo energy encourages you to take pride in how you care for yourself, including knowing when to delegate or decline.

On November 3rd, the Virgo Moon illuminates your partnership realm, making the middle of the week ideal for discussing expectations, dividing responsibilities, or spending quality time with someone important. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, shifting your attention toward intimacy, shared finances, and emotional trust. With Venus retrograde in this part of your chart, an unresolved money matter or relationship concern may deserve another conversation. Keep things transparent, especially when it comes to shared expenses or commitments. By the weekend, you’ll have a better sense of where cooperation is making your life easier and where clearer boundaries are needed.

items.title: Yohji Yamamoto on His Drawings: “I Didn’t Want to Speak”
items.description: So the story begins: in May 2024, hundreds of sheets of paper were discovered in a Tokyo warehouse, initially mistaken for ordinary paperwork. They were in fact original drawings by Yohji Yamamoto, dating back to his Paris debut in 1981 through to 1999, drawn
items.author: George Pistachio
paragraphs: So the story begins: in May 2024, hundreds of sheets of paper were discovered in a Tokyo warehouse, initially mistaken for ordinary paperwork. They were in fact original drawings by Yohji Yamamoto, dating back to his Paris debut in 1981 through to 1999, drawn to communicate his ideas to the pattern cutters who would make them clothes. There are figures that slump over, coats that seem to catch fire, ideas of dresses conjured with a handful of marks. Most have never been seen publicly. Selected by Yamamoto with fashion curator Alexandre Samson, his daughter Limi and close collaborators, with design support from Peter Saville, they make visible a part of his working life long kept private. Now, we glimpse these sketches for the first time, in a book – Yohji Yamamoto Drawings – published by Thames & Hudson.

Yamamoto’s clothes look formidable. On a hanger, a black coat might resemble the folded wings of a bird of prey, a jacket some strange instrument or weapon. His silhouettes can seem almost impossible to decipher, their proportions exaggerated and their absence of colour absolute. But to wear them is another matter entirely. The fabric softens, the shape settles and something that appeared so uncompromising becomes enveloping, flattering, even practical. I have never met Yohji-san – not many people have – but I have worn his clothes, and I know that the outward severity is only half the story.

Born in Tokyo in 1943, Yamamoto lost his father to the Second World War. His mother, Fumi, wore black in mourning for the husband she had lost and worked as a dressmaker to support them both. The image of her bent over her sewing has stayed with him. He studied law before turning to fashion, and in 1981 brought his work to Paris, where an amplified heartbeat accompanied models in voluminous black clothes, some punctured with holes. The response was sometimes vicious. Yet in an era of fashion that displayed, tightened and controlled, he offered women something close to freedom.

Which brings us back to the book – Samson recounts Yamamoto referring to them as “just drawings”. They were not intended as art objects, but as a way to communicate with the patternmakers. Often he found it easier to draw than to speak. The lines are as restless and expressive as the finished garments are composed. Looking at them again, even their maker was taken aback. “What a creative dessin I did,” he tells AnOther. “Now, I can’t draw it.”

The temptation with a book like this is to regard it as a monument, to look back on 45 years of influence and declare the work complete. Yamamoto, now 83, has a different reason for opening the boxes. He hopes the drawings might offer “inspiration, hope, freedom” to a younger generation. The anger he felt as a child, he tells me, has never left him – it appears nor has his desire to make something meaningful of it.
Over email, Yohji-san answers some questions about his book.
George Pistachio What do you remember about making these drawings? Did they help you express things you found difficult to say?

Yohji Yamamoto I used to draw for the patternmakers. For the womenswear collections, at that time I had three important patternmakers: Keiko-san and two others. I didn’t want to talk about my emotions, especially to important patternmakers. Not Keiko. She didn’t want to listen to my complicated philosophy. She feels, and because we are so close, she doesn’t need me to explain.

So, for a new collection, I thought I had to draw something for the other two patternmakers. It was a duty for me before the collection. When I started Y’s, when I began doing shows and decided to make ready-to-wear collections in Japan, Europe and the world, I suffered a lot, naturally. I didn’t want to explain myself by speaking to the patternmakers, for womenswear or menswear. I didn’t want to speak, so I used to draw. Very naturally, I started drawing dessins. It was a duty for the patternmakers a long time ago.
GP You have described a design sketch as a kind of “code” shared between the designer and the patternmaker. Does drawing still play that part in your work?
YY I cannot draw in the same way today, and I don’t use drawings anymore to communicate with my patternmakers.
“It was a long travel of misunderstanding – of my heart, my desire and my creative point of view. I didn’t want to speak, so I used to draw” – Yohji Yamamoto
GP What was it like to see these old drawings again after so many years? Did you recognise them?
YY When I rediscovered my old dessins here in Paris, very frankly, I was surprised. What a creative dessin I did. Now, I can’t draw it.
GP Are there things in these early drawings that you recognise as ideas you are still pursuing today?
YY I used to think about misunderstanding. It was a long travel of misunderstanding – of my heart, my desire and my creative point of view. I didn’t want to speak, so I used to draw.
GP The book begins with your first Paris collection in 1981. When you look back at yourself then, how much has changed?

YY Since my childhood, I have had the same anger. This has not changed. And since my first collection in Tokyo, my first show, until now, what I want to achieve with my creations, my goal, remains the same. This has not changed either.
GP When you begin a collection, what comes first – a silhouette, a feeling, a fabric or a drawing?

YY Definitely the fabric. The first moment I touch the fabric, I think about cutting. Touch is very important. Then come the pins, the scissors. I start by draping the fabric on a model or a mannequin. Fabric is the real start.
GP Can a garment ever surprise you by becoming very different from the drawing that began it?
YY Of course. In every fitting, every time, I am surprised. This is both excitement and pressure. My life is made of both – pressure and excitement.
GP Were there any drawings you deliberately decided not to include in the book?
YY There was no censorship. It all came very naturally.
GP After so many decades, what made you decide to let the public see these drawings now?
YY My wish is to give inspiration, hope, freedom to the young generation who is struggling. This is why I agreed to release these drawings and show them to the public.
Yohji Yamamoto Drawings is published by Thames & Hudson and is out now

items.title: Milan's most iconic brutalist tower is about to house 72 luxury apartments
items.description: Have you always dreamt of living in an icon of brutalist architecture? The forthcoming Torre Velasca Residences in Milan can offer a vision of just that, thanks to an exclusive new group of luxury homes that are soon coming to market.
items.author: Ellie Stathaki
paragraphs: Have you always dreamt of living in an icon of brutalist architecture? The forthcoming Torre Velasca Residences in Milan can offer a vision of just that, thanks to an exclusive new group of luxury homes that are soon coming to market.

Occupying the top eight floors of the legendary high-rise, first designed by BBPR in 1958, the 72 new residences, which have launched their first phase this autumn, have been curated to perfection by Matteo Thun & Partners.
Explore the new Torre Velasca Residences by Matteo Thun & Partners

Thun's design draws on the tower's prominent position in the Milanese skyline and its architectural avant-garde spirit. The interiors, as a result, are elegant and nod to 20th-century modernism, yet still remain perfectly tuned to 21st-century needs and contemporary mod-cons. And while the project comprises levels 19 and 26 (the rest of the building is a hotel operated by METT Hotels & Resorts), the design scope also included a rethink of some of the communal areas, such as the main reception, the welcome lobby at the rear of the ground floor, and the corridors.

Says Thun on his approach in working with such a historically significant location: 'Reinterpretation is our key methodology when engaging with a legacy. At Torre Velasca, we allowed the masters and the building itself to speak, imagining a way of living within it that could accompany the building a little further into the future, adding a new chapter to its history.'

'In our design, we did not seek contrast with the existing building; instead, we started building our colour codes from the iconic pink plaster and the green and blue tiles of Torre Velasca. Where we felt the architecture had already achieved a sense of completeness, such as at the loggias and the rooftop that have an almost sacred quality, we chose not to intervene further. Sometimes designing also means recognising when there is no need to add anything,' he adds.

'The interiors look to Milanese design from the 1950s through the 1980s, where we collaborated with some of Milan's iconic companies, such as Molteni, Oluce, Cassina and Dedar, who had shaped the city’s identity as an international design capital. Different eras and locally rooted realities come together in a shared narrative of evolution and continuity: the ability to change over time while maintaining an intact sense of identity.'

To match the existing tower and the new interiors' vision and refinement, the residences will now be operated by Sunset Hospitality, which will offer high-quality resident services that will ensure frictionless living.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Thun concludes: 'Although the project focused on interior design, Torre Velasca first and foremost challenged us to think and work as architects. Perhaps the most interesting aspect of this experience was precisely this: every time we crossed the building’s threshold, we discovered something new. It was, in every sense, a lesson in architecture.'

'Working within its walls meant constantly engaging with composition, construction details, and the relationship between the building and the city. At Torre Velasca, domestic space and urban space cannot be conceived as separate entities, but rather as parts of a single, deeply interconnected system,' the architect continues.

'In this sense, the project became a journey of discovery, in which the building itself became our first teacher,' Thun says. 'And perhaps this is the most important lesson it has left us with: in attempting to intervene in a work of architecture so rich in meaning, we received far more than we were able to give back.'

Ellie Stathaki is the Architecture & Environment Director at Wallpaper*. She trained as an architect at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece and studied architectural history at the Bartlett in London. Now an established journalist, she has been a member of the Wallpaper* team since 2006, visiting buildings across the globe and interviewing leading architects such as Tadao Ando and Rem Koolhaas. Ellie has also taken part in judging panels, moderated events, curated shows and contributed in books, such as The Contemporary House (Thames & Hudson, 2018), Glenn Sestig Architecture Diary (2020) and House London (2022).

items.title: The best new London restaurants to try now
items.description: London in the 21st century is the restaurant capital of the world. British chefs vie with the most famous names on the international food scene to secure the primest sites for their new ventures. Here you can find almost any cuisine on the planet, often made w
items.author: Ben McCormack
paragraphs: London in the 21st century is the restaurant capital of the world. British chefs vie with the most famous names on the international food scene to secure the primest sites for their new ventures. Here you can find almost any cuisine on the planet, often made with seasonal British ingredients, whether organic meats, sustainably caught fish, and regeneratively farmed vegetables, but the food is only half the story: chefs collaborate with designers to ensure that the surroundings look every bit as enticing as what’s coming out of the kitchen.
Each month, we visit some of the city’s buzziest openings to discover the most exciting new menu items and locations across the capital.
The Wallpaper* guide to new London restaurants
Florence Knight's first solo project, Lunette at London's St Clement hotel, serves up beautifully framed riverside views and picture-perfect dishes.

The mood: Flooded with early autumn light, Lunette's off-white palette, swathes of pale wood, steel tabletops, artist monographs artfully arranged on a coffee table and an abundance of Jean Prouvé's modernist ‘INSA' panels lining the walls make it resemble a curated loft apartment as much as a dining room.

What to order: Knight's cooking is precise, seasonal, ‘reasonably gentle in flavour', and inspired by nature and art. There's a painterly assemblage of raw, late-summer runner and yellow French beans with slow-cooked squid, dressed with tomato water; a sunny dish of rice cooked in crab stock, with a sauce of long peppers and tomato juice, egg-yolk jam and cock crab in crab-shell butter; a more autumnal plate of French guinea fowl with a hazelnut and celeriac sauce, beetroot purée, and a jus split with hazelnut and tarragon oils; and an edgeless chocolate tart, its super-short pastry crisp with rice flour and depth afforded by tea-soaked raisins. The full dinner menu will feature eight courses, plus sundries.
Why we love it: For artistic plates and spectacular views.
Lunette is located on the 11th floor of St. Clement at 180 The Thames, Temple, London, WC2R 2NF. Open now.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

After six years in charge of The Grill at The Dorchester, Tom Booton – the youngest chef ever to hold the role at the hotel – is opening his first solo restaurant. It is named after his Maltipoo, Ralphie, and is located on Pimlico Road, a street long known for British interior design. The cooking is equally British and influenced by Booton’s Essex childhood.

The mood: Booton designed the room himself, layering deep oxblood with Colefax and Fowler fabrics, floors and tables of dark walnut, and lighting and mirrors from Jamb, the design house just down the road. Antiques unearthed at auctions sit alongside pieces commissioned from British artisans, while the London artist Ewan David Eason has made prints for the walls.

What to order: Crispy cod cheek scampi with warm tartare sauce, then pork and mushroom pie with charcuterie sauce. To finish, warm hazelnut and fudge sauce is poured over a vanilla soft-serve sandwich at the table. On Sundays, a Yorkshire pudding comes filled with leg of lamb ‘shepherd’s pie’. Dogs get their own menu, served in William Edwards bowls.
Why we love it: For a chef who can decorate a room as well as a plate.
Ralphie’s opens on 23 November and is available to book now. It is located at 87 Pimlico Road, London, SW1W 8PH, UK

Elliot Hashtroudi, executive chef at Camille, has named his second restaurant after his grandmother Betty Penhale, a skilled home cook whose family has deep roots in Smithfield – Hashtroudi’s great-grandmother worked at the market as a butcher. He has again teamed up with Camille’s owners, Ratnesh Bagdai, Tom Hill and Clare Lattin, but this time swapping bourgeois French cuisine for the regional food of Britain and Ireland. Animals are used nose to tail, and there’s a nod to the communities that have shaped what our islands eat, from Glasgow, which claims to be the home of tikka masala, to Windrush-era London.

The mood: The Grade II-listed building, once home to Club Gascon and a Lyons tea house, has kept its Victorian shopfront and original marble, now offset by walls and ceilings with a porcelain sheen, tables laid with linen, and rush-seated chairs by Rainer Daumiller.

What to order: Begin with stout-battered oysters with bone marrow and horseradish, before sharing a Saddleback pork chop with black pudding and trotter. Then there’s tea and biscuits, served in antique teapots and cups, and Ecclefechan tart.
Why we love it: For whole-animal cooking in the shadow of London’s historic meat market.
B. Penhale opens on 16 November and is available to book now. It is located at 57 West Smithfield, London, EC1A 9DS

Spencer Large, Charlie Sims and Honey Spencer, the team behind Sune in Hackney, are opening their first pub in one of six units set around the edge of Smithfield’s Victorian General Market, which reopens as the London Museum’s new home on 28 November. In earlier lives the space has been a tailor’s, a French bistro, a dairy and a café. Now the kitchen is run by Charlie Tayler, the chef who won Simon Rogan’s Aulis its Michelin star.

The mood: Designers Version 3 have furnished the ground floor like a grand old boozer, with lofty ceilings, ornate joinery, a light-filled double-height bar and snugs beneath the mezzanine. The first-floor dining room has panelled walls, leather seats, an open kitchen and windows along its length. Early next year Envoi, a chef’s table for 10 with its own entrance, will take over the mezzanine, while Shambles, an Arts and Crafts-style cocktail bar, opens in the attic.

What to order: At the bar, pork pie and piccalilli with a pint. Upstairs, the ‘vertical’ chicken is a set menu for two that uses the whole bird, from a snack and bread through to a starter, main and even pudding, and there’s a roast every Sunday.
Why we love it: For giving the London Museum the local it deserves.
The Poet opens on 30 November and is available to book now. It is located at House 5, London Museum, General Market, Farringdon Street, London, EC4A 4AZ

Pastry chef Anna Higham, whose crowdfunded Quince Bakery has drawn queues in Islington since February 2024, is opening a 20-cover café directly across the road. Clementine was fitted out with more than £30,000 from a second crowdfunding campaign, so there’s clearly a huge appetite for what Higham is offering. At Clementine that means breakfast, elevenses and lunch from Wednesday to Sunday, with head chef Marcus Westlake, formerly of Brawn, in the kitchen. There are rumours of evening opening once the place has bedded in.

The mood: Dan Wilson Studio, which designed Quince, has carried the bakery’s look over the street, pairing the simplicity of Shaker design with Arts and Crafts details. Inside, there’s oak, a tiled fireplace and slate worktops, with carpentry by Herb Palmer and walls in a colour developed specially with Atelier Ellis.

What to order: For breakfast, choose tattie scones with scrambled Cacklebean eggs, or Staffordshire oatcakes with Gothelney Farm bacon and Appleby’s Cheshire cheese. Quince’s brown butter buns arrive for elevenses, and lunch brings chicken and tarragon pie. To drink, there’s a bespoke Postcard Teas blend made for the café and seasonal cordials such as peach and fig leaf.
Why we love it: For being a neighbourhood café paid for by its neighbourhood.
Clementine opens on 10 October for walk-ins only. It is located at 190 New North Road, London N1 7AA, UK

Ben Butterworth, Joe Haynes and Tom Hurst, the trio behind Farringdon’s Cloth, have taken over Simpson’s Tavern, the chop house that opened in 1757 on Ball Court, just off Cornhill, and counted Dickens and Thackeray among its regulars. The Grade II-listed building had been empty since 2022 and has now had a year-long restoration. The ground floor is a pub, made up of the standing-only Amy’s Bar and the old grill room, with a restaurant across two dining rooms above.

The mood: The team have changed as little as possible. The fireplaces, bow windows and tiling all survive, as do the panelling and the old books and photographs. Upstairs, most diners sit in the high-backed wooden ‘boxes’, which still have the brass rails once used for top hats and coats, and a small bar seats eight at the counter.

What to order: Hurst’s modern British menu majors on chops and steaks for sharing, such as a Barnsley chop for two with anchovy and rosemary butter, alongside lemon sole with potted shrimp and sea beet, and a Cornhill sausage with beer mustard that comes from a 1940s book of Simpson’s recipes found during the works.
Why we love it: For a restoration that gives London’s oldest chop house back to the City instead of reinventing it.
Cloth Cornhill is located at 38 Cornhill, London EC3V 9DR, UK

Endo Kazutoshi, the third-generation sushi master who won a Michelin star within six months of opening Endo at the Rotunda, has a new home in a two-storey Chelsea townhouse after his White City restaurant was closed by fire in September 2025. Downstairs is Endo, a 10-seat omakase counter. Upstairs is Moga bar, which until December can only be accessed by Endo diners. Interiors take inspiration from Japan in the 1920s and early 1930s, when ancient traditions sat alongside an influx of Western modernity.

The mood: The space, formerly the Five Fields restaurant, has been reimagined by JVAD, the Barcelona- and Tokyo-based studio of Javier Villar Ruiz, who designed Endo at the Rotunda. The centrepiece is a counter of 200-year-old hinoki with a tsukedai, the raised serving ledge, lacquered in urushi. Upstairs, an undulating ceiling made from more than 3,000 masu saké cups hangs over a rough stone bar.

What to order: There is nothing to choose: the omakase (£305) is revealed only course by course. The fish is wild, caught off the British Isles by Endo’s own fishermen; the dashi uses katsuobushi from Kyoto and kombu from Kobe, the wasabi is grown for three years in the Shizuoka mountains, and the soy sauce is double-brewed by Kajita Shoten in Ehime.
Why we love it: For a triumphant return from London’s best Japanese chef.
Endo is located at 8-9 Blacklands Terrace, London SW3 2SP, UK

Turkish cooking in London has long meant the ocakbaşı grill houses of the north-east of the capital. Sertaç Dirik grew up in one – his father’s Mangal II, which he and his brother Ferhat reinvented into a National Restaurant Awards Top 50 fixture – and after a couple of years of collabs and residencies, he’s bringing his contemporary Anatolian to his first solo restaurant, in partnership with David Carter, the restaurateur behind Oma and Smokestak.

The mood: Box 9, Carter’s long-standing design partners, have taken a Victorian corner building in Soho and introduced handmade Anatolian touches such as banquettes upholstered in hand-stitched fabric dyed burnt terracotta. Elsewhere there are tables for two and seats at the counter facing the grill, while a wine room doubles as private dining.

What to order: Start with bread from the in-house bakery – a seeded sourdough pide grilled over the mangal and brushed with kaymak butter – ahead of Cornish scallops charred over coals on horoz beans braised in roe, and sharing plates of lamb and goat from the grill and wood oven.
Why we love it: For a long-awaited first solo restaurant from one of Britain’s hottest young chefs.
Kid is located at 55 Frith Street, London W1D 4SJ, UK

Elliott Kaye worked at kitchens that take themselves very seriously – Lyle’s, The French House, Leroy – before opening Norman’s in 2020 and finding a following for a modern take on a greasy spoon. Marrion’s is his first venture alone, and this time the mood board is American as much as British, inspired by the warmth and conviviality of The Odeon in New York.

The mood: Kaye is leading on the interiors of the cosy room himself, with vintage mirrors lining the walls, a counter looking into the kitchen through a hatch, and made-to-order wooden tables. The team, most of whom have worked with him before, are kitted out in the Danish label Another Aspect.

What to order: Nostalgic comfort food all the way: devilled crab rarebit, pork schnitzel Holstein, and a tuna melt with fries and malt vinegar mayo alongside. The house martini changes monthly and kicks off with the puritan, made with Yellow Chartreuse. Sunday brunch features boiled eggs with anchovy soldiers to nurse any hangovers.
Why we love it: For a wine list that starts at £5 a glass and £30 a bottle.
Marrion’s is located at 177 Morning Lane, London E9 6LH, UK

The chefs behind two of London’s most talked-about recent residencies – Yuji Shimokawa Kelly of Urchin and Robin Kosuge of Robin’s Ramen – have been brought under one roof at this newcomer on the Kensington side of Notting Hill Gate. Both chefs came up through the Notting Hill group behind Dorian, Eel Sushi and Supermarket of Dreams, and here they take joint charge of a three-storey townhouse.

The mood: Jack Architecture & Design has restored a narrow listed Victorian building, entered beneath a custom noren. Pale timber runs across the walls, cabinetry and ceilings, with parquet flooring, satin-finished brass and hand-glazed tiles carried up all three floors. The ground floor is all open-kitchen clatter; the first floor is calmer and more restauranty.

What to order: Downstairs is where to come for a quick bowl of lobster ramen with seafood paitan and komatsuna; upstairs, take your time over quail tempura with apricot purée, and steamed turbot in red vinegar sauce.
Why we love it: For showing there’s more to Japanese food than sushi and sashimi.
Nakimushi is located at 7 Kensington Mall, London W8 4EB, UK

London diners have become used to the idea of a sushi-based omakase menu; now this Fitzrovia import – the first European outpost of Ushio Haruyoshi Bettei in Fukuoka – is introducing the capital to multi-course menus of wagyu beef. Put aside any preconceptions of fatty meat, however: the restaurant specialises in akami (lean) wagyu rather than heavy marbling.

The mood: The interiors of wood, stone and plaster are modelled on the Fukuoka original, with 27 seats spread across an eating counter and conventional tables, though wherever you sit, there is a built-in grill within easy reach. Tableware and ceramics have been sourced from Kyushu and mix Arita porcelain with hand-built Karatsu stoneware by artist Taeko Kajihara.

What to order: ‘Yakiniku’ means ‘grilled meat’ in Japanese; choose between a £95 omakase or a £55 six-piece tasting selection offering the likes of the signature wagyu sirloin seared with sukiyaki marinade, and a Fukuoka-style wagyu curry of slow-cooked beef tendon.
Why we love it: For introducing a new style of Japanese dining to London, with 12.30 am closing at the weekend (the Northern Line night tube is round the corner at Goodge Street).
Wagyu Yakiniku Ushio is located at 12 Charlotte Street, London W1T 2LU, United Kingdom
Read our full restaurant review of Wagyu Yakiniku Ushio

Chef Gabriel Waterhouse made a name for himself with the Water House Project, a communal seating fine-dining experience which closed in June after five years in Bethnal Green. This follow-up, run by Waterhouse and his wife Patricia Wakaimba, sees Waterhouse cooking food inspired by his Northumbrian background in a 24-cover dining room in a former potter’s studio on one of east London’s most photogenic streets; a wine bar will open within the Victorian warehouse in September.

The mood: Waterhouse has designed the restaurant with Rees Architects, who reworked the space so the different areas flow into one another, without losing the building’s original features – among them existing fireplaces and Crittall windows. Painted brick, British timber and stone nod to rural craftsmanship, with shelving holding the kitchen’s own preserves and ceramics.

What to order: A single seasonal tasting menu built around Waterhouse’s own courtyard garden and trusted producers. Expect dishes drawing on Lindisfarne oysters, Craster kippers and hand-dived scallops, incorporating house-made vinegars, kombuchas and misos.
Why we love it: For the pairing of Waterhouse’s Northumbrian roots on the plate with the raw, reworked warehouse setting around it.
Waterhouse is located at 7a Ezra Street, London E2 7RH, United Kingdom

It’s all going on Sloane Square: hot on the heels of Martino’s in the old Hugo Boss site, Clare Smyth’s Corenucopia round the corner on Holbein Place and a new pub from the Walmer Castle team opening in autumn comes this first international outpost of La Nouvelle Garde. The brasserie group has 10 restaurants in its native France, including five in Paris and another five stretching from Lille to Marseille. Brasserie Olivia will be open for everything from breakfast to post-theatre nightcaps. With Colbert already a firm favourite next to the Royal Court, might it be croissants at dawn in Chelsea?

The mood: The art-de-vivre inspiration might take in everything from the boulevards of Paris to the grand hotels of the Côte d’Azur, but design duties at Nouvelle Garde fall to London-based B3 Designers. Here they’ve transformed the old David Mellor cutlery boutique with a pavement terrace and a dining room where a skylit ceiling illuminates an interior of mosaic floors, checkerboard tiles and vintage advertising posters.

What to order: a petit-déjeuner of viennoiserie and crêpes ahead of an all-day menu of soupe à l’oignon, pâté en croûte, oysters shucked to order and, if the Parisian restaurants are anything to go by, a perfect rendition of a Toulouse cassoulet.
Why we love it: For bringing everyone’s favourite bistro dishes across the Channel with a vibe that feels classic, not clichéd.
Brasserie Olivia is located at 1 Sloane Square, London SW1W 8EE, United Kingdom
Read our full restaurant review of Brasserie Olivia

Man Hon Luk – founder of Vinyl Pimp, the second-hand record shop that became a DJ mecca – discovered Texas barbecue on a poker trip to Austin in 2021, trained under pitmaster John Bates at Michelin-starred InterStellar BBQ and returned to London to launch a series of pop-ups that became a two-year residency at All My Friends. The unconventional career path has led to this: a permanent 80-cover canal-side restaurant and music venue above Crate Brewery, bankrolled in part by a crowdfunder that raised £36,000 (six grand over the £30,000 target). Clearly, there’s no shortage of fans out there for Hon’s Chinese-influenced Texan barbecue.

The mood: Hon designed the space himself, with red as the primary colour layered over what remained of the zero-waste Silo restaurant that previously occupied the site. Custom furniture, from pinwheel-patterned tables to bar stools, is the work of Hun’s friend, Chinese designer Mo Tong, while the hand-built sound system comes courtesy of Noise Control Audio.

What to order: Snacks and small plates such as smoked tea egg with candied walnut to start, then the star attraction of meats smoked low and slow for 12 hours: short ribs with Sichuan peppercorn sauce, Xi’an-style lamb shoulder, or Ibérico pork ribs. Drinks are overseen by Oliver Dibben, sommelier at Brat.
Why we love it: For uniting two of the world’s greatest meat-cooking traditions on one delicious plate.
Hon’s BBQ is located at Unit 7, the White Building, Queen’s Yard, London E9 5EN, United Kingdom
Read our full restaurant review of Hon’s BBQ

This Italian seafood specialist began life on Milan’s Via Savona in 2007 before expanding to two further sites in Italy’s fashion and design capital, then opening outposts in the favoured grazing spots of the international jet-set: the Cheval Blanc Paris; Porto Cervo on Sardinia and Paraggi Bay on the Italian Riviera; a mountaintop in St Moritz. Now it’s arrived at The OWO, the former Old War Office reborn as a Raffles hotel. Needless to say, one should dress up as if for Milan Fashion Week when dining here.

The mood: Late Italian architect Carlo Samarati oversaw the look of the Milan and Paraggi Langosterias and brought Italian brio to the imperial surrounds of the OWO before his passing: hand-painted and hand-embroidered silk wall coverings sit alongside Venini lamps, Verde Alpi marble floors, custom furniture by Molteni and bespoke seating by Medea.

What to order: Kick off with something from the raw bar – perhaps a carpaccio di tonno rosso – before updated Italian classics from the open kitchen: sea bass paccheri, or a ‘chateaubriand’ of black grouper. Still hungry? There’s tiramisu for dolce.
Why we love it: Langosteria’s first UK opening brings the wow factor to The OWO.
Langosteria is located at The OWO, 57 Whitehall, London SW1A 2BX, United Kingdom
Read our full restaurant review of Langosteria

Camilla Meshiea and Ryan Sheehan’s Counter 71 earned a loyal following in Hoxton for its intimate format. Now the pair are reimagining the address as Appalachia, drawing on the culinary traditions of America’s eastern mountain range and bringing in Ali Borer, formerly of Smoking Goat, to lead the kitchen.

The mood: The space has been refreshed rather than rebuilt, its close-set counter retained, and the room warmed with new seating and updated colourings. In the basement, Lowcountry bar offers a contemporary homage to the American South.
What to order: Borer’s cooking brings together Appalachian heritage and fire-led, Thai-influenced technique: BBQ whole quail with blue cheese slaw, say, and a not-to-be-missed curried crab omelette.
Why we love it: For keeping what worked about Counter 71 and knowing the new flavours to introduce.
Appalachia is located at 71 Nile Street, London N1 7RD, United Kingdom
Read our full restaurant review of Appalachia

Jody Williams’s Manhattan hospitality empire includes not only Buvette in the West Village but Via Carota, I Sodi, The Commerce Inn and Bar Pisellino nearby. Buvette is what the James Beard Award-winning chef dubs a ‘gastrothèque’, a place equally devoted to food and drink, available all day. After a Notting Hill iteration closed in 2024, Williams is relaunching the concept in a former St John Bakery site in Covent Garden.

The mood: Williams has shaped the space herself along classic French lines: exposed brick, a vintage tin ceiling, warm wood and a long marble bar around which 80 covers are arranged on convivially close-set tables.

What to order: The menu moves through the day with confident simplicity: steamed eggs with smoked salmon and crème fraîche at breakfast, before the all-day menu brings coq au vin with thin frîtes or a properly made cassoulet for lunch, dinner and everything in-between.
Why we love it: For giving one of New York’s most influential bistros – and one of its best-loved chefs – a second bite of London.
Buvette is located at 2 Neal’s Yard, London WC2H 9DP, United Kingdom
Read our full restaurant review of Buvette

Nick Molyviatis spent his career in some of London’s most respected kitchens, including Kiln and Oma, before becoming co-owner of Singburi. For Zylia, he has teamed up with restaurateur Barry Karacostas, whose Cypriot heritage informs the menu alongside Molyviatis’s Athenian upbringing. The result is a Greek-Cypriot taverna shaped by childhood memory and professional experience.

The mood: Red Deer’s design of the 50-cover space – a former Victorian boot-lace factory in Covent Garden – blends wicker chairs and traditional Cypriot tiles with stainless steel tables and green leather booths.

What to order: Begin with handmade pitta and mezze – tirokafteri of smashed feta with roasted green chilli, grilled prawn saganaki with spiced tomato sauce – before moving to the charcoal grill for lamb kleftiko, slow-roasted with wine, garlic and bay.
Why we love it: For making the case that Greek-Cypriot cooking – a classic taste of north London – deserves a permanent home in the West End.
Zylia is located at 6 Bedford Street, London WC2E 9HZ, United Kingdom
Read our full restaurant review of Zylia

Aktar Islam is one of British-Indian cooking’s most illustrious names: his Birmingham flagship Opheem holds two Michelin stars, making it one of only two Indian restaurants in the UK to have achieved the distinction. For his London debut, Islam turns to Awadhi cuisine – the refined, courtly cooking of Lucknow, a city last year recognised by UNESCO as a Creative City of Gastronomy – and brings it to a three-floor listed building in Borough.

The mood: Designer Polina Sychova has worked with the Victorian bones of the building, layering a neutral colour palette, warm upholstery and bespoke joinery across the two dining floors, while upstairs the mood loosens with a lounge bar under a hand-painted ceiling.

What to order: Begin with nashta – street-style snacks such as soft egg yolk with spiced venison – before moving to the slow-cooked, dough-sealed dum dishes that are the heart of Awadhi cooking: smoked Wiltshire lamb shoulder baked in a lamb-fat crust, or whole turbot slow-cooked in spiced ghee with brown shrimp.
Why we love it: For giving one of India’s great culinary traditions its most high-profile London stage.
Oudh 1722 is located at 66 Union Street, London SE1 1TD, United Kingdom
Read our full restaurant review of Oudh 1772

When The Sea, The Sea opened in 2019, it quickly became one of Chelsea’s most cherished addresses – a seafood bar and fishmongers supplying not just locals but some of London’s most respected restaurants, among them Ikoyi and Kol. This May, founder Alex Hunter expands the operation with a bistro and enlarged fish shop directly across Pavilion Road, bringing a 40-cover dining room and a 28-seat terrace to one of the city’s most appealing traffic-free streets.

The mood: Downstairs, where the shop occupies the ground floor, the mood is industrial – stainless steel, dry-ageing cabinets and bespoke oak cabinetry frame an abundance of produce. The upstairs bistro is softer – skylights in a pitched roof, a small balcony flooding the room with natural light – while artworks by Patrick Caulfield and Alexander Massouras line the walls.

What to order: Fresh-as-a-daisy seafood from the fishmongers downstairs, sourced directly from small boats off the coasts of Cornwall, Devon and the west of Scotland. Start at the raw bar with pickled Fowey mussels with sunsweet melon and lovage, ahead of grilled half Cornish lobster with vin jaune sabayon.
Why we love it: For giving one of London’s best fish shops the dining room it always deserved.
The Sea, The Sea is located at 243 Pavilion Road, London SW1X 0AW, United Kingdom
Read our full restaurant review of The Sea, The Sea

Jackson Boxer has form when it comes to opening beloved local restaurants: Brunswick House has been going strong in Vauxhall since 2010, while last year Dove made Boxer’s Notting Hill restaurant Orasay more approachably laid back. For his latest venture, the chef heads to Clerkenwell with Vesper, named for the Roman word for the planet Venus as it appears at sunset: the time to enjoy one of the restaurant’s bracingly cold cocktails.

The mood: Designer Jermaine Gallacher has adapted a double-fronted corner space with timber-framed floor-to-ceiling windows, a bar by the entrance and a candlelit dining room beyond. A terrace of bistro tables occupies the pavement on warmer evenings.

What to order: The menu moves from comfort-food small plates – croquette Arnold Bennett with tarragon mayonnaise, sole fritters with curry sauce – to more substantial dishes such as glazed lamb shoulder with merguez and devilled kidney.
Why we love it: For proving, once again, that Boxer is one of London’s most reliably brilliant restaurateurs.
Vesper is located at 8-10 Exmouth Market, London EC1R 4QA, United Kingdom
Read our full restaurant review of Vesper

This new London Fields dining room has impeccable neighbourhood credentials: chef Mike Bagnall is the brains behind the ongoing Elm residency, currently at the Montpelier pub in Peckham, while his co-owner and general manager Dylan Walters is formerly of listening bar Bambi. So far, so cool London cliché, but the pair are bringing something new to the capital, with an emphasis on the cooking of the Italian region of Abruzzo.

The mood: Bagnall and Walters have designed and renovated the space themselves and hung it with artwork by Leevar Spies. Upstairs is a dinky bistro-like room centred on a charcoal grill and with a standing counter for walk-ins; downstairs is a bar to linger in afterwards.

What to order: When Bagnall lived in Abruzzo, he developed a taste for arrosticini, the region’s speciality of flame-grilled meat skewers. Expect cull yaw, liver and wild boar, washed down with Abruzzese grapes such as Montepulciano.
Why we love it: For bringing the simplicity of central Italian food and drink to a corner of east London that knows exactly how to receive it.
Auguste is located at 373 Mentmore Terrace, London, E8 3DQ, United Kingdom
Read our full restaurant review of Auguste

Olympia isn’t just a rarely used station on the District line: the Victorian venue has played host to everything from Vivienne Westwood’s first catwalk show to gigs from Pink Floyd and Jimi Hendrix. As part of a £1.3b revamp, veteran restaurateur Des Gunewardena (the co-founder and former CEO of D&D London) has launched Idalia restaurant, alongside events and live music spaces.

items.title: The Complete Works of Le Chateaubriand (2006–2026)
items.description: This is the story of Le Chateaubriand, the Paris bistro that broke every rule fine dining had. In 2006, Inaki Aizpitarte and Frédéric Peneau took over a humble, century-old bistro in Paris’ 11th arrondissement. Untucked shirts, stubble, blaring music, a photoc
paragraphs: This is the story of Le Chateaubriand, the Paris bistro that broke every rule fine dining had. In 2006, Inaki Aizpitarte and Frédéric Peneau took over a humble, century-old bistro in Paris’ 11th arrondissement. Untucked shirts, stubble, blaring music, a photocopied piece of paper as a menu: punk star chef Inaki and his disciples triggered a tsunami of gastronomic insurrection, launching ‘bistronomy’ and its devious subculture. Le Chateaubriand, originally published in French in 2024 and now translated into English by Florence Beretta and Christine Muhlke, is a memorialisation of their labyrinthine quest for adventure, experimentation, and a really good time.

Inside, a chorus of your favourite chefs’ favourite chefs, critics, regulars, and fundamental players document the uncanny dishes, drunk escapades, Michelin stars, and one-star reviews of a restaurant so notorious the conformists loosened their buttons for it.

As Inaki bows out, two decades later, he leaves behind a mythical record of an indisputable marathon to achieve something unheard of in the 2000s kitchen: freedom. At Le Chateaubriand, the customer is not always right.

Chef Inaki Aizpitarte, the son of Basque immigrants, grew up in Besançon and Bordeaux in the south of France. In 1999, at the age of 27, he travelled to Tel Aviv where he began washing dishes in a restaurant kitchen and discovered his passion for cooking. He moved to Paris in the early 2000s, where he worked at various establishments across the city, including Le Petit Marguery, La Fourchette des Anges, Ishtar Café, Le Café des Délices, La Famille in Montmartre, and Le Baratin. He then helped launch the restaurant at the MAC VAL contemporary art museum in Vitry-sur-Seine.

In 2006, he opened Le Chateaubriand at 129 Avenue Parmentier. His second venture, Le Dauphin, opened in 2010, two doors down from Le Chateaubriand. More recently, he opened Petit Grill Basque, this time in Saint-Jean-de-Luz, in the French Basque Country. Over the years, Aizpitarte has become widely regarded as the ‘godfather of bistronomy’, helping to redefine the Parisian dining scene through his distinctive, informal approach to fine dining.

items.title: Twenty-One Conversations with Architects by Arquitectura-G
items.description: Twenty-One Conversations with Architects by Arquitectura-G has been added to your shopping bag
paragraphs: Twenty-One Conversations with Architects by Arquitectura-G has been added to your shopping bag

Twenty-One Conversations with Architects brings together more than a decade and a half’s worth of interviews conducted by Barcelona-based architecture firm Arquitectura-G, published in Apartamento magazine since its very first issue in 2008. Expansive, technical, submerged, the book threads together some of architecture’s most singular minds, crossing decades, archives, disciplines, and countries, and placing multiple generations of architects side by side in a single volume. What started as a takeover of the magazine’s architecture section has now become something else entirely: a portrait of the studio itself, their own obsessions surfacing across every conversation—questions of scale, ambiguity, hedonism, bathrooms, dances, the house as a laboratory. As they open these interviews to the anthology, the architects unfold a series of choices in houses and homes that are deeply personal to those who conceived them, united by their fundamental questioning of universal needs answered by universal forms. What ties these houses together is something beyond architecture—less about having built them, and more about having gone on living inside the questions they raised. Twenty-one conversations later, Arquitectura-G draws each architect into a new one—curated together, and compiled by Moisés Puente, they are now asked to speak to each other across time.

Arquitectura-G is a Barcelona-based architecture studio founded in 2006 by Jonathan Arnabat, Jordi Ayala-Bril, Igor Urdampilleta, and Aitor Fuentes. Their practice spans ephemeral installations, residential projects, retail, and urban planning, with work published widely in international media. In 2015 they received the prestigious 2015 Mies Van der Rohe Award for Emerging Architects. They also teach, returning to the school where they first met. Since 2008 they have edited the architecture section of Apartamento magazine, a collaboration that also traces the development of their critical thinking.
