items.title: ‘I Am a Bad Roommate’
items.description: Chances are high that you’ve had a terrible roommate. Is there a more universal experience in the world? For most of us, it happens in college. It’s the first time we’ve ever lived on our own, and people don’t know how to act. Next thing you know, the girl you
items.author: Brooke LaMantia
paragraphs: Chances are high that you’ve had a terrible roommate. Is there a more universal experience in the world? For most of us, it happens in college. It’s the first time we’ve ever lived on our own, and people don’t know how to act. Next thing you know, the girl you lovingly referred to as “roomie” on week one is eating every meal from her bed, leaving clumps of her hair in the shower, and watching Netflix without headphones in the middle of the night.

Even if you skip the whole college-dorm experience, few of us venture into adulthood without a roommate or two. Don’t get me wrong: Roommates can make your life magical (I’m rewatching Jersey Shore and have felt touched by their ritual of a Sunday family dinner, despite the dysfunction in the house), but they can also make you want to never return home. We’ve seen the TikToks and tweets, and we all have a roommate horror story that we keep in our back pockets to complain about forever at parties. But what about the bad roommates themselves? Do they know their crimes? Do they feel remorse, or do they have a justification for their behavior?

Surprisingly, bad roommates generally know they suck. Most even feel bad about it. After all, people are most likely to live with a roommate when they’re young, before their frontal lobes have fully developed, and who isn’t embarrassed of something they did before they turned 25?
Here’s how your worst roommates justified their loud, disgusting, passive-aggressive, and aggressive-aggressive crimes of communal living, in their own words.

I’ll preface this by saying I was the bad roommate in this situation, but I don’t actually feel too bad about it. I had the same roommate for three years in college, as we’d become really close friends and hung out in the same social circles. At the end of our second year, she broke up with her boyfriend and asked me to check up on him over the summer to make sure he was handling it okay.

He and I ended up talking online all summer, and a few weeks into the next semester, we started hooking up in secret, as my roommate had explicitly told me she didn’t want me dating him. For weeks, I made excuses about studying at the library or rehearsing late at the theater, all while sneaking around with her ex. We were finally discovered when a mutual acquaintance spotted us making out late at night on a park bench. Word of our secret started spreading in our friend group, so we eventually came clean to my roommate. Justifiably, she was livid that I had lied to her, and it made for a pretty uncomfortable living situation for the rest of the term.

The next semester, I arranged to study abroad to distance myself from the situation, but she ended up studying in the same city as me. We worked to repair our relationship a bit, but we never lived together again. After college, we both moved to the same city for work and hung out sometimes, so I thought she’d finally forgiven me. But years later, after I sent her an invitation to my wedding, she ghosted me. I’ve been happily married to her ex-boyfriend for 12 years now and I haven’t heard a thing from her since, so I think she never actually forgave me. — M
I committed a cupcake massacre …

Before we get into it, I have to emphasize: This was in college. I was a baby. My frontal lobe had not yet fully developed. Anyway, I lived in my sorority house my junior year, where I roomed with one of my besties. We both had “roles” in the sorority. I honestly don’t remember what they were, but that spring semester she was in charge of organizing and arranging for a week of gifts that the graduating seniors would get delivered in secret from their littles. Unfortunately, it was also the week of the annual Spring Fling concert on campus, which was an excuse to get blackout drunk during the day while T.I. performed onstage. My roomie, the responsible and more sober one, got home before me to finish the next day’s gifts: homemade (by her) heart-shaped chocolate cupcakes.

A few hours later, I got home — wearing only one flip-flop, so you know where this is going. I woke up the next morning (in time for my intensive French class, thank you very much) with a vague memory of her shrieking “[Redacted], what did you do?!” and the feeling that I’d destroyed something. When I went downstairs and saw that the next-next day’s gifts, messages in a glass bottle, were still intact, I figured it was all a dream. Then I went into the kitchen, where I saw what can only be described as a massacre. I’d eaten some cupcakes, smushed and poked my finger through others, and threw some in the sink alongside dirty dishes just for the hell of it. Did I harbor some secret resentment against her or the senior girls or Betty Crocker? Who’s to say?

Luckily, my French class was really early, so I was up before any of the deliveries were supposed to happen and I had time to buy over a dozen slices of cake at the bakery down the street to make up for it. Then I spooned her, waking her up, and begged for forgiveness. I got her an extra slice, too. We haven’t spoken since graduation. — J

I’ve lived alone for five years for the simple fact that I am a bad roommate. Other people’s noises piss me off! I take everything in my home personally, probably because I’m a Taurus moon. But the time I was the worst roommate, a moment that still haunts me, was in college. I lived in an apartment with four other girls, one of whom I learned voted for Trump during the 2016 election. Our friendship immediately soured, and everything she did infuriated me.

One day, I came home from class and saw my laundry askew on the floor of my bedroom. I went to this roommate’s room to ask her if she did that. She said yes, noting the fact that I had left my clean laundry in the dryer for days. I reacted in an insane way by dumping her laundry basket of clothes onto the ground, opening her drawers and putting her clean folded clothes on the ground too. All while asking, “How does this make you feel? To have your clean clothes on the dirty ground?” — T
I weaponized therapy talk …

When I moved into a dorm during my freshman year of college, I didn’t know I had anxiety, let alone that I could treat it with medication. That’s not an excuse for what transpired, obviously, but it was probably a contributing factor. Both my roommate and I were messy to begin with, and in only a few weeks, our living space became alarmingly disorganized. We were stressed, neither of us sleeping or eating well. I made passive-aggressive comments about her clothes and folders and dirty paper plates strung across the floor, even as I dumped my laundry and books in whatever clean square inch I could find.

When she started exhibiting clear signs of burnout and depression, I tried to “encourage” her by listing examples of all the things that made me feel motivated and passionate. Basically, I sat down with her and tried to list out things we were both “passionate about,” and mine was like, “Writing! Books! Music!,” and when I asked for hers, she gave me, like, two things (which I genuinely don’t remember) because she was pissed I was asking her to do this activity that was so obviously like, “Wow, look at how passionate I am, why aren’t you as passionate as I am?” Rightfully, this pissed her off.

A turning point came when we stayed up really late together in the dorm one night, and I decided I finally wanted to go to bed. She kept the lights on and continued working on her laptop. I shifted around under my sheets, hoping she’d catch the hint to turn them off. Why didn’t I just turn them off myself? I honestly don’t remember. But I ended up sleeping in another friend’s room that night after I’d angrily stormed out. We gave each other the silent treatment for a bit, and I temporarily moved out. I still feel ashamed about how I acted back then; I wish I would have been there for her the way she needed me to be. There was so much I didn’t understand about mental health back then — not hers, and certainly not my own.

But thankfully, this story has a happy ending: My roommate and I spent some time apart, and when we started hanging out again a few months later, we realized how much we’d grown just in that brief time. I apologized. We apologized, and we forgave each other. We laugh about it now. She’s one of my best friends to this day. — L
I said the guy I just had sex with was gay …

I got sober halfway through my junior year of college, which is to say that I needed to get sober halfway through my junior year of college. At the peak of my active alcoholism, I was, among many other things, a god-awful roommate. It is something I felt an incredible amount of shame around for a very long time — and something that in the past 8.5 years, I have been able to make amends for (except for an outstanding conversation I am realizing right this second I still owe to my 2016 summer-sublet roommate).

Some of my greatest hits were: giving myself alcohol poisoning and launching on a cycle of near-constant vomiting for 12 to 14 hours, bringing hookups back to shared rooms (one time telling my roommate that, don’t worry, the half-naked man in my bed who I very obviously had sex with was actually a platonic gay friend). There were mean texts and unsanitary conditions (my mom found a used condom under my bed when she came to visit) and the occasional pizza slices left under couches. My brother visited once and I abandoned him to spend the night somewhere else, leaving my roommate to shepherd him back. I am beyond grateful I do not have to live that way anymore (and that others don’t have to live with that version of me anymore). — E
I tried to initiate a threesome (and smoked indoors) …

I moved to New York at 17 and lived with roommates until I was 28, so here’s just a tiny list of my crimes: I left my discarded fake-eyelash strips everywhere. They gathered in dusty corners, their little black fibers resembling the hairy forms of threatening spiders. This terrified each and every one of one long-term roommate’s new girlfriends — surprise, girls! A different roommate walked around shirtless, saying, “Why do you always go for guys who don’t work out?” So I stole his hand mixer, but he deserved it.

In another long-ago arrangement, a live-in friend and I attempted an acid-fueled threesome with our summer-long subletter. Poor Brian. In every one of these cases, I smoked inside … a lot. I was lovely to live with in other ways. Also, I negotiated the rent by having light phone sex with one landlord, and who else was going to take that for the team? I’m well behaved now — practically domesticated! — thanks to others’ graciousness and understanding along my merry way. — A

When I was in my early 20s, I had a roommate who worked at Beacon’s Closet, and she had a giant and ever-changing wardrobe because she had access to all the clothes, all the time. I would often borrow her clothes without asking. One memorable item was a tiered Anna Sui black lace skirt that I definitely wore in front of her. I felt justified to do this because she had SO MANY CLOTHES and they were changing all the time, and I thought she wouldn’t even notice.

This would have been marginally okay if we were friends, though actually not even. However, we were not friends. She totally knew about it but was too scared of me to ever complain. We were friendly at the outset of the roommate relationship, but that quickly cooled into mutual avoidance/gritting our teeth through coexisting. We never had a confrontation about it. Not that this justified my absolutely abhorrent behavior, but she refused to contribute to household expenses and bought her own toilet paper and took it to the bathroom with her. — EG

items.title: How to Have Sex When You Also Have Roommates
items.description: This article first ran in The Cut’s Personals newsletter, which features new sex and love stories — and date-wanted ads from interesting single people — every week. Sign up to receive the latest issue in your inbox.
items.author: Emily Leibert
paragraphs: This article first ran in The Cut’s Personals newsletter, which features new sex and love stories — and date-wanted ads from interesting single people — every week. Sign up to receive the latest issue in your inbox.

Imagine for a moment that, by the grace of Venus, you’ve reached the end of a successful date and you’re ready to see if the connection carries into the bedroom. So begin the negotiations: Your place or mine? However, you have roommates, and they are, to your abject horror, likely home and wide awake.

That’s not so hard to imagine for a lot of us. Rent is expensive, and moving into a solo apartment where one can dazzle with postcoital martinis from the bar cart might be out of reach right now. What do you do when you’re trying to do it despite the fact that your housemate who enjoys cat-forward TikToks at full volume won’t vacate the couch? Whether you’re in a relationship or bringing home a stray from the bar, we’ve gathered some advice about how to have good sex without becoming the nightmare roommate. Enjoy!

There’s nothing worse than finding Magnum wrappers (or their used contents) in a communal trash can, but leaving no trace extends to more than sex-related garbage. Ask Maria, a 25-year-old living in Lisbon who isn’t fond of her roommate (Maria finds her fussy and difficult to talk to and says she’s “always, always at home watching the same two shows”).

Maria noticed a jagged crack in their bathtub a few months ago. When Maria asked about it, her roommate seemed nervous but said she had no idea what happened. Hm! A few weeks later, Maria caught up with a friend who had recently crashed on their couch. He had apparently run into the roommate on the street, and for some reason, she “decided to describe every place she’s had sex in this house to him,” Maria said. The roommate admitted to having sex with a partner in the tub, and its acrylic sealant “ripped” under the strain. “For a month and a half, I couldn’t shower in my bathroom,” said Maria. Don’t be like Maria’s roommate. If you break something, fix it. Your housemates will respect the honesty.

It can be awkward to talk about sex with your partner, let alone with a platonic roommate. But there are benefits to giving your housemate a heads-up about hookups — like, say, avoiding a situation where you don’t hear your roommate knocking and they wind up catching you naked in the middle of performing oral.

Ruby Rare, a writer and intimacy expert for the dating app Feeld, says they are always “banging on about open and honest communication” and thus have a solution. They suggest that you don’t have to spell out the NC-17 details ahead of time — instead, a subtler approach works well. You can play it coy, like “Hey, just letting you know [partner] and I are retreating to the bedroom for some alone time.”

If you’re friends with your roommate, this might be easier — and could be especially important if you have the kind of open-door policy where you’re always barging in to hang out or borrow clothes. “My roommate and I waltzed into each other’s rooms whenever,” says Lauren, a 24-year-old living in Raleigh in a “tiny, tiny” apartment with friends. “One time, I walked in on one of my roommates and her then-boyfriend nude, mid-foreplay. He screamed ‘Get out!’ repeatedly, and I ran out in horror.”

Via trial and error and a few conversations, Lauren and her roommates agreed on some house rules: If a guy is coming over, send a warning text. If a door is shut, knock. No sex in common areas, no exceptions. “If a boyfriend is over, we have to be there, too, or at least keep him in our room,” she said. “I don’t want to wake up or get home from work and find some man sitting on my couch.”

Even if you can’t address it outright, being a good listener will get you far in all aspects of life and particularly in the quest to fuck. Paying attention to your roommates’ calendars and general whereabouts works both ways: You’ll be a more engaged, caring friend … and surreptitiously get intel to inform your hookup schedule. When they mention upcoming work trips and dinner dates, see if you can time any hot encounters to align with their out-of-the-house obligations. Do they have a Democratic Socialists of America meeting to attend Thursday night? Use that time too.

The most common roommate sex gripes are noise-related. While mutual respect is enough of a motivator for some to keep it down, others might need further seducing. Try creating tension by playing the silent game, placing a consensual hand over your partner’s mouth, or whispering dirty talk. Being called “such a good girl” for staying quiet equals real-life audio erotica.

If you really can’t keep your mouth shut (and your partner can’t shut it for you), there are work-arounds. Rosa, a 20-something in Brooklyn, said that at her last apartment, the laundry machine was just outside her room. She timed her hookups to when she was washing clothes to mask her moans. Chelsea, a 25-year-old in Manhattan, has two roommates. She leans on a common-sense approach: If someone’s home, muffle your gasps with a pillow. If the headboard creaks, secure it to the wall. If that’s not an option, hook up on the floor. If all else fails, Rare recommends minimizing movement by prioritizing oral, fingering, or hand jobs with only one person receiving at a time. “That’s quieter than anything penetrative, where two bodies are colliding,” Rare said.

Finally, to the more kink-inclined among us: If your roommate is home, your self-installed sex swing can wait. “I want people to have fun and let go in the moment, but we have a responsibility to not overtly impose our sexuality on others. If you’re in close proximity to others, it’s probably not the time to get the flogger or cane out,” Rare said. That doesn’t mean you have to totally sacrifice freaky sex. “You can lean into pain in quieter ways, like biting, pinching, or scratching,” they said. Okay, hot!
Employ a strict “no losers” policy.

Try as you might to keep your visitor out of sight, sometimes your roommates will run into your hookup anyway, e.g., fishing the Brita out of the fridge at dawn. Bring only the good ones home so any encounters are polite.

Lauren knows what it’s like when a loser makes it into the inner sanctum. Once, when she was living with four other girls, one brought a guy over. It wasn’t hard to clock him as bad news when he immediately gave a long, politically charged lecture to Lauren and the rest of the girls. He called one a “commie” because she was voting for Joe Biden, then played beer pong on their kitchen island by himself for two hours before disappearing into her roommate’s bedroom.

Around 3 a.m., Lauren heard the couple having sex in the next room — as in he repeatedly yelled “Oh yeah!” and banged around. She requested they keep it down. The suitor yelled at Lauren to “shut the fuck up” while slamming his fist against the wall. Later, the roommates discovered via Instagram that he kept a cardboard cutout of Donald Trump in his living room. Lauren’s roommate was on probation from sleepovers for a long time. They’re all still friends, though they’re haunted by this encounter over six years later.

And for the enthusiastic supporters and practitioners of first-date sex and one-night stands among us: Josh, the 24-year-old fintech intern from Tinder whom you never plan to see again, doesn’t need to sleep over. You can insist on a no-sleepover rule or blame it on one of the classics: an early Pilates class, an 8 a.m. meeting, or an ob-gyn appointment. Try this template to kick someone out with grace: “I had such a lovely time with you, but I need to wake up early for this presentation I’m giving — do you need any help figuring out how to get home?”
Be a stellar person to live with in every other respect, and you’ll get away with more.

Act like your roommates are the people to impress rather than your sexual partner. If the apartment is sparkling and you’ve taken on extra chores that week, your roommates will be more inclined to be chill if they hear something they shouldn’t have. Consider the alternative: When Maria, the 25-year-old in Lisbon, found out about the broken bathtub, she said, “If she was my friend, this would probably have been really funny. In this context, it’s annoying as hell.”

Chelsea, the 25-year-old in Manhattan, is nonconfrontational and prefers saving face over communicating directly with her roommates about sex, so she does whatever she can to keep the peace more generally — including by being understanding toward her roommate about her hookups. “Is dealing with this an inevitability if you’re not completely chaste and you live in tight quarters with people?” Probably, but trying to be a decent person outside of what you’re doing in bed will go a long way in terms of how irritating it is.
If all else fails: Just have sex with your roommate.
Angela is in her mid-30s but was once a grad student having trouble affording rent. She and a friend from her program had only known each other for six months but decided to move in together anyway.

Though they pretended otherwise, there was immediately a vibe. “There are all the obvious reasons that sleeping with your roommate can be a bad idea,” Angela said. “If a feeling emerges, there are rational reasons to suppress it.” For five years, they did … until they went to a party, took molly, and made out. Even though Angela was seeing three guys at the time, her roommate declared that if they had feelings for each other, they shouldn’t hold back.

At the time, Angela and her roommate had started watching the lesbian TV touchstone The L Word together. “It’s just too on the nose,” Angela laughs. “We’re watching The L Word in her bed. We started the series as friends, and when it ended, we were sleeping together.” Suddenly, they had a guest bedroom. “Moving into her room solved every issue in my life,” Angela said. “It solved the real-estate question. It solved my tension with my roommate. And it solved the love question too.” A year and a half ago, Angela and her roommate got married. While she can’t fully recommend fucking your roommate, it might be better than just listening to each other hook up and getting mad about it.

items.title: The Case For Doing A Couples Costume With Your Situationship
items.description: The weeks leading up to Halloween are always full of bone-chilling frights. There are vampires lurking in the dark waiting to suck the life from their next victim, oozing mummies rising up from their coffins with vengeance, and ominous black cats scampering ac
items.author: Sophie Fishman
paragraphs: The weeks leading up to Halloween are always full of bone-chilling frights. There are vampires lurking in the dark waiting to suck the life from their next victim, oozing mummies rising up from their coffins with vengeance, and ominous black cats scampering across your path. Yet, when the days get shorter and the autumn breezes start to blow, there’s only one thing scarier than skulking creatures of the night: commitment.

Dressing up together is about as hard a hard launch as you can get, and proposing the idea means laying your intentions for the relationship bare. When you don’t have a crystal ball to read your partner’s mind, is there anything more awkward than asking them to be Santana to your Brittany? If you want to make things official, proposing they be the Ilya to your Shane can feel like putting your still-beating heart on a silver platter for the taking.

Nicole, 24, (whose name, like others in this story, has been changed to avoid an awkward conversation) has been in an on-and-off situationship for almost three years, and the pair is planning on doing a couples costume as Anora and Vanya from the movie Anora. When I call her, she’s outside looking for a place to sit. “Sorry, I was literally just at Brandy Melville looking for a shirt to buy him for this,” she says.

The idea was meant to be tongue in cheek. Two years ago, the two had an explosive public fight over the status of their relationship on the subway coming home from seeing the film. Now, several fights later and still non-exclusive, she thought it was a fun call-back. With some playful begging, he agreed.

When I ask if Anora and Vanya’s toxic and ultimately tragic relationship is an apt comparison to hers, she laughs. “It definitely fits him. The guy from Anora is very haphazard and kind of boyish and immature,” she says. “But he also goes through the phase of being obsessed with someone for a period of time and then moving on from it. And that's exactly who he is.”
She’s not worried about her friends’ reactions. “I think they'll just think it's funny.” According to Nicole, “You should be doing a couples costume with your situationship as soon as possible.”

Lauren, 25, just became exclusive with her partner a few weeks ago. Still, she was nervous to pop the question to her beau. “It’s just so awkward!” she says, laughing. “You just don’t want to be the one to have to do it first.”

Thankfully, he beat her to it. “I think I’m just traumatized. Back in college when you start ‘dating’ someone at the beginning of the year, you always think, ‘Obviously by the time Halloween comes around, this is going to be real serious,’ and then it's most definitely not,” she says. “So when he was like, ‘Should we do a couples costume?’ I was like, ‘Oh wait, I'm out of jail!’”

Though she’s starting to feel more confident about where they stand as an item, Lauren is looking at their Princess Buttercup and Westley outfits as an opportunity for the ultimate test of their status: telling the world. “If anybody happens to take a picture of us, will it go on Instagram? Probably.”

That said, even for couples in it for the long haul, couples costumes aren’t sacred. Sarah, 23, has been dating her boyfriend, John, for over two years. Recently he’s been blowing up her phone with inspiration pictures of Spider-Man and MJ, Mario and Princess Peach, and The Office’s Jim and Pam. She’s yet to break the news that she’d already been planning for weeks to dress up with her best friend as Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes. “I honestly don’t want to see you in a couples costume unless you’re married,” she says. “Halloween just feels like a girl holiday and it’s cringe to pick your boyfriend over your friends.”

So to couples costume or to not couples costume? If you’re on the same page and it’s fun, absolutely. If the getup is a substitute for an honest conversation about your future? Absolutely not. And if you’re worried that not showing up as Edward and Bella means they’re going home with Jacob, maybe it wasn’t meant to be after all.

items.title: Delena’s Reunion Proves 'Princess Protection Program 2' Needs To Happen
items.description: Delena’s Reunion Proves Princess Protection Program 2 Needs To Happen
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Delena’s Reunion Proves Princess Protection Program 2 Needs To Happen
Demi Lovato and Selena Gomez got nostalgic for a new Rare Beauty collab, but why stop there?

Demi Lovato and Selena Gomez are still “One and the Same.” Over 17 years after co-starring in the beloved Disney Channel Original Movie Princess Protection Program, the former BFFs became “Delena” once again for a new collab with Gomez’s makeup line, Rare Beauty, recreating their film poster and even making one of the nostalgic YouTube vlogs they used to do as teenagers.
The Disney Channel kids are healing (both the stars and their fans), and there’s a way to make this blissful harmony last even longer. Princess Protection Program 2 needs to happen.

Let’s be real: Disney is bringing back practically every iconic DCOM they can, and rightfully so. Lovato already knows this, as she made a surprise appearance in Camp Rock 3, which premiered in August, reprising her role as Mitchie Torres.

Disney+ just wrapped production on The Cheetah Girls: Next Gen, with Raven-Symoné and Adrienne Bailon returning, and is now developing a new Halloweentown film over two decades after the fourth sequel. There have even been murmurs of more Twitches and Teen Beach movies, though that’s not official yet. So, why not Princess Protection Program next?

The 2009 DCOM follows Lovato’s Princess Rosalinda María Montoya Fioré (Disney Channel loved a long name), who is about to be crowned queen of Costa Luna when a rival nation invades her country, forcing her to enter a princess protection program. She has to hide out in a Louisiana lake town with her P.P.P. agent’s tomboy daughter, Carter (Gomez), and they have absolutely nothing in common.

The only real barrier to a sequel would be if either Lovato or Gomez didn’t want to participate, but both seem happy to revisit their Disney Channel days. Lovato helped make Camp Rock 3 happen as an executive producer, while Gomez also produced a reboot of her series Wizards of Waverly Place, sporadically popping in as her character, Alex Russo, and making her directorial debut in the final season. Plus, they did this whole Rare Beauty campaign.

If Disney wants a new movie, they can make it happen — but I have one request. The new Camp Rock and Cheetah Girls films are embracing new generations, with the OG stars serving more as mentors, which feels like the most natural way for the franchises to evolve. This is not the route a Princess Protection Program sequel should take.

It feels a bit soon for Gomez and Lovato to play mothers (ignore the Wizards reboot). And no matter their age, Rosalinda will always be a royal, which means there will always be fun stories to tell that don’t necessarily involve kids. But even if Rosalinda welcomes a princess into the royal family, Lovato and Gomez can still get up to some new hijinks, making for a fun sequel.

With Lovato’s music career and Gomez juggling Rare Beauty with acting, they might be too busy to make this happen right now. But if the returns of Cheetah Girls and Connect 3 prove anything, it’ll never be too late.

items.title: M.A.C.'s New Frost Lipsticks Have Me Feeling Like An Early 2000s It Girl
items.description: “Ladies, frost yourselves.” Matthew McConaughey was talking about diamonds when he delivered that line in How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days, but it could have just as easily been a beauty slogan. After all, when the movie came out in 2003, frosted lipstick was *the
items.author: Emma Stout
paragraphs: “Ladies, frost yourselves.” Matthew McConaughey was talking about diamonds when he delivered that line in How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days, but it could have just as easily been a beauty slogan. After all, when the movie came out in 2003, frosted lipstick was *the* look, preferably in a shade of pearly pink à la Pamela Anderson.

Flash-forward to today, and low-rise jeans are back, foot tattoos are getting another go, and apparently, we’re ready to frost ourselves all over again. According to Pinterest's 2026 Beauty Trend Report, searches for “frosted makeup” are up 286%, while “metallic lips” and “frosted lips 2000s” are both up 52% and 42%, respectively.

The only problem? Finding a lipstick with that perfectly icy shimmer hasn’t been so easy — unless you’re willing to take your chances on a 20-year-old tube from eBay. (I, for one, am not.) Luckily, M.A.C. Cosmetics just brought back its iconic Frost Lipsticks, with an updated formula and plenty of new shades. As someone who missed the frosted era the first time around, I knew I had to get my hands on them. Ahead, my full review.
- Best for: A shimmery, Y2K-inspired lip.
- What I like: The balmy formula glides on like butter.

When M.A.C.’s frosted lipsticks originally launched in the ’90s, they delivered plenty of shimmer, but it came with a catch: The formula was notoriously gritty. That’s not the kind of thing beauty lovers are likely to put up with today, no matter how pretty the finish is. So for the relaunch, M.A.C. went back to the lab, making the pearlescent pigments even smaller for a smoother, slippier feel.

If you were a fan of the OG line, though, don’t worry — not everything has changed. M.A.C. brought back three archival shades: Jet, a pearly black; Spanish Fly, a brown with a blue shift; and Chintz, a warm copper. And if those don't sound like your speed, there are 10 brand-new options to choose from, too, ranging from icy lavender to silvery greige. According to the brand, each offers medium, buildable coverage (more on that later), so you can keep the color relatively sheer or layer it up for a more intense, metallic finish.

First of all, there’s nothing better than the smell of a M.A.C. lipstick. I’m not ashamed to admit I stuck my nose right up the tube before I even swatched anything; I am, however, a little embarrassed by how few lipsticks I actually have in my makeup collection. Compared to the gazillion glosses and lip oils, I probably own two at most. Maybe I’m a little scarred from the matte era, but I guess I’ve never really gotten over the idea of lipstick being dry and chalky.

Thankfully, M.A.C.’s new Frost formula proved me wrong. It's *super* buttery — it reminds me more of a balm than a classic lipstick. It glided on without any tugging whatsoever, and there was zero grittiness, but plenty of shimmer. Even better, it’s lightweight, to the point that I forgot I was wearing anything on my lips at all.

That being said, don't expect it to be the most moisturizing lip product out there. The metallic finish can make any flakiness more noticeable. Jojoba and castor seed oils in the formula keep it feeling comfortable rather than drying, but I found that a little lip prep goes a long way. Exfoliating beforehand, then applying some Vaseline while I finished the rest of my makeup, gave me a much smoother base for the shimmer.

The shimmer itself applies beautifully — super fine, evenly distributed, and not the least bit patchy. It also made my lips look a little fuller (I can see why the 2000s It girls were such big fans). The color is definitely buildable, as M.A.C. promised, but some shades pack more pigment than others. Chintz and Rogue, for example, deliver the most with just one swipe, while TV Gold and Teddy Metal are on the sheerer side. Personally, I've been loving Teddy Metal, a dusty rose with cool undertones, especially paired with a brown lip liner. It's not too flashy for everyday wear, but the golden shimmer makes it feel a little more special than my go-to gloss.

The color doesn't have quite the same staying power as the shimmer. After eating or drinking, I noticed that most of the pigment had rubbed off, even though my lips still had a subtle sparkle. But because the balmy formula is so easy to work with (even for a lipstick novice like me), touch-ups were a breeze. With the sheerer shades, I reapplied them without even looking in a mirror.

The second coming of frosted lipstick has officially won me over. The formula isn’t particularly hydrating, and the color definitely requires touch-ups throughout the day. But the buttery texture, ultra-fine shimmer, and easy application make those trade-offs feel pretty minor.

As someone who usually gravitates toward glosses and lip oils, I appreciate that these feel more like my usual low-maintenance lip products than the finicky lipsticks I tend to avoid. Even after the pigment fades, I’m left with a subtle sparkle and a fuller-looking pout — and swiping on another layer takes approximately two seconds and zero effort. Now, all that’s left to do is master Pamela Anderson’s smoky eye, and I’m all set for the Y2K revival.

items.title: Exclusive: 'SNL' Star Grace Reiter Wants To Bring Back This Weird TikTok Trend
items.description: SNL’s Grace Reiter Wants To Bring Back Weird TikTok
items.author: Samantha Leal
paragraphs: SNL’s Grace Reiter Wants To Bring Back Weird TikTok
The comedian talks Saturday Night Live, chaotic voice memos, and Venmo etiquette.

Grace Reiter is having a pretty big year. The comedian, who first found an audience on TikTok with absurdist sketches and recently on YouTube with parodies of The Hunger Games (with Twilight up next), has officially made the jump from the FYP to Saturday Night Live. But if you’re imagining a cinematic moment when the Wisconsin native got the call, think again.

“I was in LA, and there was a mix-up with the place I was staying,” Reiter, 25, tells Bustle. After a chaotic day of hotel mishaps, she got the call that she’d been cast on Saturday Night Live. But between the early morning, unexpected travel logistics, and sheer exhaustion, it was almost too much to process in the moment.

It wasn’t until the announcement went public on Sept. 16 and the congratulatory texts started rolling in that the magnitude of it all began to sink in. “I always think my life is The Truman Show, and at any point they’re going to be like, ‘OK, and cut! That was fun, wasn’t it?’” she says. “I think it’s real now.”

Now, a few shows into her SNL tenure, Reiter is already juggling live television, internet fame, and, apparently, a second, unexpected gig. “I think my part-time job is answering emails,” she says. She’s also taking on another very 2026 problem: Venmo ghosting.

Just in time for Halloween, the comedian has partnered with the mobile payment app as its official “Venmo Ghost Medium,” a crystal-ball-wielding psychic who helps people confront the friends, dates, and acquaintances who mysteriously disappear when it’s time to split the check. As part of the campaign, launching Oct. 28, people can share their own Venmo ghosting stories in the comments on Instagram for a chance to have outstanding requests covered by the company.

And while she might be helping people recover their money, Reiter admits she’s not entirely innocent when it comes to the occasional unpaid request. Recently she saw her roommate’s two-month-old request in her Venmo. “I was like, ‘Oh, oops.’ So I have been that person for sure. Then I’m like, ‘OK, we do live together,’” she says, laughing. “‘You could also tell me.’ But that’s my bad.”
Below, Reiter talks about the TikTok trends she wants to resurrect, her chaotic voice notes, and why she could probably give a PowerPoint presentation on The Sims 3.
The Fast Follow With Grace Reiter
Are you the type to send a Venmo reminder, or do you suffer in silence?

I don’t even really do it. If it’s in your requests, I imagine you see it and ignore it for a reason. It’s there, and it won’t go away unless you decline it, but then you get notified anyway. Maybe money is hard to talk about. So I’m like, “Well, we’ll get to it.” They’ll pay me! They’ll pay me!
Do you ever snoop on other people’s Venmo transactions?
All the time. Honestly, I’ll have to scroll through my Venmo and see because I feel like people are always just lying about what they’re actually paying for because they know other people can see it.
Who’s your dream SNL host?
I said Jack Black and Melissa McCarthy before, but I’d love it if Jennifer Lawrence came on again.
What’s one internet trend you desperately want to bring back?

Honestly, the duet feature was so prominent in 2020. People would do duet chains, or if their arm went off frame, the person on the other side would make the rest of their arm. There was so much comedy to be had with that feature. Nobody uses that anymore, and I think it’s because the algorithm doesn’t favor that type of video. I’d love to see people bring back duetting in a comedic way.

Or I would say, oh my gosh, the Mafia stuff in 2020. Everyone decided to dress up as Mob bosses, but it was like a YA romance Mob-boss kind of thing where they were just looking sexy and walking in place. They’d all duet and be like, “We’re the family, meet the family.” And I’m like, “This is just awesome. This is what we should be using the internet for.”
What’s the most used app on your phone?
I feel like mostly email and Google Calendar.
Are you a Notes app comedian, or do your best ideas live somewhere more chaotic?

Probably Notes app or voice memos, because my stream of consciousness is more like pacing and talking, and the only way to know if any of it is usable is to record it and listen back. That seems to be the most natural way for ideas to come out.
So are your voice notes quick thoughts or full-length sagas?
Oh, it’s rambling. It’s a podcast. It’s a complete waste of phone storage that never really gets looked at again. But it just makes me feel good knowing that if I want to go back to it, I can.
What’s the last thing you Googled? No judgment.
An internet speed test, that Thanos quote where he’s watching the sunset in Avengers, a comedian, and then I think I was looking up the definition of “stoic.”
What’s a topic you could give an entire PowerPoint presentation on with zero preparation?
There was a time when I could give you a PowerPoint on Sims 3, go through each expansion pack, and tell you the different clothes and features. I was a big Simmer back in the day.
I also play Overwatch, and the characters have a lot of lore. So maybe a shipping chart of the characters in Overwatch — who ships to who. I could easily do that.
What’s your current internet rabbit hole?

The Atomic Twins on YouTube. I watch them react to Love Is Blind. When I’m eating food, that’s the YouTube video I’m putting on. Then I have this other guy I watch who recaps the episodes. So I’m getting double: I’m getting the clinical, just-the-facts take, and then a funny one.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

paragraphs: When giving up teaches you more than persevering ever could
Grit is all well and good, but sometimes abandoning your goals can be crucial to discovering who you are
Fear protects us from future harm, so what’s going on when we find ourselves scared of what’s already happened?
by Davide Bordini & Giuliano Torrengo
Screens and social media get the blame, but the real problem lies in how we measure intelligence in the first place
Rather than being an enemy of empiricism, belief in what can’t be known is part of how we gain knowledge, even now
Unable to handle uncertainty, AI mimics the narcissistic compulsion to fill voids with plausible but false narratives
Research on how we perceive the rate of change shows how you can be strategic about goal tracking and boost your motivation
The original optimist, Leibniz, was mocked and misunderstood. Centuries later, his worldview can help us navigate modern life
Many dismiss utopian ideas. But imagining a better world is a vital political skill for tackling today’s challenges
To protect our descendants from catastrophe, we must overcome the emotional hurdles that make it easy for us to look away

items.title: Ellah Wakatama, the godmother of African books | Psyche Portraits
items.description: Not long ago, a group of East African writers gathered at my house in Nairobi for a writing weekend. We were all working on manuscripts – novels set in Kenya and in Kazakhstan, histories of people in Ethiopia and Uganda, works we each imagined would be our mag
items.author: Carey Baraka
paragraphs: Not long ago, a group of East African writers gathered at my house in Nairobi for a writing weekend. We were all working on manuscripts – novels set in Kenya and in Kazakhstan, histories of people in Ethiopia and Uganda, works we each imagined would be our magnum opus – but the problem, invariably, was how we might turn these into published books. Over beers and pizza, we brainstormed. Maybe what we needed was to be agented in London or in New York. Maybe what we needed was to move to London or New York. Maybe we simply needed to support each other, edit one another’s manuscripts. (But how would that help us get published?) Then, a Somali author who’d won some of Africa’s most important literary prizes for shorter work, chimed in. What we needed, he said, was to be adopted by Ellah Wakatama.

To be an African writer today – especially one writing in English, especially one younger than 40 – is to reckon with the idea of Ellah. Born in Zimbabwe when it was still under the Rhodesian flag, and now based in Britain, she is an editor-at-large at Canongate, an independent publishing firm. But it is more accurate to describe her as the most powerful woman – person – in Anglophone African literature today. From friends whose books she has touched, one hears of the fury of her red pen, of what they describe as the best editing they’ve ever experienced. From those who’ve worked with her, one hears of a person who doesn’t suffer fools, nor clichés like ‘suffer fools’. No other individual has so influenced the 21st-century African canon, if there is such a thing. Wakatama calls it ‘the bookshelf that my grandchildren will refer to’. Her lifelong project is to shape that bookshelf, to turn it into a library unto itself.
The night went on, as did the weekend. We’d all laughed when he said it, but beneath our laughter were three uneasy truths:
- There were no publishers in East Africa who would put out our work.
- We were doomed to try and find our own way into publishing networks in the West.
- Having a literary godparent was what had worked for generations of African writers.

In the beginning was Chinua Achebe. It is a rule of African literature that any exegesis has to begin with him. Achebe is famous as a novelist – Things Fall Apart (1958) really is one of those great books that everyone should read before they die – but he was more important as an editor of Heinemann’s African Writers Series (AWS), which introduced Western readers to an array of African authors, fledgling and established alike. Novels by African writers had existed before Achebe but, for writers of a certain generation, the AWS was arguably the only publishing vehicle for their work. The great Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, for instance, had his first book published because he gave his manuscript to Achebe. Now we needed to give our manuscripts to Wakatama. She was editor, agent, publisher and godparent, all rolled into one.
But how had she become this person? How did a kid from Harare grow up to wield such influence? I, a kid from Kisumu, a city in Kenya, was determined to track how this had come to be.

The idea of Ellah is different from Ellah in person. In June 2025, I met Wakatama in Accra where she was leading a writing workshop for Pfumo, a Pan-African literary collective she’d recently co-founded. Who was this person in front of me, smoking a cigarette she’s rolled herself? So giggly, so cheery, a bit frilly. She squealed when we passed the store of her favourite Ghanaian designer. I wanted to gossip with her. She exuded fun.

I put to her my Achebe comparison, although I could already see holes: Wakatama’s hair is far more glorious and, unlike the grand old man of African letters, she’d never been a novelist, though she’d briefly tried to be a poet, and co-authored a book of short stories when she was 21. Wakatama, laughing, wouldn’t agree with the Achebe analogy – we both knew that would be in bad taste – but said she could see the throughline of my logic. She was, after all, a child of the age that the AWS represented and sought to shape: Africa after empire.

The second child of Winnie Ndoro and Pius Wakatama, Ellah spent her first four years in a village south of Harare with her grandparents. Winnie and Pius had met at work: she, educated, was a secretary; he, a township boy who sold newspapers, had, Ellah told me, very much ‘married up’. Pius didn’t finish high school but he could write in English; he’d read the short fiction in DRUM, a South African magazine he sold, and thought to himself: I can do that! He could, and did, and then became a novelist in the Shona language, well-known enough that he was invited for a residency at the University of Iowa.
‘I feel I have been looking for Narnia ever since. Every book I open, I’m looking for Narnia’

This time, the whole family went. In Iowa, little Ellah struggled to make friends, partly because she barely spoke English. Once, she saw a group of Black girls playing outside but they wouldn’t speak to her since all she spoke was Shona. That people who looked like her couldn’t understand her was deeply unsettling; soon after, Ellah stopped talking altogether for six months. When she resumed, she stuttered badly in English. Her mother, Winnie, enlisted a speech therapist who used C S Lewis’s The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe to help her. If you can read this word w-a-r-d-r-o-b-e without stuttering, the therapist once told her, we will have a peach melba. Ellah thought and thought, said the word without tripping over it, then snarfed down her reward.

Perhaps that’s where it started – the belief that books could be a salve against the world. A few years later, when her class went on a field trip to see a wardrobe that had once belonged to C S Lewis, Ellah packed spare socks, a sandwich and a flashlight because she was going to Narnia and not coming back. But when they opened it, it was just an empty wardrobe. ‘I was really disappointed,’ she told me. ‘And I feel I have been looking for Narnia ever since. Every book I open, I’m looking for Narnia.’

In 1976, the family moved back to Zimbabwe, where a war of liberation was being waged. A year before Ellah was born, the white minority in Rhodesia had seized power, declaring independence from Britain. Consequently, two liberation groups – ZANU and ZAPU – had started a resistance war, rejecting rule by a clique of white settlers. Pius and Winnie wanted to be home when it was won. Ten-year-old Ellah, no longer mute, had forgotten how to speak in Shona. Winnie enrolled her in the best private elementary school in Zimbabwe at the time. Only white girls were students at Bishopslea but Winnie saw no reason why her daughters shouldn’t get the best education. Neither did the school’s British headmistress. But the Rhodesian government was angry this had happened, and they deported the headmistress.

All the while, the war continued. Some of Ellah’s relatives were either fighting or living in villages fenced off because of the war. Her classmates were told to support their soldiers; one year, they had to knit balaclavas for the prime minister Ian Smith’s forces, so Ellah went home and asked her mother for green yarn. Winnie was furious; no daughter of hers was going to make balaclavas for the Rhodesians. Ellah cried and cried; all she wanted was to fit in with the other girls. As a compromise, Winnie bought her brown wool – nothing but the green of the Rhodesian flag would fit the Rhodesians.
‘It had a profound effect on me … this idea that your life has to have meaning, that you can’t just exist, that you have to be impacting the world’

This is one part of what shaped Wakatama. The memories of the war. The race laws in Zimbabwe. The fury with which her mother disregarded them while ensuring that her children were equipped to navigate them. The other part is books. Ellah moved from Nancy Drew and The Hardy Boys to Hermann Hesse and Taban Lo Liyong, working through her father’s library. She wrote Liyong a fan letter; to her delight, he responded. She and her best friend forged their mothers’ signatures so that they could borrow Georgette Heyer paperbacks from the adult library. Then, in 1980 – the year of the first free elections, of Zimbabwe’s independence, of the start of high school – she was assigned to read Doris Lessing in class.

Lessing’s The Grass Is Singing (1950) – the story of the relationship between Mary, a poor white farmer’s wife, and Moses, a Black servant on the homestead – was the first book Wakatama read that was set in Zimbabwe. She found it shocking – and confusing. ‘As a girl, I wanted to become a woman who stood at the vanguard of the battlelines that Lessing had set out, the questions she asked about selfhood and a woman’s place in the world,’ she would later say. ‘But Moses was the one who was my relative.’ It was a challenge in newly independent Zimbabwe to hold both those stories: ‘Lessing, on the one hand, speaking for my gender, and her boldly imagined Moses, on the other hand, bearing witness to my people’s dispossession.’

Enflamed by Lessing, she started writing fiction. A magazine called Moto had a monthly short-story competition, top prize $100, which she entered and won. Her story was about a prison inmate suffering an existential crisis – full of ‘deep emotion, injustice and pretty sentences’. With her prize money, she bought a pair of shoes, grey snakeskin. ‘My brother was at school with a Kenyan boy I really liked,’ she added. ‘So I took him and his friends out to lunch.’ When her father read the story, he said: ‘Yes, Miss Ellah, it’s very good.’ But he was a traditional writer; he believed stories should have a beginning, middle and end, and a moral lesson. Hers didn’t have any of that. ‘The next month, he sent in a story and he won,’ Wakatama told me. ‘It’s something a therapist would have a field day with but, in our house, it was a massive joke.’

Pius Wakatama was a man of strong opinions and believed all his children should have opinions, too. He would argue with them and expect them to argue back. ‘Are you a man or a mouse?’ he once asked Nhamu, Ellah’s younger brother, when he refused to engage. ‘Dad, I’m a mouse,’ Nhamu responded. (Ellah laughed at the memory.) Pius was also extraordinarily large-hearted, often bringing home people who were in a tight spot: struggling relatives, street families, hitchhikers. ‘I grew up with that kind of thing,’ Wakatama said. ‘I think it had a profound effect on me … this idea that your life has to have meaning, that you can’t just exist, that you have to be impacting the world.’ Once, at the school where he taught, he heard a student crying in the girls’ bathroom because her parents wanted to marry her off. ‘Don’t worry,’ Pius told the young woman. ‘Bring your suitcase with you tomorrow.’ He went home and told Winnie he was bringing her a new daughter. The next day, he knocked on Ellah’s bedroom door and said: ‘This is Florence, she’s your sister.’

Wakatama went to the same college as her mother, a small Mennonite school in rural Indiana. There, in her final year, she declared that she would not read. Specifically – and ‘with all the irritating self-riotousness of youth,’ as she once put it – she announced that she would not be reading any dead white males. Craft your own reading list, her professor told her. This was a turning point. ‘Even though it would be years later that I started working as a publisher, it defined how I approached publishing,’ she told me. ‘The bookshelf was wrong; I knew there was more to it. My professor challenged me to find that “more” – and I did.’
She put James Baldwin on her list, and Alice Walker. Then she discovered Tsitsi Dangarembga.

Dangarembga’s Nervous Conditions (1988) was the first book published in English by a Black Zimbabwean woman. It follows 13-year-old Tambu at a mission school and confronts the ‘nervous conditions’ – a phrase taken from Jean-Paul Sartre – of being caught between traditional African culture and Western colonial influence. The novel’s opening sentence – ‘I was not sorry when my brother died’ – jolted Wakatama, not least because Tambu’s brother had almost the same name as Wakatama’s brother, Nhamu. It felt as if, in exploring the dissonance of social mobility in Zimbabwe, Dangarembga was writing about Wakatama and her peers: she ‘felt that the author had peeked inside our most secret diaries and written us into being.’

More than a decade would pass before Wakatama found her way back to books. After college, she married Richard Allfrey, a British boy she’d met in the US, and, while in grad school, decided to have a child because she was ‘curious about motherhood’. She wrote her dissertation with little Gabrielle on her lap. (‘I’d breastfeed and type, breastfeed and type.’) Afterwards, the family moved to England, where she worked a series of jobs in the education sector. ‘I hated every single one,’ she said. The racism in England rankled her but, more than that, she was bored. One day, on holiday in Zimbabwe, her parents sat her down. Pius asked what she was doing with her life. Her mother added: ‘You’ve been sitting on your brain so long you’re going to forget to use it.’
‘They didn’t recognise me as a member of the tribe. I would hang out with the guys in the post room because they were Black’

Ellah cried after that intervention. She felt she was letting down her family, letting down Zimbabwe – in those early postcolonial years, the feeling was that your education was meant to improve things. Then her daughter unwittingly spearheaded another intervention. ‘We can’t live with you because you’re so unhappy,’ Gabrielle, seven at the time, told her after she returned from work one day. ‘You spend all your time and money on books,’ Richard chimed in. ‘Why don’t you just work in books?’

Gabrielle, now 34 years old, doesn’t remember giving her mother this advice, though she told me it must have been very good advice for a seven-year-old. She and her sister Rujeko, born 10 years after Gabrielle, were also in Accra. She was enjoying seeing her mother work with writers. Wakatama knew how to talk with writers in a way she hadn’t instinctively known how to talk to babies. When Gabrielle was born, Wakatama – unsure of how to interact with an infant – would read her the paper. This was the 1990s and the Soviet Union had crumbled, so she read Gabrielle stories about Boris Yeltsin. What Gabrielle remembers is struggling with dyslexia
and her mother encouraging her to read, being patient, open and supportive.

After that second intervention, Wakatama worked for a year as a temp at Penguin’s offices in London, before being hired as an assistant to both the editor of the Ancient Classics series and the editor of the Modern Classics series. She was 30. There were books everywhere, piles on the floor, spilling out of cabinets, teetering stacks on desks. I’m home, she thought to herself. But the trouble with being home is that sometimes not everyone there accepts that it is your home. ‘I knew I was with my tribe of people,’ she told me. ‘But they didn’t recognise me as a member of the tribe. I would hang out quite a bit with the guys in the post room because they were Black. Nobody was cruel to me – it just never occurred to them at the time.’
She paused. ‘I didn’t look like an editor because none of the editors looked like me.’

She’d sit at the desk looking at the Modern Classics: there were Russian writers, and Japanese writers, and French writers. She began to wonder where the African writers were. ‘How can you say you have a Modern Classics list, and you don’t have Achebe? You don’t have Ngũgĩ? It made absolutely no sense to me.’ Encouraged by her boss, she reached out to people who’d worked at the African Writers Series, and licensed some of those authors: Dambudzo Marechera from Zimbabwe, Bessie Head from Botswana, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o from Kenya. She became interested in Black writers from elsewhere, for instance championing the work of the Jamaican-born Linton Kwesi Johnson, who became the first Black poet, and the second living poet, to be included in the Penguin Modern Classics series.

‘I wasn’t at this point thinking I’m out to change literature,’ she told me. ‘I just thought this bookshelf is wrong. As a child of independence, you know you’re supposed to be changing the world, you don’t just submit and do your job. Plus, I was ambitious as fuck.’

It’s hard to write about editors. Who profiles editors? Writers are easier, at least published ones. Why did you say this 40 years ago, you might ask them; Why does the structure of your novel resemble Flaubert? While talking to Wakatama – we were discussing Wole Soyinka’s hair (‘like a cloud!’) and that time in 2010 she interviewed him – my own early obsessions returned to me: Peter Abrahams and the world of 1940s Johannesburg he created in Mine Boy (1946), Gustave Flaubert’s Parisian aristocrats in Sentimental Education (1869). I knew from an early age that I was going to be a writer; I’d been trapped by literature, deriving pleasure ever since from moments when I could do what those writers did: bring an idea in my head to life on the page, turn a half-formed thought or image into a sparkling sentence.

None of these moments would have been possible without an editor. Only a specific kind of obsessive understands Andy Elisburg’s role in the Miami Heat’s NBA championships, or Elvira Nabiullina’s in Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine, and it’s the same with editors. Writers know. Without an editor who ‘gets it’, we have little chance of succeeding – a sentence my editor most certainly did not force me to write. Or, think of musicians and their producers: there was no Michael Jackson without Berry Gordy, or Kendrick Lamar without Dr Dre. I mentioned Dre to Wakatama, specifically the way she stopped trying to be a poet and began publishing other writers, just as he killed his own rap career, and she cackled.
‘No one’s ever compared me to Dr Dre before!’

The books she is drawn to are ones ‘that feel like they had to be written’, she tells me later, when I ask about the bookshelf she is building, the one her grandchildren will refer to. ‘There has to be a message, a question, an exploration. This works best when filtered through character and place – so the story is equally important.’ In this, she has come to agree with Pius: a story needs a message and a plot. But she remains drawn to beauty. ‘It’s the layers underneath that will keep me reading and re-reading,’ she added. ‘I remain obsessed with beautiful sentences, that delicate crafting of the thought until it becomes poetry.’
Western readers should have to do the work that the African reader has always done

After Penguin, Wakatama moved to Jonathan Cape, an imprint of Random House. Among the first big writers whose books she worked on were Julian Barnes and Ian McEwan. She said: ‘I copyedited On Chesil Beach, which has one mistake in it.’
I said I would read the book to try to find it.
She laughed and said: ‘You won’t know the mistake. If you find it, tell me. Ian said it was his fault, not mine, but I still blame myself.’

Although she now had more room to commission books, her acquisitions budget was still tiny. She scoured the list of writers awarded grants by the Arts Council of England, reaching out to them to see if they had anything to publish. That’s how she published Biyi Bandele’s Burma Boy (2007), about African soldiers in the Second World War, and Nii Ayikwei Parkes’s debut novel Tail of the Blue Bird (2009), a thriller that blends forensic science and Ghanaian folklore. Both challenged the way she thought about editing. In a multi-lingual book, for instance, the non-English parts are usually italicised. But Ayikwei Parkes refused to submit to this; in Blue Bird, this convention is flipped. Typically, ‘English is the standard and the rest of us are deviations,’ she told me. But in Blue Bird, a lot of the narration is by a man who doesn’t speak English: only when he uses a non-Akan word (particular to English) do italics appear. Ayikwei Parkes’s insistence on italicising these individual words of English, rather than those of Twi or Ga, was an assertion that the centre of the world was where the writer said it was, that Western readers should have to do the work that the African reader has always done.
‘That was really, for me, political,’ she said.

Ayikwei Parkes told me how unexpected it had been to find an editor willing to change her mind about editorial style. ‘For most conventional editors, it might be baffling to accommodate such a conceit,’ he said. ‘But she fully grasped the political thrust of my stylistic choice and supported its use, protecting me from the clutches of standard copyeditors.’ When I mentioned the Achebe-Wakatama comparison to him, he disagreed. ‘I sort of resist the idea of godparents for African writing, a notion that doesn’t exist for Western writing. What I will say is that Ellah is, like Achebe, certainly interested in the dignity and autonomy of the African personality and perspective. She believes and understands that Africa is a continent from which the world can be observed, made sense of, influenced and remade.’

Growing up in Zimbabwe, Wakatama says, made her a better editor. ‘Because as an African, for my generation at least, you grow up in an education system that doesn’t include you in the literature; therefore, you have to fill in the gaps yourself. So almost any African, if they were a reader anyway, is going to be a better reader than an English person – because we’re always reading outside ourselves, as well as within ourselves.’ She paused. ‘Which I don’t think we acknowledge enough. I think, now that I’m older, especially post-menopause, and also senior enough not to care what anyone thinks, I can just say it out loud.’

It has taken decades of being dismissed for her to speak so freely: of working under bosses who paid lip-service to diversity, of going to award ceremonies and realising the only other Black people in the room were waiters, of having smaller purchasing and marketing budgets than her colleagues. She recalls trying to acquire a book once, championing it fiercely, but being turned down – mere months later, it was bought by another editor in a different division for five times the price. ‘I told them: This is nonsense – you could have had this book for five grand six months ago when I found it, but because someone else says that it’s good, you’re now going to take it. What the fuck?’

Above her desk at Random House, she’d put up a picture of Toni Morrison, previously an editor at the company. ‘I used to look at that picture and think: She survived and I can too.’ But it was after the death of Nhamu, her younger brother, that she decided things could not go on as they had. Nhamu had suffered a series of strokes, and his death a decade later catapulted Wakatama into a deep depression, a depression that would be matched in depth only by the one triggered by her later divorce from her husband. ‘[Nhamu] was one of the true loves of my life,’ she told me, dabbing her eyes. ‘I was a completely different person after he died … his dying made me think: If he’s gone and I’m left behind – if his life has ended, what am I gonna do with mine?’
‘My feeling is that, if I am sitting at that table, to not sit at that table for too long’

Shortly after, she joined Granta as deputy editor of the literary magazine. She loved its international scope and finally had what she’d always wanted: a proper budget for commissioning writers. She also began to commission authors for Granta Books. She said: ‘I am driven by a mission, I really am. I’m not a religious person, but I grew up in a religious family. Part of that is about what are you here on earth for? The most important thing to me is books. My daughters will absolutely tell you that they had to fight for my attention. And I want others to have the chance to experience what I’ve experienced. Granta finally gave me that opportunity to do that level of commissioning.’

She started doing workshops – in Nigeria, China, Sri Lanka – to train other editors, as well as more public talks and radio. Her first big interview was with Wole Soyinka. She read him a poem on stage; it was a poem he had written when younger about what he’d be like when his hair was silver. Ellah told him: ‘Look at you now, you’re pretty much all silver. You know, what do you think about the poem?’ The great man laughed.

In 2011, she was awarded an Order of the British Empire for her services to the publishing industry. Somebody noticed, she thought to herself, somebody noticed the work I’m doing. Meanwhile, some colleagues asked: Well, what are you getting that for? ‘We now call these microaggressions, which are never microaggressions,’ she said. ‘My answer was always, for surviving this.’

What does it mean to be the only person of your kind in a room, constantly having to prove you belong? For Wakatama, the cost was psychological. ‘I wish someone had said to me: This life that you’re living is really fulfilling your soul but beware of the damage it will do to you,’ she said. It is tempting to buy into the hoopla of being the first this-or-that, of having a seat at the table, ‘to get sucked into that sense of, Oh, I’m special,’ she warns. ‘My feeling is that, if I am sitting at that table, to not sit at that table for too long.’

Part of her mission, therefore, is to continue to facilitate the entry of gifted writers into the global publishing infrastructure. In this regard, the English writer Max Porter, who worked alongside Wakatama at Granta, describes her as ‘a proper writer’s editor, deeply committed to and connected to her writers, not necessarily just the one book she is working on.’ As someone new at the time to the publishing world and ‘a little suspicious of it already’, Porter was inspired by how Wakatama nurtured and protected the writers she worked with ‘in the line and on the page and in the world.’

In 2020, after the murder of George Floyd forced a new racial reckoning in the United States and beyond, Wakatama watched white agents rush to sign Black writers. ‘I was like, you’ve got to be kidding me,’ she recalled. ‘After 20 years of saying: Publish Black writers now, you have this.’ Young writers were suddenly being offered massive advances. ‘On one level, that’s great – I’m thinking: Baby, take the money and run! But when you pay half a million for a book and the book sells 10,000 copies, it’s a failure. Remember, it’s an advance against your royalties. So, the next time, you’re starting off in debt.’ The result is that the publisher thinks these books don’t sell and ‘you’ve made it impossible for those authors to be successful.’

In Accra, I sat in on some of the Pfumo sessions. One reason Wakatama co-founded the collective was her concern about how few African nonfiction writers were published internationally. As the participants discussed writing craft, she listened closely, her head tilted towards the speaker, her legs crossed. When she talked, she leaned back, her hands a vital part of her speech. Books surrounded us. (‘It’s overwhelming to realise how many of these I edited,’ she told me.)
When a participant read out her work softly, Wakatama told her to read it again because she wanted ‘a big voice’. Here are other things she said to the writers presenting their work:
‘How do you feel about that?’
‘You’re not being brave enough. I need you to be brave.’
‘Greener pastures, no. That’s a cliché. We don’t use them.’
‘I don’t want you to run away. I want you to try. I think you’ll get it.’
‘I know I said lean into the poetry, but maybe you leaned too much.’

One evening in 2017, Wakatama saw a post on Facebook by Dangarembga, the author of Nervous Conditions. That book’s opening sentence – ‘I was not sorry when my brother died’ – had shocked Ellah, but when her own Nhamu died, she returned to the novel in her sorrow. How astutely Dangarembga had written of what Ellah herself had to grapple with: ‘the psychic trauma of fitting into a world that seems to demand an erasure, a forgetting of the self before.’ Dangarembga’s second novel, The Book of Not, had come out in 2006. She was now seeking an editor for her third, which she would self-publish.

That Dangarembga would struggle to find a publisher despite her success was an indictment of an industry that still struggled to recognise African writers. Wakatama didn’t know Dangarembga personally but she reached out anyway. ‘Your writing is so important to so many of us, why are you self-publishing?’ she asked. ‘If you do self-publish, please can I offer my services for free as your editor?’

The new book – This Mournable Body (2018) – was remarkable, Wakatama thought, and she offered to introduce Dangarembga to a friend who ran Graywolf Press, an American indie publisher. Wakatama flew to Harare; Dangarembga came to the family house for lunch. Some years before, Dangarembga recalled, she had corresponded with a Zimbabwean writer called Pius Wakatama. Was he a relative, Dangarembga wondered. Pius laughed. It was him.

Graywolf bought the book. Wakatama, who had, till then, been editing it for free, added a clause in the contract stipulating that the publisher would pay her an extra fee if the book made it to the Booker shortlist. ‘Everyone was fine with it because it was never going to happen,’ she recalled, smiling. But by now Wakatama knew to bet on herself. ‘When she got shortlisted and the money hit my account, I was, like, Yeah. I told you all.’
