items.title: Bill Burr: 'I Didn't Want to Be the Angry Guy'
items.description: B ill Burr would like to make one thing crystal clear: He never wanted to be “the angry guy.”
items.author: David Fear
paragraphs: B ill Burr would like to make one thing crystal clear: He never wanted to be “the angry guy.”

Oh, the legendary stand-up knows that he has a reputation as someone who can rage with the best of them. His unparalleled ability to vent his spleen onstage and on his twice-weekly Monday Morning Podcast, which Burr started way back in 2007, has long fueled his popularity. “Believe me, dude,” the 58-year-old comedian says, “I can blow my top like anybody. I can still lose my shit. I’ve got 50-something years of practice of that.”

But Burr has been working on himself a lot over the past few years. And while there is no shortage of things that still make him mad — social media, tech billionaires, your everyday displays of blatant hypocrisy, the whole left-versus-right thing — he has finally mastered the art of anger management, as well as letting go of a lot of the pain behind it. Part of this change was spurred by a mind-blowing mushroom trip Burr took in the early 2020s, which he memorialized in his seventh comedy special, Live at Red Rocks. Part of it was the result of therapy, which Burr has credited with saving his life. Part of it involves his loved ones and realizing that he had accidentally become the very person he vowed to never be.

And part of it, as Burr will confess during our hour-plus conversation, was an unexpected moment of clarity that happened when he was preparing for his role in The Social Reckoning, writer-director Aaron Sorkin’s return to the world of Facebook, some 16 years after he helped give the world The Social Network. Burr’s character, a composite of several longtime investors, is worried that Mark Zuckerberg (played with characteristic intensity by Jeremy Strong) isn’t taking a whistleblower and a series of Wall Street Journal exposés seriously enough. Coming on the heels of his turn in the all-star Broadway revival of Glengarry Glen Ross last year, it’s a great example of both Burr’s facility as an ensemble player and his ability to parlay his comic persona into a legitimate acting career. But there was an added benefit: A spontaneous crying jag while rehearsing lines prompted Burr to finally address decades’ worth of issues and become a much happier version of himself.

Yes, Burr still blows gaskets — but on a scale of one to 10, he’s no longer “coming in at an eight because someone got my dinner order wrong.” Yes, Burr is still hilarious — probably more than he’s ever been, both in his own estimation and gauging by the dozens of record-breaking, sold-out shows he’s played everywhere from Boston to London to Greece. No, he hasn’t lost his edge, even if he knows he’s lost some fans who expect him to be a misanthrope 24/7. But as he’s been touring his latest stand-up hour around the U.S., he’s now dedicated to countering the divisiveness he believes is tearing this country apart. Enough with the angry guy. “I want to be the meet-in-the-middle guy,” Burr says.
Watch the video interview below
The Social Reckoning is not a follow-up to The Social Network, exactly. But it’s Aaron Sorkin, it’s about Facebook …

Yeah, it’s about a whistleblower that was working at Facebook. When it started to go sideways, she reached out to somebody at The Wall Street Journal, which caused all of this internal strife with the company. It put some information out there that people needed to know. Social media platforms are [still] new. We’re just seeing the fallout of them now. It started off as fun and silly, and then it got monetized, and then it just got evil.
One minute you’re using it to talk to an old high school buddy. The next, somebody’s being dragged before Congress to talk about why Instagram is evil for teenage girls.

That is kind of what happened. The internet’s this crazy place. I don’t understand why you can’t say curse words on TV, but you can post whatever you want on the internet, and there’s no rules of libel or slander and all of this stuff. And now with AI, everybody is just like, “Well, you know, it’s here … so you just have to deal with it.” It’s weird.
Who asked for this AI wave?

Nobody. Nobody wants it. That’s the thing. Maybe CEOs want AI because they don’t want to pay anybody. They’ve never wanted to pay anybody. But we’re too busy yelling at each other about red ties and blue ties, so we don’t realize we’re on the same team.
So if you’re in an ensemble with an actor who’s maybe got a certain process, a certain way that they need to kind of get into a scene …
How do you work with somebody who needs to approach things in their own specific way?

Everybody’s got a process. And if their process starts spilling over to your cup, you gotta let them know that doesn’t go in this cup. You go drink your shit over there. Whatever the fuck you need to do.
“You learn the most through the failure of bombing.”
Why are you laughing? It’s like you think I’m referring to someone in particular.
You know what? I’m going Henry Hill. “I’m just listening.” I’m just listening [laughs].

The Social Reckoning is getting into this stuff that you’ve been talking about in your act for the past few years — the lack of accountability, how the media works, the way tech is taking control of our lives. Did this seem like a natural extension of what you’ve been doing onstage?

It’s way deeper. You know, I’m a stand-up. I’m joking around. But we live in a world where if somebody tells their version of the truth of what’s going on, it’s like they’re trying to escape Russia in the Eighties. It’s insane. [Facebook] is an American company that seems to function like the CIA, which is really sort of indicative of you’re doing something wrong.

I mean, if you look at the response to the Luigi [Mangione] thing. It wasn’t “Maybe we need to look at what we’re doing if it makes some crazy person do this.” [Healthcare executives’] response was to take their faces off of the internet and get security. It’s like, “You don’t think you need to examine this? You’re just the CEO of a business. Why do you need this level of security?”

Even just touring as a comic, I’ve seen it change. It used to be we hated the Russians. Now it’s like, Texas hates California, California hates Texas. These people hate Florida. Everybody hates New York. It’s like, “Guys, same teams. We’re on the same teams here.”

I was talking about that ICE stuff onstage, talking about my people, white people. We’re not nearly as upset as we need to be, because we don’t see ourselves going into the van. I go, “Who do you think’s going in the van next?” And this guy in the crowd yells, “Liberals!” And I go, “Did you just say liberals?” Like, dude, you’re literally talking about half of your team. They’re gonna work their way back to you eventually. People think they’re in the in-group. They think they’re gonna get under the mountain or get on the spaceship. You’re not. They’re using you, and they’re making you not like me, and they’re trying to make me not like you.
Part of the impetus to start working on yourself came from an acting gig, right?
Yeah, this acting gig. The Social Reckoning role.
As my therapist would say, let’s hear more about this.

I was in my hotel room, getting ready to do this big scene the next day. I got about a page and a half in, and one of the lines was my character was disappointed, probably in the Mark Zuckerberg character. I said the line, and it made me choke up, like I was gonna cry. But it didn’t serve the scene. The scene was not at that emotional level. I was thinking, “What is this?” So I stopped myself, because that’s what you do as a guy. You’re not allowed to cry.

So then I went back to the top. I went through it again — and the same thing happened. And then I started freaking out, being like, “I’m gonna, like, emotionally lose it, I’m gonna look stupid, and they’re gonna fire me.” Some actors think if you’re crying that’s good. Well, not if it doesn’t call for it. It would have been bizarre. I literally just went, like, “OK, what is this?”

It’s almost like when you’re on mushrooms and you get an answer. For some reason, I got an answer, and I realized the way that I was raised, like 99.9 percent of my emotions were sort of shamed away. “That’s not what a man does.” I had basically three emotions. I navigated my life with laughing, being angry, or not giving a fuck. Everything else I just had in a vault.

But when I act, these characters feel emotions that are in the vault. So I’ve got to go in and get them, and then what happens is, like, a cry from 50 years ago sees the light and tries to run out. I had to sit there in this hotel room and cry for five minutes, and I didn’t even know why. Then the next day I went down and I did the scene, and it was totally fine. I realized, “OK, in my life I have the door closed. I need to open the door.”
How did you start opening the door? It’s exactly what you’re talking about in your most recent special, 2025’s Drop Dead Years, where sad men are only allowed to have, like, two emotions.
Yeah, that was the beginning of me starting to acknowledge other feelings. I will tell you what’s fucked up about my last special.

I thought that bit saying, “Why is the Ku Klux Klan still legal? Why is it that in those groups, the Proud Boys and all of them, there’s the white privilege where you can join a terrorist fucking organization?” I was thinking I’d get a lot of shit for that from racist people. Nothing. It was more people going, [mocking voice] “Do you think there’s a lot of sad men, Bill?” No one wanted to talk about the dangerous topic.

All of these years we watched [people] not do the right thing with a lot of other [countries], and now it’s happening here, and that’s why so much of the world’s like, “Well, yeah … you fucking deserve it.” But I think that we’re going to get on the other side of it.
“You’re gonna get punched. and it’s gonna hurt. But you take the hit and you get back up.”

Yeah, because the one thing I think people agree with on all sides is that people don’t want to live in an oppressive, not-free society, which is what we’re going towards. Just the amount of surveillance that they have on you and I — like, we’re not John Gotti in a social club. They have this level of surveillance on us, not because of what we’re doing but because of what they’re doing. Like, why the fuck do you need to know that I just went to 7-Eleven and got a Big Gulp? I got to walk around like Joe Pesci and [Robert] De Niro in Casino now, talking to my wife in my fucking driveway? Like, what are we doing here?
So what do you think it’s going to take for a change to happen?
I don’t know. It would have to be a fucking bloodbath. It would be like Braveheart, except everyone was wearing Lululemon shit.
Behind every massacre is a man in a suit, they say.
Let’s go back to that anger thing. So, how soon did this happen after you had taken that first big mushroom trip, which you said helped kind of open things up?

Yeah, the mushrooms helped me realize how fucked up I was. If you’re not feeling 99 percent of your feelings, how do you know that you’re sad or you’re depressed or whatever? So, the first time I took mushrooms, as they were coming on, it was the normal giggly sort of thing. And then, all of a sudden, this profound sense of sadness washed over me. So I left the room, and I was in this dark room, just, you know, having a bad trip. I started thinking about the people in my life. I’m like, “Is it my wife? No, I love her to death. Best thing that ever happened to me. I know it’s not my kids.” I just kind of went around, and then I finally ran out of stuff. And then the answer came: This is how you felt growing up. I was like, “Oh. Yep.”

Right? That bothered me. After that … I wasn’t really drinking at that point. But for like six weeks, I didn’t smoke a cigar. I didn’t do anything. I just wanted to work on myself, which is why I think that mushrooms are the best. It’s the only drug I’ve ever done that didn’t make me want to do more of it. It made me want to fix myself.

It’s funny, it’s such an East Coast thing: [Tough-guy voice] “Hey, man, don’t go out to West Coast and lose your edge.” What, don’t start enjoying my life? Don’t be a chill person to be around? In comedy, there’s this big thing of “Don’t get happy, you’re not going to be funny!” And it’s the exact opposite.

You can have access to all these emotions that you can add into your act, and you can revisit topics that you were looking at through the lens of anger and rage. This whole journey of being a comedian is when I stopped doing this and started doing a little more of that. Like, “Hey, Bill, maybe chicks aren’t psychos. Maybe you’re bringing something to the party, you know?” [Laughs.] My whole view on women is changed now. I look back on all of the dumb shit that I said, it had nothing to do with how I felt. I wanted to be married. I wanted to have kids. I just didn’t know how to do it. So what did I do? I blamed what I wanted. It’s stupid. I missed out on a lot of good times, being that brooding guy with this three-quarter Donnie Brasco leather jacket, hiding in the corner.
Only Nixon could go to China, and only Bill Burr can get guys to go to therapy and deal with their shit.

I know a lot of angry people that like my comedy. I want to tell them, “Look, if I can get on the other side of it, anybody can, because I was a first-ballot lunatic.” I didn’t want to be the angry guy.

My whole career, it’s “Oh, you’re the angry comic.” It was always embarrassing to me. Anger was embarrassing because it reminded me of my dad, who had no control, and I used to always be like, “I’m not going to be like him.” And what happens? You’re doing exactly what he was doing. So I always felt shame. Then that would make me hate myself, which made me go darker, which made me get angrier. I didn’t know how to get out of it. It was just this spinning-down thing.
When you started to lose the anger, were you afraid you had gotten rid of your creative fuel?

No, I felt liberated. Before, it was like, “You’re going to write a song on this piano — but you can only use these notes.” As opposed to, you can use the whole piano now. The best thing that happened to me, in terms of learning, was becoming a comedian. Because you learn the most through the failure of bombing. You can learn other things faster by just going into the same mindset.

Oh, recently. I was in Vegas, and I opened with that Luigi shit. Oh, my God! That ate a big dick. And then — this is what’s good about getting on the other side of my emotions. So it didn’t work, and rather than judge them and blame them, I went, “All right, I get it. You came to Vegas, you’re blowing off steam. I get it. I was wrong. I came out too hard. So … how’s everybody doing?” [Laughs.] And then, like, they were all laughing because I did, I came out guns a-blazing.

Yeah, bombing never goes away. If you’re continuing to try new jokes and push yourself, it’s a part of it. It’s like boxing. You’re gonna get punched, and it’s gonna fucking hurt. Even if you win. But you take the hit and you get back up.
You’re raising a son now, right?
Yeah. I’ve got a daughter and a son.
So how are you helping him avoid some of that “men can’t cry” shit?

I just let him be who he is. I let my daughter be who she is. And then I just go, “Hey, a little too much of this or that, guys! Ease up.” I expose them to all different kinds of music and sports and stuff, and I see what they gravitate towards. My wife is amazing with that. I learn a lot by watching her. And it helps that I remember what it was like to be a kid. To be scared, to not be listened to, and all of that awful stuff. I learned how to be a really good father by not doing what I saw. I remember the first time I felt it was working was when my daughter, who was probably two at the time, there was something that was upsetting to her. I was sitting on the stairs, and I said, “Well, come over here and talk to me about it.” And she walked over, and both of us just held each other’s hands. It was like … [Starts crying.] Sorry.
That’s all right. I don’t know what your growing-up situation was necessarily …
It was the exact opposite of that.
“This is not a battle of left and right. This is the working man vs. robber barons.”
It must have made you feel good to have an organic connection like that with your kid. That’s huge.

Yeah! Yeah, it is. I mean, it’s funny, because my kids are not afraid of me at all, which I love. But then sometimes when I’m going, “Dude, I’ve told you three times, go to bed,” they’re still just doing a dance, thinking I’m joking around.

They’re hilarious. They roast me. Like my daughter one time, I was like, “How are you still up? Go to bed. Come on. I’ve asked you like 10 times.” I said, “This isn’t fair.” And she just goes “Life isn’t fair.” I was like, “Shouldn’t I be telling you that?” And she comes back with: “Yeah, well, you didn’t.” I was like, “Well, I lost that one” [laughs]. They’re good kids. They’re emotionally intelligent, and you know, kind of everything I’m not.
Is there an itch that acting scratches that stand-up doesn’t?

Yeah. The collaborative thing. I really like working with other people and seeing what they’re gonna do. I like hearing other actors say a line and thinking, “Wow, I never would have thought to do it that way.” I’ve gotten better just watching the choices, and to see somebody fearless as an actor. The way I gravitated towards a fearless comedian, to then be like, “OK, what is being fearless as an actor?” And then seeing that, and it’s the same thing. Like, “Oh, that’s like some Dave Attell stuff, but in the acting world.”
How did doing Glengarry Glen Ross on Broadway for a four-month run make you think differently about acting?

It combined stand-up and acting. In stand-up, I say the thing, you guys react positively or negatively. I get immediate feedback, and silence is bad. On a set, silence is a good thing. If somebody doesn’t come up to you after a take, that means you did a good job. With theater, there’s feedback. And when you’re with the other actors, you’re seeing how everyone else does it and how it changes every night. It made me love theater. I was a typical sports guy. I thought theater was Cats. It’s like, I don’t want to watch a bunch of people dressed like fucking felines.

I never read plays growing up. That was for the kids that got beat up. I was trying not to get beat up in high school. So I went back and I read a bunch when we were doing Glengarry. Sam Shepard plays and The Motherfucker With the Hat. Just great stuff that made me want to do more of it.
I hear there’s a revival of Cats. You might want to look into that.
You started your podcast before Joe Rogan and Marc Maron started theirs, right?

Before they eclipsed me, you mean? “Bill, didn’t you do a podcast before those other guys became vastly more rich and famous than you?” [Laughs.] Yeah, I was there early. I still just do it into my phone. It’s just random thoughts. I don’t have guests a lot. I got into this to have fun, and I felt when you took it to the next level with a studio, employees, guests, it became a job. Not saying I would have done what Rogan and Maron did. I just kept it my way out of laziness.
When did you feel like you first found your voice as a comic?

I feel like I’m finding it now. Before, that was Traumatized Me. Fight-or-flight mode, alopecia, losing clumps of hair and shit. I was a fucking mess. That tropey sad-clown thing. How many years was I going to go up there and take out my childhood on the crowd?

When you were doing press for Drop Dead Years, you talked about how the country is divided and you wanted people to feel like they could find common ground at your show. How’s that working with the hour you’re touring now?

Oh, it’s been really fun. I just did a casino gig, and it was a really MAGA crowd, and my opener was a joke making fun of Trump, and half the room laughed, and then the other half really enthusiastically booed. So I was able to go up there, and just by what I was talking about, make it what I think it’s about.

This is not a battle of left and right. This is the working man versus this new era of robber barons. So I just was saying we got to stop these nerds with apps. They keep fucking over the working man. But then I was able to make fun of Trump, and they’re still laughing. And then I go, to the left, “Well, you know, you can’t laugh at them. You elected Joe Biden. I mean, both of these guys should be in a fucking home.” Like, we both kind of fucked up here.
How are you judging success now?

A lot of liberals don’t like me and a lot of conservatives don’t like me, which makes me feel like I’m doing something right. The extremes on both sides are pretty vocal, but I feel like the people in the middle aren’t like these butt-hurt idiots. I travel everywhere. Eighty-five percent of people are cool. They can listen to somebody. “Oh, that’s how you see it. OK, cool. You want to get a sandwich?”
Let’s end on something less fraught. How did you get into flying helicopters as a hobby?

I got into reading about the Federal Reserve, and I’m like, “The dollar could collapse at any moment. I live in L.A. I can barely get out of this city in two hours when it works. What happens when the shit hits the fan?” Up and out was the easiest way.
So this is your version of a mobile panic room?

The thing about a panic room is once you go in it, you can’t get the fuck out of there. The thing I like about a helicopter … I can put one gallon of fuel in there, maybe take off and fly the pattern. But I still have to come back. I have nowhere to go. There is nowhere to go. You should stay and fight. All these fucking people moving to other countries. It’s just, like, that’s not what you do. You stay and fight.

items.title: Martha Stewart Responds to Halloween Costume Backlash: ‘Homelessness’ Is ‘Something That I Care Deeply About’
items.description: Martha Stewart has issued a statement after drawing hefty backlash for dressing up as a homeless person for Halloween. The media mogul’s choice of costume for Saturday’s holiday, which included her dressed up in tattered clothing, dirt-inspired face makeup and
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: Martha Stewart has issued a statement after drawing hefty backlash for dressing up as a homeless person for Halloween. The media mogul’s choice of costume for Saturday’s holiday, which included her dressed up in tattered clothing, dirt-inspired face makeup and a sign that read, “I am hungry. Help me!!,” was quickly deemed offensive and in poor taste by fans. (The photo she’d posted of the costume to Instagram was promptly deleted.)

“I am distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention,” Stewart told Page Six in a statement issued on Sunday.

She continued: “Homelessness continues to remain one of America’s greatest challenges and ongoing crises, something that I care deeply about and I have spent a significant amount of time and effort supporting charities that combat this ongoing social epidemic.” The businesswoman also shared that she remains “committed to continuing to make a difference.”

On Saturday, Stewart also shared a carousel of images of her yard with festive decor captioned, “Halloween night Waiting for those who trick or treat!” In the days leading up to the holiday, Stewart appeared on “Today” to share Halloween entertaining ideas, “including my no-bake spiderweb cheesecake, witches’ brew, and a ghastly goulash,” she wrote on social media. “I always enjoy getting dressed up in fun and creative costumes when my busy schedule allows.”

Variety previously reported that Cate Blanchett is set to star as Stewart in the upcoming biopic “Good Thing” about the career of the lifestyle media mogul, with “Zola” director Janicza Bravo helming the project.

items.title: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Clayface’ Fighting for No. 1 in Quiet Halloween Weekend
items.description: A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, which includes a memorable discussion about the classic comedy routine “Who’s on First,” sparked questions about whether the movie itself could take first place over Clayface as the two films battled a
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, which includes a memorable discussion about the classic comedy routine “Who’s on First,” sparked questions about whether the movie itself could take first place over Clayface as the two films battled at the box office during a subdued Halloween weekend.

Sunday figures show the two movies still neck and neck for the top spot domestically, with directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s You Can See Everything looking like the early winner at $10.6 million in its third weekend to bring its North American cume to $63.8 million. Currently playing in 3,243 North American locations, the Oscar-buzzed documentary eyes its first No. 1 finish. It looks to decline around 43 percent for the weekend that saw the studios avoid releasing new titles as Halloween fell on a Saturday.

If this holds, the three-hour You Can See Everything would follow previous features True Grit, Argo and 1917 as films that hit No. 1 in their third frames. Despite the meager overall turnout for this weekend’s moviegoing, the domestic box office’s 2026 take of $8.46 billion still puts it around 20 percent ahead of last year’s total sum to this point, according to Rentrak.

Just behind You Can See Everything for the time being is Clayface, as filmmaker James Watkins’ body horror feature looks to gross around $10.4 million in its sophomore frame for a two-week North American sum of $44.1 million. Tom Rhys Harries and Naomi Ackie star in the $44 million-budgeted Warner Bros. release that marks DC Studios‘ third theatrical title for bosses James Gunn and Peter Safran after 2025’s Superman and this summer’s underperforming Supergirl. Clayface looks to decline around 56 percent for the weekend from 3,478 domestic theaters.

Overall, this weekend is headed for one of the lowest domestic totals of the year with $55.6 million, down a frightening 42.1 percent from last weekend, per Rentrak. This still marks a roughly 4.2 percent uptick over the $49 million collected from the equivalent weekend in 2025. Last year, Halloween fell on Friday as Black Phone 2 led the frame with $8.3 million in its third weekend.

“Historical challenges can spook studios away from launching a major film into the marketplace,” Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian tells The Hollywood Reporter of competition from parties and trick-or-treating on moviegoing’s biggest day of the weekend. He points out that the lack of a splashy opener “limits the opportunity for a major new release to give October a big closing boost. [But] the broader horror picture remains remarkable. A quieter Halloween weekend can coexist with an exceptionally strong year for the genre.”

In third place is Laika‘s stop-motion animated feature Wildwood, which earned around $7.5 million in its second weekend to bring its domestic sum to $25.8 million. Carey Mulligan, Peyton Elizabeth Lee and Jacob Tremblay lead the voice cast for director Travis Knight’s movie that eyes an impressive decline of around 38 percent from 2,712 North Americans theaters and was likely dinged by families’ weekend attention focusing away from cinemas. Wildwood has generated Academy Awards buzz and carries a 99 percent critics approval rating from Rotten Tomatoes, but it will need to continue to show legs, given its hefty reported production budget of $100 million.

Registering a similarly enviable hold with a decline around 28 percent is Black Bear’s Wicker, as the romantic fantasy grossed $4.1 million from 2,374 North American theaters for a domestic total of $13.2 million after its second weekend. Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgard star in directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer’s movie about a woman in a quiet village who gets a wicker husband. It holds a strong 94 Rotten Tomatoes score from critics.

Closing out the top five is Paramount and Legendary’s Street Fighter, picking up $3.2 million in its third weekend as its domestic cume reaches $53 million in its third weekend. Starring Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji, director Kitao Sakurai’s adaptation of the Capcom video game added $3.2 million internationally as the global total stands at $91.9 million for the $82 million-budgeted feature.

Likely landing in seventh place is Sony’s Resident Evil, which crossed $400 million at the global box office in its seventh weekend of release. Its projected $2.5 million domestically for the frame will bring the North American total to $157.3 million for director Zach Cregger’s Austin Abrams-led adaptation of the video game.

After launching on six screens last weekend, Sony Pictures Classics’ The Only Living Pickpocket in New York expanded to 1,112 North American locations for a sophomore frame of $1.9 million, likely in ninth place. Holding a $2.1 million cume, writer-director Noah Segan’s feature stars John Turturro as an aging pickpocket dealing with a theft gone wrong. In his review for THR, chief film critic David Rooney heralded it as “contemplative, cool-headed and transfixing.”

Despite the slow weekend, analysts see the box office as likely to pick up dramatically as the 2026 holiday corridor approaches. Remaining high-profile titles for 2026 include The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Avengers: Doomsday, Dune: Part Three and more.

“This is the first time since the pandemic that Halloween has landed on a Saturday, and studios are wise to avoid competing with parties or trick-or-treating events, on top of the usual packed football schedule in the States this time of year,” Fandango director of analytics and Box Office Theory founder Shawn Robbins tells THR. He notes that such a gap can precede a busy stretch, which is likely this year “as holiday moviegoing picks up, and the cadence of tentpole releases resumes, crescendoing with a December that may be one for movie theater record books and cap off a strong year for the industry.”
Next weekend sees the releases of The Cat in the Hat, Godzilla Minus Zero and Wild Horse Nine.

items.title: Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself at L.A. Gun Range
items.description: Michael Mann was hospitalized on Saturday after accidentally shooting himself at a gun range in Los Angeles, The Hollywood Reporter has learned.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: Michael Mann was hospitalized on Saturday after accidentally shooting himself at a gun range in Los Angeles, The Hollywood Reporter has learned.

“On Saturday, at a gun range, a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered resulting in a superficial injury to film director Michael Mann. He was treated and is being released,” a rep for the four-time Oscar-nominated filmmaker shared in a statement.

The Los Angeles Police Department said officers responded to The Range LA at around 4 p.m. for a call about shots fired. “Responding units’ investigation determined the shooting to be accidental. The subject was transported to a local hospital in stable condition,” authorities said.

Sources told TMZ that Mann was apparently trying to holster his gun during target practice at a sanctioned gun range when the firearm went off. He was later taken to a local hospital for minor injuries. Mann has been an experienced target shooter for decades.

Mann is currently in pre-production on Heat 2, which reportedly has Leonardo DiCaprio, Stephen Graham and Christian Bale attached to star. The film comes more than three decades after the 1995 crime drama Heat that starred Al Pacino, Robert De Niro, Val Kilmer and Jon Voight.

He’s also best known for directing 1981’s Thief, 1999’s The Insider, 2001’s Ali, 2004’s Collateral, 2006’s Miami Vice, 2009’s Public Enemies and 2023’s Ferrari, among others. Throughout his career, he’s received four Academy Award nominations, including best director, best picture and best adapted screenplay for The Insider, and best picture for 2005’s The Aviator.

items.title: Best Celebrity Halloween Costumes 2026: Paris Hilton as Britney Spears, Lisa Rinna as Kylie Jenner and More
items.description: Hollywood stars are celebrating Halloween with a wide range of costumes, from recreating iconic on-screen characters to paying tribute to fellow celebrities.
items.author: Lexi Carson; Hilary Lewis
paragraphs: Hollywood stars are celebrating Halloween with a wide range of costumes, from recreating iconic on-screen characters to paying tribute to fellow celebrities.

Whether it’s Camila Mendes and Madelaine Petsch channeling Betty and Wilma from The Flintstones, Kim Kardashian transforming into her daughter, North West, or Paris Hilton debuting multiple costumes throughout the holiday, celebrities are getting into the Halloween spirit.

Below, see a roundup of this year’s costumes from a host of stars, including some of The Hollywood Reporter’s favorites. (This is an ongoing story that will be updated throughout the weekend as more celebrities reveal their costumes.)
The Halloween superfan introduced a new character this year: Phish Boy, complete with impressive prosthetics that have become a signature of her costumes.

The Dynasty star, who is known for her elaborate Halloween costumes and often shares looks with her fellow Victorious alum Ariana Grande, opted for another niche look this year, dressing as Luke from the 1998 Disney Channel Original Movie Halloweentown.
Rapper Tyga is a Martian from Tim Burton’s 1996 sci-fi movie, Mars Attacks!
Tyga also dressed as vampire Count Orlok, as portrayed by Bill Skarsgard in Robert Eggers’s Oscar-nominated 2024 horror film Nosferatu.

The ‘Burbs actress paid tribute to Janet Jackson with one of her Halloween costumes this year, as she and her three-year-old son recreated Jackson’s iconic black-and-white 1995 music video for “Scream,” which she performed with her brother, the late Michael Jackson.
Camila Mendes & Madelaine Petsch
The Riverdale co-stars celebrated the holiday in duo costumes, channeling Betty and Wilma from The Flintstones.
In one of her several Halloween costumes so far this year, Paris Hilton recreated Britney Spears’ “I’m a Slave 4 U” performance at the 2001 MTV Video Music Awards.
Robert Downey Jr. and Pedro Pascal

Robert Downey Jr. and Pedro Pascal did a Marvel character switch this Halloween, dressing up as each other’s respective Avengers: Doomsday characters. Yes, the Oscar winner portrayed Reed Richards/Mister Fantastic of the Fantastic Four, and the Emmy nominee dressed up as Doctor Doom.

The Today show brought NBC’s 100th-anniversary celebration to Halloween, as the morning show hosts dressed up to highlight memorable programming from the past century. Dressed as an NBC page, Savannah Guthrie led a group of tourists, who closely resembled some Today hosts, through 30 Rockefeller Plaza. They first encountered Willie Geist as Tonight Show host Johnny Carson’s Carnac the Magnificent, followed by Dylan Dreyer as I Dream of Jeannie’s title character, played by Barbara Eden, and Al Roker as Eddie Murphy’s Saturday Night Live character Gumby. When the tour got to Must-See TV, Guthrie donned a second costume, dressing as Friends’ Rachel Green alongside Jenna Bush Hager’s Phoebe Buffay. The Today show also honored itself with Carson Daly dressing as Ella Langley to celebrate his Today PopStart segment. And NBC’s unscripted programming was also highlighted, specifically its Olympic coverage: Laura Jarrett dressed as Simone Biles and Craig Melvin transformed into Snoop Dogg, who’s become known for his memorable Olympics appearances in recent years. The real Martha Stewart even joined Melvin’s Snoop Dogg. And, to celebrate NBC’s holiday traditions, including the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade and Christmas in Rockefeller Center, Sheinelle Jones joined the Radio City Rockettes for a sparkly dance routine. Guthrie’s page even got a visit from 30 Rock page Kenneth Parcell, with Jack McBrayer reprising his role from the beloved NBC comedy that recently celebrated its 20th anniversary.

Live! With Kelly and Mark brought back former co-host Ryan Seacrest for its New Year’s Eve-inspired Halloween Shockin’ Eve. Seacrest appeared at the beginning of the show as the hosts honored Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Consuelos, dressed as the webslinger, swung through the New York streets as Ripa’s Yelena Belova held on. The hosts took the stage as Bad Bunny and Lady Gaga from the 2026 Super Bowl halftime show before changing costumes at the commercial break to Anne Hathaway’s Penelope and Matt Damon’s Odysseus in The Odyssey before they ended the show joined by producer Michael Gelman and DJ Deja Vu, with the whole Live team all dressed as Toy Story 5 characters. Live’s Halloween episode featured more than 60 costumes, including pretaped segments in which Ripa dressed as Inde Navarrette’s Nikki from Obsession, who can’t get enough of a different kind of Bear in Consuelos’ squishy creature, and Elizabeth Holmes as shown in You Can See Everything as part of a Traitors parody. Guest Lisa Rinna also got in on the action, dressing as Kylie Jenner alongside Gelman’s Timothee Chalamet, as Rinna and Gelman sported Jenner and Chalamet’s memorable orange looks from Marty Supreme’s Los Angeles premiere late last year.
Kim Kardashian dressed up as her daughter North West.
Hello, Barbie! Brandy’s costume this year was channeling the Mattel toy. “Being the first Black woman to have a Barbie made in my likeness will always mean so much to me,” she wrote on Instagram.
Usher and his wife and kids dressed up as the characters from Pixar’s Toy Story. “Happy Halloween from the Raymond family,” he wrote in his Instagram caption.
Talk about a deep cut: Comedian Rickey Thompson recreated Zendaya’s red carpet look from the 2011 premiere of Justin Bieber: Never Say Never.
Grammy winner Lizzo dressed up as Dolly Parton, who died in August. She later debuted another costume as Gina Byrams, Playboy’s first International Bunny of the Year in 1970.

Gotta blast! Teyana Taylor dressed up as Jimmy Neutron for Halloween this year. “BTS: Jimmy pants wasn’t letting me be great but STAY TUNED….. Jimmy, Goddard and Sheen gotta blastttttttt,” she captioned her video.

For Halloween this year, Zendaya’s longtime stylist Law Roach posted the actress channeling Halle Berry’s iconic Lanvin Fall 2000 ensemble that she originally wore to the New York City premiere of X-Men.
Model Alex Consani went full Spy Kids, dressing up as one of villain Fegan Floop’s Thumb-Thumbs from the 2001 film.

items.title: When the ‘Mommune’ Isn’t All It’s Cracked Up to Be
items.description: When Anilese Haney and her best friend, Nicole, were growing up outside of Eugene, Oregon, they used to fantasize about what their lives would be like when they were older. They wanted to be in each other’s weddings and hoped they would be pregnant together. B
items.author: Erica Schwiegershausen
paragraphs: When Anilese Haney and her best friend, Nicole, were growing up outside of Eugene, Oregon, they used to fantasize about what their lives would be like when they were older. They wanted to be in each other’s weddings and hoped they would be pregnant together. But by the time they were 25, Nicole was divorced with 3-year-old twins and a baby; Anilese was living with her boyfriend and her 3-year-old, but her relationship was on the rocks. “I told Nicole, ‘If we break up, I need you to move in with me.’ We’ve always wanted to live together. We’ve always wanted to raise our kids together,” Anilese says. Her apartment had four bedrooms, and they could each have their own bathroom. A few weeks later, Anilese and her boyfriend split, and Nicole moved in. “We were so excited. It was kind of like a dream come true,” says Anilese.

For the two mothers, living together wasn’t just a way to save money on rent. Combining their households under one roof made their lives easier in all sorts of ways. “My daughter’s dad was not helpful at all,” says Anilese. “He drank a lot, and he barely worked. He didn’t have a lot of motivation. My mom was helping us pay for diapers.” Moving in with Nicole, she felt as though she suddenly had an extra set of hands. The moms split groceries and shared clothes, and in the mornings, they helped get each other’s kids dressed and loaded up in the car. They dropped the kids off at their gym day care so they could work out together, and they decided to start a cleaning business. Anilese and Nicole both had split custody, so when the kids were with their dads, they would work long days and then lie around watching Love Island. When the kids were there, they had built-in playmates for crafts and movie nights. The arrangement seemed ideal for everyone — at least at first.

The economics of raising kids as a single mom has always been brutal. With inflation and soaring rents, moving in with another mom just makes sense: You can split the bills, switch off cooking dinner, and have someone there to watch the kids when you need to run an errand. On TikTok, plenty of women are taken with the idea. This summer, 38-year-old single mom Bernie Sinclaire went viral documenting her life sharing a three-bedroom apartment in Harlem with her best friend and their three kids, an idyllic-seeming living situation she calls “the mommune.” Sinclair is adamant she’ll never go back to living with a man. But even if you can find a mom willing to sign a lease with you, sharing a kitchen and a living room with another parent and their brood is a complicated proposition. What if your kids don’t get along or you have wildly different approaches to discipline? How do you avoid becoming a de facto babysitter? What if your roommate’s boyfriend decides to move in too?

For Kristen Dill and Rachel Zachry, becoming roommates was a last-ditch attempt to avoid having to live with their parents again. After she split with her husband, Rachel bought a four-bedroom house in Fort Worth, Texas. But once she moved in with her kids, who are 13, 11, and 9, she felt overwhelmed by the realities of homeownership. Her ex lived across the country, and she was working full time waiting tables. Between property taxes, insurance, and utilities, the bills were endless. She felt she was constantly behind. “I would wake up in the mornings completely anxious. Like, How am I supposed to do this without a man? My lawn needs to be mowed. I don’t even know how to fix a sink if it’s leaking.” Rachel was on the verge of selling the house when Kristen — who was going through a divorce of her own and had been crashing with her mom and stepdad — asked how she would feel about her and her 9-year-old daughter moving in. “I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, absolutely,’” says Rachel.

At first, they were just going to try it out for a week. Two months later, it still feels like the honeymoon phase. Sure, there were some kinks to work out early on; now, they don’t go into each other’s rooms without asking, and Kristen stays out of Rachel’s way when she’s trying to get her kids out the door in the morning. “It takes a lot of communication, just like a marriage would,” says Kristen. But as longtime friends, they take pride in anticipating each other’s needs. Someone is always there to move the laundry to the dryer, and they can tag-team cooking dinner and helping with homework. Kristen bakes sourdough and packs all the kids’ lunches the night before. She set up a Skylight smart calendar with a morning checklist to remind the kids to brush their teeth, wash their faces, and remember their water bottles and Chromebooks for school. “As the wife, you feel like you’re solely in control of taking care of the house and the kids, and also you still have to work. The dynamic between two moms or two best friends is so different,” says Kristen. “And there’s no sexual tension, like, After this I’m gonna have to go and have sex with my husband.”

But no matter how well you get along with your roommate, living with someone else’s kids comes with its own set of challenges. With babies and toddlers, noise is a constant, and even a house that seems spacious can quickly start to feel cramped. When a friend of a friend needed a place to stay, Shannon Foote was happy to let her and her 4-year-old move into a spare bedroom in the house she shared with her four kids outside of Reno, Nevada. But the woman’s daughter had a hard time going from being an only child to suddenly being one of five. They ended up having to stagger their custody schedule so the kids were together only a few days a month. In the end, the other woman decided living with four more kids was just too chaotic. “She was like, ‘I want to read a book in quiet,’” says Shannon, who adds that she gets it. “I mean, she was also sharing a bedroom with her daughter. That sucks.”

And like any living arrangement, when it goes wrong, it can really screw up your life. After Heather, a 37-year-old single mom in New Jersey, got divorced, she started renting a house with her son, who was 5 at the time. When she found out a childhood friend was getting evicted, it seemed like a no-brainer to invite her and her 4-year-old to move in and split the rent. “I said to her, ‘Neither of us have men, so why not?’” At first, everything seemed fine. Her new roommate worked long shifts as a nurse, so Heather would help out with day-care drop-off and pickup. Then things started to get weird. The roommate accused Heather’s son of hitting her daughter and wouldn’t let it go. One morning, her car was blocking Heather’s, but she refused to move it until Heather’s son apologized to her daughter. “She was yelling at me, and I started laughing,” Heather says. “She got really close to my face, and I bumped her, like, Back up.” The next thing she knew, they were on the ground wrestling in front of their children, who were terrified. After that, Heather told the woman she would have to move out — but she refused and called child protective services on Heather. In the end, she had to get a temporary restraining order to force the other woman to leave.

Then there’s the question of where men fit into the arrangement. Kim Cosby, a mother of four in Georgia, has lived with multiple single mothers, and she always tells them up front she doesn’t want boyfriends around. “I love to be half naked, in a spaghetti-strap shirt and leggings,” she says. She doesn’t want to “get fully dressed” just because her roommate’s boyfriend is coming over — and she doesn’t want men who aren’t family around her kids, either. She does a “heavy vetting process” before moving in with anyone. “I have rules and regulations: I don’t smoke, I don’t drink, and I don’t want those influences around my children.” She hasn’t had any problems yet. But others aren’t so lucky.

If you don’t take a hard line on keeping men out of the house, you may suddenly find your roommate’s boyfriend crashing there all the time. For Anilese and Nicole, things fell apart when Nicole started dating someone. “He was kind of a bum, in my opinion. He was basically homeless,” Anilese says. Since he didn’t have anywhere to go, he started staying with them — and brought along two kids of his own. The women had already been struggling to make ends meet; adding three people to the mix just felt impossible. Then Anilese also started seeing someone. “We were like, ‘What are we gonna do? We can’t all live here.”’ Finally, they had a blowout fight and Nicole moved out. The friends eventually made up, but they don’t plan to live together again.

Kristen and Rachel told me, as much as they love it, they know their current roommate situation won’t last forever. Kristen would be happy never to date a man again, but Rachel really wants another husband. When she starts dating someone, she’ll be up front about her lifestyle. “Like, this is what my household looks like. No, we’re not lesbians. We’re best friends trying to make this economy work.” She wants to make sure a man doesn’t come in and expect to kick out Kristen and her daughter: “And he better respect that. If he doesn’t, then that’s an absolute ‘no.’”

Still, as much as Rachel would like to remarry, she has yet to meet the “mature, fabulous” man of her dreams. “So it’s, like, either settle for a man I don’t like or have my best friend move in,” she says. “It was an obvious answer.”
- The ‘Sex Diaries’ That Brought Roommates Into the Mix
- ‘I Wish I Could Move Out, But My Parents Need the Rent Money’

items.title: Синоптик спрогнозировал наступление метеорологической зимы в Москве
items.description: Синоптик спрогнозировал наступление метеорологической зимы в Москве
items.author: Иван Адоньев
paragraphs: Синоптик спрогнозировал наступление метеорологической зимы в Москве

Метеорологическая зима в Москве, которая характеризуется устойчивым переходом среднесуточной температуры через ноль в сторону отрицательных значений, ожидается во второй половине ноября. До этого в столице завершится затянувшийся период тёплой осенней погоды, рассказал синоптик Евгений Тишковец.

В ближайшие выходные в Москве сохранится сухая и относительно тёплая погода. Ночью температура составит от нуля до плюс трёх градусов, днём — от плюс восьми до плюс 11. Осадки маловероятны, временами будет появляться солнце.

Октябрь в столице оказался на 3,2 градуса теплее климатической нормы, а количество осадков было на 54% ниже обычного. Среднемесячная температура составила плюс 9,2 градуса — столько же фиксировали в рекордно тёплом октябре 2020 года.
Первые снежинки в Москве могут появиться поздним вечером во вторник. Начиная со среды мокрый снег будет регулярно примешиваться к дождю, что станет началом климатического подсезона предзимья.

В ноябре среднемесячная температура в средней полосе России, в том числе в Центральном регионе, ожидается примерно на два градуса выше многолетней нормы. Для Москвы климатическая норма составляет около минус 3,3 градуса ночью и плюс 1,1 градуса днём.
Количество осадков ожидается близким к обычным значениям — для Москвы ноябрьская норма составляет около 52 миллиметров.

items.title: В Италии нашли гробницу возрастом 2300 лет, предположительно принадлежавшую жрице Деметры
items.description: В Италии нашли гробницу возрастом 2300 лет, предположительно принадлежавшую жрице Деметры
items.author: Данил Самойлов
paragraphs: В Италии нашли гробницу возрастом 2300 лет, предположительно принадлежавшую жрице Деметры

В итальянской Мандурии археологи обнаружили захоронение женщины, которая могла служить жрицей богини Деметры. О находке, представленной 29 октября в Лечче, сообщает Arkeonews со ссылкой на региональное управление охраны культурного наследия.
Вырезанную в скале погребальную камеру первоначально закрывали три крупные плиты. Снаружи исследователи прочитали женское имя, имя отца и слово thabara, которое связывают с жреческим статусом.

Внутри уцелели красные и синие надписи, орнамент и изображения, предположительно обозначающие храмовый ключ и сосуд для благовоний. Один из фрагментов текста может содержать имя, связанное с Деметрой.
Ранее гробницу разграбили, однако в ней остались бронзовые застёжки, серебряные кольцо и монета. Человеческие останки сохранились плохо, что затрудняет идентификацию погребённой.
Связь захоронения с культом Деметры пока не доказана. Специалисты продолжают расшифровку и планируют реставрацию расписных поверхностей.

items.title: «А нужен ли нам вообще перезапуск?» Как фанаты «Glee» реагируют на возвращение сериала
items.description: Сериал Райана Мерфи выходил с 2009 по 2015 год и растянулся на шесть сезонов, на протяжении которых зрители следили за отношениями героев, школьными драмами, соревнованиями хоров и каверами хитов — от Канье Уэста до Ареты Франклин.
items.author: Афиша Daily
paragraphs: Сериал Райана Мерфи выходил с 2009 по 2015 год и растянулся на шесть сезонов, на протяжении которых зрители следили за отношениями героев, школьными драмами, соревнованиями хоров и каверами хитов — от Канье Уэста до Ареты Франклин.

После завершения проекта шоураннер неоднократно говорил о возвращении к этой истории. В 2020 году в честь 11-летия сериала Мерфи опубликовал пост с идеей переснять пилотный эпизод с Леа Мишель, Беном Платтом и Бини Фелдштейн, но позже удалил публикацию. В 2022 году в подкасте, который ведут бывшие актеры «Хора» Кевин МакХейл и Дженна Ушковиц, Мерфи рассуждал, что можно было бы сделать с «Хором» — то ли ребут, то ли бродвейский мюзикл. Фанаты тогда не восприняли его слова всерьез.

В 2026 году настойчивому желанию Мерфи вернуться к проекту все же поверили. В июле в интервью People он отметил, что сериал снова становится популярным среди молодых зрителей, а уже в сентябре сказал, что закончил сценарий нового «Хора». Тогда же он добавил, что обсуждал возвращение примерно с десятью актерами оригинального состава. Теперь мы точно знаем, что проект увидит свет, но что это будет — продолжение истории или перезапуск, — неясно.

Кто снимется в новом сезоне, также точно не известно, но актриса Хизер Моррис намекнула, что вновь наденет форму чирлидерши Бриттани С.Пирс. «Бриттани С.Пирс все это время действительно пропадала в канализации. Но я здесь, чтобы сообщить вам: она жива, здорова… и возвращается», — написала актриса, опубликовав архивное фото со съемочной площадки.

Корд Оверстрит (Сэм Эванс) и Кевин МакХейл (Арти Абрамс) также намекнули на свое возвращение. После новостей о перезапуске Оверстрит написал: «Как же здорово снова быть вместе!» А МакХейл ответил: «Вызов принят» — на твит Genius от марта 2020 года о том, что Дрейк обошел «Хор» по количеству песен, попавших в американский чарт Billboard Hot 100. Источники Variety также сообщают, что Леа Мишель вновь исполнит роль Рейчел Берри в сериале.

Издание считает, что Джонатан Грофф сыграет эпизодическую роль Джесси Сент-Джеймса. Даррен Крисс, вероятно, тоже появится в сериале, учитывая, что он до сих пор исполняет многие песни Блейна Андерсона из «Хора». «Крис Колфер, сыгравший Курта Хаммела, две недели назад заявил, что ничего не слышал о потенциальной перезагрузке, но затем Колфер и Крисс воссоединились, чтобы спеть в Лондоне песню „Baby, It’s Cold Outside“ из сериала „Хор“. Совпадение? Мы так не думаем», — подчеркивает Variety.
На новость о новом сезоне «Хора» быстро отреагировали поклонники, и их мнения разделились.
«Лучший день в моей жизни».
«Только пусть это не будет ремейк».

«Клянусь, ты ненастоящий фанат „Хора“, если не ждешь провала. „Хор“ был плохим еще на момент выхода — в этом и заключалась его прелесть. Я вообще не надеюсь, что получится что-то хорошее, и я в восторге».

«А нужен ли нам вообще перезапуск „Хора“? Иногда лучше оставить что-то в прошлом. „Хор“ был продуктом своего времени. Не зря мир делится на эпохи до и после „Хора“ — это был уникальный момент в истории. Я не хочу смотреть, как Рейчел Берри перепевает Оливию Дин».
«Хм… Я обожал „Хор“, и планка была задана очень высоко. Если они собираются повторить этот эксперимент, надеюсь, у них получится достойное продолжение».

Блогер Лили Дока выпустила в своих соцсетях ролик, в котором отметила, что не знает, как реагировать на возвращение «Хора», радоваться или бояться. «Давайте бояться, потому что Райан Мерфи сейчас творит какую-то дичь с „Американской историей ужасов“», — ответил ей один из подписчиков. «Нам страшно? Да. Будем смотреть? Еще как», — добавил другой. «Боюсь, он испортит и этот перезапуск, но мне не терпится услышать все каверы из „Хора“!» — подытожил третий.

В оригинальном сериале актеры перепевали песни из мюзиклов — от «Бриолина» до «Злой», — а также хиты Мадонны, Бритни Спирс и Леди Гаги. В сериале также появлялись звезды Бродвея, среди которых Кристин Ченовет, Патти ЛюПон, Идина Мензел и Бернадетта Питерс. Музыка — то, на чем держался проект, и сейчас фанаты гадают, какие треки перепоют новые «хористы». «Они же сделают в перезапуске „Хора“ целый эпизод с музыкальным противостоянием Сабрины Карпентер и Оливии Родриго, да?..» — надеются фанаты, предлагая также треки Тейлор Свифт, Чаппелл Роан и Кендрика Ламара.

«Хор» вырастил целое поколение миллениалов и ранних зумеров и стал для них не просто сериалом о школьном хоре, а историей о принятии себя, поиске своего места и людях, с которыми можно быть собой. И несмотря на то, каким получится продолжение, люди массово выкладывают видео под песни из сериала, радуясь, что вновь смогут окунуться в подростковые будни.
