items.title: Sourav Ganguly’s ‘Bigg Boss Bangla’ Among Highlights as Indian Media Giant JioStar Revenues Climb 10%
items.description: JioStar, the Indian media giant backed by Reliance Industries, grew revenue from operations 10.1% year-on-year to INR68.1 billion ($710 million) in the July–September quarter despite a weak advertising market. Profit after tax fell 13.2% to INR11.5 billion ($1
items.author: Naman Ramachandran
paragraphs: JioStar, the Indian media giant backed by Reliance Industries, grew revenue from operations 10.1% year-on-year to INR68.1 billion ($710 million) in the July–September quarter despite a weak advertising market. Profit after tax fell 13.2% to INR11.5 billion ($120 million).

Former India cricket captain Sourav Ganguly hosted the first-ever “Bigg Boss Bangla,” which launched this quarter on streaming service JioHotstar. The reality franchise rolled out in six languages, and all editions together pulled in more than 90 million viewers in their first three weeks. That makes “Bigg Boss” the biggest entertainment property on the platform.
Reliance Industries credited JioStar’s revenue growth to subscriptions and to advertising on digital entertainment. Gross revenue rose 9.8% to INR79.4 billion ($829 million).

Margins came under pressure. EBITDA from operations dropped 10.5% to INR13.7 billion ($143 million), and the margin fell to 22.1% from 28.1% a year earlier. A 36.6% drop in investment income pulled total EBITDA down 13.6% to INR15 billion ($157 million). The quarter was also well below April–June, when JioStar booked INR109.5 billion ($1.1 billion) in revenue from operations.

JioHotstar averaged about 440 million monthly active users over the three months, up 10% on the prior year. In September, the platform relaunched under the JioHotstar name in the U.K., Canada and Singapore. Reliance said active subscribers in those three territories have grown about 30% since then.

The company also introduced “Pay Kisi Aur Se” (“Ask Others to Pay”), which lets users send a subscription payment request to a friend or relative. Reliance said the feature raised payment initiations by 10%. Subscribers on mobile plans now get up to two hours a month of viewing on connected TVs. The average JioHotstar viewer on a connected TV watches three times as much as one on a phone.

Watch time for entertainment content grew more than 15%, with Hindi and regional markets performing well. Reliance said titles including “India Ke Top 1%,” “Khatron Ke Khiladi,” “Hustle” Season 5 and “Bhojpuri Bawaal” strengthened JioStar’s position as the country’s top entertainment network.

“Resort” became the most-watched title in the streamer’s history, which Reliance cited as evidence that its bet on long-running series is paying off. Rajkumar Hirani’s “Pritam & Pedro” set the platform record for a short-running series. “Heart Beat” Season 3 and new series “Court” both opened strongly, and Hindi drama “Thukra Ke Mera Pyaar” Season 2 improved on its first season. Tadka also grew its catalog, adding nearly 100 titles spanning reality, sports and other categories.

In sports, the England–India cricket series gave JioHotstar its biggest audience yet for a bilateral series played abroad. Wimbledon, the U.S. Open and the opening weeks of the 2026–27 Premier League season drew steady audiences and were monetized more effectively, according to the company. JioStar also expanded its commerce integrations, which had been limited to cricket, to all three events.

The results came two days after Jio Platforms, Reliance’s separate telecom and digital arm, listed on Indian stock exchanges. Reliance said the INR301.9 billion ($3.15 billion) IPO is the largest in India to date. Mukesh Ambani, Reliance’s chairman and managing director, said the issue was subscribed more than 22 times.

items.title: Patrick Stewart Changed Genre Acting Forever With ‘Star Trek’ and ‘X-Men’
items.description: I will never claim to be a true Shakespeare buff, save for having read plays like “Romeo & Juliet” or “Julius Caesar” in school many years ago. But ever since I learned of the death of Sir Patrick Stewart, a line from “Hamlet” has been at the forefront of my m
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: I will never claim to be a true Shakespeare buff, save for having read plays like “Romeo & Juliet” or “Julius Caesar” in school many years ago. But ever since I learned of the death of Sir Patrick Stewart, a line from “Hamlet” has been at the forefront of my mind.
“He was a man, take him for all in all, I shall not look upon his like again.”

They quite simply do not make men like Patrick Stewart very often. He was a man of incredible gravitas, a man of dignity and grace. His baritone voice could stir you to action or tears in equal measure, often within the space of a single scene.

Yet he also possessed a remarkably sharp sense of humor, never taking himself so seriously that he was unwilling to do or say truly outlandish things that made you laugh even harder given his well-honed Shakespearean bearing. I can’t think of Stewart as Avery Bullock on the animated series “American Dad” saying lines like “You are a complicated man, Smith. I would love to do mushrooms with you” and not burst out laughing.
To put it simply, Patrick Stewart was not just an actor. He was an Actor, capital A.

Every fiber of his being was devoted to the pursuit of perfection in his craft. Even when he was of an age when he could have easily walked away and lived a comfortable life of leisure anywhere in the world, he continued to pursue work on the stage and screen. Because acting drove him, always striving to be better than he was before.

And that, I think, is what I found so inspiring about him. Stewart’s iconic performances did not just leave you in awe of his ability; they made you want to be better. To look inside yourself and tap into the better angels of our nature. You wanted to live up to the example that he set, for that example represented the finest qualities of humanity.

Stewart will probably never get the credit he deserves for how he changed this business. While everyone will point to stars like Robert Downey Jr. for the shift in perception around genre content like superhero movies and shows, Stewart was breaking new ground in that way more than two decades before the MCU came into existence.

“Star Trek” was still popular before “The Next Generation” debuted due to reruns of the original series and the many movies the original cast did together, but it was not considered high art by any means.

Stewart changed that. He brought years of experience from the Royal Shakespeare Company to the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, turning the character not just into a starship captain, but rather a universally recognized noble leader that even a casual viewer would no doubt follow into the darkest corners of the galaxy.

That ability and dedication elevated the entire show. His “TNG” castmates have often spoken of the fact that the bar Stewart set as Picard inspired them to up their game. Life imitated art as he became the show’s leader both onscreen and off, bringing “Star Trek” to a new generation and cementing Picard as one of the greatest characters in Hollywood’s history.

An actor achieving so much with one character is the kind of thing you can hang a career on. But Stewart brought that same level of power and skill to the “X-Men” film franchise as Professor Xavier, blowing away the dogma of the time surrounding the campy nature of movies based on comic book characters.

Professor X was the teacher we wish we all had growing up. He was not mean, nor overly strict, nor immovably rigid. He was kind and gentle, but with an unquestionable authority that he wielded with the tender care that children (and even adults) need.

To see him play opposite his dear friend and fellow acting legend Ian McKellen’s Magneto was to see two men at the top of their game fully committed to performances that some more self-serious actors would never deign to attempt. Now, every actor worth their salt is lining up to be in the next big superhero film. That simply would not be the case were it not for Patrick Stewart.

While “Star Trek” and “X-Men” are often the first roles modern audiences associate with Stewart (myself included), I would be remiss to not acknowledge the decades of work he did across theater, film and television outside of those franchises. He possessed an almost unmatched range, playing every single role to the best of his ability no matter how small. Whether hero, villain, or comic relief, you never had to be concerned about whether Stewart would deliver something memorable.

I had the privilege of meeting Stewart in person just once. A friend and colleague was doing a cover story for Variety tied to the launch of “Star Trek: Picard” in early 2020. We were both big Trekkies, so he worked it out so I got to be on set for the cover’s photo and video shoot. The idea was that I would interview Stewart for a career retrospective video that would be released alongside the print story.

They say never meet your heroes, but those people never met Stewart. He was exactly what I hoped he would be. He was professional, courteous, and so, so funny. He wasn’t feeling well that day, so he asked if we could limit the number of video interview questions to spare his sore throat. I said that was fine, I would simply cut out my 10 or so questions about “American Dad.” To my great pleasure, he laughed.

What struck me the most about interviewing him that day was how he would take questions about himself and turn them into praise for his co-stars and collaborators. It was never about him or his ego. It was about making the best work possible and acknowledging all those who contributed to that process.

Now, at 86 years old, Stewart has left us. The world is worse off with his absence, but the lifetime of hard work and love that he leaves behind will endure as he takes his well-deserved place among the stars.
Hailing frequencies closed, sir.

items.title: Reese Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine Cuts 50% of Employees After Actress Buys Back Company
items.description: Reese Witherspoon‘s Hello Sunshine is majorly shrinking.
items.author: Selome Hailu
paragraphs: Reese Witherspoon‘s Hello Sunshine is majorly shrinking.

Earlier this month, Witherspoon bought her production company back from Candle Media, the Blackstone-backed label that had acquired a controlling stake in 2021. With the support of the French conglomerate Mediawan, the actress was reportedly able to reacquire the banner for just a fraction of the $900 million that Candle Media had paid for it. Now, after just a few weeks in the driver’s seat, Witherspoon has let go some 30 employees — roughly 50% of Hello Sunshine’s staff.

Variety learned the layoff news from multiple sources, who noted that Hello Sunshine will now focus primarily on film and television projects and the Reese’s Book Club brand, with the direct-to-consumer division being gutted. Reps for Hello Sunshine declined a request for comment.

Though Witherspoon and Mediawan’s control of Hello Sunshine is new, the company is no stranger to layoffs. Under Candle Media’s leadership, it saw at least four rounds of staff reduction in the last two years alone, impacting the unscripted department and the Gen Z-oriented lifestyle brand Sunnie in particular. Candle Media also shuttered Hello Sunshine’s kids and animation unit in 2023. In 2024, it consolidated its live-action division, including that of Hello Sunshine, into Candle Studios, which was led by Hello Sunshine CEO Sarah Harden until she stepped down a year later.
When Witherspoon re-acquired Hello Sunshine, she wrote in a statement that “the best is still ahead.”

“Mediawan has built a global, independent studio by putting creators first. That has always been my vision for Hello Sunshine,” her statement said. “I’m investing alongside Mediawan and joining Pierre-Antoine Capton and his teams because this is the perfect home for this new media landscape. It’s also a homecoming. Peter Chernin and Jesse Jacobs believed in Hello Sunshine from day one. I’m deeply proud of what our incredible team has built, and grateful to Blackstone and Candle Media for their partnership and unwavering support.”

items.title: ‘Harry Potter’ HBO Series Casts Sorting Hat, Nearly Headless Nick, and More Hogwarts Ghosts and Portraits
items.description: HBO‘s upcoming “Harry Potter” series is casting Revelio on some more Season 1 roles.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: HBO‘s upcoming “Harry Potter” series is casting Revelio on some more Season 1 roles.

David Threlfall (“Shameless,” “Nightsleeper”) has been cast as the voice of the Sorting Hat, while Leo Bill (“The Living and the Dead,” “Alice in Wonderland”) will play Gryffindor House ghost Nearly Headless Nick. Andrew Brooke (“PhoneShop,” “The Agency”) will play Slytherin House ghost The Bloody Baron. Daniel Fearn (“Things You Should Have Done,” “Slow Horses”) will play The Fat Friar, house ghost for Hufflepuff. And Laura Smyth (“Baby Reindeer”) will play The Fat Lady, the portrait that guards the entrance to Gryffindor House.
Bill is repped by Curtis Brown. Brooke is repped by United Agents. Smyth is repped by United Agents. Fearn is repped by GDA Management. Threlfall is repped by Independent Talent.
Season 1 of the show, based on “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone,” will debut on HBO and HBO Max on Dec. 25. It features an expansive cast, which includes:

Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger, Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley, John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagall, Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape, Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid, Rory Wilmot as Neville Longbottom, Lox Pratt as Draco Malfoy, Leo Earley as Seamus Finnigan, Elijah Oshin as Dean Thomas, Tristan Harland as Fred Weasley, Gabriel Harland as George Weasley, Ruari Spooner as Percy Weasley, Alessia Leoni as Parvati Patil, Sienna Moosah as Lavender Brown, Finn Stephens as Vincent Crabbe, William Nash as Gregory Goyle, Warwick Davis as Filius Flitwick, Sirine Saba as Pomona Sprout, Daniel Rigby as Vernon Dursley, Bel Powley as Petunia Dursley, Paul Whitehouse as Argus Filch, Johnny Flynn as Lucius Malfoy, Bertie Carvel as Cornelius Fudge, Luke Thallon as Quirinus Quirrell, Katherine Parkinson as Molly Weasley, Amos Kitson as Dudley Dursley, Gracie Cochrane as Ginny Weasley, Richard Durden as Cuthbert Binns, Louise Brealey as Rolanda Hooch, Bríd Brennan as Poppy Pomfrey, Leigh Gill as Griphook, Anton Lesser as Garrick Ollivander, Harry Gilby as Charlie Weasley, Jasper Talbot as James Potter, and Hannah Chinn as Lily Potter.

Work is already underway on Season 2, which is based on “Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets.” New cast members already announced for that season include: Kit Harington as Gilderoy Lockhart, Bonnie Hill as Ginny Weasley, Lenny Rush as Dobby, Billy Barratt as Tom Riddle, Rafe Spall as Arthur Weasley, Molly Hewitt-Richards as Moaning Myrtle, and Jasper Ambrose as Colin Creevey.

Season 1 is written and executive produced by Francesca Gardiner. Mark Mylod will executive produce and direct multiple episodes of the series for HBO in association with Brontë Film and TV and Warner Bros. Television. The series is executive produced by author J.K. Rowling, Neil Blair, and Ruth Kenley-Letts of Brontë Film and TV, David Heyman of Heyday Films, Laura Neal, and Jon Brown.

items.title: 2026 Daytime Emmy Awards: ‘General Hospital’ Wins Best Daytime Drama
items.description: The 2026 Daytime Emmy Awards were presented Friday night, with General Hospital taking home the top prize of best daytime drama.
items.author: Hilary Lewis
paragraphs: The 2026 Daytime Emmy Awards were presented Friday night, with General Hospital taking home the top prize of best daytime drama.

The series, which went into Friday night’s show up for 13 awards, won three other awards and saw its Genie Francis receive the lifetime achievement award. Beyond the Gates also won four awards, with star Tamara Tunie winning best actress in a daytime drama series. Best actor in a daytime drama went to The Bold and the Beautiful‘s Scott Clifton.

Tunie, who won her first Daytime Emmy, paid tribute to the “host of Black actresses who paved the way for me, and I feel them as I stand here tonight, beginning with the legendary Cicely Tyson, the first Black woman to appear on a daytime television show, The Guiding Light.”
Fellow best actress nominee Heather Tom, from The Bold and the Beautiful, was eyeing a record-setting seventh trophy, which would have made her the most awarded actress in daytime history.

The Young and the Restless led this year’s nominees with 18 nominations. Though it only won three awards, two of those came in the supporting performer categories. Roger Howarth was named best supporting actor, and Beth Maitland was named best supporting actress.

The Kelly Clarkson Show won five awards, including best daytime talk series, but the singer-host of the now-completed talk show didn’t appear to be at the Daytime Emmys. And Clarkson didn’t win the award for best daytime talk series host. Instead that honor went to fellow former talk show host Sherri Shepherd, whose eponymous talk show was canceled after four seasons.

Other notable winners include Tracee Ellis Ross, who won best travel and adventure program for her Solo Traveling show; Keke Palmer, who won for her work executive producing Glam Through the Ages; and Ina Garten, who won best culinary host for her Be My Guest Food Network series, which was named best culinary instructional series.

Midway through the ceremony, NATAS chair Terry O’Reilly offered a timely, political speech, just days ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Speaking about a congressman who was jailed in 1798 after criticizing the president in print, O’Reilly highlighed the power of the people.
“The free press in 1800 was not saved by a court. It was saved by citizens who were engaged and informed,” he said.

Turning to the present day, O’Reilly called out “the most sustained effort to control what Americans see and hear in this country that were faced in my lifetime.” He cited specifically journalists being banned from covering the Pentagon and president, the DOJ antitrust investigation into the White House TV press pool and the challenge to the news exemption enjoyed by late night and daytime programs, including The View.

“It is not much of a leap, from silencing political speech, to suppressing creative expression,” O’Reilly added. “The characters, the storylines, the points of view that someone in power decides are no longer welcome. Here, in the cradle of Hollywood, this town of all towns, we know where that can lead. We have seen what happens when those in power begin drawing up lists of people and pops and ideas that they are willing to label as un-American. We should never wish to see that again.”
Turning to the “consequential” midterms on Tuesday, O’Reilly issued a call to those in the audience: “Let’s stand together to resist those who would seek comfort in a quieter media.”

And NATAS additionally inducted a number of individuals into its Gold and Silver Circle Society, recognizing industry leaders who’ve demonstrated enduring contributions to television through their 50 or 25 years in industry. The 2026 Gold Circle inductees are Allen Media Group CEO Byron Allen, performer Patrika Darbo, actor-director-producer Francesca James and host-producer Meredith Vieira. The Silver Circle inductees are Fox TV Stations executive vp, programming and development Stephen Brown and announcer warm-up host Rubin Ervin.
The Hollywood Reporter won its first Daytime Emmy, taking home the award for best arts and popular culture program for THR’s Off Script roundtable series.
Fellow PMC brand IndieWire additionally won best editing for a daytime studio program for its craft roundtables, with Trevor Wallace accepting for the brand.
The 53rd Daytime Emmy Awards ceremony took place on Friday, Oct. 30 at the Hollywood Palladium.

items.title: William Shatner, Seth MacFarlane, Hugh Jackman, Minnie Driver, More Remember Patrick Stewart: “He Was a Singular Talent”
items.description: Patrick Stewart‘s former co-stars and fellow Hollywood notables and executives are paying tribute to the sci-fi icon following his death at age 86.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: Patrick Stewart‘s former co-stars and fellow Hollywood notables and executives are paying tribute to the sci-fi icon following his death at age 86.

The actor, best known for playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor X in X-Men, died on Wednesday after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” his longtime rep Kelly Bush Novak previously shared.
Kevin Feige, Ian McKellen, William Shatner, Seth MacFarlane, Hugh Jackman, Minnie Driver, Marvel Studios and Lea Thompson are among those who have taken to social media to remember Stewart.

Feige, the head of Marvel Studios, shared in a statement with The Hollywood Reporter, “I’ll never forget the first time I saw Sir Patrick Stewart on the set of the first X-Men. After years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe — and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas. Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor.”

“It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him,” he added. “His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.”

McKellen, who played Magneto/Erik Lehnsherr opposite Stewart in the original X-Men franchise, shared a lengthy tribute on X. “Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love,” he wrote in part.

Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk alongside Patrick in 1994’s Star Trek: Generations, wrote on X, “What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed.”

Jackman, who starred as Wolverine in several X-Men films, shared in a tribute on Instagram, “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”

Marvel Studios also shared on social media, “All of us at Marvel Studios are deeply saddened by the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart. Sir Patrick brought Professor Charles Xavier to life with extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from X-Men to Logan to Avengers: Doomsday. He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman. Our hearts go out to his wife Sunny, his children, his friends, and the countless fans around the world whose lives he touched with his art.”

MacFarlane, who worked with Stewart on numerous projects, including Family Guy, Ted, Blunt Talk and American Dad!, took to Instagram, writing, “Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us. I grew up as a fan, and was later gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend, working with him for many years on “American Dad!”, “Family Guy”, and “Ted”. He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come.”

“I remember exchanging emails with him a number of years ago when he was beginning day 1 of a new film,” MacFarlane continued. “He commented to me that he always walked onto a new set feeling like the biggest novice there. My stunned reaction was the same as anyone’s would be. I said, “Patrick, if you feel that way, the rest of us are screwed.” We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet.”

Minnie, who starred in 2017’s The Wilde Wedding with Stewart, wrote, “Is this year some kind of portal to a much, much better place that all the greatest people know about and so have gently made their exits ? Dearest Patrick. Who always had the best advice, the funniest story, the patience to listen. I’m just bereft. All love to your family, and you, in my heart forever.”

Jonathan Frakes, who played Commander William Riker in Star Trek: The Next Generation series with Stewart, posted on his Instagram Story, “Rest in peace my friend.” Wil Wheaton, who also played Wesley Crusher in the series, shared a photo of him with Stewart on Instagram with the caption, “Godspeed, Captain.”

Thompson, who directed Stewart in two episodes of Star Trek: Picard, shared on social media, “This astonishing actor was kind enough to take a chance on me as a director. Always hardworking intelligent and so very good you could play the whole scene on him. @sirpatstew Patrick Stuart was indeed a Sir. To sir with love. #rip you were one of a kind.”
Kumail Nanjiani shared on Bluesky, “Sir Patrick Stewart was the best. I don’t know what else I can say.”

George Takei, who played Lieutenant Hikaru Sulu in Star Trek: The Original Series, wrote on Threads, “Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend. As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.”

items.title: Canadian Rock Icon Bryan Adams Takes Aim at Trump, Says His Protest Song Gets Standing Ovations in Red States (Exclusive)
items.description: He never says him by name — not in the songs and not in this interview.
items.author: Seth Abramovitch
paragraphs: He never says him by name — not in the songs and not in this interview.
But there can be no mistaking who Bryan Adams is taking aim at in his recent musical output, a string of Canadian protest songs like “51st State” and his latest, the plaintive “Lake Ontario.”
Adams has Donald Trump on the brain.
Both of those songs appear on How’s It Goin’, a Canadian concept album which drops Nov. 6 and features a dozen new tracks about Adams’ homeland.

It’s the 17th studio album for the rocker — whose catalog of indestructible hits includes “Summer of ’69,” “Run to You” and “(Everything I Do) I Do It for You” — and easily his most politically pointed, having found a new muse in the deterioration of relations between his homeland and the United States.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has placed punishing tariffs on Canadian goods, repeatedly threatened to make Canada the “51st state” and even ordered Lake Ontario renamed “Lake America” in U.S. federal records, inflaming tensions with the country’s longtime ally north of the 49th parallel.

Adams, for one, has had enough. He checked in with The Hollywood Reporter from a tour stop in Las Vegas — he’s in the middle of a five-show run at the Wynn — to share where his head is at these days. It’s firmly grounded in the waning months of 2026, about as far as you can get from the summer of ’69.
I’ve lived in L.A. for 25 years, but I grew up in Montreal. I’m still very much a proud Canadian. And I’ve got to say, listening to “Lake Ontario,” I got a little choked up.
Wow, that’s super nice. Now wait till you hear the rest of the album.
Half my family is still there, and it’s been a really rough couple of years. You put those dark feelings into these angry, beautiful words that really helped me process it a bit.
I mean, it’s not even angry.
It’s not angry. It’s stating the facts. I’m just commenting on current affairs and feeling the temperature in the room, basically.
So you might not be angry, but I know people there are very angry.
No, I mean, listen, I might be angry, but I don’t think the songs are angry. I think there’s a lot of irony in there.

And they’re heartfelt and funny. But it’s helping process what feels like a betrayal. You say it in the song: We’ve had so many years of peace and harmony, and it just takes “one dude” — and I’m wondering if “dude” was the original word you wanted to use — to fuck it all up.
Yeah, “dude” was the original word. There are other expletives you could put in there, but I consider myself respectful as well, even under the circumstances.

But the thing I really wanted to say is that if you have that much power, why would you not want to channel it for good? You could do so much good in the world with that much power, and it’s just not happening.
So I think that’s the thing that perplexes me more than anything. Put Canada aside for one second and just look at the global situation. It’s baffling.
How did the idea for the album come to you? Did it come out of this frustration?

It started out that I was asked to write a song for a documentary on Canada, about Canada’s East Coast. When I write, I don’t just focus on one thing. I just start writing. Looking back on my notes, I noticed there were a few things I had that were potentially interesting.

So I went down and finished that one, then I finished another one, and then I started getting into the current affairs thing. Before I knew it, I had three or four songs that seemed like part of a concept album. So I just kept going, and the whole album was written and recorded in three months.
“51st State,” that was the first song on the album that was quite political. How did people react to it?

We debuted that song in St. Louis on our tour this summer, and we weren’t sure how it was going to go down in America. But the first night we did it, standing ovation. Second night we did it, standing ovation. Got into Texas, into the red states, standing ovation.

And I suddenly thought to myself, I’m not sure that the people in this country, in America — I’m in Las Vegas at the moment — I’m not sure everybody agrees with what’s going down. And that was the way of testing the temperature in the room, because if you play it live, you can see automatically what people think. We were getting just full-on cheers.
Well, we’ll see in a few days what people really think, with the Nov. 3 election.
It’s not worth predicting it at all. I’m just writing my truth.

I want to bring up this viral thing that happened, and I return to it whenever I want to smile. It’s when that drunk guy came onstage during “Summer of ’69,” and you let it happen, and then you continued the song without missing a single beat. Not only is it funny, but it says something about you, I think.
A lot of people would have been angry, would have been reactive, would have said, “Get this guy off the stage!” But you let the universe just happen.
That’s what I’m getting at. I feel that I saw the real you at that moment.

Well, that’s nice. I think that’s actually very much what I am like. I let the universe do its thing. And when I saw that guy coming, I mean, I could have easily backed off, but I saw him coming and just thought, “Go for it, have a crack.”
As he climbed onto the stage, he whacked his head. And I remember that moment, thinking, “He’s not going to make it all the way up here.” But he did. Oh dear. I’m glad somebody filmed it.
Since we’re on the subject of “Summer of ’69.” I’m just curious, how much of those lyrics are true? Do you remember your summer of ’69? Did you really have a band with friends?
The song is obviously bittersweet, and it’s a song of nostalgia, but it’s not about the year.
Someone told me it’s about another kind of 69. I was like, “There’s no way.”
Well, it’s just a metaphor. It’s about first love. It’s about first figuring out where you’re going, what you’re doing, and it’s about reflecting on how that summer went.
But there’s no double entendre in there.
OK then! My friend is right. I was like, “Are you crazy? No, it’s about the summer of 1969!”
Nowhere in the song do I say [1969].
Where did you get your first real six-string?
Well, I’m glad he got it for you.

items.title: How Vaginal Fillers Gave Me My Life Back Postpartum
items.description: I hit my breaking point on a Monday night outside a club in Hollywood.
items.author: Casey Gates Frey
paragraphs: I hit my breaking point on a Monday night outside a club in Hollywood.
I had been riding high, emerging in the afterglow of the dance floor. I bet no one even knew I was a mom, I thought, strolling back to my car-seat-filled SUV.

Then I looked down. A puddle of urine had spread across my crotch, identical to when my toddler refuses to stop playing and has an accident. I had been savoring this moment of rare freedom from my responsibilities, but my body once again betrayed me.

I began to struggle with incontinence after the birth of my older daughter in 2020. At first, I thought the liquid that sometimes dribbled out of me without warning was leftover amniotic fluid. At my postpartum checkup, though, my doctor told me I was actually peeing myself. She referred me to pelvic-floor physical therapy and assured me that would likely solve the problem.

But soon I was pregnant again. My second daughter, whom I delivered vaginally, weighed a whopping ten pounds, ten ounces. After her birth, my incontinence got even worse, but with two young kids, I had my hands full.

I wasn’t entirely passive about the problem. I followed my doctor’s advice and did physical therapy — my bird dogs, my squats, and my bridges. I did my effing Kegels. I told myself that because I experienced incontinence only on occasion and managed it relatively well by modifying my activities, I probably wasn’t eligible for any other treatment. Oh, you had a kid and now sometimes you pee when you sneeze? Welcome to the club, I told myself. For three years, I accepted sporadic urine leakage as my new normal.

But my new normal began to weigh on me. Not long after my little “oopsie” on the dance floor, I was mindlessly scrolling social media hoping to stumble upon some hidden gem that would change my life. I found a post from a woman who said she had also struggled with postpartum incontinence and had gotten vaginal fillers to solve the problem. I was sat.

At my annual physical, I brought up the idea with my primary-care physician. After I assured her that I didn’t mean “labial puffing” — a.k.a. restoring volume of the labia for aesthetic purposes — she referred me to a urogynecologist named Dr. Michele Torosis. At my first appointment, Torosis listened to my symptoms and performed a cough stress test. She then formally diagnosed me with stress urinary incontinence, or SUI, the involuntary leakage of urine caused by sudden physical pressure or strain on the bladder and urethra. SUI can occur after having kids because pregnancy and childbirth stretch, weaken, and sometimes damage the complex system of muscles, nerves, and tissues that normally hold urine in the bladder, Torosis told me, adding that you’re at higher risk if you’ve had a vaginal delivery.

I was also given a more thorough explanation of these so-called fillers, which are officially called “bulking agents.” The treatment consists of injecting a soft gel into the walls of the urethra, the tube that carries urine out of the bladder.
This solution to my woes is relatively new. The material used for the treatment was approved by the FDA only in 2020, and Torosis says it has made the procedure much easier to do.
“We’ve actually seen on a national scale the rates of bulking have gone up,” she says.

Not until Torosis performed a pelvic exam on me during my appointment did I realize how much shame I’d been carrying over my incontinence. She confirmed that my pelvic muscles felt strong and that I had good control. It was liberating. I’d done weeks of physical therapy, Kegels, and everything else I was supposed to do to prevent leaks, then blamed myself when it didn’t work. But the problem wasn’t just my pelvic muscles.

Torosis tells me that while pelvic-floor physical therapy can be hugely helpful in regaining strength postpartum, it alone can’t cure more severe cases of incontinence. Johanna Hanley, the Los Angeles–based physical therapist I worked with, agrees. She says she sees patients racked with “shame and guilt” about birthing experiences over which they had no control.

“Sometimes, it’s just how we’re made and the size of our baby — a confluence of factors we can’t necessarily control in the moment,” Hanley tells me. “We do the best we can, but at some point, we may need more of an intervention. And that’s also okay.”

After years of adapting, avoiding, and modifying how I moved through life, solving my SUI took only about 15 minutes. The doctor inserted a numbing jelly into my urethra, followed by a local anesthetic before the fillers, and the pain was mostly tolerable. The sensation felt similar to having an extremely full bladder. No one directly said “Wow, what a champ” in response to my bravery, but I could tell they were thinking it.
The immediate discomfort subsided within a couple of hours, and I was back to weight lifting the very next day. But the real triumph for me? It worked.
Two days after my procedure, I went dancing and stayed magically dry. I tried jogging for the first time in years. No leaking.

According to Torosis, the treatment is expected to last about two or three years, at which time I can go back and get the fillers again. But I’ve also learned I am now in a position to train my muscles in a way I wasn’t able to before the treatment, so it’s possible I may be able to restore better control.

Either way, I am thrilled to know I will be out on those streets running, dancing, and doing dry-ass dead lifts for decades to come. Last week, I even said “yes” to a moms-only potato-sack race at my daughter’s preschool — an act of public-facing jumping I would never have done pre-fillers. And I won.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: October 30, 2026
items.description: Positive energy between the sun and moon (in water signs Scorpio and Cancer, respectively) improve your chances of having a cheerful morning. But things are likely to get more contentious in the afternoon, when Mercury and Mars (in Scorpio and Leo) square off.
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: Positive energy between the sun and moon (in water signs Scorpio and Cancer, respectively) improve your chances of having a cheerful morning. But things are likely to get more contentious in the afternoon, when Mercury and Mars (in Scorpio and Leo) square off. Expect to encounter some stubbornness and impatience in those around you. Avoid initiating conversations about sensitive subjects; given everyone’s pent-up frustration, those discussions could quickly devolve into arguments. Try to find a healthy way to channel your own energy, too, so that you don’t snap at people who haven’t done anything wrong.

Today, you’ll feel motivated to start new projects — the wilder and more ambitious, the better. But you might not necessarily have the dedication to follow through on them, especially if they require long-term commitment. Once the project gets challenging — or worse, boring — you could quickly lose interest, leaving things half-finished. Keep in mind that the enthusiasm you feel right now won’t necessarily last, so think carefully before initiating anything new.

You might be uncharacteristically prickly today. Anything and everything others say could rub you the wrong way; even if you know they mean no harm, you’ll struggle not to get irritated. Being aware of this might help you avoid overreacting or saying things you’ll regret — but if you truly can’t help your crankiness, it might be best to avoid other people for the time being. You can reconnect later, when you’re in a better mood for it.

You might have some ambitious ideas about how to save yourself time today. You’ll imagine that if you take a shortcut or two, you’ll reach your destination much faster; if you rush through the unimportant tasks, you’ll have more energy for the activities you actually enjoy. But right now, anything you do to “save time” could end up costing you more time in the end. You might encounter unexpected complications, and dealing with them will take longer than if you’d just done things thoroughly in the first place. For now, stick to your original plan, and take it slow and steady.

Resist the temptation to change your life with stuff today. You might tell yourself that new clothes will fix the parts of your personality you don’t like; new gadgets will allow you to work harder and be “better.” But right now, new things won’t be nearly as satisfying as you had hoped. Instead, strive to determine what’s actually wrong with your life — and reflect on how you might address it in a deeper, more lasting way, rather than simply throwing money at the problem.

You know you can’t expect everyone to like you. But sometimes it’s hard! In your opinion, people should like you! You make an effort to be friendly and appealing, and you wish everybody responded the way you wanted. When you sense that someone is indifferent, even disapproving, your impulse might be to try harder to win their admiration — and, failing that, you might lash out. But today, none of that will work out well. Try to focus on the people who do like you, and put everyone else out of your mind.

There are perfectly good reasons to keep some of your ideas to yourself. Maybe you’re not yet sure you want to pursue something, and you want to think it through privately before asking for advice. Maybe some of your friends can be competitive, and you don’t want to deal with that right now. But remember that if the people around you don’t know what you’re thinking, it’s unreasonable to be annoyed when they fail to support you. If you want help, you have to ask for it.

You might come across pushy today, even if you don’t intend to. Well-meaning efforts to help others might feel, to them, like attempts to control their lives. When you think you’re simply offering useful insight, they might feel you’re being disrespectful. Right now, advice — especially if it’s unsolicited — isn’t likely to be received well, so avoid offering it. If you must make your voice heard, don’t be surprised if the reaction isn’t as positive as you’d anticipated.

If someone tells you what to do today, you’ll be inclined to do exactly the opposite. It’s about the principle of the matter; you want to demonstrate that you won’t be pushed around. But while standing up for yourself is important, don’t let your reactivity go unchecked. Make a point of doing what’s actually best for you, not simply what’s contrarian.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

Your loved ones might not seem particularly talkative today — and you might be tempted to read into their silence. You might speculate that they’re judging you, that they’re mad at you, or that there’s some other issue in your relationship that’s weighing on them. But try not to jump to conclusions, because you’re unlikely to land on the right ones. People are probably dealing with things that have nothing to do with you. Ask what’s going on before you assume the worst.

You might feel the urge to burn bridges today. If someone gets in your way or irritates you, you might convince yourself you’re better off without them. This attitude might seem freeing at first, but chances are you’ll come to regret it. You do need other people to support and help you, so don’t let your momentary frustrations create a lasting rift.

Just about everything might feel unfair to you today. When you look around, you’ll feel that everyone else has more than they deserve, while you have less — luck is somehow always on their side, never on yours. Try not to act on those feelings. Even if you are seeing things accurately — and that isn’t likely — reacting in anger or bitterness won’t do anything to remedy the situation. Wait to act until you have a clearer head.

Today, you’re likely to notice all the little things other people are doing wrong — and you’ll want to tell them about it. Your intention isn’t to be rude or critical; you’re only trying to be helpful, calling attention to areas for improvement. But it’s probably safe to assume that your advice, however well-meaning, will only make them defensive. So unless you have something truly urgent to share, it might be best to keep it to yourself.

items.title: ‘I Wish I Could Move Out, But My Parents Need the Rent Money’
items.description: A third of adults under 35 are living at home with their parents, a growing trend that reflects the bleak housing market and rising cost of living. But contrary to popular sentiment, they aren’t all 20-somethings freeloading off Mom and Dad. More than 70 perce
items.author: Charlotte Cowles
paragraphs: A third of adults under 35 are living at home with their parents, a growing trend that reflects the bleak housing market and rising cost of living. But contrary to popular sentiment, they aren’t all 20-somethings freeloading off Mom and Dad. More than 70 percent of young adults who live with their parents contribute to household costs, and in some cases, they’re actually the breadwinners. “There’s this perception that if you’re approaching 30 and living with your parents, you’re just doing it to save money,” says one woman I spoke to. (At 25, she still sleeps in her childhood bedroom and contributes at least $2,500 a month to her parents’ household costs — help they very much need.) “In my case, that couldn’t be further from the truth. I just have to smile and nod.”
Below, three adults who live with — and financially support — their parents share the frustrations, rewards, and surprising perks (free laundry!) of their roommate situation.
“I didn’t know how unprepared my parents were until my dad got sick.” —a 28-year-old accountant for a health-care company in Southern California

My family is from Mexico, and my parents moved to California right before I was born. When I was growing up, they worked multiple jobs to support my siblings and me and send money back home to their relatives. I was taught that you take care of your family, especially your elders.

I have always lived with my parents. When I was in school, it was great — I didn’t have to pay rent, though I did help with the bills, usually a few hundred dollars a month. I was expected to contribute to the household pretty early on, around age 16. I think I gave half of whatever I earned to my parents and kept half for my own spending money. I worked all kinds of jobs: fast-food restaurants, retail. Then I majored in accounting at a local college and got a job at a health-care company. I’ve worked there for about five years now. I make more money than anyone in my family ever has: about $80,000 a year.

After I got the job at my current company, I started taking care of more household bills. Now, I pay my parents’ mortgage and property taxes, about $2,000 a month. That coincided with my dad having some health problems and going on disability two years ago. My mom is still working but only part time.

Even though I pay a big portion of our bills, it was hard to get my parents to open up to me about their finances. They’re not secretive, exactly, but they’re very traditional. I don’t think they even talk to each other about money. I wasn’t super-surprised that they didn’t have a retirement plan, but I didn’t know how unprepared they were until my dad got sick. They don’t have much savings, and while their house is almost paid off, it’s not like they could sell it. They’d still need a place to live, and it would be hard to find something comparable that they can afford. Also, their community is here, their church is here, their doctors are here. So I’m basically paying all their housing costs, which are also my housing costs. I can’t afford to move out and still pay their mortgage, so it is what it is. Maybe when the house is paid off in about four years, I could move out, but I’ll probably still need to help them financially. Both of my younger siblings are in the military, so they’re not really in a position to help at this point.

As far as roommates go, my parents are pretty good. Sometimes, I wish I could just come home at the end of the day and have a glass of wine and decompress by myself, in my own space, like a normal adult. I watch all these TikToks where women in their 20s come home from work to their clean apartments and make dinner in their own kitchens, and it looks so glamorous — I come home and my parents are eating dinner on the couch. And it’s hard to date. If I go out with my friends, I’ll usually spend the night at one of their houses so I don’t come home late and get an earful of questions about where I was and what I was doing.

I try not to get too down about it. Right now, financially, this is what’s best for everyone. I’m proud to be helping my parents, but I don’t want to put my own kids in this position someday. I’m putting money in my own 401(k) already, and I try to save. I’m definitely not living a super-adventurous, fun life in my 20s, but that’s okay. I mean, I’m an accountant, you know? I would like to have a family of my own someday, and sometimes I worry that living with my parents is making it harder to find someone to do that with. But I should probably put myself out there more, too.
“I feel like we’re turning into some weird version of Grey Gardens.” —a 33-year-old marketing manager in Texas

I moved back in with my mom two years ago after I got divorced and my dad died suddenly. At first, there were a lot of nights when we both hit the wine a little too hard together, feeling sorry for ourselves. I’m so lucky I had her to lean on. She was really supportive of me leaving my marriage and welcomed me home with open arms.

For some reason, my dad didn’t have life insurance. Or maybe he did and the payout was really small. For whatever reason, his death left my mom financially unstable. She was a stay-at-home mom for my siblings and me, so it’s not like she could just up and get a job. My dad owned his own business, which had been suffering since the pandemic. He had retirement savings, but it’s not enough for my mom to live on for the rest of her life. My dad clearly anticipated he’d be working for another decade at least. And my mom didn’t know a lot about their finances, period. Soon after I moved in, I realized she needed my help if she was going to stay in her house. My parents bought the home in 2021, when mortgage rates were really low.

I work in marketing, and my job is remote. I was used to living in a two-income household while I was married, and now I’m living in a one-income household with my mom. It’s not ideal, but I’m glad I can help her. I’m just not sure where the off-ramp is. Like, if I move out, what will she do? My brothers are both pretty distant, with their own families and their own lives, and I don’t think they know about our mom’s financial situation. She’s been too proud to tell them, and I don’t think she wants them to worry. Maybe at some point, she could sell the house, but there’s still a lot of years left on the mortgage and the rate is so low it’s hard to see how that would make sense.

Right now, I contribute about $3,000 a month toward my mom’s living expenses, including utilities and groceries. My mom definitely feels bad that I’m financially taking care of her. As a result, she does a lot of momlike stuff for me: She makes my bed, cleans the house, does most of the cooking and grocery shopping. It’s nice, and I’m grateful but sometimes it feels regressive, like I’m home from college or something. Occasionally, it feels intrusive. Sometimes, I’ll be on a Zoom call for work and she’ll come into my room to get my dirty laundry. Either way, I don’t think either of us wants to be in this position. Just a few years ago, I was a fully launched adult with a spouse and a nice apartment and a life of my own. Now I feel like we’re turning into some weird version of Grey Gardens. I don’t miss my ex-husband, but I do miss my independent life. I’m not dating at the moment, but if I ever do, I’m not sure how I’d even manage the question of my mom.
“My fiancé says we’re first-generation wealth builders. Which sounds nice, but sometimes I’m like, ‘Where’s the wealth?’” —a 25-year-old nurse in New Jersey

My fiancé and I would love to get married and move in together, but both of us currently live with our respective parents and help support their households. A big part of it is cultural. Our parents are immigrants, and they come from cultures where children are expected to take care of their parents as they age. But that system only works if the cost of living is low enough for their children to be able to do that and support themselves, too. Right now, where we live, it’s not.

I met my fiancé at work. I’m a nurse practitioner, and he’s a radiology technician. We’d love to save up for a big wedding and a house — you know, the American Dream. But right now, it’s hard to pay our student loans and help our parents with their bills.

I have a younger sibling who’s still in high school and also lives with my parents and me. I’m hoping that after she graduates, maybe my parents can sell their house and downsize and both my sister and I can move out. But that’s at least two years off, if not significantly longer. There’s also a chance my parents might need to live with one of us. My fiancé is in a different position; his parents will probably need some financial support here and there, but they’re in better shape than my family.

I’m trying to be patient. My fiancé is really into personal finance and always listens to podcasts and sends me stuff. He’s looking into side hustles and does DoorDash delivery to make extra money. He says we’re first-generation wealth builders. Which sounds nice, but sometimes I’m like, “Where’s the wealth? It’s all going to our families’ utility bills!” I’m grateful for all the opportunities my parents gave us, but it’s hard not to compare myself to other people my age who are having these big weddings and starting families already.

It’s also hard for my fiancé and me to spend time together. We see each other at work, obviously, but that’s not the same. Luckily, my parents really like him, so we do spend a lot of time at my house. But it’s hard to be romantic when your whole family’s on the other side of the wall, you know?
Email your money conundrums to mytwocents@nymag.com (and read our submission terms here.)
