items.title: Четыре минуты в день: простая тренировка для силы и равновесия после 65 лет — Reminder
items.description: Встать со стула, подняться по лестнице, удержать равновесие — это те движения, от которых зависит, насколько самостоятельно человек может обходиться в повседневной жизни. С возрастом выполнять их бывает сложнее, особенно если физической активности мало. Исслед
items.author: Ксения Зернова
paragraphs: Встать со стула, подняться по лестнице, удержать равновесие — это те движения, от которых зависит, насколько самостоятельно человек может обходиться в повседневной жизни. С возрастом выполнять их бывает сложнее, особенно если физической активности мало. Исследователи из Университета штата Пенсильвания проверили, может ли с этим помочь короткая домашняя тренировка: участники занимались всего четыре минуты в день на протяжении 12 недель.

В исследовании участвовали 97 человек старше 65 лет. Средний возраст составил 74 года. Все участники вели малоподвижный образ жизни, испытывали трудности при ходьбе и до начала эксперимента занимались физической активностью в среднем всего около 18 минут в неделю. Силовыми упражнениями они не занимались.

Исследователи случайным образом разделили добровольцев на две группы. Первая ежедневно выполняла четырехминутный комплекс FAST-2, а вторая в течение 12 недель жила в привычном режиме, после чего тоже получила возможность пройти программу.

В начале и в конце исследования ученые проверяли, сколько раз участники могут встать со стула за 30 секунд, как долго удерживают равновесие на одной ноге и сколько времени им требуется, чтобы пять раз подряд сесть на стул и встать с него. Эти тесты помогают оценить физические возможности, от которых зависит самостоятельность в повседневной жизни.

Через 12 недель участники, выполнявшие упражнения, по сравнению с контрольной группой могли в среднем на 4,2 раза больше встать со стула за 30 секунд. Они также удерживали равновесие на одной ноге на 3,6 секунды дольше, а пять вставаний со стула выполняли на 2,3 секунды быстрее.
Участники тренировались регулярно — в среднем 5,6 дня в неделю. Результаты показали, что короткий комплекс может улучшить некоторые показатели силы и подвижности даже у малоподвижных пожилых людей.

Для тренировки понадобятся стул без колес, резиновая лента с ручками и невысокая ступенька. Каждое упражнение выполняют в течение 30 секунд, затем отдыхают 30 секунд перед следующим. Весь комплекс занимает около четырех минут.

Когда упражнение станет даваться легче, можно перейти к отжиманиям от столешницы. Чем ниже расположена опора, тем больше нагрузка. В исследовании участники начинали с подходящего им варианта и постепенно усложняли упражнение.
Когда выполнять движение станет легче, попробуйте вставать, скрестив руки на груди.
Старайтесь не округлять спину и не раскачивать корпус. Если тянуть ленту трудно, выберите вариант с меньшим сопротивлением. Следите, чтобы лента не соскальзывала со стоп во время движения.

В исследовании участники начинали с небольшой высоты и увеличивали ее по мере того, как выполнять упражнение становилось легче. Не используйте шаткие предметы или обычный стул вместо ступеньки. Если вам трудно удерживать равновесие, выполняйте упражнение рядом с опорой и при необходимости держитесь за нее.

items.title: Eric Bauza to Make Posthumous ‘Simpsons’ Debut: Late ‘Looney Tunes’ Voice Actor Plays Two Characters
items.description: In recent years, Eric Bauza had become one of the most successful and popular voice-over artists in the business, including his command of the entire library of Bugs Bunny and other “Looney Tunes” characters. But there was one iconic show that had eluded him u
items.author: Michael Schneider
paragraphs: In recent years, Eric Bauza had become one of the most successful and popular voice-over artists in the business, including his command of the entire library of Bugs Bunny and other “Looney Tunes” characters. But there was one iconic show that had eluded him until recently: “The Simpsons.”

Bauza recently made that dream come true — and his “The Simpsons” premiere is set to take place on Nov. 15 on Fox, with the episode “Dream Scenari-Moe.” But sadly, Bauza’s “Simpsons” debut is now posthumous, following his death Sunday at the age of 46. Bauza’s passing, a result of hypertensive cardiovascular disease, stunned the animation community — including “The Simpsons” writers who had just worked with him.
“The Simpsons” co-exec producer Cesar Mazariegos, who is the co-showrunner of the episode, shares that Bauza plays two characters: restaurateur “Mr. Fong” and newspaper editor “Harry Metsali.”

“Everything people have said about Eric, before and after his untimely passing, is absolutely true,” Mazariegos told Variety. “He was so funny, kind, creative and just immensely talented. We reached out to him to play two New-Yorky characters for our ‘Dream Scenari-Moe’ episode, and he knocked it out of the park. He seamlessly dipped in and out of dozens of voices, both to give us options and just hilariously riffing while off-mic. He signed our Wall-of-Fame and drew an amazingly rendered Bugs Bunny on it. That’s how we found out he started as an animator! He was such a longtime fan of animation and kept saying that he felt like the luckiest guy in the world.”

Mazariegos said Bauza came in to record in two sessions, and that they had recently bumped into him at last month’s Creative Arts Emmys. Also, exec producer Matt Selman had just seen Bauza at another event last week.

“He was absolutely someone we were excited to have come in again and again, and then we heard the news. It was such a shock,” Mazariegos said. “His passing just checks off so many boxes that make this such a devastating loss. To his young family, to a generation of animation fans, to an industry that’s being hobbled by greed and AI. We join his countless friends, colleagues and fans in mourning his loss.”

Bauza was heard in this year’s “Coyote vs. Acme” as Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tweety, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig, Road Runner, Charlie the Dog and others. But he had more than 400 acting credits to his name, including “Avatar: The Last Airbender,” “Chowder,” “Alvin and the Chipmunks: The Squeakquel,” “Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated,” “Fanboy & Chum Chum,” “Ben 10 Omniverse” and, in 2026 alone, “Chibiverse,” “Minions & Monsters,” “Forgotten Island,” “Rick and Morty,” “Superkitties” and “Avatar: Seven Havens,” among others.

Besides Bauza, “Dream Scenari-Moe” guest voices also include Meg Ryan (who plays “Sam”) and “Saturday Night Live” cast member James Austin Johnson as “Dr. De La Manana.” Here’s the logline to the episode: “When Moe has trouble sleeping, he enrolls in a brand new sleep study that gives him the greatest romantic comedy dreams of his life. But unbeknownst to him, his beautiful fantasy comes at a nightmarish price.”

“The Simpsons” recently made headlines for another big voice-over headline: The return of Apu, now voiced by Sunil Malhotra. In an Instagram post this week, Malhotra shared the congratulatory note that Bauza had sent him when the Apu casting news was revealed, as well as a photo from the first time they met.

“A picture from when Eric Bauza and I first met,” he wrote. “It was on a panel for animation students at LMU in 2017. He was already a legend, and I was in awe of him. And he was a fellow Asian American, someone truly to look up to. But the thing about Eric was, in addition to his enormous talent, he had boundless generosity and grace. He made me feel like a peer. Over the years, we’d gotten to work together a few times and it was always ridiculous fun. We alternated between talking about being boy dads and then just being silly with each other. The next picture is the last time I talked to Eric. He had just messaged me on Tuesday with the most beautiful congratulations on my new role. That text was so emblematic of his generosity and kindness. As much as we all will miss him, his talent, his laugh, his warmth, I can only imagine the loss his family must be feeling. I’m sending them all my love. The world is an unfair place. But it was a little brighter, better and funnier when Eric was here. I will miss him.”
Besides “The Simpsons,” Bauza will next be heard voicing the upcoming short “Daffy Season,” which will run in theaters as the opener to “The Cat in the Hat.”

items.title: Before ‘Star Trek,’ Patrick Stewart Proved His Sci-Fi Chops in ‘Dune’
items.description: Before there was Jean-Luc Picard, there was Gurney Halleck. Several years before Star Trek: The Next Generation sent his career into the cosmos, Sir Patrick Stewart played Halleck, the Warmaster of House Atreides in David Lynch’s Dune in 1984. Stewart, who die
items.author: Julian Sancton
paragraphs: Before there was Jean-Luc Picard, there was Gurney Halleck. Several years before Star Trek: The Next Generation sent his career into the cosmos, Sir Patrick Stewart played Halleck, the Warmaster of House Atreides in David Lynch’s Dune in 1984. Stewart, who died this week at age 86, was then a seasoned stage veteran in his native England, but Dune was merely his third film. It was also his introduction to science fiction, a precursor to his career-defining role as Picard. He imbued his character with the kind of presence and dignity that only classical stagecraft can summon — much as his English forebear Alec Guinness had in Star Wars.

In his new memoir, Fictional Selves (recently excerpted in The Hollywood Reporter), actor Kyle MacLachlan recalled the surreal, formative experience of shooting Dune in the Mexican desert alongside Stewart.

“The first thing I noticed when I met Patrick was his voice,” writes MacLachlan, who was 24 at the time and, like Stewart, new to film. “I went to school for three years to learn how to speak onstage, but I’ll never sound like him. Coming from the prestigious Royal Shakespeare Company, Patrick has the most mellifluous tones, regal and elegant. No one can make the line ‘Behold, as a wild ass in the desert go I forth to my work’ sound correct except for him. He is Gurney Halleck, master swordsman and troubadour. And because he’s also Patrick Stewart, he’s suave and debonair about it. When he puts on the Atreides battle jacket or the Fremen stillsuit, it’s like he’s lived in it all his life. He also has the most marvelously shaped head of any human I’ve ever seen, and I tell him so. He gives me a ‘thank you, I think’ kind of look.”

A longtime fan of Frank Herbert’s Dune franchise, MacLachlan writes that he knew more about the works than most of the people involved in the film, including Lynch. As such, he became something of an authority on the subject matter. Stewart came to rely on MacLachlan’s expertise in order to get deeper into his character.

“Patrick is a mix of stately confidence and thoughtful inquiry. He regularly leans over and, sotto voce, asks me questions about what’s going on,” writes MacLachlan. “Though he presents a very cool and collected mien, he is just trying to figure shit out like me. We connect on our theater background — I did Shakespeare the previous summer — and laugh at the exponential difference between simple theater productions and … whatever this is. The size and scope of the film often leave us speechless, and I feel less alone with him beside me.”

The following passage from Maclachlan’s memoir well illustrates Stewart’s refusal to treat popular entertainment with any less seriousness than Shakespeare, a trait that would serve him well throughout his career.

On his first day of shooting, he and I took our seats in a half-built “ornithopter,” which is like a giant, multifaceted bee that flies over the desert. We were seated in front of a gigantic blue screen, where the landscape would be matted in later. I could feel Patrick’s nervousness as we prepared to “fly” over the shield wall and the Great Desert of Arrakis. He leaned forward and quietly asked, ‘Kyle, what are we looking at here?’
I leaned back and spoke in an undertone: “There’s a sandworm down there bigger than a tractor trailer.”
“Aha. And there?” he asked, pointing lower down. “It’s swallowing one of the harvesters.”
“It’s like a large metal factory on wheels.”
“Seems like a risky mission,” he said, a trace of somber gravitas. “Tremendous risk,” I said quietly.
Patrick’s key line in the scene is “The worm is eight minutes away, sire.” After the first take, he had a question. “Pardon, David?”
“YES, PATRICK,” David said in his distinctive honk.
“How exactly would I know how far out the worm is?” I’m impressed that Patrick exists deeply enough within his character to ask such a thing.

David stopped, re-calculating in his mind. “EXCELLENT QUESTION, PATRICK,” he said, like a supportive teacher. “THANK YOU.” He then dispatched a propman to construct a gauge, with analog hands to be inserted later.

The above quotes are from FICTIONAL SELVES: A Memoir by Kyle MacLachlan. Copyright © 2026 by Kyle MacLachlan. Published in the United States by Crown, an imprint of the Crown Publishing Group, a division of Penguin Random House LLC. All rights reserved.

items.title: ‘X-Men’ Stars Ian McKellen, Hugh Jackman, Halle Berry, James Marsden Honor “Fellow Mutant” Patrick Stewart: “One of the Greats”
items.description: Patrick Stewart‘s X-Men family is paying tribute to the late sci-fi icon.
items.author: McKinley Franklin; Lexi Carson
paragraphs: Patrick Stewart‘s X-Men family is paying tribute to the late sci-fi icon.
Stewart died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles at 86 following “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” longtime spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak announced.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

The actor led the original X-Men franchise, an adaptation of the Marvel comic books, for 20th Century Fox. Starring as Prof. Charles Xavier, he brought the role to the big screen in the first film in 2000, and went on to appear in X2: X-Men United (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006), X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014) and Logan (2017).

He had subsequent cameos in Origins: Wolverine (2009) and The Wolverine (2013), and will reprise the role in Marvel’s upcoming Avengers: Doomsday this December. He’ll be joined in Doomsday by a few of his original X-Men co-stars from the Fox era, including Ian McKellen, James Marsden, Kelsey Grammer, Alan Cumming and Rebecca Romijn.

McKellen, whom starred as Magneto/Erik Lehnsherr, Prof. X’s rival turned friend in Fox’s X-Men movies, shared a tribute on his social media platforms on Thursday. He commemorated his Yorkshire roots, writing, “Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.”

The Oscar nominee went on to reflect on how they first crossed paths at the Royal Shakespeare Company, and later a few years in London “when he told me about an offer to take over a leading part in Star Trek.”

He continued, “‘But Patrick think of your stage career in the U.K. Do you really want to risk — getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?’ Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did for not just his devoted Trekkies but film and theatre audiences, who marvelled at his using international celebrity to star in a string of cinema successes (X-Men of course) and in great classical plays by Shakespeare, Ibsen, Arthur Miller, Peter Shaffer, Pinter and Beckett at Stratford-upon-Avon, in London’s West End and on Broadway.”

McKellen concluded his statement by noting Stewart’s final film, which they will appear in together as Magneto and Prof. X, respectively: “His farewell performance in Avengers: Doomsday is yet to be seen.”

Hugh Jackman, who graced the silver screen alongside Stewart in the X-Men movies as Wolverine/James “Logan” Howlett, wrote on Instagram, “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”
Berry, who portrayed Storm (Ororo Munroe), shared a tribute on her Instagram Stories Thursday, writing, “Rest in peace sweet friend,” with a red heart emoji.

Marsden, the original Scott Summers/Cyclops, posted a photo on Instagram of Stewart, Berry and himself in X-Men, writing, “We’ve lost a very special man. Kind and generous, with extraordinary talent and a wicked sense of humor, it was impossible not to feel charmed, enlightened and downright joyous in his presence. I’m grateful to have spent the time I did with you, Patrick. Rest well, my good friend.”
Marsden is reprising his X-Men role in Doomsday, where he and Stewart will reunite onscreen.

Romijn, the original Mystique/Raven actress who will also star opposite Stewart in Doomsday, shared a video on Instagram. “I just heard the very sad news about the passing of my dear friend Patrick Stewart. I feel so grateful to have known him for the last 25 years, and to have been in his orbit for the last 25 years, both as a fellow mutant and as a fellow member of Starfleet,” she said.

“He was positively delicious, hilarious, naughty, incredible sense of humor,” Romijn continued. “And that booming voice of his that always spoke to the very back of the room. As every classically trained Shakespearean great needs to master, has always been an inspiration. I wanna send my condolences to his family, and I’ll miss my friend dearly. Rest in peace, Patrick.”

The Emmy nominee’s fellow Star Trek: The Next Generation and X-Men co-star Famke Janssen, who portrayed Jean Grey/Phoenix in the film franchise, said in a statement shared with The Hollywood Reporter, “Patrick was a legend. One of the greats.”

“I had the pleasure and honor of working with him over several decades. First as Kamala opposite him as Captain Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and later on as Jean Grey with Patrick embodying Professor X in the X-Men movies,” Janssen said. “You will be missed, Patrick, but never forgotten.”

Vinnie Jones, who played Cain Marko/Juggernaut in X-Men: The Last Stand, shared photos of himself and Stewart on set. “Getting to grips with the legendary Patrick Stewart on the set of X-Men: The Last Stand. RIP my old friend!” he wrote on Instagram.

Longtime X-Men director shared a series of photos with the actor on Instagram, writing, “It’s been a while since I last posted, but Patrick Stewart’s passing has brought back decades of memories, and I wanted to share a few candid photographs from our time together.”

“I could never recount all the experiences Patrick and I shared, both professionally and personally, in a single post. He was far more than a cast member and a friend. He was a teacher,” he wrote. “I feel fortunate to have known Patrick, to have learned from him, and to have called him my friend. I will cherish those memories for the rest of my life. He will be deeply missed.”

Grammer, in a statement given to THR, wrote, “Sending love to Patrick and all of his fans and family. He was just terrific. Gave one of the greatest turns as a guest on Frasier — ever! A marvelous man. I liked him so. Time spent with him was always time well spent.”

As the Emmy winner noted, Stewart made a guest appearance on Frasier in the sitcom’s 11th season. They also collaborated on Fox’s X-Men movies, where Grammer played Beast/Dr. Hank McCoy, plus Marvel’s upcoming Doomsday.

Kevin Feige, the head of Marvel Studios, shared in a statement with THR, “I’ll never forget the first time I saw Sir Patrick Stewart on the set of the first X-Men. After years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe — and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas. Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor.”

“It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him,” he added. “His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.”

Marvel Studios additionally shared on social media, “All of us at Marvel Studios are deeply saddened by the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart. Sir Patrick brought Professor Charles Xavier to life with extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from X-Men to Logan to Avengers: Doomsday. He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman. Our hearts go out to his wife Sunny, his children, his friends, and the countless fans around the world whose lives he touched with his art.”

Zak Penn, one of the screenwriters of the second and third X-Men movies, posted behind-the-scenes images of Stewart with the cast along with his tribute: “Patrick Stewart was an incredible guy, the most generous actor and an absolute pleasure to be around,” Penn wrote. “A true legend.”

items.title: Byron Allen Sells His Stake in Starz
items.description: Byron Allen is out of the Starz business.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: Byron Allen is out of the Starz business.
The media mogul has sold his entire 10.7 percent take in the pay-TV and streaming company that spun out from Lionsgate last year.
Allen had acquired his stake through his family office from former Treasury Secretary Steve Mnuchin’s Liberty 77 investment fund earlier this year, paying $25 million for the shares.

A new disclosure filed with the SEC Thursday afternoon however shows that Allen sold off his entire holdings over the course of August and September, netting him a bit less than $45 million, the filings indicate.
Starz adopted a poison pill to prevent Allen from taking a larger stake after he disclosed the purchase, but he told The Hollywood Reporter that he nonetheless had his sights on the premium service.
“When I decide to buy the whole company — I will buy the whole company — I do plan on controlling Starz,” he said, adding that he wanted an SVOD service to complement what he is doing with BuzzFeed.
He has since, however, changed his mind, it seems, as the filing indicates.
Starz is in the midst of a transformation, and the company reported growing revenue and declining losses in its Q3 earnings report Thursday, driven by franchises like Power and Outlander.

Allen, of course, owns properties like The Weather Channel and HBCU Go, and hosts and produces Comics Unleashed, which airs on CBS at 11:30 p.m. He also acquired a controlling stake in BuzzFeed earlier this year, with plans to leverage that digital company’s scale to build a streaming video and advertising business.

items.title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’: First Reactions
items.description: He’s back, and he’s angrier than ever! Godzilla Minus Zero had a series of screenings this week for press and the first reactions have been flooding social media. The verdict? We have another kaiju-sized hit on our hands.
items.author: Abid Rahman
paragraphs: He’s back, and he’s angrier than ever! Godzilla Minus Zero had a series of screenings this week for press and the first reactions have been flooding social media. The verdict? We have another kaiju-sized hit on our hands.

Despite having its world premiere at the New York Film Festival on Sept. 26, legendary Japanese studio Toho held more press screenings this week for Godzilla Minus Zero ahead of the film’s Centerpiece gala screening at the Tokyo International Film Festival on Nov. 1. The film is released in theaters in Japan on Nov. 3 and North America on Nov. 6.

Written and directed by Takashi Yamazaki, Godzilla Minus Zero is a direct sequel to the Japanese filmmaker’s 2023 epic Godzilla Minus One, that scored over $100 million at the global box office from a $15 million budget and won an Oscar for best visual effects in 2024.

A synopsis from Toho of Godzilla Minus Zero reads: “War reduced Japan to zero, and Godzilla plunged it into minus. Two years have passed since then, and the country has faced agonizing struggles to achieve recovery and finally reclaim its daily life. Just as humanity managed to cling to a hard-won peace, a new threat strikes, crushing hope in an instant. There is no third time. Everything ends here.”
Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe, Hidetaka Yoshioka and Kuranosuke Sasaki are among the cast returning for the sequel. Newcomers include Min Tanaka and Masami Nagasawa.
Shot entirely in Japan, notably, Godzilla Minus Zero is the first-ever Japanese production to be filmed for Imax.

The Hollywood Reporter‘s David Rooney reviewed Godzilla Minus Zero after seeing it NYFF, and described the film as a “radioactive blast.” In a rave review, Rooney praised Yamazaki for topping the spectacle of his first film. “The resulting clash of the legendary kaiju is a rip-roaring smackdown in a movie that keeps awing the audience with exhilarating action and then continually one-upping itself in the dustups that follow,” Rooney writes. “I’m fairly sure I stopped breathing during a tense scene in which Godzilla bears down on a seaplane attempting a hurried liftoff.”
Godzilla Minus Zero currently holds a score of 92 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 50 reviews. On Metacritic it holds a score of 78 and on Letterboxd it is rated at 4 stars.

items.title: The Unclassifiable Talent of Hervé Guibert
items.description: Hervé Guibert’s ultimately unclassifiable talent brilliantly evokes the shadows, the moments of dread and paranoia, that are part of the experience of love. Doom lurks everywhere in Guibert’s world, in large part because love, as Guibert expresses it, is synon
items.author: Hilton Als
paragraphs: Hervé Guibert’s ultimately unclassifiable talent brilliantly evokes the shadows, the moments of dread and paranoia, that are part of the experience of love. Doom lurks everywhere in Guibert’s world, in large part because love, as Guibert expresses it, is synonymous with longing, and what is longing but a pit stop on the way to hurt, loss, and the lover’s need to control the beloved?

Born in 1955, into a middle-class family in a suburb of Paris, Guibert, who wrote about photography in addition to taking pictures himself—he also published more than two dozen books of fiction, autofiction, and essays—was a gay man who came of age during the AIDS epidemic, a time of incalculable devastation. Guibert describes the epoch with what feels like a preternatural calm in his now classic 1990 novel, “To the Friend Who Did Not Save My Life,” in which we meet some of his friends, thinly disguised, including the philosopher Michel Foucault and the actress Isabelle Adjani. I remember reading about the book when it came out in the U.S. the following year—the year that Guibert died, at age thirty-six, of AIDS-related causes. Some people condemned the work for outing Foucault as a fellow AIDS sufferer. What right did Guibert have to tell someone else’s story? At some point, I read the book, and then I put the memory of reading it away: it was too potent, too sharp a reminder of what I had experienced during those years when quick and slow disasters were all around, and I felt ashamed of my helplessness and relative good health.

But then, about a decade ago, the writers Bruce Hainley and Jennifer Krasinski told me about a video that Guibert had made some months before his death. Titled “Modesty, or Immodesty” (1991), the hour-length work, shot by Guibert himself between June, 1990, and March, 1991, shows the artist going about his daily life in his final months, writing, talking on the phone, bathing, exercising, undergoing a medical procedure, then playing back the footage so that he can witness it, taking a holiday, and finally typing on a word processor, which continues to produce his text after he has moved on. This piece, Guibert’s single work on video, is an extraordinary film of self-dramatization: life and illness as a form of theatre. It is not a brave work—that’s too paltry a word for it. It is a powerful record of the isolating effects of AIDS, and of a patient who is running out of time and holding onto the act of creation as evidence that he has lived. As with “To the Friend Who Did Not Save My Life,” I did not want to remember the film after I had seen it; its solitude spoke of universal solitude, all those rooms filled with lost potential and the memory of the dead.

So it was with some trepidation, but also curiosity and not a little excitement, that I began looking at the volumes of Guibert’s photographs that were published recently, in elegant editions, by the Magic Hour Press. “The Only Face” is a version of the catalogue for a show that Guibert had in Paris, in 1984. The images are in black-and-white, and are romantic in a way that reminds one almost immediately of the photographer Duane Michals, another artist who worked with image and text. In the introduction to the original catalogue, Guibert wrote:

Love doesn’t necessarily make a good photograph, but the photographer’s interest, and the intelligence and imagination behind it, can contribute to the making of a picture that interests us. It’s important to remember that Guibert was a very young man when he was taking these photographs, because sometimes the romanticism of his vision draws out a kind of artificiality that feels distinctly Gallic in its love of surface beauty; one longs to go deeper, to be allowed to go deeper, into the image.

The photographs are titled—“The mother,” “The father,” and so on—and the dominant visual theme in the work is the photographer’s fascination with the play of light in black-and-white. Too often Guibert goes for mood, as in “The fiancé” and “Sienna.” In the former, we see a figure shot from the front, draped in tulle. At first it’s not clear what sex the person is, but, looking closer, you can make out black hair across his chest. It’s a self-conscious study in texture, the kind of Photography 101 assignment you’re proud of yourself for having carried to completion, but Guibert’s lyricism topples over into kitsch in “Sienna.” In that picture, we see light pouring through a window. There’s smoke in the light. Is it cigarette smoke, or angels’ breath? A thin, shirtless figure sits in a chair with arms and head bent over a table. Again, it’s not a photograph but an image about photography, and Guibert’s too-romantic love of it.

Guibert’s love of Michals-influenced gay narrative also plays out in a piece called “The friend.” A white male hand rests on a broad, darker-skinned chest. That is all we see, in medium closeup, and the contrasts are obvious—light and dark, older and younger—but the picture stops there; what we are meant to register is not so much the bodies, their stories, as the photographer in the act of becoming one. (Helmut Newton is another influence. In Guibert’s portrait “Agathe,” a wavy-haired young woman looks out at us, her open jacket exposing her small breasts.)

Sometimes, though, Guibert is helped by a subject who works with him to make an emotionally legible picture that succeeds graphically as well. I don’t think I’ll soon forget his terrific portrait “Isabelle,” in which we see Adjani lying on a bench, her face turned to the camera. She wears a light-colored garment; her right arm rests on her belly. Adjani’s dark hair, the openness of her gaze, feels less like a study in grays and blacks than like a photograph about stillness. You can see how in their time together, the time it took to take this picture, Guibert was able to move past his love of the art of photography to the point of understanding it as an instrument of connection.

Like Adjani, the subjects of Guibert’s brilliant book “Suzanne and Louise” are so extraordinary that you can’t look away from them, and neither can the artist. Guibert called this book, originally published in France in 1980 and now available in English for the first time, a photo-novel, and that’s fine, but the category seems too limiting for what “Suzanne and Louise” is: a work as great as Jean Genet’s “The Maids,” and just as chilling. We’re in another black-and-white world, this time in a hôtel particulier in the Fifteenth Arrondissement, where two sisters, Suzanne and Louise, have lived for more than forty years. The fairly reclusive ladies, Guibert’s great-aunts, have had different lives: Louise was a Carmelite nun until she was convinced to leave the order by Suzanne, a widow who was once married to a pharmacist. Suzanne has money, and Louise does not. They share a dog named Whysky, and a marriage of sorts: Suzanne is the dominant figure, and Louise her poor relation who waits on her. The prose in the book is written from the inside; when Guibert was a child, he and his family made weekly visits to these sisters, who ultimately fascinated him enough that he was able to sidestep his overly aestheticized sensibility and let these singular beings speak and act and be in ways that are constantly startling and new. “Five years ago, I proposed to my great-aunts that I make a film about them; I had started writing a script, but their refusals were so categorical that I lost of [sic] all hope of ever making it,” Guibert writes. He was able to take photographs, though, and, as the contact sheets piled up, he decided to print some of the images, “just to see, to show them.” In a book of astonishing acts of intimacy, the most revealing is in a series of pictures that Guibert shot of Louise taking down her hair—her “most intimate thing.” Long ago, a woman would send a missed loved one a photograph of herself taking her hair down. In this case, Louise’s washing of her long gray tresses is less an erotic image than an act of self-dramatization in the theatre of being. It’s not a statement so much as a reckoning, a way of showing love to the young relative behind the camera who refuses to let these women not be in the world and then leave it, forgotten. ♦

items.title: How Can Sports Teams Possibly Be Worth This Much?
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Gary Sernovitz
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
Pity James Dolan: According to the stock market, he is not as rich as he thinks he should be.

Unlike most teams in the Big Four North American pro-sports leagues, the Knicks and Rangers have been owned by a publicly traded company, MSG Sports Corp. The Dolan family trust owned a fifth, and legally controlled all, of MSG Sports, which, as of last week, was valued at $9.5 billion. Or, in the mind of James Dolan, which was valued at only $9.5 billion. Earlier this year, Bob Iger and Josh Kushner said they would buy the Lakers for $12.5 billion; a trio of investors just bought an eighth of the NHL team in Raleigh, North Carolina (where God did not mean for people to play hockey) at a valuation of $2.7 billion. Dolan can check the Forbes and Sportico websites. Both estimate the teams should be worth about $7 billion more.

So, this week, Dolan tried some Wall Street hocus-pocus: One company became two, and the Rangers and Knicks are now owned by separate entities. Their combined value is still $9.5 billion, but Dolan hopes that a more transparent daily measure of how undervalued the teams are will move their value closer to the $17 billion estimate.

That dream can be hard to understand for an outsider. Ten years ago, Forbes estimated the teams’ value below $5 billion. Has the value of the Rangers and Knicks tripled because they have become a great business recently? No. In the fiscal year ending on June 30, the company generated $32 million in earnings before interest, taxes, and depreciation. (That is, for context, the operating profits of a distributor of laundry equipment; it is two-thirds less than MSG Sports made in 2022.) Are the teams worth a lot more because Dolan — after 27 years of being seen as a talentless, short-tempered nepo baby — oversaw the Knicks finally winning an NBA championship? No again. The team would likely be worth the same had Jalen Brunson missed every shot or if Dolan had won five rings over his reign.

The truth is that the prices of American sports teams are post-logic. Their value has, in Wall Street lingo, technical trading dynamics independent from the fundamentals (or the basic rules of finance). In the past few years, prices of sports teams have rapidly accelerated — suddenly in the case of the NBA, relentlessly in the case of the NFL, incredibly in the case of the MLB. In the NBA, Kushner and Iger are buying the team from Mark Walter (who purchased the team himself last year with money that may not have been exactly his) for twice what the Celtics sold for in 2025 — and three times the recent “get-in price” for teams in Minnesota and Phoenix. In the NFL, prices have quadrupled between David Tepper’s purchase of the Panthers for $2.3 billion in 2018 and Vinod Khosla’s purchase of the Seahawks for $9.6 billion in 2026. In the MLB, the Padres (the small-market winner of one World Series game in their entire history) sold for $3.9 billion, 62 percent more than what Steve Cohen paid for the Mets only six years ago.

The most common explanation for all this is that the rich are getting richer, and that the Big Four leagues — the NFL, NBA, MLB, and NHL — rarely make more teams. As Mark Cuban, who sold his stake in the Mavericks in 2023 at a reported profit of over $3 billion, explained to me by email: “When there is a big jump in individual wealth, typically tied to the NASDAQ or an industry like AI creating new fortunes, teams are going to increase in value.” The median fortune on the Forbes 400 list of the richest Americans was $8.3 billion this year. It was $1.8 billion 20 years ago.

A spreadsheet doesn’t capture the appeal of the product of sports-team ownership any more than it does a painting. No one asks for the EBITDA multiple of a Rothko. Why would they for a franchise? And yet the making of new billionaires doesn’t fully explain the specific acceleration in the value of sports teams; the prices of franchises are going up way more than in the case of other things billionaires enjoy, like art and Hamptons houses.

When I began writing this article, I assumed that the inexplicable then had the usual explanation: It’s a bubble. Sport teams’ leaps in price look familiar, like other markets right before a crash. There’s a long way down in valuation for things like the Rangers and Knicks from 313 times the $32 million they made last year. (The median large American company trades at 15 times cash flow.) And it would follow that if our current economy seems optimized solely to inflate billionaires, market history teaches us that there always come periods when economies (or societies) deflate billionaires — and the bubbles caused by their whims. “When markets decline,” Cuban told me, “you will see what happened to team valuations from 2002 to about 2012 happen again.” But in those bad ten years? Values of teams still doubled.

Something else is happening. Sports teams have become a product with unusual and special characteristics. They have the unshakable appeal to billionaires of personal transformation — they can make Steven Cohen, once an unsmiling hedge-fund manager, “Uncle Steve” — and the unparalleled financial characteristics of as-sure-as-the-calendar-advances rising value. The logic behind this is circular, but also imperishable, as long as there are buyers. And the buyers are still lining up, paying valuations on a vibe even more loosey-goosey than before.

In the olden days, when gamblers and moguls with loud ties owned teams, they did not really try to make money. Three weeks after the Mets won the World Series in 1986, the New York Times reported that for the next season, “box seats would cost $10 and reserved seats, with one exception, would cost $8.50, an increase of 50 cents in both cases.”

One part of the current values of sports franchises is simply the end of this era. Sports teams get revenue from four sources — sponsorships, local media rights, national media rights, and ticket sales (along with the $65 parking, $200 jerseys, and $18 beers that come with them) — and have become particularly good at squeezing the last two. Teams “own” their fans and their fans’ children. (Hello, Jets dads.) So where else can a fan — or Fox Sports — go? An investor told me that something would be wrong if the Seattle Seahawks didn’t sell for 50 percent more than the Washington Commanders; the NFL got 80 percent more for its new 11-year TV package between the two sales.

As Ian Charles, a co-founder of Arctos, the dominant private equity buyer of minority interests in sports team, explained to me, “Every team is actually two things: It’s a piece of the league and a local live entertainment business. The league piece is the same for everybody. The value of the license to operate a protected local live entertainment business is a function of the market, the building deal, and the skill of the operator.” For some, the local entertainment business is actually a liability — I’ll spare the feelings of the team he mentioned — and the team is worth less than the (rapidly appreciating) generic piece of the league.

Still, none of this has made sports teams a great business, if we define a great business by how much profit it makes or how consistently those profits grow. (Which, for the record, is how we define a great business.) NFL teams make an average of $127 million dollars per year pretax. With a few exceptions, other teams are “break-evenish.” Some lose money.

When I spoke to Marc Lasry, the billionaire founder of Avenue Capital and former co-majority owner of the Milwaukee Bucks, he said he bought into the Bucks at about 100 times cash flow in 2014. He thought he had a straightforward plan to boost the profits of the team. What he soon realized was that the easiest way to “increase profits was by not investing in the team” and giving higher salaries for better players. “But the problem with that is very simple: You don’t want to be horrible.”

So in a business with inverted economics in which the desire to show the world who’s boss competes with a theoretical need to make money, Lasry’s strategy shifted. “We pretty much spent all the money we made every year to try to compete,” he said. It worked on the court. The Bucks won the NBA championship in 2021. It worked out fine for Lasry too. He sold his stake in 2023 at nearly seven times the valuation of what he paid for it.

The inverted economics is why sports teams have never traded on earnings, which is how you’d assess the right price to buy stock in Amazon or a pet-grooming business down the block. They also don’t quite trade like art, on some hazy combination of aesthetics and scarcity. Teams trade by mutual agreement, in a market with enough buyers, on revenue, roughly 6 to 10 times for those in the NHL and MLB, and 10 to 14 times revenue for teams in the NFL and NBA. (Iger and Kushner’s bid for the Lakers is higher than that: 18 times revenue.)

In other industries, like tech, revenue multiples are usually valuation’s opening act before companies become profitable (like Amazon). But pro sports teams have been around for decades. The Green Bay Packers, 107 years old, are the eighth or so most popular team in America’s most popular sport. They publicly report their finances to their public owners. Their revenue grew from 2015 to 2025 by about 6 percent per year. That is the same aggregate growth rate as companies in the S&P 500.

No, sports teams aren’t becoming more valuable because they are suddenly more profitable businesses. (They also have challenges: in labor costs, changing viewer habits, imploding regional cable networks, competition from other sports, declining cultural hold.) Sports teams also aren’t becoming more valuable because of another clichéd reason I hear all the time: institutional private equity buyers. According to Charles of Arctos, because of the severe restrictions on which and how private equity firms can buy minority stakes (and only minority stakes), his firm has about 75 percent of the market. It has a Padres’ worth of capital, not enough to shape the value of 124 teams worth about a half-trillion dollars in total. Private equity funds are lending money to sports teams, such as the bulk of capital in the widely misreported transaction between Apollo and the Yankees; they are also investing in emerging sports and the awful professionalization of youth sports. But these are speculative, riskier (if potentially higher returning) infusions of capital into new ventures, not the safer bets into Big Four teams.

In fact, private equity buyers aren’t even usually the best buyer of a minority stake in a team. When I spoke to Sal Galatioto, a blunt, high-energy 74-year-old pioneering sports-team banker, he said in his last 16 assignments, he’s not once sold a minority stake to private equity: “High-net-worth individuals, because of ego-gratification value, because of the perks they get, and because their investment horizons are 30 to 40 years whereas a private equity fund has to sell this thing in 7 to 10 years — they’re always willing to bid more.”

If we are generous to clichés, we could say that private equity dudes are partly shaping the team market. The people buying majority control of sports teams nowadays are almost all in finance (VC, hedge funds, private equity), tech, or the intersection thereof. That is, of course, because that’s the way you can frictionlessly and scalably make billions in America today — maybe second only to inheriting a pro sports team.

For these majority buyers, the product of sports-team ownership has way more ego-gratification benefit than for minority owners, whose rights might not extend much past taking your brother-in-law to fist-bump Kevin Durant in practice. Being the controlling owner of a team can make you a local god, a maker of dreams, a buddy to heroes. At this year’s New Orleans mayoral inauguration, after the new mayor, Helena Moreno, sat down, Gayle Benson, the owner of the Pelicans and Saints, walked into the ceremony surrounded by security. At that moment, I realized that I live in a constitutional monarchy on the Mississippi.

Being a majority owner has tax benefits, too. But its most amazing feature — the core of its differentiation from other glamorous money-pit investments like restaurants — is that every owner, for as long as anyone can remember, has always made money when they sell, with maybe no down years. Charles told me about the returns of one team investor. “There’s nothing amazing about a 13 percent growth rate,” he said. “What’s amazing is how long he compounded 13 percent.”

And so James Dolan’s move underlines an unflattering fact: there remains a “Dolan Discount” of $7.5 billion, the difference between the value the stock market places on the Knicks and Rangers owned by his public companies compared to what almost everyone thinks they could fetch in a sale. Because, yes, someone would almost certainly today pay him $4 billion for the Rangers and a Lakers price for the Knicks. New York is bigger; the sports fans are better. Majority-control transactions remain rare, about four per year. There are multiple bidders for everything for sale, including the Seahawks. Marc Lasry suspects the Lakers would have gone for more than $12.5 billion had Mark Walter had a competitive auction for the team.

Whether it’s the Knicks or another team, for the product of owning a sports team to lose its most attractive feature something almost unimaginable would seem to have to happen after 50 years. Team buyers would have to start losing money.

There is a recent catalyst to the unthinkable in other industries: AI. But in the sports-team market even this seems to be working in owners’ favor. In sports, people cite AI as the reason why the market won’t change. Constantly, people told me that owning a team is “a hedge against AI.” This is yet another stupid cliché in this market — not because it can’t be true, but because it’s incomplete. A farmer doesn’t “hedge against corn”; he hedges against corn prices falling. Hedges need verbs.

Charles told me that the relative AI impact could be modest, with sports-team values simply resilient, increasing by a couple of percentage points faster than the market as a whole. But the press release introducing the Kushner firm that would go on to bid on the Lakers had darker undertones: Thrive Eternal is seeking to invest, it said, in “assets with qualities that cannot be replicated by technology. Iconic franchises and cultural institutions rooted in tradition, identity, and shared experience. In a world shaped by abundant intelligence where creation scales and distribution fragments, we believe they will matter even more.”

In other words, everything else is likely to matter less or wither away. Or as Galatioto said to me, “I’d bet you anything that the Yankees are more likely to be around in 100 years than Apple.” Apollo, for its part, recently called the Yankees, lovingly, “AI-resistant leisure.”

And so the most recent logic underpinning the prices of sports teams is not a hedge against AI. It’s just another bet on AI, that teams will get more valuable as AI gets more disruptive. No one is going to want to watch robots play football, the thinking goes. People are likely to be even more hungry for hug-a-stranger, heart-stopping, consequential-against-all-common-sense unscripted experiences.

Dolan’s dream of $17 billion for the Rangers and Knicks is not just a circular-logic valuation — the teams will be worth more because people will pay more; and people will pay more because teams keep on rising in value — but also an AI-vibe valuation. Owners and wannabe owners think so much could fail in society. But not your team. You will keep watching them, no matter what happens. And somehow, inexplicably, as always, this means that the owners will get richer still.

items.title: Reece King on His Career, Mental Health and Social Media
items.description: Model Reece King on His Career, Mental Health and Social Media
items.author: Justin Moran
paragraphs: Model Reece King on His Career, Mental Health and Social Media

Born in the late '90s, 23-year-old British model Reece King was raised by a single mother and family overflowing with aunties. While caring, King's family wasn't very well off, so he began working long retail hours for minimum wage to contribute to their expenses. Once his modeling career took off and stardom came knocking, he left his job to eventually shoot major campaigns for brands like Diesel and grace magazine covers across the globe.

But when the flashing lights subdue, King remains himself. In fact, he is hyper aware of the concept of self. Reserved, and not wanting to reveal too much, he said, "I have such a hard time trying to talk about myself, because I have this situation where I disassociate myself from job. When I'm at home, I don't really check social media. I don't like to focus on it. I don't talk about it. I pretend it's not real."

A model whose image has been seen by thousands but doesn't like attention may seem like the ultimate paradox, but in reality his shyness is not out of the ordinary at all. "I'm just a little introvert, but I think on social media it probably looks like I'm this big, big character that's always doing something, and loves my picture taken, even though I don't," he said. It's true that once you enter the digital sphere, some people will only listen and some people will only look and formulate ideas of what and how public figures should be.

King's Instagram reaches those who are listening and watching beyond surface. Struggling with depression and severe anxiety throughout most of my life, King's posts have been a visual representation of what it means to stand at the intersection. He talks openly about his battle with mental health and how he manages to juggle everything. "It's been kind of hard," he said. "I've had problems with anxiety, and insomnia, even stuff just to do with my weight, and my mental health. I'm the only person in my family that's managed to get a situation, or job, like this. So it's hard to speak to people about what I feel, or deal with, because some people just can't relate from their perspective."

I share with him how as a younger version of myself, I experienced a feeling many young black people across the globe know too well — the idea that constant stress, worry or fear were all just aspects that come with life, an everyday normality we all go through. Now being much older, I see that things I couldn't quite place my finger on before could be diagnosed and treated. King agrees, "I don't think I actually knew anything about mental health. And it sounds crazy, but thinking back, I don't think I've ever had a serious conversation with someone, that's actually explained, 'You're feeling like this, because of this.' Or, 'Your body's like this, because your mind is here.' I never really had that growing up."

King has managed to find a healthy balance and manifest positive energy into most aspects of his life, saying, "I've just had to learn through a lot of lessons, a few bad moments. I've had to learn what's acceptable and what's not. I found that eating and drinking clean really helps me feel better inside. I also found meditating and reading and some time alone helps. I have plants and a little zen garden that I try to do morning and night. I try to stretch and workout a little bit. And I have three dogs, so it's really good energy with them. The best thing that probably helps me is just knowing that everyone is actually going through something as well."

And when things get really rough, there is always one person he can rely on. "My mom definitely has helped me," he said. "But she doesn't really know a whole bunch about what I do. And I still have to explain the difference between a casting and a request casting, and a campaign. Because it's just not her world."

King's most profound advice regards changing ways of thought. "I think it's a personal journey of learning that there's different ways of thinking. That's something that the person, the individual, has to just go through. Sometimes you have to do some stupid things to know that. I don't actually think I actually understood that sort of advice when I was younger, because your mind space just isn't there. With a little bit of age, I kind of understand you are your own world. If you feel good, then it's good. I've had to learn self-care."

Coming to terms with his sexuality as a bisexual black man was a large part of that journey to self-care. For King, understanding his sexuality was not an easy journey. "Just being a bit younger, like 18 or 19, you just don't know. It's very confusing. I think for a year, I was really, really convinced that I was asexual, because I was so confused that I didn't have a preference," he said. But he soon came to understand himself better, realizing, "I don't really care if it's a woman or a man, because it doesn't make a difference if I'm in love. But then I also felt so insecure towards that subject and I had put it off for so long, I didn't actually know who I really was. I knew what I liked in my head, but when it came to real life, I didn't really know how to interact."
"I was really, really convinced that I was asexual, because I was so confused that I didn't have a preference."

He said he kept putting off his feelings until he and then I eventually realized that this is me for the rest of my life, so I don't really have a choice. I can either make peace with who I am or hate myself or lie. So I think the Gay Times interview came at the right time and I was like, 'You know what, people? I've already said that I'm bisexual, but I guess it could be inspiring and helpful if I actually took that and put it into the modeling influences situation of things.''
As a public figure, King battles the negative stereotypes and tropes applied unfairly to bisexual people.

"With the whole picking sides thing," he says, "I've had situations where I've been talking to a girl and then someone will say something like, 'Oh, girl, you can't talk to him because you know he's messed with boys before.' I've had situations where I'm talking to a guy and then it's like, 'Is that girl a friend or is she more?' If I posted pictures with my friends in the past, it would always just get turned into, 'Oh, that has to be someone he's romantically seeing or sexually seeing, because he likes guys and girls.' But I kind of have to tell people, I'm not interested in every human being."

King also addresses society's desire to pigeonhole black men and fetishize them into lustful objects, saying, "Being biracial, I definitely think I've been sexualized a lot. Sometimes, if people know I'm bisexual, they kind of just think, based on the way I look that it's like, 'Oh, he's only interested in one thing.' I guess that's a fetish on their end. I've tried to find more positives in the situation, but when I was younger, it was definitely harder. I definitely had to smile through a lot of uncomfortable situations, but everything comes around."

Throughout his career, King has helped young people all over the world simply by way of being himself. Standing tall at 5'11 inches, he has a unique aura of positivity that draws you in. In a world consumed with the digital realm, he remains centered, introspective and optimistic for the future. "I believe in the law of attraction," he says. "I think I manifested a lot of things that I've wanted in my life where I'm at right now. And I had to learn that not everything I thought I wanted is actually necessary. It's a process of learning who I am and just growing as an adult. I mean 23, that's barely anything, yet."

items.title: Let Them Eat Olive Spheres: Inside Airbnb’s Star-Studded Charity Gala
items.description: Nothing says billionaire-hosted gala quite like an olive sphere. What’s an olive sphere, you ask? Imagine a bite-sized gelatinous membrane filled with olive juice that is served on a tiny silver platter, and requires two servers—two!—to pass out: one to offer
items.author: Maxwell Adler
paragraphs: Nothing says billionaire-hosted gala quite like an olive sphere. What’s an olive sphere, you ask? Imagine a bite-sized gelatinous membrane filled with olive juice that is served on a tiny silver platter, and requires two servers—two!—to pass out: one to offer guests the savory blobs, and another to collect the discarded platters.

Before taking the stage at Milk Studios in Los Angeles on Wednesday night, Jimmy Kimmel walked past two olive sphere servers and a third handing out caviar. He told me he’d been listening to The Howard Stern Show on the drive over, and something so X-rated came on that he had to quickly turn down the volume when he pulled up alongside another car. Evidently, it put him in a silly mood by the time he welcomed guests to the first ever gala for Airbnb’s independent nonprofit—or “gay-la,” as he put it, “depending on your sexual orientation.”

Kimmel had been tapped to serve as master of ceremonies at the fundraiser for the home-sharing behemoth’s nonprofit, which was created in 2020 to provide free temporary housing to people displaced by disasters and other crises. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky announced a $500 million funding commitment over the next five years, allowing the organization to expand its services to families traveling for medical treatment and survivors of domestic violence.

Among the guests were people who had lost their homes in the devastating Eaton Fire in 2025. They shared a room with a group of people who presumably have little need for emergency housing: Charlize Theron, Serena Williams, Matthew McConaughey, Katie Couric, Joaquin Phoenix, Rooney Mara, Cynthia Erivo, and Demi Lovato, among others. It was a collision of two Los Angeleses: People who had lost everything, and people who wore bling worth as much as a house in Altadena.

Most of the men were dressed in tuxedos. Williams shined in a sparkly animal-print gown. Paul Bettany wore a black Chairman Mao-style shirt. Jaden Smith wore jeans, apparently missing the black-tie memo.

Kimmel, decked out in a perfectly tailored black tuxedo, had some ground rules as the emcee. Guests were expected to wash their dishes. No pets, except service animals, “which we know none of them really are.” “And absolutely no sitting naked on the furniture or on chef José Andrés.”

Chesky, who hard-launched his relationship with girlfriend designer Carly Helfrich on the red carpet, delivered his remarks with the cadence of Vanessa Bayer’s Jacob the Bar Mitzvah Boy Saturday Night Live character, staring down at the teleprompter positioned on the floor. “People are fundamentally good,” he declared, explaining that Airbnb’s business would have never worked otherwise.

On the red carpet, I asked Chesky whether the Trump administration had made it harder for his nonprofit to house people fleeing tragedy. “No, absolutely not,” he insisted, describing emergency housing as a cause that transcends partisan politics. This was a rather diplomatic answer from a man whose company once ran advertisements welcoming refugees in pointed opposition to Trump’s 2017 Muslim travel ban. But Chesky wasn’t taking the bait. “This is a very united kind of issue,” he said.

The night took an emotional turn when Kimmel talked about his son Billy’s three open-heart surgeries before introducing a video of a young boy receiving cancer treatments who was the beneficiary of the charity’s efforts. At that moment, the child, who was in attendance with his mom and grandma, stood on his chair and made a heart symbol using his two hands. The crowd went wild.

José Andrés, whose name appeared on the menu but who was rather noncommittal when asked whether he had actually designed it, insisted that the evening’s charitable mission was more than an excuse for Hollywood to get dressed up.

By dessert, Kimmel was shaking down the wealthy guests. “Don’t cheap out,” he warned, noting that anyone who could afford the new folding iPhone (which retails at roughly $2,000) could surely spare $110 to provide a family with a night of emergency housing. He also accidentally revealed the evening’s secret musical guest: Charli xcx.
“Oh shit!” he exclaimed, realizing his mistake. “Okay, it’s not a surprise anymore.”
Charli eventually took the stage, with will.i.am and Greta Lee dancing from the front row. “That was soooooo good,” Lee said to me on the way out.
And although the set wasn’t particularly long, Charli rocked it, sending heads banging everywhere. She got the Hollywood room doing what it does best: partying for a cause.

items.title: Inside Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s Beloved 730-Acre Country Estate
items.description: On any given day at Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s sprawling 730-acre privately owned estate in Gloucestershire, one might spy the 76-year-old checking in on her prized Highland cows, a scarf tied firmly over her famous bouffant. At the estate’s cutting-edge s
items.author: Hadley Hall Meares
paragraphs: On any given day at Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s sprawling 730-acre privately owned estate in Gloucestershire, one might spy the 76-year-old checking in on her prized Highland cows, a scarf tied firmly over her famous bouffant. At the estate’s cutting-edge stables, her daughter, Zara Tindall, may be riding with her daughter and nieces, coaching them as they jump through courses designed by her father Mark Phillips. Meanwhile, Zara’s husband, rugby star Mike Tindall, may be playing beer pong in the “party barn” with his brother-in-law Peter Phillips, while Princess Anne’s husband Sir Timothy Laurence watches rugby in the cozy, cluttered parlor of the estate’s main Georgian mansion.

The scene is that of an idyllic country estate, a beloved family home that is also a working farm. It may also serve as an example to Prince Harry and Meghan Markle as they search for their own private estate in the British countryside. “Being able to take on a place like this—for me, I’ve got to make it work,” Princess Anne once said. “This is not something that comes free, this has got to pay its way, otherwise I can’t stay here."

Since the ’70s, Gatcombe Park has been Princess Anne’s place of refuge from endless royal duties, a place to live the country life she loves. “Every year, month and day, I realise how fortunate and privileged I am to have grown up and spent most of my life in the countryside,” she told Country Life in 2020. “It’s not only the space, appreciating the seasons, the wildlife, the plant life, the arable crops and the livestock, but, most importantly, it’s the people who live and work there and understand the complexity of their environment.”

The estate was the perfect wedding present from the late Queen Elizabeth to her athletic, no-nonsense daughter and her first husband, Mark Phillips. The two Olympic equestrians first met at a party in 1968, although the meeting was not auspicious. “We had to be told that we’d met in 1968 before we remembered,” Anne recalled.

They later reconnected and found they shared many things, including an obsession with nature, country life, and the world of elite equestrian competitions. “Anne couldn’t marry her horse, so she’s marrying Mark,” the then Prince Charles reportedly joked about his future brother-in-law. Princess Anne approached their upcoming wedding with the same stoicism she did everything. When asked if their relationship could withstand the pressure of publicity and public duties, the Princess was blunt. “Can? It’s got to, hasn’t it.”

The two were married on November 14, 1973, in a lavish ceremony at Westminster Abbey. From the start, Phillips, an active captain in 1st The Queen’s Dragoon Guards, proved to be cut from a different cloth. He refused all the Queen’s offers of titles and was not popular with some royals and their courtiers, with the protective Prince Charles reportedly nicknaming him “fog,” because he was “so thick, according to Kitty Kelley’s The Royals.” British journalist Auberon Waugh (the eldest son of novelist Evelyn Waugh) was even more brutal. He unkindly described him as “Princess Anne’s grinning, speechless husband, who, if you whistle at him, wets himself.”

In spite of naysayers, the couple forged ahead and began searching for the perfect country estate (“I’ve never been a city girl,” Anne noted). In 1976, former Home Secretary Lord Rab Butler, suggested the couple check out Gatcombe Estate, his family home outside of the village of Minchinhampton.

The estate featured over 700 acres of woods and cultivated farmland, stables, a fine herd of Hereford-Friesian cattle and a trout lake, “netting an income of between 14,000 and 18,000 pounds a year.” The five-bedroom neoclassical main house, built with Cotswold stone, was originally built in 1774. In 1820, the famous economist Davis Ricardo had the house redesigned. The exterior was covered in roses and wisteria, and the couple were instantly smitten. The interior was not as picturesque, with one friend describing it as “rather dreary, in some disrepair, with suspicions of dry rot.”

But the couple loved it. “We stood on the front steps and looked out at the view; it was quiet, it was secluded, it was peaceful with woods down each side of a long valley,” Phillips recalled. “I thought to myself—well, whatever is inside, we can change, given time. But this we can never change. This is just what we have been looking for.”

A week later, Princess Anne took Queen Elizabeth to view the property. In June 1976, it was announced the Queen had purchased the home for the couple for a reported 500,000 to 750,000 pounds at the time. Workers on the estate suggested to reporters that Anne could help on a tractor. “Since the Princess can drive a tank, why not?” one quipped.

There was immediate backlash to the private purchase. “When members of the Labour Party government heard that the Queen was buying her daughter and son-in-law the farm and woodland property at such a price, left-wing members called for the introduction of a wealth tax,” the Australian Woman’s Weekly reported. “They pointed out that last year Parliament voted the royal family an extra $600,000 to help it pay its bills.”
MP Willie Hamilton took it a step further. “They’re gold-plated parasites. The lot of them. All parasites.”
For their part, the palace was tight-lipped, claiming the purchase was “an absolutely private matter.” Lord Butler also scoffed at the reported price, claiming it was not nearly as high.

Ignoring the noise, the couple began working to improve their new estate, insisting they would pay their own way. “People never believe me when I say that we’re just like any other young married couple with a mortgage,” Phillips said. Princess Anne did indeed drive a tractor, and Prince Andrew and Prince Edward were said to come down to help during harvest season. While his wife stayed at her apartment working in Buckingham Palace in London during the week, Phillips worked tirelessly on the farm, “so tired that I fell asleep in front of the television.”

Making good on their dream to turn Gatcombe into an A+ equestrian facility, the couple in 1983 hosted the inaugural Gatcombe Park Festival of British Eventing. The event became a mainstay on the elite equestrian calendar. Held every August, it featured Olympians competing in cross-county (courses often designed by Phillips), jumping and dressage events. Thousands attended the televised program each year, and many more visited at the annual craft fairs and the Gatcombe Food Festival.

Phillips found many ways to monetize the estate, even turning brushwood cleared from the courses into paintbrushes. Meanwhile, the couple raised their children Peter and Zara at Gatcombe, where life revolved around horses. “One enjoys riding, but when you get back there’s still half a day’s work to do just to keep the darn things on four legs,” Anne noted, per The Princess Royal by Helen Cathcart. “You have time for nothing else.”

Tindall has noted that she had an “amazing” country childhood on the estate, far from the hustle and bustle of royal life. “It was a great place to grow up around horses, looking after animals—the respect and partnership that you have to build with the animals, it teaches you so much you know growing up and as a kid,” she said.

But this didn’t mean that growing up on the farm wasn’t hard work. The Phillips children (whose parents declined for them to have titles) were expected to carry their weight. “We had to do everything with them,” Zara recalled. “We had to clean our tack. We had to muck them out.”

Zara, who eventually became an Olympic rider herself, recalled that her parents had very different ways of training. “Mum’s very relaxed. She’s like, Just, you know, just do what you do, whereas my father’s like, More of this, more of that, she said. “My father was quite critical... Very rarely you would get a, Yeah, that was good, out of him. So it was always striving to try and get that comment. He was a tough coach.”

There was also tension inside the home. Both Princess Anne and Phillips were unfaithful (Phillips even had a daughter, Felicity, with a New Zealand woman in 1985) and in 1989 they separated. But Phillips did not go far, moving to Aston Farm on the estate and continuing to run Gatcombe’s events (he finally left Aston Farm in 2013). Princess Anne stayed in the main house with her new husband, Sir Timothy Laurence, who she married in 1992.

According to those who have visited the main house, life there is surprisingly “unroyal” and laid-back, filled with bric-a-brac and cozy, worn decor. “Journalists and biographers who visit Gatcombe for the first time are still struck by the informality of the place,” Anne’s biographer Nicholas Courtney told Glocester Live. Gatcombe Park has become a true family compound, with Peter Phillips and his family reportedly having a cottage there. Zara and Mike Tindall have raised their children at Aston Farm since 2013.

Running the estate has also become a family affair. Peter Phillips helped organize the annual Gatcombe Park Festival of British Eventing in later years. Princess Anne would present trophies and Zara would compete, as photographers took pictures of Anne’s grandchildren frolicking.

Farming operations have also continued, a practice Anne clearly relishes. “I have lived at Gatcombe for more than 42 years,” Anne wrote in Country Life in 2020. “We were not looking for a farm, but it has been a real privilege to try to work with what we have. Ours is an organic, extensive grass enterprise, usually complicated by running the horse-trial championships in early August. The woodland is a real mix of trees—mostly beeches, but huge numbers of ash of all ages. Who knows how many will survive, but I feel the naturally selected mix could be an important part of the answer.”

That same year, the official royal website also noted the extensive livestock on the property that included 230 Wiltshire Horn sheep, 14 White Park cows, 6 Highland cows, and 2 Gloucester Old Spot sows. There is also a prized herd of rare Suffolk Punch horses, which Anne is passionate about saving. The estate also includes a kitted out party barn, which includes catering facilities, large screens and bar/lounge areas.

The last few years have been eventful, in both good and bad ways. In 2021, Zara gave birth to her third child, Lucas, on the bathroom floor at Aston Farm. In 2023, the estate hosted their last Eventing Festival, citing rising costs and COVID as the reason.

“The horse trials at Gatcombe and more recently the Festival of British Eventing have been a major part of my life for over 40 years when The Princess Royal and I first had the dream,” Mark Phillips said in a statement at the time. “It’s truly a great sadness that the original model and indeed the sport has changed so much. Since COVID, costs, particularly insurance, have risen so much that the numbers no longer add up. It is an end of an era, the next 40 years of the sport will be different, let’s hope it can be equally special.”

In 2024, Princess Anne was reportedly injured by a horse on the property, which resulted in her being hospitalized for a concussion. But there was happier news in June of 2026, when Peter Phillips and his new wife Harriet Sperling reportedly celebrated their wedding reception at the party barn.

Although Princess Anne still continues with her punishing schedule of official engagements, staying in her London apartment in St. James Palace when she must, it is clear her heart lies at Gatcombe Park, surrounded by her loved ones, beloved animals and the crisp country air. “It’s very normal; there isn’t any standing on ceremony, and she’s the only one with a title,” royal historian Robert Hardman told Hello!. “She’s a very good grandmother. She’s hands-on, but like all grandchildren, I think they can get away with things. She dotes on them.”

In fact, the normally tight-lipped Anne has said so herself. “It’s really nice to come back and just be yourself in an area like this.” Former royal courtier Ailsa Anderson agrees. “Gatcombe is her bolthole, where she is not the Princess Royal—she is Anne.”

items.title: Anthony Boyle Talks Sam Bankman-Fried and ‘The Altruists,’ a Tale of Sex and Crypto
items.description: Given how many venal tech billionaires have grabbed our attention over the last several years, you’d be forgiven for having only a hazy memory of Sam Bankman-Fried. He was the cryptocurrency whiz kid whose exchange, FTX, made him one of the richest men in the
items.author: Joy Press
paragraphs: Given how many venal tech billionaires have grabbed our attention over the last several years, you’d be forgiven for having only a hazy memory of Sam Bankman-Fried. He was the cryptocurrency whiz kid whose exchange, FTX, made him one of the richest men in the world, and who forged a charmingly slackerish persona: a shabbily dressed nerd with good intentions. As a believer in the effective altruism movement, SBF planned to donate his riches to charity. Instead, he is now serving a 25-year prison sentence for fraud and conspiracy.

Anthony Boyle slips under SBF’s skin in The Altruists, the new Netflix limited series chronicling the rise and fall of FTX—as well as the relationship between Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner), his on-and-off romantic and business partner. The Belfast-born Boyle is best known to American audiences for his roles in historical dramas like House of Guinness (as 18th-century Irish lord Arthur Guinness), Say Nothing (as IRA leader Brendan Hughes), and Masters of the Air (as WW2 Air Force officer Harry Crosby). He got his break while still in college when he was cast as Scorpius Malfoy in the original cast of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child in London’s West End.

Ellison’s character would love that. The geek love she and SBF share in the series is complicated and cringe-inducing. She writes Harry Potter fanfic and considers herself polyamorous; he’s a virgin wowed by her brainy sophistication. They egg each other on, bound together by their hunger for risk and their desire to win, whatever the game and whatever the cost. Throughout it all, they remain convinced that they are the good guys.

The Altruists drops November 19, in the midst of a Hollywood tech billionaire reckoning that includes the Sam Altman biopic Artificial, Musk, the Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything, and Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network, The Social Reckoning. Boyle says he hasn’t seen any of those films yet, though he was originally set to play SBF in another movie that fell through. “I was sort of heartbroken,” he tells me, “because I’d spent a couple of months prepping, I had turned down other projects, and then it was taken away from me. I was like, I’m never gonna be able to do that voice that I worked so hard on!”

Yet when his agent called with news of the Netflix project, Boyle was hesitant. “My heart was already broken by [SBF] once,” he says. But the scripts for The Altruist—written by Graham Moore, the screenwriter of The Imitation Game—changed his mind. “It’s so funny and more about the relationship between him and Caroline,” the actor says now, “about their love story and them goading each other to do all this.”
During his initial meeting with Moore, Boyle stayed in character as Bankman-Fried. “I

was complaining about getting off of a Zoom with Mark Zuckerberg, because that’s the tone of the show. It can be quite irreverent at some points, and then other scenes are kind of heartbreaking.” It won him the part. “Thankfully,” he says, “all my prep didn’t go to waste!”
Vanity Fair: It’s funny that you were so eager to live in Sam Bankman-Fried’s head. He is such an anxious figure.

Boyle: There’s a lot of anxiety in him. You can even tell in his speech patterns: He corrects himself and goes back and forth, like his internal metronome is going so quickly at all times. He’s like a hummingbird, like his heart’s beating so quick. But thankfully I didn’t take any of that home with me.
