At a couple of points in the series, he says, “I know I’m not a normal person.” There’s an ongoing public conversation right now about a lot of these tech moguls believing they know better than the rest of us. Did you think of SBF as someone with that kind of Superman complex?

I think the opposite. I played him as someone who was profoundly insecure. There’s this thing of broken men building empires. He has this idea of: I am FTX. So if I can make FTX the biggest, the richest, if I can have the most of something…. That’s not someone who’s comfortable in his own skin. I was interested in what possessed someone to become the world’s youngest billionaire. I’m not really interested in money or crypto or finance. It was: What makes them do the things that they do?
Sam is a nerdy guy, but as soon as he gets successful, he hangs giant posters of himself everywhere. Is he burning for the world to recognize him and admire his empire?

Do you know the poem “Ozymandias” [by Percy Bysshe Shelley]? There’s a bit in the show where I’m looking up at this great poster of myself, and it reminded me of that line: “Look on my works, ye mighty, and despair!” I asked Graham, “Can I quote that poem in the show?” And he said, “Originally called that episode ‘Ozymandias!’”

Talking about wanting to be recognized—when I was prepping for this, I went to a crypto guy’s birthday party in Los Angeles. He was paying a DJ a million dollars for one evening, but he built this plinth above the DJ decks for him and his friends so you had to look at him. A lot of these crypto people, who maybe didn’t have buzzing social lives—wallflowers who didn’t know how to communicate—became billionaires. And what this guy had done with it was to throw money at a very famous DJ, and then raise himself above him. It reminded me of the scene where Sam has a 100-foot poster behind him. It was like, Wow, this is that sort of man in his mum’s basement who just wants the world to see him.

In Sam’s case, his roaring egotism is somewhat awkward because he’s also obsessed with the idea of being altruistic. At one point in the show, a leader of the Effective Altruism movement sees this lavish party he’s thrown and says, “Uh, this isn’t very altruistic.”

Yes, he’s spent a lot of money on confetti cannons! That dichotomy is what’s really fascinating about him, because I think both of those two things are true. I think he really is altruistic, and I think he does have narcissistic tendencies.
I read that you corresponded with him in prison. What did you want to know?

Annoyingly for this interview, I promised him that I wouldn’t divulge anything. I asked him to open his heart up to me, and he really did. He was very forthcoming with over 100 questions in emails. He answered, I’d say, 98% of them. Even the ones that he didn’t answer were very telling for me, because you’re like a detective, trying to figure out how he answers them and in what way. And can you trust it?
As we see in the series, he insisted on doing interviews throughout the scandal. Even when his lawyers were telling him to stop.

When I was playing those scenes, it was like: I can outsmart this; I can get in front of it. I can just explain this to them. You know, he went to jail for stealing the money—but if he didn’t go to jail, a year later to the day, all of that money would have been back, and tenfold. He invested in Anthropic. He invested in the biggest AI companies. His argument was: Look, I know the markets. What you all see is a bird falling to certain death. What I can see is that the bird is swooping, and will come back up. I read last week that said Sam might have been the world’s first trillionaire had he not gone to jail, because all the AI companies are now flourishing.
The show frames Sam and Caroline as a love story. But it’s hard to tell if they are egging on each other’s delusions, or if this is kind of a game that’s fueling their relationship.

They’re obsessed with games. Even the first time they meet, they are playing a game. This isn’t in the show, but in my head, the scene that I sort of created for myself to understand him was: He’s playing World of Warcraft, and on the same screen he loses $100 million, and then he dies in World of Warcraft. He’s like, Fuck!, and feels more emotional about the game than about other people’s money.
It does feel like the real-life consequences are very abstract to him. Like he’s busy trying to outplay everyone and not thinking: This is going to cause somebody to go bankrupt and ruin their lives.

I think that’s the great tragedy of it, because people did go bankrupt, and people unfortunately died by suicide through this. Marriages broke up. Families tore apart because all of their money was in this. And that’s something that we have to remember when talking about the show. There were real-world consequences because of this crash.
There’s a whole spate of movie projects this fall that suggest tech bros are the new supervillains. But it sounds like you didn’t approach the character that way at all.

My viewpoint on it is that Sam wants to do good. But I think the best-laid plans of mice and men often [go awry]. It’s easy to say I’m going to give away all these billions—and then suddenly you’re not in your mum’s basement, and you’re hanging out with Katy Perry, and you think, This feels pretty good to me. I don’t think people should have that amount of power.
You are Mr. Period Actor. Is this the first time that you’ve played a character living in the present?

I feel like it is. It’s the first time I had to act with a laptop and an iPhone, and it’s so annoying. There’s no one there that you’re looking at. You’re just looking at a green screen. And then it [causes problems]—like, Oh, we saw the camera in the reflection when you turned it that way. These things that I didn’t have to deal with before because I was, as you said, Mr. Period Man.
Even Say Nothing was set in the 1970s and ’80s, well before cell phones.
That was more handguns than iPhones.

One of your most recent period characters is Arthur Guinness in House of Guinness, and there’s been some buzz about your full-frontal nude scene on that show. I’m just curious if there’s anything that you would not do on screen.

That’s such a funny question. I guess whatever they write in the script, I’d look at it and see if I wanted to do it, but probably not! Like when I did that scene, it was in service of the character and in service of the moment. I wanted that character to feel like he's in control of the world and that these are all peasants that are beneath him and he doesn’t care. Very opposite to Sam, who I think has a lot of body shame.
Somehow, I don’t know that the world wants to think about Sam Bankman-Fried naked.
You never know, man. There’s something out there for everyone.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

items.title: Heidi Klum Teases Her Latest Halloween Costume
items.description: Halloween is just around the corner—and what does that mean? It means that Heidi Klum, the undisputed queen of the scariest night of the year, will soon reveal her incredible new costume. After dressing up as an anthropomorphic worm, an incredibly realistic ET
items.author: Alfredo Toriello
paragraphs: Halloween is just around the corner—and what does that mean? It means that Heidi Klum, the undisputed queen of the scariest night of the year, will soon reveal her incredible new costume. After dressing up as an anthropomorphic worm, an incredibly realistic ET, and a chimpanzee complete with prosthetic facial features and ears, the supermodel is ready to amaze us once again.

Back in September, she revealed to People that she was already hard at work planning her next big costume. While she didn’t reveal any details—which is perfectly understandable—she did hint that it would be a “very, very bloody” look and that it “goes very well with red wine.” She’s given a few clues; the latest one she shared on her Instagram profile.

“What’s my costume?” the supermodel asked her followers, attaching a spooky close-up of some prosthetics ready to transform her into who knows what. The image appears to include a shiny brain, a blue tube resembling a sea creature, fleshy tissue, and a yellow sac that could be a honeycomb, coral, earwax—in short, anything.

Of course, many have tried to come up with an answer. Some suggested it might be Ursula from The Little Mermaid; others noted similarities to the vanity monster portrayed by Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley in The Substance, while another user pointed out that the image resembles the appearance of the zombies in The Last of Us.

In an interview with NBC’s Hollywood ReelTime, special effects makeup artist Mike Marino—who has created some of the model’s most iconic Halloween looks—revealed that this year’s costume is the most complicated one he’s ever worked on.

It seems almost impossible for Klum to follow last year’s incredible costume; on the 25th anniversary of her famous Halloween party, she appeared as the mythological Medusa. Her body was entirely covered in green scales; she had a long tail and moving snakes instead of hair, while her husband, Tom Kaulitz, dressed as a Greek soldier turned to stone.

It’s quite the challenge to top that legendary getup. Yet we’re certain the former Victoria’s Secret Angel won’t disappoint. So mark your calendar for this weekend to find out whom Heidi Klum will be impersonating.
Originally published by Vanity Fair Italia.

items.title: The Traitors: New Blood Recap: The Game Finally Moves Forward
items.description: We left the roundtable last week in chaos. Who won the power of the pardon? Will they pardon Victor? I mean, yes. Obviously yes. The anticlimax of then kicking him off anyway. The producers would not let it happen. Also, who else is going to take the reins of
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: We left the roundtable last week in chaos. Who won the power of the pardon? Will they pardon Victor? I mean, yes. Obviously yes. The anticlimax of then kicking him off anyway. The producers would not let it happen. Also, who else is going to take the reins of the Faithful after Victor leaves? Jay tried being loud, and everyone hated it. I know I’ve been vocally anti-Victor, but I acknowledge that this group is giving very little, leaving room for Victor to do the most. I also acknowledge that I fully believed Tomica when she said she accidentally said Katie’s name, and my sister-in-law judged me heartily for this.

Shane wins the power of the pardon. Shane voted for Victor, but Shane also seems like a kind, thoughtful man who might change his mind (damn him). And change his mind he does! “Bro, bro, bro,” an eloquent Wyatt proclaims. Shane says he used his power as a New Yorker to discern truth from lies and determined that Victor was telling the truth. Morgan looks how I feel. Shane is on board with Fruitgate now! Victor is slowly winning over the castle.

In the Traitors’ turret, Katie and Tomica are able to have it out over Tomica saying Katie’s name as a potential Traitor, and Katie then voting for Tomica. Katie didn’t think Tomica was going to go home (she says). Tomica doesn’t know if she said Katie’s name. I wish we had more time in these damn episodes so we could hear more of the conversations. Why isn’t Tomica tossing Wyatt’s name out there? Why are the Traitors constantly thrown when asked to name other potential Traitors? Wyatt is in love with Victor, so you’re not going to lose his loyalty if you name him. Just have some names ready to go! Come on, people. Why am I doing your job for you? I still want Joe and Katie to win, but I’m gonna need some better playing. They lasted this long because no one in this castle knows what they’re doing. Except Victor, I guess?

They decide that the choice for murder is down to Victor, Abby L, or Clyde. Even aside from my dislike of him, they should objectively kill Victor. They can say someone was trying to frame them, and if the other players don’t believe that, Victor is not going to give up on trying to get Tomica and Joe out anyway. But they decide to kill Abby L. to put heat on Wyatt. Does that work? No. No, it does not.

The next morning, when the players find out that Abby L. has been murdered, they all immediately decide that Wyatt is being framed. Even Morgan! I love Morgan, but she is terrible at this game. So if they had murdered Victor, would everyone assume that someone was framing Tomica? Maybe! I do not like strategy games, but even I am like, you guys, can someone think a few moves ahead, please? Everyone but damn Victor is playing in a real reactionary way. This is making me miss Rob, even though he crushed Moira’s heart.

Alan has harvested a Truffula tree for his boutonniere and comes in to tell everyone that they are all going to have a gossip sesh and then head straight to the roundtable. Victor takes this opportunity to follow Tomica from room to room, which, sure. Why not? What else is he gonna do? Kriste says she doesn’t have any brain cells left and needs someone to tell her what to do. GUYS. She is shocked that her mom experience is not helping her more in this television game show. Look, I am also a mom, but it’s wild that that was her pitch to get on the show and it worked. Kriste tells us that her superpowers are constipated. Between this and Joe’s roughage comment, is everyone doing okay in the castle? Seems like not. Victor follows Tomica out of the room, leaving Joe and Katie alone to agree that they messed up by not killing him. Yes! You did! But now this game will finally move forward, I guess.

At the morning roundtable, Alan tells the players that Marathon, Agincourt, and Waterloo were all decisive battles fought early in the day. And now we have these low-key influencers sitting at a table ready to vote someone out. The parallels. No one talks, and then Victor accuses Tomica (surprise) and says that people who lie are more prone to messing names up. Are they? Kriste launches into some menopause education, which Victor doesn’t know how to respond to. “How am I supposed to say anything to menopause?” “Read an article!” That’s fair; you probably should read an article, Victor. I don’t particularly care about what, but I would like you to expand your mental horizons beyond “girls are pretty,” “I am a sweaty boy,” and “I don’t know what to say about menopause.”

Joe speaks up when Wyatt declares that no one is defending Tomica, but only to say how he has tried to be as authentic and honest as possible. Smooth, Joe. When Victor asks him to name a Traitor other than Victor, Joe says that if it’s not Victor, it’s probably Tomica. Daaaaaamn. Okay, this is fine. At some point, Traitors have to sacrifice other Traitors. We see such a pared-down version of the roundtable, and based on the vote, the winds were blowing pretty hard against Tomica.

The vote is Jay (Victor), Morgan (Tomica), Shane (Tomica), Kriste (Tomica), Tomica (Victor), Katie (Tomica), Victor (Tomica), Abbey B (Tomica), Clyde (Tomica). That means Tomica is banished, but the other players voted: Ben (Tomica), Joe (Tomica), Wyatt (Tomica).

Tomica stands in front of them all and tells the players that she flew her plane a little too close to the sun and got burned because she’s a Traitor. The biggest “we caught a Traitor” celebration ever happens, because they have been wrong so many times. It’s so ridiculous that Alan starts laughing and then gets teary! Aww, Alan! Clyde cries because he feels betrayed by his friend. Oh nooo, the downside of this game of relationships and trust!

Then Joe cries in the interview chair because he feels awful for voting for Tomica, and then Katie is sad because she knows that this all but confirms Joe for people. Victor is “the messiah of the castle,” according to her. So kill him! Literally, what do you all have to lose? I am genuinely so curious as to who Joe and Katie are going to murder, because who on earth else could it be? Wyatt? That won’t do anything to shift the outcome. Clyde is just a sad choice. Abbey B is giving us nothing and killing her would do nothing. Kriste would be confusing, I guess, but Kriste is literally telling people to tell her what to do. Morgan wouldn’t do anything; Jay is a shield … I guess they could kill Ben. Or Shane. But they should kill the loudest person.

Who would I vote for on Traitors? It’s hard to judge what one would do without having the insider knowledge, because who knows the full context of what’s happening in that castle, but based on what’s presented, here are my picks:
No Insider Knowledge: I would vote for Tomica. Everyone else did it, except Tomica and Jay, and I’m not singling myself out like that.

Yes Insider Knowledge: I mean … okay, I’ve said Victor every week, so let’s switch it up and have them kill Abbey B. It won’t change anything, but there needs to be consequences for a lack of contribution.

items.title: The Lowdown Recap: Never Split Up
items.description: Ethan Hawke continues to repulse/delight as The Lowdown’s gross/hot, dumb/talented, obnoxious/charming anti-hero, but “Raw Milk” belongs to the series’ newcomers. Betty Gilpin’s plucky oddball Ginger hits a personal high-water mark of desperation now that she
items.author: Amanda Whiting
paragraphs: Ethan Hawke continues to repulse/delight as The Lowdown’s gross/hot, dumb/talented, obnoxious/charming anti-hero, but “Raw Milk” belongs to the series’ newcomers. Betty Gilpin’s plucky oddball Ginger hits a personal high-water mark of desperation now that she knows Mekko is on the run from something dangerous. Steve Earle reappears as a small-town journalist holding a mirror up to Lee’s devil-may-care, anything-for-the-story style of local journalism. Tommy Lee Jones, previously confined to the immediate vicinity of Hoot Owl Books, finally gets somewhere to go and something to do.

And we get our first glimpse of Martha Plimpton — impeccably cast as Woodrell County sheriff Vela Thorne. Vela’s bottle-blonde hair is shellacked into a helmet; her cowboy boots are made for walking down Main Street USA. She’s a woman in a man’s job. She’s a stone-cold bitch thriving in a sea of corruption. Tulsa might be rotten just below the surface, but in Woodrell, the snakes don’t even bother to hide in the brush.

“Raw Milk” is a fun ride, but there are elements of the nonsensical to the hour, which I found distracting. The first is the pairing of Marty, Ray, and Frog. Like Lee before him, Marty is finding the dig story a little dry for his taste. But he is intrigued by a related scoop: archeological looting. According to Ray — the bitchy antiques dealer — there’s a highly illicit, highly lucrative black market for misappropriated Native American artifacts in Tulsa. Tonight, Ray and Marty are attending an auction run out of the same private members’ club from which Lee lifted a Joe Brainard sketch in season one.

They’re doing preliminary research in the stacks of Hoot Owl when Frog comes in looking for a copy of As I Lay Dying, which he finds shelved in the “Lee’s Picks” section. (The Lowdown loves to intimate that the fallen apple overestimates its distance from the tree.) Frog regales Marty and Ray, who already make an exceptionally odd couple, with what must be a bullshit account of the time he spent as a runaway in Durango, Mexico, on the set of The Treasure of the Sierra Madre. Frog insists that the John Huston classic was an elaborate cover for unauthorized excavation. Intrigued, Ray and Marty invite Frog to come along to the soirée.

Marty needs Ray to get into the auction, but why do either of them want an eccentric like Frog there? He capably poses as a swaggering archeologist, but before long he’s visiting the open bar too often, lingering too long over the curios of pottery shards and Mississippian carvings. Frog has such palpable “I’m gonna take something” energy that it’s shocking he’s able to walk out of the place with the owl-shaped shell gorget he’s been eyeing since they walked in. Ray is scandalized, but Marty doesn’t mind — he leaves the auction with enough sources to pick up his story. As for Frog, you can’t really steal something that’s already stolen, can you? He wants to see Marty take the Tulsa robber barons down in print and make a little trouble for his son at the same time. In place of the repurloined gorget, Frog leaves a Hoot Owl Books promotional pin under glass at the auction.

That Lee is graceless under pressure is well established on The Lowdown, but even so, his bungling of the Lonnie predicament is so extreme that the story line felt like it was scripted chiefly for laughs. (In which case, touché. I did laugh a lot.) At the end of episode three, Johnny and Lee were left wondering what to do with the cop lying unconscious by Johnny’s shed. In the minutes between then and when “Raw Milk” picks up, they apparently decided the best course of action was to load said cop into the trunk of Johnny’s car and drive him over to Cyrus’s office. Except he’s not that unconscious — he’s yelling to be let out. And when they arrive at Tulsa Beat, Cyrus is yelling because it’s bad manners to bring the cop you battered to someone else’s yard. Lee wants Cyrus’s help to interrogate Lonnie, and Draymond agrees to join Lee’s legal team for a retainer. Lee doesn’t live by the code of “act first, think later.” It’s act, act, act, act, act all the time.

But when the gang heads back outside to grab Lonnie, he’s already escaped the trunk. To me, this seems like a good outcome. Lee didn’t have any actual questions to ask. Cyrus wasn’t interested in becoming an accessory to cop-napping. Draymond, the only level head among them, points out that Tulsa isn’t in Woodrell County, where Lonnie’s badge is from, so he likely wasn’t creeping around Johnny’s hot tub in a professional capacity. (Also, Lee did pants Lonnie before throwing him in the trunk — an “intimidation” tactic — so if he was super keen to question him, he could overtake Lonnie waddling down the street with his jeans at his ankles.)

By the time Lee recounts the night’s events for Ginger, they’ve been embellished with his half-true heroics. This particular strain of Lee’s sleaziness comes off as harmless, though, because Ginger doesn’t hang on his every word. To the extent she even likes Lee, it’s in spite of her better judgment. She’s a public defender, professionally trained to perceive when people have drifted from the truth. There’s more to any case than the facts.

Luckily for their floundering investigation, Lee did stumble onto a critical point of coincidence. Mekko had told Angie that he’d been forced to remain with a dead body in prison, but when Ginger looked into it, the only recent inmate death had been Nathan Spence, a young offender being held at county lockup in Woodrell. The Woodrell sheriff’s office maintains that particular jail — the same office where Lonnie serves as deputy. The good news is that they have a fresh lead. The bad news is that the home intruder with the SS neck tattoo Ginger shot a few episodes back is actually a cop.

Lee wants to rush up to Woodrell and start peppering people with questions. Which questions? He doesn’t say. Which people? He’ll know them when he sees them. But first, Johnny is going to fix up the tooth Lee half-lost during his fisticuffs with Lonnie. He’s never been to the dentist before, and he’s hoping Ginger will stick around to offer moral support. Their relationship is evolving. Lee is helping Ginger to find her AWOL fugitive boyfriend; Ginger spends the morning with Lee and Lee’s ex-wife’s husband ripping nitrous. There’s a give and a take, I suppose. It’s entertaining, but I couldn’t shake the feeling that the scene was reverse-engineered from its gruesome end shot: Lee laughing maniacally into the camera, his teeth hopelessly mangled.

“Raw Milk” finally hits its stride when it gets out of Tulsa. Ginger has a connection in Woodrell. With Lee’s smile refreshed, they drive out to meet her old colleague, Jeff, at the depressing roadhouse that doubles as his office. As they wait for him, Lee and Ginger get to talking about something other than the case. Last time Lee saw Frog, Frog went off his meds, and Lee was compelled to have his old man hospitalized. But those are just the facts. Ginger asks if father and son were ever close, which makes Lee laugh. How can you be close to a guy as unreliable and irascible and egomaniacal as that? Ginger’s a public defender, though, professionally trained to cut to the chase. She wants to know: Is it possible to be close to Lee?

Jeff’s belated arrival saves Lee from having to answer the question. Crucially, it saves him from having to think too hard about the question and about the tendencies he may have inherited from a man he despises. It also gives Ginger and Lee another chance to introduce themselves as a non-couple. They were a hit at the dentist’s office; Johnny loved Ginger for his buddy. And Jeff, who was transferred out of the Tulsa PD’s office — probably for drinking on the job, but perhaps just for being horny and inappropriate — gives Lee his meaningless nod of approval. The series seems to be slow-building the case for this odd coupling.

Jeff represented Nathan. He claims to have gotten the kid a good plea deal — placement in a diversion program where he could work off his sentence. But Nathan died in county lockup before ever making it to his placement. The sheriff’s office is calling it a medical emergency, but that doesn’t satisfy Nathan’s mother. Jeff warns them that Sheriff Thorne is a cunt, but, equally, he seems like he might say that about any woman in power.

Usually, it’s a bad sign when the good guys split up, but so far it’s taken Lee and Ginger half a television season just to discover that the man they’re looking for is missing by choice. They’re not exactly making great inroads together. Ginger and Jeff head to see Nathan’s mom, who overcomes her initial wariness to confide in Ginger that she thinks someone murdered her son.

But that’s not what’s being reported in the Woodrell County Monitor. Lee separately heads to the newspaper’s offices to confront their columnist, Dale Slater — the same guy who gave Lee a safe ride home from McMann’s house last episode. Dale didn’t tell Lee about his day job then, but he did recognize Lee from his car-crash acceptance speech at the Tulsa journalism awards, which has gone low-key viral in a very small corner of Oklahoma. Dale wasn’t impressed. In fact, he sees the project of local journalism very differently.

Dale practices selective journalism: Tell only the productive truths. If there’s no responsible way to tell the story of Nathan Spence’s tragic, mysterious death, then it shouldn’t be told. It’s no wonder that Dale believes that “Truth’s Easy”; he’s only telling the easy truths! But Dale’s conservative journalism is so toothless as to be misleading. If the town paper ignores the suspicious death of a young inmate, how can a community hold its leaders to account?

Luckily for the people of Woodrell, Lee Raybon Jr., Tulsa truthstorian, is here to do some good old-fashioned shoe-leather reporting. He follows Dale over to the 4-H Fair to uncover police corruption at the market lamb competition, which will be judged by Sheriff Thorne. Thorne is something of a celebrity in town. When Lee finds her, she’s coaching her daughter, who worries that one of the boys is destined to win the lamb contest. Thorne tells her that steady eye contact and a firm handshake are the secret to being a woman in a man’s world, but I’m pretty sure being the sheriff’s daughter can’t hurt. As Thorne progresses through the livestock tent with her husband’s arm slung over her shoulders, she gets pulled into grip-and-grins with her constituents. Lee, standing nearby, offers to take the photos.

Vela’s already heard about Lee, the busybody out-of-towner who’s been hanging out at the Boontill strip club. Just beyond the lamb pen, Lee asks to see the coroner’s report for Nathan Spence, but Vela counters that she’d be happy to sit down for a Heartland Press interview at a later date at a more appropriate venue. She’s brushing him off. Even after Lee mentions her deputy Lonnie turning up at his ex-wife’s house, she won’t be intimidated.

Neither is Lee cowed by the sheriff’s bravado, though he is obliged to accept her terms. Because, well, he has the shits. Since arriving at the fair, Lee’s been haphazardly guzzling down unpasteurized milk. Now, at the critical moment, his digestive tract is rebelling. Just when he should be screaming truth to power, he finds himself holed up in a porta-potty. Many of you will delight in these high jinks, but Lee is already too gross and greasy for me. From the moment I saw him dribbling raw milk down his beard, I lived in fear of how this would end up.

Lee is still imprisoned in the porta-potty when Deputy Lonnie arrives at the fair, asking for his badge and gun. Lee hands him back his wallet, but the gun he’s left in Dan’s safekeeping. So Lonnie hauls Lee in. This isn’t Tulsa. We’re in Lonnie’s neck of the woods now. When Lee wants to know what he’s being charged with, Vela teases the murder of Chili Franks. Or maybe she’ll just charge Lee with harboring a fugitive. See, Woodrell is a small town. The head prison guard McMann is Vela’s cousin, and he thinks Lee knows exactly where Mekko is.

Eventually, Lee asks for his phone call and reveals he’s got the phone number for “Big D” written on the inside of his boot. At first, I assumed he must be about to call Draymond, the most recent addition to his investigative team, but there’s an even bigger D in Oklahoma who owes him a favor after season one.

Either way, my takeaway from “Raw Milk” is that Ginger and Lee really should never split up. It’s not just that Lee finds himself in trouble in her absence, but that the series itself feels less rich when she’s missing from action. We’ve already watched Lee successfully swagger his way through a season of reckless reporting. We’ve turned up every week to be charmed and repulsed by the same guy, rooting for him to win in spite of ourselves. But Lee’s bluster is less grating on the audience when Ginger is there to contradict him or, even better, simply ignore him.

items.title: Survivor Recap: Soul Crushing
items.description: The switch to three tribes is really screwing with this season, huh? There have been bright spots in these three post-tribe-swap episodes, especially Kilby and Lewis (and Maggie!)’s flashy move at last week’s Tribal Council, but it’s hard to escape the feeling
items.author: Ben Rosenstock
paragraphs: The switch to three tribes is really screwing with this season, huh? There have been bright spots in these three post-tribe-swap episodes, especially Kilby and Lewis (and Maggie!)’s flashy move at last week’s Tribal Council, but it’s hard to escape the feeling that season 51 is stalling when it could really be cooking. Based on the previews for next week, the merge will be upon us very soon, so I’m not actually super worried about this tailspin continuing — but that doesn’t make it super fun to experience in real time.

Problem tribes were common in the New Era, a frequent effect of the three-tribe format (plus the exponential weakening effect of shedding tribe members while losing out on important food-based rewards). Those tribes can sometimes produce engaging underdogs, like the Tika 3 on season 44 or Emily Flippen and Kaleb Gebrewold on season 45. But that isn’t quite the case with the dwindling nü-Savu tribe on season 51. Instead, watching this group go to Tribal Council over and over is just dull, especially because it means missing out on seeing new dynamics get tested elsewhere.

So much of the screen time in “I Love Crying” is spent on just three characters: Devin, Jelly, and Ori. And while each of them has some charm (Jelly most of all), we don’t actually learn that much about them in this episode. Sure, there are plenty of talking heads where Devin and Jelly express how much fun the three of them are having together, and how strong the banter is between the core two in particular, but barely any of the actual connection makes it to the screen. I’m not sure seeing Dev teach Ori his model walk was enough for me to feel sold on this lovable trio in this episode, or to feel heartbroken (rather than just annoyed) when they fell short during the immunity challenge. Jelly says that yesterday was one of the best days of her life, but that didn’t quite come across.

Besides, the edit made it obvious from the beginning of this episode that Savu would be heading back to the chopping block. How many times did Devin or Jelly mention how desperately the three wanted to avoid turning on one another? The amount of gameplay available to the Savu players was already scarce in the previous two episodes, but the options are even scarcer this time. Credit to Jelly for at least flexing her idol and refusing to let herself be considered — though Devin could’ve blindsided her if he really wanted to — and credit to Ori for his valiant attempt to sway the other two into viewing their closeness as a liability instead of a strength. But it was never going to work, and it doesn’t.

Ori does seem like a nice guy, and I’m not actively happy to see him go. It would’ve been nice to see the helicopter alliance make it deeper into the game, especially considering how common it is for Black players to leave pre-merge. But after seeing women get slaughtered in tribal after tribal this year, it’s at least a relief to see one of the men (and not necessarily one of the most dynamic characters) go home. It’s just a shame that his big emotional sendoff doesn’t work as it should. Six episodes isn’t too soon to build real investment in a character dynamic, but whether it’s a result of casting or editing, this outcome is more sad-in-theory than actually sad.

The other big event of the episode is the summit, which is essentially a New Era-style journey where each tribe picks a representative and sends them off for some unknown task. Cristian smartly makes sure one of his people is chosen when they draw rocks, so Sharonda goes; Maggie and Thien An push for Kristin to go in order to keep power out of Mike’s hands; Ori rounds out the mission. The three representatives have a supposedly difficult choice before them: Two of them will take food back to their camps, while one stays behind on Exile and receives a tethered idol (which can only be used on the other two players) for their trouble.

Kristin is basically the only one who even cares about getting this weird non-idol, so it’s not difficult for the three to come to a consensus (though the edit frames this partially as some smart, subtle manipulation on Sharonda’s end). It seems like a weird power to begin with — it protects Sharonda and Ori, not Kristin herself, so why would she sacrifice so much to get it? But of course there’s a twist: If both of the other players are voted out, the tethered idol will become a personal immunity idol for Kristin. And now that Ori’s out, that could happen in the near future! Things are looking up for Kristin, and we love that. Not sure I needed the gratuitous backstory montage about her decades-long Survivor fandom, though. We’ve already been over that ad nauseam. If anything, Kristin’s depth of nerdy super-fandom is the one thing keeping me from totally embracing her as my favorite of the season.

Speaking of nerds, it seems likely Mike would’ve been the one to go if his tribe went to tribal this time. Most of the Toka content is still hitting the usual beats: Everyone knows Mike is suspicious and playing for himself, so they’re keeping him at arm’s length, even Kristin. “Either I’m going home next, or I’m going to win this damn thing,” Mike says, and personally, I’m hoping for the former. He’s clearly an intelligent guy, but I’m not riveted by his screen presence.

There’s a general slackness to the pacing in “I Love Crying,” possibly because the non-Savu tribes are just sitting around and waiting for something to happen. Like, it’s charming to watch Carter apply his skills to create a sack swing, but the scene gets overexplained with some more on-the-nose confessional talk about the necessity of taking time away from game talk. Besides, real entertainment on Survivor usually comes from friction, especially Maggie’s annoyance with her tribemates (and Brady’s irritation in return).

Dina has a bit more going on in the wake of Kilby’s game-changing move. Eric is as emotional as you’d expect about this grave betrayal, though he still cares about the guy, and I suspect he’ll still try to keep him around if he can. Sharonda is playing things smart by recognizing that Eric needs love and attention to be kept on side, but Eric still seems more connected to Kilby on a personal level, and her unconvincing summit story might not help. So much of building a trusting alliance is about instinct, and Eric’s once-in-a-lifetime soul connection with Kilby may actually win out in the end.

The tribe swap has put the narrative in a weird spot these last few weeks: The game once felt like an open board, where anybody could be taken out (even pantsless Patt!), but stretching the cast thin by sticking them in smaller groups has limited the options severely. That will hopefully change next week, with everybody on the same beach again and fighting for their individual agendas. It’s just too bad we had to slog through another predictable three-tribe massacre for a bit before we got there. We know how these things go; nothing new to see here.

• The challenge itself was … fine? I’ve actually found some of the challenges this season somewhat refreshing and raw, but this one didn’t have a ton of standout moments, and it always felt inevitable that Savu wouldn’t come through.

• Cristian is finally starting to emerge as a strategic player, if not a well-developed character. He seems keen to abandon the sinking Savu ship and use Kilby and Lewis for their Toka relationships, partly just to cause chaos and indulge his fun side. I mean, hey, I support chaos.

• Devin and Jelly’s praise of Ori during tribal felt a tad condescending to me, even if it came from a genuine place. I would not be happy to pal around in this moment. Ditto Jeff’s inspirational monologue about how getting voted out isn’t failure, since almost everyone loses Survivor. Let the guy be sad about his crushed dreams for a sec, guys! It makes for memorable TV!
• That said, the show did make sure to include every instance of Ori claiming that his Shot in the Dark was absolutely, 100 percent going to work, only to fail.

items.title: Microdrama Platform FlareFlow Sets Thailand Launch on AIS Play (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Microdrama platform FlareFlow will launch in Thailand on Nov. 2 through AIS Play, the entertainment service of Thai telecom operator Advanced Info Service (AIS), in a deal brokered by Singapore-based distributor Rock Networks.
items.author: Naman Ramachandran
paragraphs: Microdrama platform FlareFlow will launch in Thailand on Nov. 2 through AIS Play, the entertainment service of Thai telecom operator Advanced Info Service (AIS), in a deal brokered by Singapore-based distributor Rock Networks.

FlareFlow, the vertical video service owned by COL Group, will cost subscribers THB39 ($1.15) a month. AIS Play users will find a branded FlareFlow section stocked with curated English-, Chinese- and Korean-language series, every one of them carrying Thai subtitles.
Romance, drama, fantasy and reality shows feature in the lineup, alongside a selection of LGBTQ+ titles.

Launch titles include the English-language “From Janitor to Mrs Billionaire,” the Chinese-language “Rise of Aurora’s Fallen General” and the Korean Boys’ Love series “My Team Leader Is Working Late Again.” Also on the slate is “SupermodelMe: Make It or Break It,” a reality contest franchise shot in vertical format and fronted by Thai TV personality, actor and model Cindy Bishop.

“Thailand is one of Southeast Asia’s most creative, connected and culturally influential entertainment markets,” said Timothy Oh, general manager of COL Group International and chief marketing officer of FlareFlow. “Our launch with AIS Play is about making premium vertical entertainment accessible to more Thai audiences. At THB39 per month, viewers will be able to discover thousands of mobile-first stories backed by the scale, content library and industry experience of COL Group.”

“It is also an opportunity to introduce Thai audiences to a broader range of stories, genres and creative perspectives from around the world, while building a foundation for future collaboration with Thailand’s creators, producers and entertainment industry.”

Rock Networks, FlareFlow’s exclusive partner for telco and OTT integration across Asia, negotiated the commercial terms with AIS. The Singapore-headquartered company will also run the relationship for FlareFlow, handling integration, the launch itself and co-marketing.

“AIS Play is the right home for FlareFlow’s launch in Thailand,” said Beatrice Lee, CEO of Rock Networks. “Our role is to match world-class content with the region’s leading telcos and platforms, and this partnership brings a global microdrama leader to one of Thailand’s largest customer bases. Thailand is the first of several markets where we’ll be bringing FlareFlow to telco and OTT partners across Asia.”

COL Group was among the early movers in microdramas in both China and the U.S. FlareFlow has released more than 5,000 series to date, supports 14 languages and claims upward of 50 million registered users in over 200 countries and territories.

The Thai rollout forms part of what the company calls its Vertical 2.0 strategy. The plan is to push the format past standard microdramas with higher production values, a wider spread of genres and new formats such as reality, documentary and drama.

AIS and FlareFlow also plan to look beyond distribution. The two sides will explore Thai content development, work with local creators, localization and new mobile entertainment formats for Thailand and the wider Southeast Asian region.

AIS counted 53.9 million customers across its businesses as of June 2026. That includes 47.1 million subscribers on its 5G mobile network and 5.3 million on its fixed broadband service, AIS 3BB Fibre3. Microdrama platform ReelShort entered Southeast Asia through a partnership with AIS in April.

items.title: Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’s’ Captain Picard and ‘X-Men’s’ Charles Xavier, Dies at 86
items.description: Patrick Stewart, the English actor with impressive stage and film credits who will be remembered most for his roles as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and as Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” films, died Wednesday at his Los A
items.author: Carmel Dagan
paragraphs: Patrick Stewart, the English actor with impressive stage and film credits who will be remembered most for his roles as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and as Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” films, died Wednesday at his Los Angeles home. He was 86.
According to a statement on his Instagram account, Stewart died after a brief battle with Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia.

“His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre. He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise,” the statement read. “His professional accomplishments were humbly matched by his philanthropy and activism on behalf of human rights, survivors of domestic violence, global refugees, veterans’ mental health services, and animal welfare, particularly his cherished foster pitties. He was a Knight, Chancellor, motor sport enthusiast, and lifelong Huddersfield Football fan. He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life.”

Stewart and his “Star Trek: TNG” co-stars took their characters to the big screen for several films before the “Star Trek” film franchise was rebooted by J.J. Abrams with characters from the original series. He returned to the franchise for “Star Trek: Picard,” which ran from 2020 to 2023.

In the high-profile “X-Men” film franchise, Stewart played Professor Xavier opposite his good friend Ian McKellen as the villainous Magneto. He reprises the role in this December’s “Avengers: Doomsday” alongside McKellen.

In a 2008 profile describing Stewart’s return to his roots in classical theater by starring in a production of “Macbeth,” the New York Times in its mash-up headline pithily referenced the two very different paths the actor had followed in his career: “To Boldly Go Where Shakespeare Calls.”
In addition to being nominated for four Emmy awards, Stewart won three Olivier awards for his theater work and was nominated for a Tony Award.

It is hard to emphasize enough how dramatically Stewart’s life changed when he began his run on “Star Trek: The Next Generation” in 1987. For the two decades prior he had been a mainstay of the Royal Shakespeare Company. He had made time for some film and television work, but was kept busy appearing in more than two dozen RSC stage productions, including as Astrov in “Uncle Vanya” in 1974, Oberon in “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” in 1977, Shylock in “The Merchant of Venice” in 1978, and in the title role in “Titus Andronicus” in 1981.

Stewart played Picard throughout the 1987-1994 run of “Star Trek: TNG,” and then in the features “Star Trek: Generations” (in which he appeared with William Shatner), “Star Trek: First Contact,” “Star Trek: Insurrection” and “Star Trek: Nemesis.” He played Professor Xavier in “X-Men” (2000), “X-Men 2,” “X-Men: The Last Stand,” “X-Men Origins: Wolverine,” “The Wolverine” and “X-Men: Days of Future Past.”

Assessing Stewart’s contributions to “Star Trek: TNG,” the New York Times said, “With his aura of stern yet fair authority and seriousness of purpose, Mr. Stewart made Capt. Jean-Luc Picard the moral center of ‘Star Trek: The Next Generation’ across seven seasons, helping to keep it from sliding into camp or self-parody. Hollywood took to him, and he took to Hollywood.”

In general, Stewart seemed to keep a good sense of humor about his ties to popular culture, never publicly displaying the angst that Shatner and Leonard Nimoy each revealed at times. He did voicework on “The Simpsons,” “Family Guy” and “American Dad” and showed a willingness to make forays into comedy, playing a comically snooty waiter in Steve Martin’s 1991 gem “L.A. Story” and King Richard in Mel Brooks’ 1993 “Robin Hood: Men in Tights,” and hosting “Saturday Night Live” in 1994.
He recently voiced Sir Ritchfield in the animated “Sheep Detectives.”

In a very different vein, he was the best thing in 1995 gay comedy “Jeffrey”; the New York Times said Stewart “has some of the best lines and delivers them with a dignified brio that is only enhanced when he happens to be wearing a fuchsia beret, the uniform of an anti-gay-bashing group called the Pink Panthers.” Later the actor would serve as the narrator for Seth McFarlane’s scabrous comedy “Ted” and its sequel.

Stewart appeared in the 2015 film “Match,” based on the play by Stephen Belber, in which the actor played a vain, flamboyant dance instructor and — in a very different vein — in the Jeremy Saulnier horror-thriller “Green Room,” in which he played the leader of a band of neo-Nazis. He also starred in the Starz series “Blunt Talk,” about a substance-abusing English newscaster who moves to L.A. to host a talkshow.

Stewart continued his stage work even during the run of “Star Trek: TNG,” playing George in “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” at the Young Vic in 1987 (he would return to the role at Minneapolis’ Guthrie Theatre in 2001) and repeatedly appearing in seasonal stagings in Los Angeles and on Broadway of a one-man version of “A Christmas Carol” that he adapted himself from the original Dickens.

After “TNG” ended, Stewart ramped up his theater work. He appeared on Broadway as Prospero in “The Tempest” in 1996, essayed the title role in a “photo-negative” staging of “Othello” at the Shakespeare Theatre in Washington, D.C., in 1997 and returned to Broadway to star in “The Ride Down Mt. Morgan” in 2000. In Britain, his work on the boards, starring in “Antony and Cleopatra,” in “The Tempest” and soon triumphing in “Macbeth,” won back the critics who had written him off when he had ventured into American television’s version of outer space years earlier. Also in 2008, Stewart played Claudius in a production of “Hamlet” that starred David Tennant, winning Stewart the Olivier award for best supporting actor.

Stewart had had a productive association with McKellen. In addition to starring as adversaries in the “X-Men” films, during the filming of which they developed a close friendship, the pair appeared on the West End in “Waiting for Godot” in 2009 and in repertory on Broadway in 2014 in that Beckett play and another existential classic, Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land.”

The actor made his first cinematic forays into fantasy and science fiction with John Boorman’s take on the Arthur legend, 1981’s “Excalibur,” in which Stewart played Leondegrance, and director David Lynch’s 1984 adaptation of Frank Herbert’s “Dune,” in which he played Gurney Halleck, a top officer in the Atreides household who becomes the trusted lieutenant to Paul (Kyle MacLachlan).

Earlier, on British television, he starred in the 1975 BBC miniseries “North & South,” an adaptation of the Elizabeth Gaskell novel, and then played Sejanus on “I, Claudius.” In the BBC’s “Maybury” from 1981-83 he starred as a psychiatrist at a hospital.

Patrick Hewes Stewart was born in Mirfield, Yorkshire, acting as a youth with various amateur drama societies in the region and leaving school at 15. He held a job as a newspaper reporter but ultimately chose acting over journalism. He lost his hair at age 18.
Stewart began his acting career at Manchester’s Library Theatre, after which he became a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966.
The actor lent his voice to a number of videogames associated with the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises.
He was thrice married, the first time to choreographer Sheila Falconer, the second to Wendy Neuss, a producer of “Star Trek: The Next Generation.”

Survivors include third wife Sunny Ozell, whom he married in a 2013 ceremony presided over by Ian McKellen, as well as a daughter, Sophie Stewart, and son, actor Daniel Stewart, both from his marriage to Falconer.
Donations may be made to Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources.

items.title: William Shatner and ‘Star Trek’ Family Mourn Patrick Stewart With Picard Tributes: ‘Godspeed, Captain’
items.description: Tributes from across the “Star Trek” franchise are pouring in for Patrick Stewart following the news of his death at 86.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: Tributes from across the “Star Trek” franchise are pouring in for Patrick Stewart following the news of his death at 86.

Fellow USS Enterprise captain William Shatner posted a statement on Stewart to his Facebook page, writing, “What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed.”

Stewart’s “Next Generation” cast members also paid tribute to the actor, with Wil Wheaton (aka Wesley Crusher) posting a photograph of the two with the caption, “Godspeed, Captain.” Likewise, Cmdr. Will Riker actor Jonathan Frakes released a statement that read, “There’s no one on this planet that I have acted with or directed more often than my late great friend Patrick Stewart. He will be with me forever. May he rest in Peace.”

George Takei, who starred in “Star Trek: The Original Series” with Shatner, wrote on Bluesky “Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend. As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before. He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.”
Alex Kurtzman, who co-created “Star Trek: Picard” with Akiva Goldsman, Michael Chabon and Kirsten Beyer, wrote:

“It’s hard, impossible really, to express how grateful I am to have shared this moment with him. Grateful in a ‘once in a career’ kind of way. Right from our first meeting, he made it known that the only reason to play Picard again was to break new ground. His challenge was clear: Picard needed to be the man we knew and loved, but also entirely different, just as Patrick himself was 30 years after last wearing the uniform. The world of the Federation had to feel fresh and mirror many of the big issues the world faces today, issues that he wanted to face as a human and an artist, which meant interrogating an ideal to expose something more honest. He demanded truth. And in perhaps the trickiest high wire act, he wanted to reward fans with the nostalgia they would rightly demand, while subverting their expectations.”

“More than anything, he wanted to be proud of the work because he knew that Jean-Luc Picard would be his legacy,” Kurtzman continued. “I am heartbroken, and also deeply proud, to know that legacy lives on as of today. A legacy that also includes being fearless when it came to speaking out about the things he believed in. A legacy that includes the way he loved his wife and cared for his family. A legacy that was so beautifully evident in the way he’d snuggle up to any pitbull he saw, and the way these supposedly fearsome creatures simply snuggled back. He was magic. He was my colleague. He was my friend. He taught me what ‘Star Trek’ was really about. And in the end, he was and always will be, my captain.”
Goldsman, co-showrunner and co-creator on “Star Trek: Picard,” said in his own statement:

“Patrick was not only a true lion of the profession, he was the rarest of alchemists, one who could literally turn the written word into flesh and blood. Patrick was kind, strong, fiercely intelligent, collaborative, vulnerable and wise. His Captain Jean-Luc Picard permanently expanded the universe of Star Trek without measure. He will be deeply missed by this one fan and by so many more.”

Stewart originated the role of Capt. Jean-Luc Picard on “Star Trek: The Next Generation” beginning in 1987. He then went on to play the character in four “Star Trek” films between 1994 and 2002 before returning to the role in the Paramount+ series “Star Trek: Picard” in 2020 for three seasons.

LeVar Burton, who played Geordi La Forge on “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and “Star Trek: Picard”, along with four Star Trek films, said, “He was family. There is no other context in which to hold him that makes sense. I am lucky to have known and loved so many of the facets of a soul so rich in talent and generous of heart. Of all the Dames and Knights I’ve known he was deep down-the silliest.”

“Star Trek: Picard” EP and co-showrunner Terry Matalas said, “Patrick Stewart was a singular talent, a passionate artist with an infectious sense of humor. He had a warmth felt by everyone around him. Patrick could quite literally command a room simply by being in it. We were all so fortunate to have him in our lives, and the world feels a little less bright without him.”
Stewart died Oct. 28 following what was described as “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.”

items.title: Matthew Weiner Exits Peacock, 101 Studios Series ‘The Chairman’ Starring Eddie Murphy (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Matthew Weiner is no longer involved with the drama series “The Chairman” that is currently in development at Peacock, Variety has learned exclusively from sources.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: Matthew Weiner is no longer involved with the drama series “The Chairman” that is currently in development at Peacock, Variety has learned exclusively from sources.

The project was first reported to be in the works at the streamer less than a month ago, with Eddie Murphy attached to star. According to sources, creative differences between Weiner and the show’s producers caused them to part ways.
A new showrunning team is already said to be in place and will be announced in the coming days. The show’s writers’ room has been placed on a two-week hiatus as the new creative leads come onboard.

Exact plot details for “The Chairman” remain under wraps. Should it get picked up to series, it would be the first live-action series in which Murphy has starred since his days as a cast member on “Saturday Night Live.”

The series will be produced by Universal Television and 101 Studios, which is run by “Yellowstone” executive producer David Glasser. 101 is currently under a first-look film and television deal at NBCUniversal that began in January. “The Chairman” will also be the first project to come out of ex-Paramount boss Chris McCarthy’s deal at NBCUniversal, which was first reported in November 2025 and put him in a consulting role on the studio’s relationship with Glasser and 101. Murphy serves as a producer “The Chairman” in addition to starring.

Weiner is best known for creating the seminal TV drama “Mad Men,” which aired for seven seasons on AMC and won 16 Emmy Awards. “The Chairman,” assuming it is to be greenlit, would have marked Weiner’s first TV writing credit since 2018, when he created the Amazon Prime Video series “The Romanoffs.”

items.title: ‘Monarch: Legacy of Monsters’ Eyes Season 3 Renewal at Apple TV With New Writers, Showrunner
items.description: Apple TV and Legendary Television are currently in talks for a third season of “Monarch: Legacy of Monsters,” but with some major changes.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: Apple TV and Legendary Television are currently in talks for a third season of “Monarch: Legacy of Monsters,” but with some major changes.

According to an individual with knowledge of the situation, Season 3 of the show would be helmed by a new showrunner and new writers, and would feature new Titans from Legendary’s Monsterverse. No word yet on if that would mean characters from the first two seasons would not carry on into the third. Sources say that multiple individuals have been approached about potentially taking over showrunning the series.
The series originally debuted on Apple TV in 2023, with the second season launching in Feb. 2026.

Still in the works, though, is the spinoff series starring Wyatt Russell as Col. Lee Shaw. That show will follow Shaw on a mission in 1984 as he tries to prevent the Soviets from unleashing a devastating new Titan.

Chris Black and Matt Faction originally created “Monarch,” with Black serving as showrunner and executive producer on Season 2. Joby Harold and Tory Tunnell of Safehouse Pictures are also executive producers on the show, with Jen Roskind, Matt Shakman, Lawrence Trilling, and Andrew Colville executive producing Season 2. Hiro Matsuoka and Takemasa Arita executive produce on behalf of Toho Co., Ltd., the owner of the Godzilla character.

Harold will serve as showrunner on the spinoff series, with Harold also developing multiple series within the world of the Legendary Monsterverse. In addition to Russell, the cast includes Millie Brady, Pilou Asbaek, Corey Stoll, Ralph Ineson, Nyasha Hatendi, Connie Nielsen and Stana Katic.

items.title: China’s First Fully AI-Generated Movie Flops at the Box Office
items.description: Just as the first chapter of Elon Musk’s AI-produced version of The Odyssey was turning off viewers in the United States, the first feature-length AI-generated movie widely released in China was flopping at the box office.
items.author: James Hibberd
paragraphs: Just as the first chapter of Elon Musk’s AI-produced version of The Odyssey was turning off viewers in the United States, the first feature-length AI-generated movie widely released in China was flopping at the box office.
The film, the sci-fi thriller Sanxingdui: Future Past, was released last week and only grossed an estimated $198,000, according to the French wire service Agence France-Presse.

There have been several other AI-generated feature films in limited release in other countries. But with 10,000-plus opening-day screenings, Future Past marks the first longform AI film to get a true wide release with reported box office numbers in a major territory, arguably marking the first real commercial test of the technology for feature-length projects. The film’s early ticket sales were reportedly about 12 percent of its 10 million yuan budget (about $1.5 million).

According to the AFP, Jiang Defu, CEO of the film’s production company Bona Film Group, told Chinese film outlet Yuli that the film nonetheless represented an important experiment. “We are the first to try it, the first to get a theatrical release permit and the first to be tested by the audience. I think that is not easy at all.”
One moviegoer told the outlet, “In terms of quality, compared with human production, it still falls short.”

That said, the technology is hardly bound to the fate of a single film. In China, AI has taken over the production of short online films (microdramas), with 95 percent being AI-generated, according to Fortune. A feature-length AI-generated hit seems only a matter of time.

Future Past is a 100-minute film inspired by archaeological finds from the Sanxingdui civilization. Appropriately enough, the film is about a future when a superintelligent AI has spread across the globe and humanity has handed control to algorithms, which plunges the world into a crisis.

Previous feature-length movies that gained limited release include India’s Love You, a 95-minute musical, released in May 2025, and Malaysia’s Pirate Queen: Zheng Yi Sao, which was released in January.

In the United States, the first AI-generated feature film is scheduled for limited release Dec. 4. The film is called Gods Don’t Give Gifts, distributed by Fable and created by YouTuber Gossip Goblin, and is an R-rated anthology of four sci-fi stories.

items.title: Patrick Stewart’s Career Was a Rare and Thrilling Marriage of the Prestigious and the Populist
items.description: In the first two decades and change of Patrick Stewart’s distinguished professional career, he spent 16 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, made his Broadway debut alongside Ben Kingsley and Frances de la Tour in a legendary production of A Midsummer Nig
items.author: David Rooney
paragraphs: In the first two decades and change of Patrick Stewart’s distinguished professional career, he spent 16 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, made his Broadway debut alongside Ben Kingsley and Frances de la Tour in a legendary production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream directed by influential theater giant Peter Brook, and became a frequent presence on the storied stages of the prestigious Royal National Theatre.

It’s a telling insight into the hermetically sealed bubble of Hollywood that a renowned classical actor with years of notable work behind him, when cast in 1987 in the sci-fi TV spin-off Star Trek: The Next Generation, was identified in the Los Angeles Times as an “unknown British Shakespearean actor.” Stewart, who died Wednesday at 86, now runs no risk of being called unknown.

That wealth of stage experience was deeply embedded in his layered characterization as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, commander of the USS Enterprise, allowing Stewart to project steely authority without ever losing sight of the man’s kindness and compassion, his mentorship and familial protectiveness toward his crew.

While longtime friend and colleague Ian McKellen urged him not to toss away his prime Shakespeare years — the trajectory that ideally leads from Hamlet and Macbeth all the way to King Lear — Stewart took the Star Trek job. He signed the standard six-year contract despite quiet assurances from his agents and other industry associates that the show would likely last a single season, after which he could pocket his television earnings and return to his first love, the British stage.

But the spacetime continuum has a way of scrambling well-made plans. Not only did the show run for 178 episodes over seven seasons — peaking at 12 million viewers until the 1994 series finale, which was watched by more than 30 million — it also spawned four feature films, plus an additional spinoff, Star Trek: Picard, for which Stewart returned to the role for a three-season run.

The endlessly regenerative sci-fi phenomenon made Stewart a wealthy man and gave him global recognition, but by all accounts, the rigorous discipline he had acquired over all those years treading the boards was instrumental in shaping the work ethic of the entire company. As Picard, he also played a decisive role in making bald sexy.

With his crisp, cut-glass diction, stentorian delivery and regal bearing, it’s hard to believe Stewart grew up in a working-class Yorkshire family, such was his unquestionable natural command. But perhaps that upbringing in an unstable household — where he was often forced in explosions of domestic violence to get between his mother and father, a World War II veteran who suffered from undiagnosed PTSD — was part of what made Stewart such a warmly empathetic screen presence.

That quality, along with his Shakespearean gift for language and dramatic nuance, informed another defining role, that of Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise, starting in the late ‘90s. Back then, the Superhero Industrial Complex was in its infancy, and casting actors of the caliber of Stewart and McKellen gave it a legitimacy that helped turn those films into pop-cultural powerhouse events.

Stewart’s Professor X, like Picard, was a stern but nurturing figure, a telepathic mutant who founded the Xavier School for Gifted Youngsters, providing a refuge for youths displaced or discriminated against and a safe environment for them to better understand and control their extraordinary powers. The professor’s integrity and honor shone brightly when seen alongside the Machiavellian Magneto, the supervillain on a quest to impose mutant supremacy over mankind. Making for what might be the most perfect pairing in Marvel Comics movies, McKellen took on that role.
Between 2000 and 2017, Stewart made seven X-Men features, collectively grossing $3.32 billion, in addition to appearances in two separate Marvel Cinematic Universe films.

While fans of the series will no doubt have a range of personal favorites, for me, Stewart’s best performance as Charles Xavier was his last, in James Mangold’s haunting, Western-adjacent Logan. Starring opposite Hugh Jackman as a battle-weary Wolverine, Stewart brought enormous pathos and heart to the ailing Professor X, his telepathic gifts turned glitchy by an unknown brain disease. The emotional depth and the heavy burdens of the past in both leads’ performances — but Stewart’s in particular — make Logan one of the most unexpectedly poignant MCU films, transcending the comic-book genre to become a moving character study.

I was fortunate to drink in Stewart’s magnificent stage presence in three plays on Broadway. The first was in 2008, in director Rupert Goold’s hyper-kinetic horror-movie reimagining of Macbeth. Stewart was 68 at the time, older than most actors cast in the title role, his advancing age fueling a rich current of resentment at being too long passed over for leadership roles despite his valor on the battlefield. Casting Kate Fleetwood as a ruthlessly ambitious trophy wife some three decades younger added even more tension to that famously conspiratorial spousal dynamic.

Stewart’s Macbeth was absolutely a murderous fiend, willingly goaded into action by his slinky missus, but the actor brought steadily amplified frailty, paranoia and befuddlement to the tyrant that made us see him in a different light. He didn’t go so far as to turn the character from villainous to sympathetic, but he made it impossible not to be touched by this once-great man undone by the encroaching shadows of his treachery.

He returned to Broadway in 2013, reuniting with McKellen in a blistering doublebill of Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land and Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot. Stewart and McKellen first shared a stage in 1977 at the RSC, and their spiky interplay, more than three decades and many adversarial X-Men encounters later, was thrilling to watch.

Absurdist dramas that trace the treacherous limbo between birth and death, the companion pieces assumed the cutting double edge of tragicomic vaudeville. Humor and cruelty consistently overlapped in the actors’ portrayals of two men trapped in an unbreakable cycle of existential unease and futility.

While Stewart’s death is a sad occasion, his legacy is a robust one, demonstrating that classical training and a firm grasp of bardic poetry can enrich even the most seemingly unlikely genre material with dramatic weight, psychological complexity and emotional impact. Not bad for an “unknown British Shakespearean actor.”

items.title: Jacob Elordi's New Cartier Is Secretly Extra Fancy
items.description: Last month, Jacob Elordi did the impossible and made goatees not just socially acceptable but somehow sexy; the month before, the tall Aussie actor wore a suit to The Dog Stars film premiere alongside his canine co-star, and the internet started interrogating
items.author: Mike Christensen
paragraphs: Last month, Jacob Elordi did the impossible and made goatees not just socially acceptable but somehow sexy; the month before, the tall Aussie actor wore a suit to The Dog Stars film premiere alongside his canine co-star, and the internet started interrogating the length of his trousers.

People care a lot about Jacob Elordi and his appearance. That’s one reason he’s in the running to be the next James Bond; it’s also why I don’t think he will be 007. How could we possibly increase our thirst for the 29-year-old? It’s not possible really—unless we talk about his personal watch collection, where there’s quite a lot to talk about.

As a longtime friend of Cartier, Elordi likes to keep things pretty consistently Tank-coded. Over the past year, I’ve spotted him wearing different types of Tanks: a Française, à Guichet, a diamond-set one, green and black Tank Musts, you name it. He wears Cartier very well because, despite his imposing frame, he's comfortable wearing rather dainty pieces of horology.

The man has simple tastes and doesn’t seem to want his watches to do anything other than tell the time in a quaint, uncomplicated way. Second hands? Elordi doesn’t need them. Hour and minute hands will suffice.

Over the weekend, while on a date with girlfriend Kendall Jenner at the Academy Museum Gala in LA, Elordi wore his fanciest Tank yet. Although you really have to study the watch to see how special it is. Zoom in a little on the watch, which could be mistaken for a stainless-steel Cartier Tank, but is actually a new platinum version on a semi-matt burgundy alligator leather strap. The telltale sign is the shinier-than-usual case. Platinum is a heavier, prettier, and more expensive metal than stainless steel.

Unlike some of the vintage Cartiers he’s rocked recently—the majority of which have quartz movements inside—this one is packing a very handy automatic winding, calibre 1899 MC. So it's the real deal, and also makes the watch a tiny bit larger (38.1 x 27.75 mm) than his previous flexes.

No matter what Tank Jacob Elordi has worn, the dials always remain pretty much the same. The word timeless is bandied around far too often in the watch world, but the Tank can legitimately make such claims because the dial design has hardly changed in more than 100 years. Roman numerals, minimalist geometry, and a clear rectangular shape in the centre of the dial inside a very rectangular case make these watches unmistakably Cartier.
This story originally appeared on British GQ.

items.title: I Waited Years for Bvlgari to Make This Watch. It Was Worth It
items.description: It’s been so long that I can’t even remember when I first started asking for a smaller version of Bvlgari’s award-winning, record-breaking ultra-thin watch, the Octo Finissimo. I do remember that it became something of a tradition to badger Fabrizio Buonamassa
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: It’s been so long that I can’t even remember when I first started asking for a smaller version of Bvlgari’s award-winning, record-breaking ultra-thin watch, the Octo Finissimo. I do remember that it became something of a tradition to badger Fabrizio Buonamassa Stigliani, Bvlgari’s product creation executive director and design director. His reaction was always the same. He would flash his signature heavily bearded, friendly smile from behind a desk in the presidential suite of Geneva’s Hotel President and say, “Everybody asks me for this watch!”

This spring, Bvlgari finally made good on my long-standing wish. The brand unveiled a new 37-mm version of the Octo Finissimo, a much more wearable size for most wrists. The new diameter is especially important for this particular model’s shape. “The demand wasn’t driven only by the trend toward smaller watches,” Buonamassa Stigliani told me during an interview in April. “The Octo Finissimo is a square watch, so it wears larger than its dimensions suggest.”

The Octo Finissimo is an icon of modern watchmaking, which made the lack of a Goldilocks-size version even more glaring. Since Bvlgari debuted the OF in 2014, the collection has accumulated 10 world records for ultra-thin watchmaking, including two for the thinnest mechanical watch. The original Automatic, sized at 40 mm, followed a few years later and has since been made available in numerous iterations: sandblasted titanium, stainless steel, 18k gold, ceramic, and more.

Bvlgari rewarded my patience handsomely. The brand debuted three versions of the new OF37: in matte sandblasted titanium; brushed and polished titanium, and yellow gold. Excited beyond what should reasonably stir the emotions of a 36-year-old man, I requested to spend a week with the sandblasted titanium version—which, to my mind, struck a fine balance between graceful futurism and the utilitarian look of a classic tool watch.

Having the OF37 on my wrist really drove home that it looks and feels like nothing else on the market. For almost my entire adult life, I’ve worn a Rolex Submariner, which is in many ways the standard-bearer for modern watch design, and I was immediately struck by how much wearing the OF37 felt like a daring adventure. While I’ve come to love the weight and heft of the Sub, the legendary lightness of the OF was both lovely and slightly alarming. Looking down and seeing this thing—whose matte titanium body completely changes color from steel grey to black to light graphite depending upon the ambient light—is fascinating. On the other hand, I’m a fairly active guy: I’ve taken my Sub swimming and diving without thinking about it, I’ve owned it for 24 years and worn it for 15 without ever servicing it, I’ve donned it during patrols in the military, I’ve banged it into every conceivable surface and (almost) never worried about it. I’m not sure I’d be comfortable wearing the OF37 the same way.

The OF37 is the product of many years of refinement. “We’ve been collecting feedback for years—about the buckle, the case size, the movement finishing, and the needs of both clients and collectors,” says Buonamassa Stigliani. “This watch reflects all of that feedback. We explored several sizes—36, 37, 38, and 39 millimeters. Ultimately, 37 mm was the smallest size that allowed us to preserve the watch’s technical features.”

The change is what made a slightly imperfect watch perfect to me—looking at the older version was like seeing a painting hanging just slightly crooked. I’m of the mind that a well-designed watch should be framed by one’s wrist—not sit right up against the edge of it. This was precisely the quality that the condensed size offered: smaller, incredibly thin, and so comfortable I forgot it was there.

The OF’s similarities to other modern watches begin and end with the fact that it uses three hands to tell the time. You can certainly perceive some of the Gerald Genta-inflected heritage of Bvlgari’s watchmaking division, particularly in the obsession with eight-sided bezels. But compare it to even the luxury sports watch stalwarts out there—timepieces such as the Royal Oak and the Patek Philippe’s Nautilus—let alone to something like a Submariner, and you’re left scratching your head going, this is different.

What distinguishes the design is the clever octagon-within-a-circle-within-a-square architecture. The design starts with one of Buonamassa Stigliani’s famous hand sketches. The angular look is inspired by ancient Roman architecture (and its ample use of the octagon); Italian design; automotive motifs (Buonamassa Stigliani loves cars); and Bvlgari’s own jewelry. In fact, the OF37 wears much more like a piece of modernist sculpture on the wrist than a conventional wristwatch.

The OF37, regardless of material, boasts the brand-new Bvlgari BVF 100 movement. Measuring just 2.35 mm thick, it uses a platinum micro-rotor activated by the movement of your wrist to automatically wind the watch. The case itself at 6.45 mm is actually thicker than the 40mm version’s case at 5.15 mm, though you likely wouldn’t notice this given its smaller diameter and the fact that it’s only as thick as a few credit cards stacked together. The power reserve on the 40-mm version is 60 hours; impressively, that of the 37mm—a watch 20% smaller in volume—is 20% higher, at 72 hours.

The OF is almost a victim of its own success in differentiating itself from the rest of the market. I’m almost certain that the watch couldn’t be my personal daily driver. But could it be a part of my rotation? Hell yes. I can’t wait till the first celeb pairs one of these with black tie, frankly. Josh O’Connor, can you help me out there? The list price warrants discussion here: $16,600 for the sandblasted titanium version ($17,300 for the satin/polished titanium version and $48,300 for the gold version) is no joke. This probably won’t be someone’s first watch but rather the province of somebody for whom watch collecting is already a practiced sport.

Once or twice while wearing the OF37, I caught a glimpse of its sleek angles and strange profile in the window reflection of a parked car, or even the mirror in my bathroom. That it looks quite unlike anything that came before it means that it doesn’t have simple answers to simple questions: Is this an everyday watch? A dress watch? Something for serious collectors or splashy newcomers? What makes the OF37 special is that it refuses to be any one of those things.

items.title: 5 Products That Changed My Life in October
items.description: Late October officially lands us at the start of the holiday season, a typically chaotic period I have never been very effective at managing. There are costumes to plan, parties to throw and attend, and between it all, many end-of-year deadlines to meet. A lit
items.author: Alyssa Bereznak
